  rw [map_le_iff_le_comap] at hx hy

applications.title: Certify an infinite monomial family
applications.inputs: In the real polynomial vector space R[X], take v_n=X^n for every natural n.

steps.text: Define the induced outer mass of an event S as the supremum of finite subsums with indices inside S.
If S is finite, its own subsum is among these subsums. Every subsum over a finite subset F of S is at most the sum over S, since the omitted masses are nonnegative.
Thus the supremum is at least and at most the sum over S, and the two are equal.
For S empty, the only subsum is 0, so the formula still holds. This argument applies to every finite event without a sigma-algebra assumption.

steps.text: Suppose the outer mass of S is 0. For any a in S, its singleton subsum p(a) is at most the outer mass of S, so p(a)=0.
The zero-outside-support lemma gives a outside the support for every a in S. Thus S is disjoint from the support.
Conversely, if S is disjoint from the support, every p(a) with a in S is zero. Every finite subsum inside S is then zero.
Their supremum, the induced outer mass of S, is zero. This argument applies to arbitrary S, including an empty event.

results.name: An event has mass 1 exactly when it contains the support
results.statement: For a probability mass function p and any subset S, its induced outer probability is 1 if and only if S contains the support.
hypotheses: p is a probability mass function on A.
S is any subset of A.
Outer probability is the sum of p over S.

prerequisites.reason: Support containment makes every omitted mass vanish.

source.excerpt:
theorem toOuterMeasure_apply_eq_one_iff : p.toOuterMeasure s = 1 ↔ p.support ⊆ s := by
  refine (p.toOuterMeasure_apply s).symm ▸ ⟨fun h a hap => ?_, fun h => ?_⟩
  · refine by_contra fun hs => ne_of_lt ?_ (h.trans p.tsum_coe.symm)
    have hs' : s.indicator p a = 0 := Set.indicator_apply_eq_zero.2 fun hs' => False.elim <| hs hs'
    have hsa : s.indicator p a < p a := hs'.symm ▸ (p.apply_pos_iff a).2 hap
    exact ENNReal.tsum_lt_tsum (p.tsum_coe_indicator_ne_top s)
      (fun x => Set.indicator_apply_le fun _ => le_rfl) hsa
  · classical suffices ∀ (x) (_ : x ∉ s), p x = 0 from
      _root_.trans (tsum_congr
        fun a => (Set.indicator_apply s p a).trans
          (ite_eq_left_iff.2 <| symm ∘ this a)) p.tsum_coe
    exact fun a ha => (p.apply_eq_zero_iff a).2 <| Set.notMem_subset h ha

results.name: Set.prod_eq_prod_iff
results.statement: A times B equals A1 times B1 if and only if A=A1 and B=B1, or both products have an empty factor.
hypotheses: U,V are arbitrary sets. A,A1,A2 are subsets of U. B,B1,B2 are subsets of V. Empty factors are permitted unless excluded below.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Equal factors give equal products, and an empty factor makes either product empty. These facts prove the reverse implication.

Suppose the common product is nonempty. Both factors on each side are nonempty. First-coordinate projection gives A=A1. For any y in B, choose x in A. The product equality puts (x,y) in A1 times B1, so y belongs to B1. Conversely, choose x in A1 for any y in B1 to prove y in B. Hence B=B1.
If the common product is empty, the product nonemptiness lemma implies that each product has an empty factor. This completes all cases.

prerequisites.reason: The proof detects empty products through their factors.
Coordinate projections recover each nonempty factor. The second-coordinate proof is identical after exchanging the coordinate names.

source.excerpt:
theorem prod_eq_prod_iff :
    s ×ˢ t = s₁ ×ˢ t₁ ↔ s = s₁ ∧ t = t₁ ∨ (s = ∅ ∨ t = ∅) ∧ (s₁ = ∅ ∨ t₁ = ∅) := by
  symm
  rcases eq_empty_or_nonempty (s ×ˢ t) with h | h
  · simp_rw [h, @eq_comm _ ∅, prod_eq_empty_iff, prod_eq_empty_iff.mp h, true_and,
      or_iff_right_iff_imp]
    rintro ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
    exact prod_eq_empty_iff.mp h
  rw [prod_eq_prod_iff_of_nonempty h]
  rw [nonempty_iff_ne_empty, Ne, prod_eq_empty_iff] at h
  simp_rw [h, false_and, or_false]

results.name: Function.bijective_iff_existsUnique
results.statement: A function f:A->B is bijective if and only if every b in B has exactly 1 preimage in A.
hypotheses: A,B,C are arbitrary sets. Every function has its displayed domain and codomain.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Bijectivity gives a preimage by surjectivity. Any two preimages agree by injectivity, so the preimage is unique.
Conversely, existence of each preimage is surjectivity. If f(x)=f(y), x,y are preimages of the same point. Uniqueness gives x=y, so f is injective.

source.excerpt:
theorem bijective_iff_existsUnique (f : α → β) : Bijective f ↔ ∀ b : β, ∃! a : α, f a = b :=
  ⟨fun hf b ↦
      let ⟨a, ha⟩ := hf.surjective b
      ⟨a, ha, fun _ ha' ↦ hf.injective (ha'.trans ha.symm)⟩,
    fun he ↦ ⟨fun {_a a'} h ↦ (he (f a')).unique h rfl, fun b ↦ (he b).exists⟩⟩

results.statement: In a lattice, meet(a,b)<join(a,b) if and only if a is not equal to b.
hypotheses: L is a lattice. The symbols join and meet denote its least upper bound and greatest lower bound operations.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: If a=b, both meet and join equal a, so strict inequality is false.
Always meet(a,b)<=a,b<=join(a,b). If meet and join are equal, these inequalities squeeze both a,b to that common value by antisymmetry. Thus a=b.

results.name: mem_closure_iff
results.statement: A point x lies in closure(A) if and only if every open neighborhood of x meets A.
hypotheses: X is any topological space. A,B are subsets of X. Empty subsets are permitted.

steps.text: If an open neighborhood O of x missed A, then its closed complement would contain A. Minimality would put closure(A) inside that complement, so x could not lie in the closure.

applications.title: Approximate nonnegative reals by rational squares
applications.inputs: Take the dense inclusion f:Q->R and g:R->[0,infinity), g(x)=x^2. The codomain has its subspace topology.
applications.hypotheses: Assume the standard density of Q in R. Squaring is continuous, and every nonnegative real is a square.

steps.text: At a real a, |x^2-a^2|=|x-a||x+a|. If |x-a|<1, then |x+a|<2|a|+1. Choosing delta=min(1,epsilon/(2|a|+1)) proves continuity of squaring.
For each t>=0, the values at 0 and t+1 bracket t, because 0<=t<(t+1)^2. The intermediate value theorem gives a real x with x^2=t. Thus g is surjective and has dense range.
The dense-composition theorem proves that rational squares are dense in the nonnegative reals. Rational approximations 1.4,1.41 and 1.414 give the following concrete values near 2.
The rational 1.41 has square 1.9881, which is closer to 2 than the first square.
The rational 1.414 has square 1.999396. The exact difference from 2 is 0.000604.

applications.conclusion: Every neighborhood of every nonnegative real contains a rational square. The displayed exact computations give 3 examples near 2.

results.name: abs_pow_eq_one
results.statement: For a real a and positive natural n, abs(a^n)=1 if and only if abs(a)=1.
hypotheses: All displayed scalars are real numbers. Division by 0 follows the source convention x/0=0 only where explicitly permitted.
n is a positive natural number.

steps.text: Put t=abs(a)>=0. The absolute-power lemma gives abs(a^n)=t^n.

If 0<=t<1, induction gives 0<=t^n<1 for n>=1. The base n=1 holds. If u=t^n is in [0,1), then 0<=ut<=u<1. If t>1, the base t^1>1 holds, and u>1 implies ut>u>1. Thus every positive power stays strictly below or strictly above 1 in these two cases.
Thus t^n=1 forces t=1 by trichotomy. Conversely, t=1 gives t^n=1.

prerequisites.reason: The power identity reduces the claim to a nonnegative real power.

lemma abs_pow_eq_one (a : α) (h : n ≠ 0) : |a ^ n| = 1 ↔ |a| = 1 := by
  convert pow_left_inj₀ (abs_nonneg a) zero_le_one h
  exacts [(pow_abs _ _).symm, (one_pow _).symm]

hypotheses: G is a group with a seminorm N:G->[0,infinity). It satisfies N(1)=0, N(g inverse)=N(g), and N(gh)<=N(g)+N(h). The operation need not commute.
n is any natural number, including 0.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: For n=0, the power is 1 and both sides are 0. Suppose the bound holds at n.
Since g^(n+1)=g^n g, the triangle axiom gives N(g^(n+1))<=N(g^n)+N(g)<=n N(g)+N(g)=(n+1)N(g). Induction finishes the proof.

source.excerpt:
lemma norm_pow_le_mul_norm : ∀ {n : ℕ}, ‖a ^ n‖ ≤ n * ‖a‖
  | 0 => by simp
  | n + 1 => by simpa [pow_succ, add_mul] using norm_mul_le_of_le' norm_pow_le_mul_norm le_rfl

results.statement: In a seminormed abelian additive group, the norm of a finite multiset sum is at most the sum of the norms.

The induction hypothesis bounds the last norm by the sum of the norms in M. Adding N(x) gives the required sum for the enlarged multiset.

results.name: norm_prod_le
results.statement: In a seminormed abelian multiplicative group, the seminorm of a finite product is at most the sum of the seminorms of its factors.
hypotheses: G is a group with a seminorm N:G->[0,infinity). It satisfies N(1)=0, N(g inverse)=N(g), and N(gh)<=N(g)+N(h). The operation need not commute.

Remove one factor g_j. The triangle axiom bounds the seminorm of the product by N(g_j) plus the seminorm of the remaining product.

results.statement: For a map f:X->V into a normed additive group, the real function N composed with f has compact support if and only if f has compact support.

results.name: linearIndependent_of_ne_zero_of_inner_eq_zero
results.statement: Every pairwise orthogonal family of nonzero vectors in a real or complex inner product space is linearly independent.
hypotheses: V is a real or complex inner product space. The first slot is conjugate-linear and the second is linear. The norm satisfies N(x)^2=<x,x>.
The norm separates 0. I is any index set. v_i is nonzero for every i, and <v_i,v_j>=0 whenever i is not equal to j.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Consider any finitely supported relation sum_i c_i v_i=0. Fix an index j in its finite support.
Take the inner product with v_j in the first slot. Repeated right-slot linearity expands the finite sum. Orthogonality removes every term except c_j<v_j,v_j>, so this product is 0.
Since v_j is nonzero, the zero-diagonal criterion gives <v_j,v_j> nonzero. Division in the scalar field gives c_j=0.
This holds for every index in the support. All other coefficients vanish by definition of support. Therefore every finite relation is trivial, which is linear independence.

prerequisites.reason: Each nonzero vector has a nonzero diagonal inner product.

source.excerpt:
theorem linearIndependent_of_ne_zero_of_inner_eq_zero {ι : Type*} {v : ι → E} (hz : ∀ i, v i ≠ 0)
    (ho : Pairwise fun i j => ⟪v i, v j⟫ = 0) : LinearIndependent 𝕜 v := by
  rw [linearIndependent_iff']
  intro s g hg i hi
  have h' : g i * ⟪v i, v i⟫ = ⟪v i, ∑ j ∈ s, g j • v j⟫ := by
    rw [inner_sum]
    symm
    convert Finset.sum_eq_single (M := 𝕜) i ?_ ?_
    · rw [inner_smul_right]
    · intro j _hj hji
      rw [inner_smul_right, ho hji.symm, mul_zero]
    · exact fun h => False.elim (h hi)
  simpa [hg, hz] using h'

applications.title: Certify independence through orthogonality
applications.inputs: Use v1=(1,1,0), v2=(1,-1,0), v3=(0,0,2) in R^3 with the usual dot product.
applications.hypotheses: The Euclidean inner product has a separating norm. The theorem requires each vector nonzero and each pair orthogonal.

steps.text: The first two vectors have dot product 1-1+0=0.
The dot product of the third vector (0,0,2) with the first vector (1,1,0) is 0*1+0*1+2*0, which is 0 because the third coordinate of the first vector vanishes.
The dot product of the third vector (0,0,2) with the second vector (1,-1,0) is 0*1+0*(-1)+2*0, which is 0 for the same reason.
The squared norms of the first two vectors are both 2, so neither vector is zero.
The third vector has squared norm 4 and is therefore nonzero. All pairwise orthogonality conditions now hold.
Apply the orthogonal-independence theorem. A finite relation c1 v1+c2 v2+c3 v3=0 must have every coefficient zero.

applications.conclusion: The 3 vectors are linearly independent. The certificate uses 3 dot products and positive squared norms, without row reduction.

results.name: norm_eq_sqrt_re_inner
results.statement: For every x in an inner product space, N(x)=sqrt(real part of <x,x>).
hypotheses: V is a real or complex inner product space. The first slot is conjugate-linear and the second is linear. The norm satisfies N(x)^2=<x,x>.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Norm compatibility gives real part of <x,x>=N(x)^2. The norm is a nonnegative real number.
The nonnegative square root of the square of a nonnegative real t is t by the definition of square root. Substitute t=N(x).

theorem norm_eq_sqrt_re_inner (x : E) : ‖x‖ = √(re ⟪x, x⟫) :=
  calc
    ‖x‖ = √(‖x‖ ^ 2) := (sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _)).symm
    _ = √(re ⟪x, x⟫) := congr_arg _ (norm_sq_eq_re_inner _)

results.statement: If v,w are orthogonal in a real or complex inner product space, then N(w-v)=N(w+v).

results.name: Polynomial.root_or_root_of_root_mul
results.statement: In an integral domain R, a root a of pq is a root of p or a root of q.
hypotheses: R is a commutative integral domain. p,q are polynomials over R and a belongs to R. Evaluation of pq at a is 0.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Multiplicative evaluation with the identity coefficient map gives (pq)(a)=p(a)q(a). The root assumption therefore gives p(a)q(a)=0.
An integral domain has no zero divisors, so p(a)=0 or q(a)=0. These are exactly the two root alternatives.

prerequisites.reason: The root of the product gives a product of scalar evaluations equal to 0.

  | n + 1 =>

      _ ≤ (n + 1) * (n + 1) ^ n := Nat.mul_le_mul_left _ (Nat.pow_le_pow_left n.le_succ _)

results.name: Nat.ascFactorial_mul_ascFactorial
results.statement: For natural n,l,k, the product of l consecutive factors from n times the product of k consecutive factors from n+l equals the product of l+k consecutive factors from n.
hypotheses: n,l,k are natural numbers. The ascending factorial n^(over r) is the product n(n+1)...(n+r-1), with the empty product equal to 1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: The first product contains factors n through n+l-1. The second contains factors n+l through n+l+k-1. These two adjacent ranges concatenate to the range of l+k factors.
Associativity of multiplication identifies the product of the two finite products with the product over the concatenated range. Empty ranges follow from the identity factor 1.

source.excerpt:
theorem ascFactorial_mul_ascFactorial (n l k : ℕ) :
    n.ascFactorial l * (n + l).ascFactorial k = n.ascFactorial (l + k) := by
  cases n with
  | zero =>
    cases l
    · simp only [ascFactorial_zero, Nat.add_zero, Nat.one_mul, Nat.zero_add]
    · simp only [Nat.add_right_comm, zero_ascFactorial, Nat.zero_add, Nat.zero_mul]
  | succ n' =>
    apply Nat.mul_left_cancel (factorial_pos n')
    simp only [Nat.add_assoc, ← Nat.mul_assoc, factorial_mul_ascFactorial]
    rw [Nat.add_comm 1 l, ← Nat.add_assoc, factorial_mul_ascFactorial, Nat.add_assoc]

results.name: Nat.choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial
results.statement: For natural k<=n, C(n,k) k! (n-k)!=n!.
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: An n-element set has n! orderings: the empty set has 1 ordering, and a nonempty set chooses its first element and orders the rest. Induction with the factorial recurrence gives this count.
An ordering determines its first k elements as an unordered subset S. Conversely, choose S, order its k elements, and order the remaining n-k elements. Concatenation recovers a unique ordering.
This is a bijection between orderings and these three independent choices. Their counts are C(n,k), k! and (n-k)!. Multiplication of finite counts proves the identity, including k=0 and k=n.

prerequisites.reason: The recurrence counts orderings by the choice of their first element.

theorem choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial : ∀ {n k}, k ≤ n → choose n k * k ! * (n - k)! = n !
  | 0, _, hk => by simp [Nat.eq_zero_of_le_zero hk]
  | n + 1, 0, _ => by simp
  | n + 1, succ k, hk => by
    rcases lt_or_eq_of_le hk with hk₁ | hk₁
    · have h : choose n k * k.succ ! * (n - k)! = (k + 1) * n ! := by
        rw [← choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial (le_of_succ_le_succ hk)]
        simp [factorial_succ, Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_left_comm, Nat.mul_assoc]
      have h₁ : (n - k)! = (n - k) * (n - k.succ)! := by
        rw [← succ_sub_succ, succ_sub (le_of_lt_succ hk₁), factorial_succ]
      have h₂ : choose n (succ k) * k.succ ! * ((n - k) * (n - k.succ)!) = (n - k) * n ! := by
        rw [← choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial (le_of_lt_succ hk₁)]
        simp [factorial_succ, Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_left_comm, Nat.mul_assoc]
      have h₃ : k * n ! ≤ n * n ! := Nat.mul_le_mul_right _ (le_of_succ_le_succ hk)
      rw [choose_succ_succ, Nat.add_mul, Nat.add_mul, succ_sub_succ, h, h₁, h₂, Nat.add_mul,
        Nat.mul_sub_right_distrib, factorial_succ, ← Nat.add_sub_assoc h₃, Nat.add_assoc,
        ← Nat.add_mul, Nat.add_sub_cancel_left, Nat.add_comm]
    · rw [hk₁]; simp [Nat.mul_comm, choose, Nat.sub_self]

results.name: Nat.choose_mul
results.statement: For natural s<=k, C(n,k) C(k,s)=C(n,s) C(n-s,k-s).
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Count pairs of subsets S subset T of a fixed n-element set with sizes s,k. First choose T, then S inside T. This gives C(n,k) C(k,s) pairs.
Alternatively choose S, then choose k-s additional elements from its complement of size n-s. This gives C(n,s) C(n-s,k-s) pairs.

Both methods enumerate the same finite pairs bijectively, so their counts are equal. If k>n, there are no such pairs. If also s>n, both counts vanish. If s<=n<k, then k-s>n-s and the second factor on the right vanishes.

source.excerpt:
theorem choose_mul {n k s : ℕ} (hsk : s ≤ k) :
    n.choose k * k.choose s = n.choose s * (n - s).choose (k - s) := by
  obtain hnk | hkn := lt_or_ge n k
  · grind
  have h : 0 < (n - k)! * (k - s)! * s ! := by apply_rules [factorial_pos, Nat.mul_pos]
  apply Nat.mul_right_cancel h
  calc
    _ = n.choose s * s ! * ((n - s).choose (k - s) * (k - s)! * (n - s - (k - s))!) := by
      grind [choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial]
    _ = n.choose s * (n - s).choose (k - s) * ((n - k)! * (k - s)! * s !) := by
      grind

results.name: Nat.choose_le_middle
results.statement: For all natural n,r, C(n,r)<=C(n,floor(n/2)).
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.
All indices are natural numbers, including 0 unless an additional inequality excludes it. Factorial n! is the product of integers from 1 to n, with 0!=1.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: If r>n, the left count is 0, so the bound follows from nonnegativity. Assume r<=n. The factorial identity gives C(n,j)=n!/(j!(n-j)!) for all j<=n, since both denominator factors are positive.
For j<n, cancellation in this formula gives C(n,j+1)=C(n,j)(n-j)/(j+1). If j<floor(n/2), then n-j>=j+1, so C(n,j+1)>=C(n,j). All divisions here have positive denominators.

If r<=floor(n/2), repeat this inequality from r to the middle. If r>floor(n/2), replace r by n-r, which is at most the middle. The factorial formula gives C(n,r)=C(n,n-r) by exchange of the two denominator factors.
The preceding increasing sequence bound now applies to n-r. Thus every r has the stated bound, including n=0.

prerequisites.reason: The proof derives the coefficient ratio and reflection identity from the factorial formula.
The factorial denominators are positive.

  rcases le_or_gt r n with b | b
  · rcases le_or_gt r (n / 2) with a | h
    · apply choose_le_middle_of_le_half_left a
    · rw [← choose_symm b]
      apply choose_le_middle_of_le_half_left
      lia
  · rw [choose_eq_zero_of_lt b]
    apply zero_le

results.name: Nat.multichoose_eq
results.statement: For natural n,k, the number of multisets of size k from n types equals C(n+k-1,k), with natural subtraction in the upper index.
hypotheses: n,k,s,i,j are natural numbers. C(n,k) is the number of k-element subsets of an n-element set. It equals 0 when k>n. The empty subset gives C(n,0)=1.
A multiset records a nonnegative multiplicity for each of n types, with total multiplicity k.

proof.verification: complete readable proof; agent review required; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: If k=0, there is exactly 1 empty multiset and C(n-1,0)=1, including n=0. If n=0 and k>0, no such multiset exists and C(k-1,k)=0.
For n>=1 and k>=1, write each multiset uniquely as a nondecreasing sequence 1<=a1<=...<=ak<=n. Map it to the strict sequence b_t=a_t+t-1 for t=1,...,k. These indices satisfy 1<=b1<...<bk<=n+k-1.
Conversely, from such a strict sequence set a_t=b_t-t+1. The strict index spacing gives nondecreasing a_t and a_t>=1. Since b_t<=n+k-1-(k-t), it gives a_t<=n.
These transformations are inverse. Strict sequences correspond to k-element subsets of an (n+k-1)-element set, whose count is C(n+k-1,k). This proves the formula in every case.

prerequisites.reason: The worked application converts the subset count into an exact factorial quotient.
The factorial quotient has a positive denominator.

theorem multichoose_eq : ∀ n k : ℕ, multichoose n k = (n + k - 1).choose k
  | _, 0 => by simp
  | 0, k + 1 => by simp
  | n + 1, k + 1 => by
    have : n + (k + 1) < (n + 1) + (k + 1) := Nat.add_lt_add_right (Nat.lt_succ_self _) _
    have : (n + 1) + k < (n + 1) + (k + 1) := Nat.add_lt_add_left (Nat.lt_succ_self _) _
    rw [multichoose_succ_succ, Nat.add_comm, Nat.succ_add_sub_one, ← Nat.add_assoc,
      Nat.choose_succ_succ]
    simp [multichoose_eq n (k + 1), multichoose_eq (n + 1) k]

results.name: Euler's criterion for quadratic residues
results.statement: Let p be an odd prime and let a be an integer with p not dividing a. Then a is a square modulo p (that is, x^2 = a mod p has a solution x) if and only if a^((p-1)/2) = 1 mod p. If a is not a square modulo p, then a^((p-1)/2) = -1 mod p.
hypotheses: p is an odd prime number.
a is an integer and a is not divisible by p, so the class of a in the field Z/pZ is not zero.
The exponent (p-1)/2 is an integer because p is odd. For p = 2 every class is a square, and the statement is not needed.

prerequisites.reason: Fermat's little theorem gives y^(p-1) = 1 for y not 0, which is used for squares and for the square of a^((p-1)/2).
Lagrange's theorem on polynomial congruences bounds the number of roots of x^((p-1)/2) - 1 modulo p by its degree.

definitions.name: square modulo p
definitions.text: An integer a is a square modulo p if some integer x satisfies x^2 = a mod p.

definitions.name: F_p
definitions.text: F_p is the field Z/pZ. It has p elements and p is prime.

theorem euler_criterion {a : ZMod p} (ha : a ≠ 0) : IsSquare (a : ZMod p) ↔ a ^ (p / 2) = 1 := by
  apply (iff_congr _ (by simp [Units.ext_iff])).mp (euler_criterion_units p (Units.mk0 a ha))
  simp only [Units.ext_iff, sq, Units.val_mk0, Units.val_mul]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨y, hy⟩; exact ⟨y, hy.symm⟩
  · rintro ⟨y, rfl⟩
    have hy : y ≠ 0 := by
      rintro rfl
      simp [mul_zero, ne_eq] at ha
    refine ⟨Units.mk0 y hy, ?_⟩; simp

source.alignment: The Lean statement is for a nonzero element a of ZMod p and uses p / 2 (natural division). For odd p this equals (p-1)/2. The authored statement adds the value -1 for non-squares, which Lean states as ZMod.pow_div_two_eq_neg_one_or_one.

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Work in the field F_p and put k = (p-1)/2. Let S be the set of squares y^2 with y in F_p and y not 0. If y^2 = z^2 then (y-z)(y+z) = 0, so z = y or z = -y. Since p is odd, y is not -y for y not 0. Hence every square in S has exactly two square roots, and S has exactly k elements.
Every element s = y^2 of S satisfies s^k = y^(2k) = y^(p-1) = 1, by Fermat's little theorem for y not 0. So every element of S is a root of the polynomial x^k - 1 over F_p.

The polynomial x^k - 1 has degree k, and F_p is a field, so it has at most k roots in F_p. By step 1, S already gives k distinct roots. Hence the roots of x^k - 1 in F_p are exactly the elements of S.

Take a not 0 in F_p. If a is a square, then a is in S and a^k = 1 by step 2. If a is not a square, then a is not in S, so by step 3 a is not a root of x^k - 1, and a^k is not 1. This proves: a is a square if and only if a^k = 1.

Now let a be a non-square. By Fermat's little theorem (a^k)^2 = a^(p-1) = 1, so a^k is a root of x^2 - 1 = (x-1)(x+1). A field has no zero divisors, so a^k = 1 or a^k = -1. Step 4 excludes 1, so a^k = -1. This completes the proof.

applications.title: Decide whether 3 and 2 are squares modulo 13
applications.inputs: The prime p = 13, so k = (13-1)/2 = 6. The integers to test are a = 3 and a = 2.
applications.hypotheses: 13 is an odd prime and neither 3 nor 2 is divisible by 13, so Euler's criterion applies.

steps.text: Compute 3^6 = 729. Since 13 * 56 = 728, the remainder of 729 modulo 13 is 1. So 3^6 = 1 mod 13.
Euler's criterion says that 3 is a square modulo 13. A check: 4^2 = 16 and 16 - 13 = 3.
Compute 2^6 = 64. Since 13 * 4 = 52, the remainder of 64 modulo 13 is 12, which is -1 modulo 13.
The value 12 = -1 is not 1. So Euler's criterion says that 2 is not a square modulo 13. A direct list of the squares 1, 4, 9, 3, 12, 10 modulo 13 does not contain 2.

applications.conclusion: 3 is a square modulo 13 and 2 is not. Each answer needs only one modular power and no search for square roots.

results.name: Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol
results.statement: Let p be an odd prime. For an integer a, the Legendre symbol (a/p) is 0 if p divides a, 1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and -1 if a is not a square modulo p. Then (ab/p) = (a/p)(b/p) for all integers a and b.
hypotheses: p is an odd prime number.
a and b are arbitrary integers. The case where p divides a or b is included, and both sides are 0 there.
The Legendre symbol takes values in the integers {-1, 0, 1}, and the equality is an equality of integers.

prerequisites.reason: Euler's criterion gives (a/p) = a^((p-1)/2) mod p, which makes the symbol multiplicative modulo p.

definitions.name: Legendre symbol
definitions.text: For an odd prime p and an integer a, (a/p) = 0 if p divides a, (a/p) = 1 if p does not divide a and a is a square modulo p, and (a/p) = -1 if a is not a square modulo p.

steps.text: First claim: for every integer c, (c/p) = c^((p-1)/2) mod p. If p divides c, both sides are 0 mod p. If p does not divide c, Euler's criterion gives c^((p-1)/2) = 1 mod p when c is a square and c^((p-1)/2) = -1 mod p when c is not a square. These are the values 1 and -1 of (c/p).
Apply the claim to a, b and ab. Then (ab/p) = (ab)^((p-1)/2) = a^((p-1)/2) b^((p-1)/2) = (a/p)(b/p) mod p. The middle step is the law (xy)^n = x^n y^n in the commutative ring Z/pZ.
Both (ab/p) and (a/p)(b/p) are integers in {-1, 0, 1}. Their difference is an integer with absolute value at most 2. By step 2 it is divisible by p.
Since p is an odd prime, p is at least 3. The only integer with absolute value at most 2 that p divides is 0. So the difference is 0, and (ab/p) = (a/p)(b/p) as integers.

steps.text: Case p = 2. Here 1^2 = 1 = -1 mod 2, so -1 is a square. Also 2 mod 4 = 2, which is not 3. Both sides of the equivalence are true.
Now let p be odd and put k = (p-1)/2. The class -1 is not 0 modulo p. Euler's criterion says: -1 is a square modulo p if and only if (-1)^k = 1 in Z/pZ.

The classes 1 and -1 are different in Z/pZ because p is odd (their difference 2 is not divisible by p). So (-1)^k = 1 in Z/pZ if and only if k is even. If k is even, (-1)^k = 1. If k is odd, (-1)^k = -1, which is not 1.

Finally, k = (p-1)/2 is even if and only if p - 1 is divisible by 4, that is, p = 1 mod 4. For odd p, the residue p mod 4 is 1 or 3. So 'p = 1 mod 4' is the same as 'p is not 3 mod 4'. This proves the equivalence, and the formula (-1/p) = (-1)^k follows from step 2 and the value of the symbol.

applications.title: Test x^2 = -1 modulo 13 and modulo 7
applications.inputs: The primes 13 and 7. The question is whether -1 is a square modulo each prime.
applications.hypotheses: 13 and 7 are odd primes, so the theorem applies and the residue modulo 4 decides the answer.

steps.text: For p = 13, the residue 13 mod 4 is 1, because 13 - 4*3 = 1. So -1 is a square modulo 13.
The theorem does not name a root. A root is 5, because 5^2 + 1 = 26 = 2 * 13. Hence 5^2 = -1 mod 13.
For p = 7, the residue 7 mod 4 is 3, because 7 - 4*1 = 3. So -1 is not a square modulo 7.
A check: the squares modulo 7 are 1, 4, 2 (from 1, 2, 3). The class -1 = 6 is not in this list. The Euler value is (-1)^3 = -1, as the criterion predicts.

applications.conclusion: -1 is a square modulo 13 (with root 5) and not a square modulo 7, as the residue modulo 4 predicts.

steps.text: Let K = F_{p^2}. Since p is odd, p^2 = 1 mod 8, so 8 divides p^2 - 1, the order of the cyclic group K*. A cyclic group has an element of every order dividing its order, so K contains an element z of order 8. Then z^4 is a root of x^2 - 1 and z^4 is not 1. So z^4 = -1, because K is a field.

Put tau = z + z^(-1). Then tau^2 = z^2 + 2 + z^(-2). Put i = z^2. Then i^2 = z^4 = -1, so i^(-1) = -i, and z^2 + z^(-2) = i - i = 0. Hence tau^2 = 2. In particular tau is not 0, since 2 is not 0 in K.

By the Frobenius rule, tau^p = z^p + z^(-p). Since z has order 8, z^p depends only on p mod 8. Suppose p = 1 mod 8 or p = 7 mod 8. Then z^p = z or z^p = z^(-1), so z^p + z^(-p) = tau. Hence tau^p = tau.
Suppose p = 3 mod 8 or p = 5 mod 8. Then z^p = z^3 or z^p = z^(-3). Use z^4 = -1: z^3 = z^4 z^(-1) = -z^(-1), and z^(-3) = z^(-4) z = -z. In both cases z^p + z^(-p) = -(z + z^(-1)), so tau^p = -tau.

Since tau is not 0, divide by tau: tau^(p-1) = 1 in the first case and tau^(p-1) = -1 in the second case. Also tau^(p-1) = (tau^2)^((p-1)/2) = 2^((p-1)/2). So 2^((p-1)/2) = 1 if p = +-1 mod 8, and 2^((p-1)/2) = -1 if p = +-3 mod 8.

The class 2 is not 0 modulo p, because p is odd. By Euler's criterion, 2 is a square modulo p if and only if 2^((p-1)/2) = 1. By step 5 this holds if and only if p = 1 or 7 mod 8. The formula (-1)^((p^2-1)/8) equals 1 exactly for these p, because (p^2-1)/8 is even for p = +-1 mod 8 and odd for p = +-3 mod 8.

applications.title: Decide whether 2 is a square modulo 17, 11 and 13
applications.inputs: The odd primes 17, 11 and 13. The question is whether x^2 = 2 has a solution modulo each prime.
applications.hypotheses: All three numbers are odd primes, so the second supplement applies and only p mod 8 matters.

steps.text: For p = 17, the residue 17 mod 8 is 1, since 17 - 8*2 = 1. So 2 is a square modulo 17.
For p = 11, the residue 11 mod 8 is 3, since 11 - 8 = 3. So 2 is not a square modulo 11. Check with the formula: 2^5 = 32 and 32 - 33 = -1, so 2^5 = -1 mod 11.
For p = 13, the residue 13 mod 8 is 5, since 13 - 8 = 5. So 2 is not a square modulo 13. This agrees with the value 2^6 = 12 = -1 mod 13.

applications.conclusion: 2 is a square modulo 17 (root 6) and not a square modulo 11 or 13. The test needs only the residue of p modulo 8.

steps.text: Let N = {1, 2, ..., n}. For each k in N, the number g = gcd(k, n) is a positive divisor of n. So N is the disjoint union of the sets A_e = {k in N : gcd(k, n) = e}, taken over the positive divisors e of n. Hence n = sum over e | n of |A_e|.

Fix a divisor e of n and put d = n/e. Define a map f from {j : 1 <= j <= d, gcd(j, d) = 1} to A_e by f(j) = e j. Then 1 <= e j <= e d = n, and gcd(e j, n) = gcd(e j, e d) = e gcd(j, d) = e. So f(j) is in A_e.

The map f is injective, because e j = e j' implies j = j' for e > 0. It is surjective: if k is in A_e, then e divides k, so k = e j with 1 <= j <= d. Then e gcd(j, d) = gcd(k, n) = e, so gcd(j, d) = 1. Hence |A_e| = phi(d) = phi(n/e).

Substitute this into step 1: n = sum over e | n of phi(n/e). As e runs over the positive divisors of n, the number n/e runs over the same set of divisors exactly once each. Hence n = sum over d | n of phi(d).

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Prime powers. Let p be prime and k >= 1. An integer j in 1..p^k fails to be coprime to p^k exactly when p divides j. The multiples of p in 1..p^k are p, 2p, ..., p^(k-1) p, so there are p^(k-1) of them. Hence phi(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1) = p^(k-1)(p - 1).
Multiplicativity, part 1. Let gcd(m, n) = 1. The map x -> (x mod m, x mod n) from Z/mnZ to Z/mZ x Z/nZ is a bijection by the Chinese remainder theorem.

Multiplicativity, part 2. For an integer x, gcd(x, mn) = 1 if and only if gcd(x, m) = 1 and gcd(x, n) = 1, because a prime divisor of mn divides m or n. Coprimality to m depends only on x mod m, and coprimality to n depends only on x mod n. So the bijection of step 2 maps the classes coprime to mn exactly onto the pairs (u, v) with u coprime to m and v coprime to n.
Counting the two sets in step 3 gives phi(mn) = phi(m) phi(n) for coprime m and n.

Now let n = p_1^k_1 ... p_r^k_r. The factors p_i^k_i are pairwise coprime, and the product of the first j factors is coprime to the next factor. By induction on r and step 4, phi(n) = product of phi(p_i^k_i). By step 1 this equals product of p_i^(k_i - 1)(p_i - 1).
Finally p_i^(k_i - 1)(p_i - 1) = p_i^k_i (1 - 1/p_i). Multiplying over i and using n = product of p_i^k_i gives phi(n) = n * product of (1 - 1/p_i).

steps.text: Let gcd(m, n) = 1. Let D(m) and D(n) be the sets of positive divisors of m and n, and let D(mn) be the set of positive divisors of mn. Define phi: D(m) x D(n) -> D(mn) by phi(d1, d2) = d1 d2. This is well defined, because d1 d2 divides mn.
Phi is injective. Let d1 | m and d2 | n. Since gcd(m, n) = 1, d2 is coprime to m. So gcd(d1 d2, m) = gcd(d1, m) = d1. In the same way gcd(d1 d2, n) = gcd(d2, n) = d2. So d1 d2 determines d1 and d2.

Phi is surjective. Let d | mn. Put d1 = gcd(d, m) and d2 = gcd(d, n). Then d1 and d2 are coprime, since they divide the coprime numbers m and n. Both divide d, so d1 d2 divides d. Conversely, let a prime power q^e divide d. Then q^e divides mn, and q divides only one of m and n, so q^e divides m or n and thus divides d1 or d2. So d divides d1 d2. Hence d = d1 d2.

Because phi is a bijection and (d1 d2)^k = d1^k d2^k, we get sigma_k(mn) = sum over d | mn of d^k = sum over (d1, d2) of d1^k d2^k = (sum over d1 | m of d1^k)(sum over d2 | n of d2^k) = sigma_k(m) sigma_k(n). Also sigma_k(1) = 1.

For a prime power p^a, the positive divisors are 1, p, ..., p^a, by unique factorization. So sigma_k(p^a) = 1 + p^k + ... + p^(ak). For n = p_1^a_1 ... p_r^a_r the prime powers are pairwise coprime, so repeated use of step 4 gives the product formula.

theorem lucas_primality (p : ℕ) (a : ZMod p) (ha : a ^ (p - 1) = 1)
    (hd : ∀ q : ℕ, q.Prime → q ∣ p - 1 → a ^ ((p - 1) / q) ≠ 1) : p.Prime := by
  have h : p ≠ 0 ∧ p ≠ 1 := by
    constructor <;> rintro rfl <;> exact hd 2 Nat.prime_two (dvd_zero _) (pow_zero _)
  have hp1 : 1 < p := Nat.one_lt_iff_ne_zero_and_ne_one.2 h
  have : NeZero p := ⟨h.1⟩
  rw [Nat.prime_iff_card_units]
  apply (Nat.card_units_zmod_lt_sub_one hp1).antisymm
  let a' : (ZMod p)ˣ := Units.mkOfMulEqOne a _ (by rwa [← pow_succ', tsub_add_eq_add_tsub hp1])
  calc p - 1 = orderOf a := (orderOf_eq_of_pow_and_pow_div_prime (tsub_pos_of_lt hp1) ha hd).symm
    _ = orderOf a' := orderOf_injective (Units.coeHom _) Units.val_injective a'

steps.text: Since a^(n-1) = 1 mod n and n - 1 >= 1, we have a * a^(n-2) = 1 mod n. So the class of a is a unit in G = (Z/nZ)*. Let d be the order of a in G. From a^(n-1) = 1 we get d | n - 1.

Claim: d = n - 1. Suppose d < n - 1. Then (n-1)/d is an integer greater than 1, so it has a prime divisor q. Then q divides n - 1 and d divides (n-1)/q. Hence a^((n-1)/q) = (a^d)^((n-1)/(qd)) = 1 mod n. This contradicts the hypothesis. So d = n - 1.
By Lagrange's theorem the order d of a divides |G|. Hence |G| >= n - 1.

The group G consists of classes of integers in 1..n-1 that are coprime to n. (The class 0 is not a unit when n >= 2.) So |G| <= n - 1. With step 3, |G| = n - 1, so every integer in 1..n-1 is coprime to n.
Suppose n has a divisor e with 1 < e < n. Then gcd(e, n) = e > 1, so e is an integer in 1..n-1 that is not coprime to n. This contradicts step 4. So n has no such divisor. Since n >= 2, n is prime.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are coprime. For m = 0, gcd(F_0, F_1) = gcd(0, 1) = 1. If gcd(F_m, F_(m+1)) = 1, then gcd(F_(m+1), F_(m+2)) = gcd(F_(m+1), F_(m+1) + F_m) = gcd(F_(m+1), F_m) = 1.

Addition formula: F_(a+b) = F_a F_(b+1) + F_(a-1) F_b for a >= 1 and b >= 0. For b = 0 it reads F_a = F_a * 1 + 0. For b = 1 it reads F_(a+1) = F_a + F_(a-1). If it holds for b and b + 1, adding the two equations and using the recurrence on both sides gives it for b + 2. So it holds for all b by induction.

Shift lemma: for m >= 1 and n >= 0, gcd(F_m, F_(m+n)) = gcd(F_m, F_n). By step 2 with a = m and b = n, F_(m+n) = F_m F_(n+1) + F_(m-1) F_n. The first term is a multiple of F_m, so gcd(F_m, F_(m+n)) = gcd(F_m, F_(m-1) F_n). By step 1, F_m is coprime to F_(m-1), so this equals gcd(F_m, F_n). For m = 0 both sides equal F_n.
Repeating step 3 shows gcd(F_m, F_(r + t m)) = gcd(F_m, F_r) for every t >= 0. Take N = r + t m with r = N mod m. Then for m >= 1: gcd(F_m, F_N) = gcd(F_m, F_r) with r = N mod m < m.

Now prove gcd(F_m, F_N) = F_gcd(m,N) by strong induction on m, for all N. If m = 0, both sides are F_N. If m >= 1, step 4 gives gcd(F_m, F_N) = gcd(F_r, F_m) with r < m. By the induction hypothesis this is F_gcd(r, m). By the Euclidean algorithm, gcd(r, m) = gcd(m, N mod m) = gcd(m, N). So gcd(F_m, F_N) = F_gcd(m, N).
If m divides n, then gcd(m, n) = m, and the identity gives gcd(F_m, F_n) = F_m. So F_m divides F_n.

applications.title: Find gcd(F_12, F_18) without factoring
applications.inputs: The Fibonacci numbers F_12 = 144 and F_18 = 2584. The indices are m = 12 and n = 18.
applications.hypotheses: m and n are non-negative integers, and the Fibonacci values are from the recurrence F_(k+2) = F_(k+1) + F_k with F_0 = 0 and F_1 = 1.

steps.text: The Euclidean algorithm on the indices: 18 = 1 * 12 + 6 and 12 = 2 * 6. So gcd(12, 18) = 6.
The identity predicts gcd(144, 2584) = F_6. The sequence F_0..F_6 is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so F_6 = 8.
Check by division: 144 = 8 * 18 and 2584 = 8 * 323.
The numbers 18 and 323 are coprime. By the Euclidean algorithm, 323 = 17 * 18 + 17, 18 = 1 * 17 + 1, so the gcd is 1.

applications.conclusion: gcd(F_12, F_18) = 8 = F_6, as the identity says. Also F_6 = 8 divides F_12 and F_18.

results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the recurrence of the Fibonacci numbers, induction and the Euclidean algorithm for the gcd.

results.name: There are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 modulo 4
results.statement: For every integer N >= 2 there is a prime p with p > N and p = 1 mod 4. Hence the set of primes congruent to 1 modulo 4 is infinite. More precisely, every prime divisor p of (N!)^2 + 1 satisfies p > N and p = 1 mod 4.
hypotheses: N is an integer with N >= 2, so N! is even.
N! is the product 1 * 2 * ... * N.
The statement is the case k = 4 of the theorem on infinitely many primes congruent to 1 modulo k. The proof here is elementary and does not use cyclotomic polynomials.

prerequisites.reason: The first supplement shows that a prime p for which -1 is a square must satisfy p = 1 mod 4 when p is odd.

definitions.name: N!
definitions.text: The product of the integers 1, 2, ..., N.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration states that for every k >= 1 there are infinitely many primes p with p = 1 mod k. The authored statement is the case k = 4, with an elementary proof and an explicit bound on the prime.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Put M = (N!)^2 + 1. Since N >= 2, M >= 5, so M has a prime divisor p. Let p be any prime divisor of M.
Claim: p > N. If p <= N, then p divides N!, so p divides (N!)^2. Since p divides M = (N!)^2 + 1, p divides the difference 1. This is impossible for a prime.
Claim: p is odd. Since N >= 2, N! is even, so (N!)^2 is even and M is odd. So p, a divisor of M, is odd.
From p | M we get (N!)^2 = -1 mod p. So x = N! is a root of x^2 = -1 modulo p. Thus -1 is a square modulo p.
By the first supplement, a prime p for which -1 is a square satisfies p mod 4 not equal to 3. Since p is odd, p mod 4 is 1 or 3, so p = 1 mod 4.
For every N >= 2 we have found a prime p > N with p = 1 mod 4. If there were only finitely many such primes, take N larger than all of them. This gives a contradiction, so there are infinitely many.

applications.title: Produce a prime above 4 that is 1 mod 4, using N = 4
applications.hypotheses: N = 4 is at least 2. To locate the prime divisors of M it is enough to test the primes up to the square root of M, which is below 25.

steps.text: Test the primes below 25. Remainders of 577: by 2 it is 1, by 3 it is 1 (576 = 3 * 192), by 5 it is 2, by 7 it is 3, by 11 it is 5, by 13 it is 5, by 17 it is 16, by 19 it is 7, by 23 it is 2. None is 0, so 577 is prime.
So the only prime divisor of M is p = 577, and p > 4. The theorem predicts p = 1 mod 4. Indeed 577 = 4 * 144 + 1.
A root of x^2 = -1 modulo 577 is x = 24, because 24^2 + 1 = 577.

applications.conclusion: The number 577 is a prime above 4 with 577 = 1 mod 4. The same recipe with larger N gives primes of the form 4k + 1 above any bound.

results.name: Characterization of the integers that are sums of two squares
aliases: Fermat-Euler theorem on sums of two squares for composite numbers
results.statement: Let n >= 1 be an integer. Then n = x^2 + y^2 for some integers x and y if and only if, for every prime q with q = 3 mod 4, the exponent of q in the prime factorization of n is even.
hypotheses: n is a positive integer. (For n = 0, both sides hold: 0 = 0^2 + 0^2.)
x and y are integers; their signs do not matter, so one may take x, y >= 0.
The exponent of q in n is the largest e with q^e dividing n. It is 0 when q does not divide n, and 0 is even.

prerequisites.reason: The first supplement shows that -1 is not a square modulo a prime q = 3 mod 4, which excludes such primes from a coprime sum of two squares.
Fermat's theorem on two squares writes every prime p = 1 mod 4 as a sum of two squares, which gives the sufficiency part.

definitions.name: exponent of q in n
definitions.text: The number v_q(n), which is the largest e >= 0 such that q^e divides n.

definitions.name: two-square identity
definitions.text: For all integers a, b, c, d: (a^2 + b^2)(c^2 + d^2) = (ac - bd)^2 + (ad + bc)^2. Expanding both sides gives a^2 c^2 + a^2 d^2 + b^2 c^2 + b^2 d^2 in each case, because the terms -2abcd and +2abcd cancel.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Sufficiency, part 1. Let every prime q = 3 mod 4 have an even exponent in n. Write n = 2^a * P * Q^2, where P is the product of the prime powers p^b with p = 1 mod 4, and Q^2 collects the primes q = 3 mod 4 (their exponents are even, so they form a square). The prime 2 satisfies 2 = 1^2 + 1^2.

Sufficiency, part 2. Every prime p = 1 mod 4 is a sum of two squares by Fermat's theorem. The two-square identity shows that a product of two sums of two squares is a sum of two squares. By induction on the number of factors, 2^a * P is a sum of two squares u^2 + v^2.
Sufficiency, part 3. Multiply by Q^2 = Q^2 + 0^2 with the identity: (u^2 + v^2)(Q^2 + 0^2) = (uQ)^2 + (vQ)^2. So n = (uQ)^2 + (vQ)^2.
Necessity, part 1. Let n = x^2 + y^2 with n >= 1. Then x and y are not both 0. Let g = gcd(x, y), x = g x', y = g y'. Then gcd(x', y') = 1 and n = g^2 m with m = x'^2 + y'^2.

Necessity, part 2. Claim: no prime q = 3 mod 4 divides m. Suppose q divides m. If q divided y', then q would divide x'^2 = m - y'^2, so q would divide x'. This contradicts gcd(x', y') = 1. So y' is invertible modulo q. Put w = x' * (y')^(-1) mod q. Then w^2 = x'^2 / y'^2 = -1 mod q, because x'^2 + y'^2 = 0 mod q. So -1 is a square modulo q.
Necessity, part 3. By the first supplement, -1 is not a square modulo a prime q = 3 mod 4. This contradicts step 5. So no such prime divides m.
Necessity, part 4. For a prime q = 3 mod 4, v_q(n) = 2 v_q(g) + v_q(m) = 2 v_q(g), because q does not divide m. This number is even. This proves necessity.

applications.title: Decide whether 450 and 210 are sums of two squares, and build the representation of 450
applications.inputs: The integers 450 = 2 * 3^2 * 5^2 and 210 = 2 * 3 * 5 * 7. The primes 3 and 7 are the primes congruent to 3 modulo 4.
applications.hypotheses: Both integers are positive. The test needs only the exponents of 3 and 7, which are the primes congruent to 3 mod 4 in these factorizations.

steps.text: Check the factorization of 450 by multiplying the prime powers.
In 450 the prime 3 has exponent 2, which is even. The prime 7 has exponent 0. So 450 is a sum of two squares.
Next multiply by 3^2 = 3^2 + 0^2 with the identity: (5^2 + 5^2)(3^2 + 0^2) = 15^2 + 15^2.
Check 210 = 2 * 3 * 5 * 7. The prime 3 has exponent 1 and the prime 7 has exponent 1. Both exponents are odd, so 210 is not a sum of two squares.

applications.conclusion: 450 = 15^2 + 15^2 is a sum of two squares, and 210 is not. The factorization alone decides the question.

results.name: gcd(a^m - 1, a^n - 1) = a^gcd(m,n) - 1
results.statement: Let a >= 2 be an integer and let m, n >= 0 be integers. Then gcd(a^m - 1, a^n - 1) = a^gcd(m, n) - 1. In particular, a^d - 1 divides a^m - 1 whenever d divides m, and the numbers 2^p - 1 and 2^q - 1 are coprime for distinct primes p and q.
hypotheses: a is an integer with a >= 2, so that a^k - 1 is strictly increasing in k.
m and n are non-negative integers. We use gcd(m, 0) = m and a^0 - 1 = 0, so gcd(x, 0) = x.
All quantities are non-negative integers.

definitions.name: geometric factorization
definitions.text: For x and an integer q >= 1: x^q - 1 = (x - 1)(x^(q-1) + x^(q-2) + ... + x + 1).

source.alignment: The Lean statement holds for all natural numbers a, b, c with truncated subtraction. The authored statement takes a >= 2, the case in which the identity is used.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let n >= 1 and write m = q n + r with q >= 0 and 0 <= r < n. Put x = a^n. By the geometric factorization, x - 1 divides x^q - 1 = a^(qn) - 1.
Now a^m - 1 = a^r (a^(qn) - 1) + (a^r - 1). The first term is a multiple of a^n - 1 by step 1. So a^m - 1 = a^r - 1 mod (a^n - 1).

Since a >= 2 and r < n, we have 0 <= a^r - 1 < a^n - 1. So a^r - 1 is the remainder of a^m - 1 on division by a^n - 1. By the Euclidean step, gcd(a^m - 1, a^n - 1) = gcd(a^n - 1, a^r - 1) with r = m mod n.
Let G(m, n) = gcd(a^m - 1, a^n - 1). Prove G(m, n) = a^gcd(m,n) - 1 by strong induction on n, for all m. If n = 0, then G(m, 0) = gcd(a^m - 1, 0) = a^m - 1 = a^gcd(m,0) - 1.

Let n >= 1 and assume the claim for all smaller second arguments. By step 3, G(m, n) = G(n, r) = G(r, n) with r = m mod n < n. By the induction hypothesis G(r, n) = a^gcd(r,n) - 1. By the Euclidean algorithm gcd(r, n) = gcd(n, m mod n) = gcd(m, n). So G(m, n) = a^gcd(m,n) - 1.

For the consequences: if d divides m then gcd(d, m) = d, so gcd(a^d - 1, a^m - 1) = a^d - 1, which means a^d - 1 divides a^m - 1. For distinct primes p and q, gcd(p, q) = 1, so gcd(2^p - 1, 2^q - 1) = 2^1 - 1 = 1.

applications.title: Find gcd(2^12 - 1, 2^18 - 1) and test two Mersenne numbers
applications.inputs: The numbers 2^12 - 1 = 4095 and 2^18 - 1 = 262143. The exponents are 12 and 18. Also the Mersenne numbers 2^7 - 1 and 2^5 - 1.
applications.hypotheses: The base a = 2 satisfies a >= 2 and the exponents are non-negative integers, so the identity applies.

steps.text: Compute the first number. The second is 2^18 - 1 = 262143.
The Euclidean algorithm on the exponents: 18 = 1 * 12 + 6 and 12 = 2 * 6. So gcd(12, 18) = 6.
The identity predicts gcd(4095, 262143) = 2^6 - 1.
Check by division: 4095 = 63 * 65 and 262143 = 63 * 4161. The numbers 65 and 4161 are coprime because 4161 = 64 * 65 + 1.
For the Mersenne numbers 2^7 - 1 = 127 and 2^5 - 1 = 31, gcd(7, 5) = 1, so their gcd is 2^1 - 1 = 1. Check: 127 = 4 * 31 + 3.

applications.conclusion: gcd(4095, 262143) = 63 = 2^6 - 1, as predicted by gcd(12, 18) = 6. The Mersenne numbers 127 and 31 are coprime.

results.name: Cancellation law for congruences
aliases: dividing a congruence by a common factor
results.statement: Let m >= 1 and c be integers. Put d = gcd(m, c). If c a = c b mod m for integers a and b, then a = b mod m/d. If gcd(m, c) = 1, then a = b mod m. The modulus m/d is the best possible: for some a and b with c a = c b mod m, a = b mod m/d fails modulo any larger multiple m/d * t with 1 < t.
hypotheses: m is a positive integer.
a, b and c are integers. The factor c may share factors with m.
d = gcd(m, c) is positive because m is positive.

prerequisites.reason: Bezout's identity shows that m/d and c/d are coprime, and it gives Euclid's lemma used to remove the factor c/d.

definitions.name: congruence
definitions.text: x = y mod m means that m divides x - y.

steps.text: Let d = gcd(m, c) and write m = d m', c = d c' with integers m' >= 1 and c'. Bezout's identity gives integers u and v with d = u m + v c. Divide by d: 1 = u m' + v c'. So gcd(m', c') = 1.
The hypothesis c a = c b mod m says that m divides c (b - a). In terms of m' and c' this reads d m' | d c' (b - a).
Cancel the positive factor d: m' divides c' (b - a). Here d > 0, so it is allowed to divide both sides of the divisibility d m' | d c' (b - a) by d.
Use 1 = u m' + v c' from step 1 and multiply by (b - a): b - a = u m' (b - a) + v c' (b - a). The first term is divisible by m'. The second term is divisible by m' by step 3. So m' divides b - a.
Hence a = b mod m' = m/d. If gcd(m, c) = 1, then d = 1 and a = b mod m.
Sharpness. Take a = 0 and b = m/d. Then c b = (c/d) m = 0 mod m, so c a = c b mod m. Here a = b mod m/d, but a is not b mod (m/d) t for any t > 1, since 0 < m/d < (m/d) t.

applications.title: Solve 12 x = 36 mod 30
applications.inputs: The modulus m = 30, the factor c = 12 and the right side 36 = 12 * 3. The aim is to cancel 12 from 12 x = 12 * 3 mod 30.
applications.hypotheses: m = 30 is positive. The factor 12 is not coprime to 30, so ordinary division by 12 is not allowed, but the cancellation law applies with d = gcd(30, 12).

steps.text: Find d = gcd(30, 12) with the Euclidean algorithm: 30 = 2 * 12 + 6 and 12 = 2 * 6. So d = 6.
The new modulus is m/d = 30/6.
By the law, 12 x = 12 * 3 mod 30 gives x = 3 mod 5. So x is in {3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28} modulo 30.
Check one value that is not 3: x = 8. We get 12 * 8 - 12 * 3 = 60 = 2 * 30.
So 12 * 8 = 12 * 3 mod 30, but 8 is not 3 mod 30, since 30 does not divide 5. This shows the modulus must be divided by d.

applications.conclusion: The solutions of 12 x = 36 mod 30 are exactly x = 3 mod 5, which are 6 classes modulo 30 and 6 = gcd(30, 12).

results.name: Chinese remainder theorem for moduli that are not coprime
aliases: compatibility condition a = b mod gcd(n, m)
results.statement: Let n, m >= 1 be integers and let g = gcd(n, m) and L = lcm(n, m). For integers a and b, the system x = a mod n, x = b mod m has a solution x if and only if a = b mod g. In that case the solutions form exactly one residue class modulo L.
hypotheses: n and m are positive integers; they need not be coprime.
a and b are arbitrary integers.
g = gcd(n, m) and L = lcm(n, m) = n m / g. If g = 1, the condition a = b mod g is empty and the statement is the usual theorem.

prerequisites.reason: Bezout's identity gives integers u and v with n u + m v = g, which is used to build an explicit solution.

definitions.name: lcm
definitions.text: L = lcm(n, m) is the least positive common multiple of n and m. It equals n m / g, and every common multiple of n and m is a multiple of L.

def chineseRemainder' (h : a ≡ b [MOD gcd n m]) : { k // k ≡ a [MOD n] ∧ k ≡ b [MOD m] } :=
  if hn : n = 0 then ⟨a, by
    rw [hn, gcd_zero_left] at h; constructor
    · rfl
    · exact h⟩
  else
    if hm : m = 0 then ⟨b, by
      rw [hm, gcd_zero_right] at h; constructor
      · exact h.symm
      · rfl⟩
    else
      ⟨let (c, d) := xgcd n m; Int.toNat ((n * c * b + m * d * a) / gcd n m % lcm n m), by
        rw [xgcd_val]
        dsimp
        rw [modEq_iff_dvd, modEq_iff_dvd,
          Int.toNat_of_nonneg (Int.emod_nonneg _ (Int.natCast_ne_zero.2 (lcm_ne_zero hn hm)))]
        have hnonzero : (gcd n m : ℤ) ≠ 0 := by
          norm_cast
          rw [Nat.gcd_eq_zero_iff, not_and]
          exact fun _ => hm
        have hcoedvd : ∀ t, (gcd n m : ℤ) ∣ t * (b - a) := fun t => h.dvd.mul_left _
        have := gcd_eq_gcd_ab n m
        constructor <;> rw [Int.emod_def, ← sub_add] <;>
            refine Int.dvd_add ?_ (dvd_mul_of_dvd_left ?_ _) <;>
          try norm_cast
        · rw [← sub_eq_iff_eq_add'] at this
          rw [← this, Int.sub_mul, ← add_sub_assoc, add_comm, add_sub_assoc, ← Int.mul_sub,
            Int.add_ediv_of_dvd_left, Int.mul_ediv_cancel_left _ hnonzero,
            Int.mul_ediv_assoc _ h.dvd, ← sub_sub, sub_self, zero_sub, Int.dvd_neg, mul_assoc]
          · exact dvd_mul_right _ _
          norm_cast
          exact dvd_mul_right _ _
        · exact dvd_lcm_left n m
        · rw [← sub_eq_iff_eq_add] at this
          rw [← this, Int.sub_mul, sub_add, ← Int.mul_sub, Int.sub_ediv_of_dvd,
            Int.mul_ediv_cancel_left _ hnonzero, Int.mul_ediv_assoc _ h.dvd, ← sub_add, sub_self,
            zero_add, mul_assoc]
          · exact dvd_mul_right _ _
          · exact hcoedvd _

source.alignment: The Lean definition constructs a natural number k with k = a mod n and k = b mod m from a proof that a = b mod gcd(n, m). The authored statement adds the converse and the uniqueness modulo lcm(n, m).

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Necessity. Let x satisfy both congruences. The number g divides n and n divides x - a, so g divides x - a. Likewise g divides x - b. Hence g divides (x - b) - (x - a) = a - b, that is, a = b mod g.
Sufficiency, set-up. Let a = b mod g. Write b - a = g t for an integer t. By Bezout's identity there are integers u and v with n u + m v = g.
Sufficiency, construction. Put x_0 = a + n u t. Then x_0 = a mod n, since the second term is a multiple of n.
Sufficiency, check modulo m. Use n u = g - m v. Then x_0 = a + (g - m v) t = a + g t - m v t = b - m v t. So x_0 = b mod m. Hence x_0 solves the system.

Uniqueness. Let x and x' both solve the system. Then n divides x - x' and m divides x - x'. So x - x' is a common multiple of n and m. Every common multiple is a multiple of L: if t = n s and m divides n s, then m/g divides (n/g) s, and gcd(m/g, n/g) = 1, so m/g divides s and L = n m / g divides t. Hence x = x' mod L.
Conversely, if x_0 is a solution and x = x_0 mod L, then x is a solution, since n and m both divide L. So the solutions are exactly the class of x_0 modulo L.

steps.text: Compute the lcm L = n m / g = 12 * 18 / 6.
Test compatibility. The difference b - a = 17 - 5 is divisible by 6, so a solution exists.
The construction gives x_0 = a + n u t = 5 + 12 * (-1) * 2.
Reduce modulo 36: -19 + 36 = 17. Check: 17 = 5 mod 12, because 17 - 5 = 12. And 17 = 17 mod 18.

applications.conclusion: The first system has the solution class x = 17 mod 36, and the second system has no solution. The test a = b mod gcd(n, m) decides both cases.

  rw [Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Nat.card_eq_fintype_card]

    calc

        card_congr (Equiv.sigmaFiberEquiv (@Quotient.mk'' _ (orbitRel G α))).symm

      _ ≡ ∑ _a : fixedPoints G α, 1 [MOD p] := ?_

    refine

steps.text: The orbits of G partition X, because the relation x ~ y if y = g.x for some g is an equivalence relation. So |X| is the sum of the sizes of the distinct orbits.
By the orbit-stabilizer theorem, the size of each orbit divides |G| = p^n. A divisor of p^n is p^k for some k with 0 <= k <= n, because p is prime.

An orbit has size 1 if and only if its point x satisfies g.x = x for all g. So the orbits of size 1 correspond one to one to the points of X^G. All other orbits have size p^k with k >= 1, and p divides this size.
Hence |X| = |X^G| + (a sum of orbit sizes that are all divisible by p). The sum is divisible by p. Therefore |X| is congruent to |X^G| modulo p.

steps.text: Define psi from the left cosets of H ∩ K to the product set (G/H) x (G/K) by psi(g(H ∩ K)) = (gH, gK). The map is well defined: if g' = gc with c in H ∩ K, then g'H = gH and g'K = gK.
The map psi is injective. Suppose gH = g'H and gK = g'K. Then g^-1 g' is in H and in K. So g^-1 g' is in H ∩ K, and g(H ∩ K) = g'(H ∩ K).
The target set has [G : H] * [G : K] elements, which is finite. An injective map into a finite set shows that G/(H ∩ K) is finite and that [G : H ∩ K] <= [G : H] * [G : K].
Equality of the two finite numbers holds if and only if psi is a bijection, so we must find when psi is surjective. The pair (xH, yK) is in the image if and only if some g lies in both xH and yK.
Suppose psi is surjective. For any y in G take the pair (eH, yK). Some g lies in H and in yK, so g = h = yk. Then y = hk^-1 is in HK. Hence G = HK.
Suppose G = HK. Take any x and y in G. Write x^-1 y = hk with h in H and k in K. Then g = xh = yk^-1 lies in xH and in yK. So every pair is in the image, and psi is surjective.

applications.title: Index of 4Z intersected with 6Z in the integers
applications.inputs: Let G = Z under addition, H = 4Z and K = 6Z. Then [G : H] = 4 and [G : K] = 6. Also take H' = 3Z and K' = 5Z.
applications.hypotheses: Both subgroups have finite index. The intersection of two subgroups of Z is the set of common multiples, which is the multiples of the least common multiple.

The intersection 4Z ∩ 6Z is 12Z, because lcm(4, 6) = 4 * 6 / gcd(4, 6). So its index is this number, and it is less than 24.

source.alignment: The declaration states that the commutator subgroup lies in the kernel of every homomorphism to an abelian group. The authored statement also gives normality, the criterion for quotients, and the factorisation, which the same module proves.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: For g in G, g[a, b]g^-1 = [gag^-1, gbg^-1], because conjugation by g is a homomorphism. So conjugation maps the set of commutators into itself. It therefore maps the subgroup G' generated by them into itself, and G' is normal. This proves (1).
Let N be normal. In G/N the elements xN and yN commute if and only if xyN = yxN. This holds if and only if x y x^-1 y^-1 is in N, which means [x, y] is in N.

So G/N is abelian if and only if every commutator [x, y] is in N. Since N is a subgroup, this holds if and only if the subgroup G' generated by the commutators is in N. This proves (2). With N = G' it also shows that G/G' is abelian.

Let f: G -> A be a homomorphism with A abelian. For all a and b, f([a, b]) = f(a) f(b) f(a)^-1 f(b)^-1 = 1, because f(a) and f(b) commute. So every generator of G' is in ker f. Hence G' is contained in ker f.
Define f'(gG') = f(g). It is well defined. If g' = gc with c in G', then f(g') = f(g) f(c) = f(g), because c is in ker f. It is a homomorphism, since f'(gG' hG') = f'(ghG') = f(gh) = f(g) f(h).
The map f' is unique. Every element of G/G' has the form gG', and any homomorphism f'' with f''(gG') = f(g) agrees with f' on all these elements. This proves (3).

steps.text: The product c = ab = (12)(13) is a 3-cycle. Since a^-1 = a and b^-1 = b, the commutator [a, b] = abab = c^2. It is also a 3-cycle, and it is not the identity.
The quotient S_3/A_3 is abelian, so by part (2) G' is contained in A_3. The subgroup G' contains the non-identity element c^2. By Lagrange, the order of G' divides 3 and is not 1. So G' = A_3.
By part (3), the abelianization S_3/G' has order equal to the group order divided by 3.

applications.conclusion: [S_3, S_3] = A_3, and the abelianization of S_3 is the group of order 2. Every homomorphism from S_3 to an abelian group factors through the sign map.

source.alignment: Mathlib defines the sign homomorphism Perm α →* ℤˣ for any finite type by another construction. The authored statement uses the classical product formula on {1, ..., n} and adds the kernel and uniqueness properties.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: For a pair {i, j} of distinct points put F_s(i, j) = (s(j) - s(i)) / (j - i). Swapping i and j changes the sign of both the numerator and the denominator, so F_s(i, j) = F_s(j, i). Thus P(s) is a product over unordered pairs. Each factor is non-zero.

P(s) is 1 or -1. Since s is a bijection, s maps the set of unordered pairs onto itself. So the products of the absolute values |s(j) - s(i)| and |j - i| over all pairs are equal. Hence |P(s)| = 1. The sign of P(s) is (-1)^inv(s), because a factor is negative if and only if the pair is an inversion.

P(st) = P(s) P(t). For i != j, write (s(t(j)) - s(t(i))) / (j - i) = F_s(t(i), t(j)) * F_t(i, j). Take the product over all unordered pairs. The pair {t(i), t(j)} runs over all unordered pairs once, and F_s is symmetric, so the product of F_s(t(i), t(j)) equals P(s).

Let t = (k k+1) be an adjacent transposition. It has exactly one inversion, the pair (k, k+1). Any pair that does not contain both k and k+1 keeps its order: points outside {k, k+1} are fixed, and a point on one side of both k and k+1 stays on that side. So P(t) = (-1)^1 = -1.

Let (a b) be any transposition. Choose a permutation r with r(k) = a and r(k+1) = b. Then r (k k+1) r^-1 = (a b). Since P is a homomorphism into the abelian group {1, -1}, P((a b)) = P(r) P((k k+1)) P(r)^-1 = -1.
P is onto {1, -1} because P(id) = 1 and P((1 2)) = -1. By the first isomorphism theorem, S_n / ker P has 2 elements, so A_n = ker P is normal of index 2. By Lagrange, |A_n| = n!/2.
Let Q be any homomorphism S_n -> {1, -1} with Q(t) = -1 for each transposition t. Every permutation is a product of transpositions, so Q and P agree on all of S_n. This proves uniqueness.

source.alignment: The declaration states that two finite subgroups of a cyclic group are equal if their orders are equal. The authored statement adds the existence of a subgroup of order d for each divisor d and the count of subgroups.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: By Lagrange's theorem, the order of every subgroup divides n. So subgroups can only have orders that divide n.

Let d divide n. The element g has order n, so g^m = e if and only if n divides m. The element h = g^(n/d) satisfies h^k = e if and only if n divides k n / d, which holds if and only if d divides k. So h has order d and the subgroup <h> has d elements.

Let S_d be the set of x in G with x^d = e. Write x = g^m. Then x^d = e if and only if n divides m d, which holds if and only if (n/d) divides m, after division by n/d. So x is a power of g^(n/d), and S_d = <h>.
Now let H be any subgroup of order d. By Lagrange's theorem, the order of each element of H divides d, so x^d = e for every x in H. Hence H is contained in S_d.

The sets H and S_d are finite with |H| = d = |S_d|, and H is contained in S_d. So H = S_d = <g^(n/d)>. The subgroup of order d is therefore unique. Counting one subgroup for each divisor gives the number of subgroups.

steps.text: Let X = G/H be the set of left cosets. It has p elements. G acts on X by g.(xH) = gxH. This defines a homomorphism phi: G -> Sym(X), and Sym(X) has order p!. Let K = ker phi. It is normal in G.
K is contained in H. If g is in K, then g fixes the coset eH = H, so gH = H, which means g is in H.
By the first isomorphism theorem, G/K is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sym(X). By Lagrange, m = [G : K] divides p!. By Lagrange, m also divides |G|, because |G| = m |K|.
Also [G : K] = [G : H] [H : K] = p [H : K], by Lagrange applied to K <= H <= G. So p divides m.
Let q be a prime that divides m. Then q divides |G|, so q >= p, because p is the smallest prime divisor of |G|. Also q divides p! = 1*2*...*p, so q <= p. Hence q = p. So m is a power of p.

p^2 does not divide p! = p * (p-1)!, because (p-1)! is a product of integers smaller than p, and the prime p divides none of them. Since m is a power of p that divides p!, and p divides m, we get m = p.
Now [G : K] = p = [G : H], so |K| = |H|. Since K is contained in H, K = H. So H is the kernel of phi and H is normal in G.

The group H has order p^n and acts on X by h.(xH) = hxH. By the fixed-point congruence, |X| is congruent to |X^H| modulo p. Since p divides |X|, p divides |X^H|.
Compute the fixed points. The coset xH is fixed if and only if hxH = xH for all h in H, which means x^-1 h x is in H for all h. That is, x^-1 H x is contained in H.

The sets x^-1 H x and H are finite and have the same size p^n. So the inclusion x^-1 H x <= H means x^-1 H x = H. This holds if and only if x is in N_G(H). Hence the fixed points are the cosets xH with x in N_G(H).
These cosets are the left cosets of H in N_G(H), because H is contained in N_G(H). So |X^H| = [N_G(H) : H], and p divides [N_G(H) : H].
The index [N_G(H) : H] is at least 1 and p divides it, so it is at least p >= 2. Hence N_G(H) is strictly larger than H.

source.alignment: The declaration states that in a nilpotent group a subgroup is maximal if and only if its index is prime. Finite p-groups are nilpotent. The authored statement is for finite p-groups, proves normality, and gives index exactly p for maximal subgroups, which is one direction of the declaration.

steps.text: By Lagrange's theorem, |H| divides p^n, so |H| = p^m for some m. Since H is a proper subgroup, |H| < |G| and m < n. Hence p^(m+1) divides p^n.
By the theorem on normalizers, N_G(H) is strictly larger than H. Now H <= N_G(H) <= G and H is maximal, so N_G(H) = G. Hence gHg^-1 = H for all g, and H is normal.
So Q = G/H is a group of order p^(n-m) > 1. Let S be a subgroup of Q. Its preimage in G is a subgroup that contains H. By maximality it is H or G. So S is the trivial subgroup or Q.
Take x != e in Q. The subgroup <x> is not trivial, so <x> = Q and Q is cyclic of order p^k with k = n - m >= 1.
Suppose k >= 2. Then x^p has order p^(k-1) > 1, and <x^p> has p^(k-1) < p^k elements. It would be a subgroup that is neither trivial nor Q. This is a contradiction, so k = 1 and [G : H] = |Q| = p.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Existence, by strong induction on deg f. If f = 0 or deg f < deg g, take q = 0 and r = f. These cases need no further work.
Now let m = deg f and n = deg g with m >= n. Let a be the leading coefficient of f and b the leading coefficient of g. Since k is a field, b has an inverse, so the element c = a/b exists.

Define h = f - c x^(m-n) g. The term c x^(m-n) g has degree m and leading coefficient c b = a. So the coefficient of x^m in h is a - a = 0, and every higher coefficient is 0. Hence h = 0 or deg h < m.
By the induction hypothesis, h = q' g + r with r = 0 or deg r < deg g. Then f = h + c x^(m-n) g = (q' + c x^(m-n)) g + r. This gives the existence of q and r.
Uniqueness. Let f = q g + r = q' g + r' with both remainders zero or of degree less than deg g. Subtract to get (q - q') g = r' - r.
Suppose q is not equal to q'. A field has no zero divisors, so the leading coefficients of q - q' and g multiply to a nonzero element. Hence deg((q - q') g) = deg(q - q') + deg g >= deg g.
But r' - r is zero or has degree less than deg g, because each of r and r' has this property. This contradicts the bound above. So q = q', and then r = r'.

steps.text: The leading term x^4 of f is cancelled by x^2 g = x^4 + x^3 + x^2. The difference is x^3 - x^2 - x + 5.
The term x^3 is cancelled by x g = x^3 + x^2 + x. The difference is -2x^2 - 2x + 5. The next quotient term is -2.
Now (-2) g = -2x^2 - 2x - 2. The difference is the constant 7, which has degree less than 2. So q = x^2 + x - 2 and r = 7.
Check the identity at x = 2. The value of f(2) is computed first.
The value of q(2) g(2) + r is the same number, as the theorem requires.

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: N(z) = z * conj(z), where conj is complex conjugation. Conjugation respects products. So N(z w) = z w conj(z) conj(w) = N(z) N(w). This holds for all complex z and w.

Let alpha and beta be given with beta != 0. In the field Q(i), the quotient alpha/beta equals alpha conj(beta) / N(beta). Write it as x + y i. The numbers x and y are rational because N(beta) is a positive integer.
Choose integers m and n with |x - m| <= 1/2 and |y - n| <= 1/2. Such integers exist: take the nearest integer to each rational number. Put gamma = m + n i, which lies in Z[i].
Put rho = alpha - gamma beta. It lies in Z[i] because Z[i] is a ring. It satisfies rho = (alpha/beta - gamma) beta in the complex numbers.
By the multiplicativity of N, N(rho) = N(alpha/beta - gamma) N(beta), where N(u + v i) = u^2 + v^2 is used for real u and v. Here N(alpha/beta - gamma) = (x - m)^2 + (y - n)^2 <= 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
So N(rho) <= N(beta)/2. Since N(beta) is a positive integer, N(beta)/2 < N(beta). Therefore N(rho) < N(beta). Together with N(z) >= 1 for nonzero z, this shows that N is a Euclidean function on Z[i].

applications.title: Divide 11 + 7i by 2 + 3i in the Gaussian integers
applications.inputs: alpha = 11 + 7i and beta = 2 + 3i. The norm of beta is 13.
applications.hypotheses: beta is not zero and both numbers lie in Z[i], so the theorem gives gamma and rho with N(rho) <= 13/2.

steps.text: Compute alpha conj(beta) = (11 + 7i)(2 - 3i). Its real part is 11*2 + 7*3.
Its imaginary part is 7*2 - 11*3.
So alpha/beta = 43/13 - (19/13) i, which is about 3.31 - 1.46 i. The nearest integers are m = 3 and n = -1, so gamma = 3 - i.
Now gamma beta = (3 - i)(2 + 3i) has real part 3*2 + 1*3.
Its imaginary part is 3*3 - 1*2. So gamma beta = 9 + 7i and rho = alpha - gamma beta = 2.
The norm of rho is 4. The norm of beta is 13. The bound of the proof gives 13/2, and 4 is less than 13/2.

applications.conclusion: 11 + 7i = (3 - i)(2 + 3i) + 2 with N(2) = 4 < 13 = N(2 + 3i). This is one step of Euclid's algorithm in Z[i].

Its proof rests on the lemma mod_mem_iff pinned here, which says x % y lies in an ideal S exactly when x does, for y in S. proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let I be an ideal of R. If I = 0, then I = (0) is principal. Assume I is not 0.
The set of values N(x) for x in I with x != 0 is a nonempty set of natural numbers. By well-ordering it has a least element. Choose b in I, b != 0, with N(b) equal to this least value.
Since b is in I and I is an ideal, every multiple r b is in I. So (b) is contained in I.
Let a be in I. Divide with remainder: a = q b + r with r = 0 or N(r) < N(b). Since a and q b are in I, the difference r = a - q b is in I.
If r were not 0, then r would be a nonzero element of I with N(r) < N(b). This contradicts the choice of b as an element of least N. So r = 0 and a = q b is in (b).
Hence I is contained in (b), and I = (b). For the last claim, apply this to I = (a, b). The generator d lies in (a, b), so d = a x + b y. Also a and b lie in (d), so d divides both.

applications.title: The ideal (11 + 7i, 2 + 3i) of the Gaussian integers is the whole ring

applications.hypotheses: Z[i] is a Euclidean domain, so the ideal is principal and Euclid's algorithm finds its generator.

steps.text: Division with remainder gives 11 + 7i = (3 - i)(2 + 3i) + 2. The remainder 2 has N = 4, which is less than N(2 + 3i) = 13.
Divide 2 + 3i by 2. Take quotient 1 + i, so (1 + i) * 2 = 2 + 2i and the remainder is (2 + 3i) - (2 + 2i) = i. Its norm is 1, which is less than N(2) = 4.
Now 2 = (-2i) * i, so the next remainder is 0. The last nonzero remainder i is a generator of the ideal, by the proof above. Since i is a unit, the ideal contains 1.
Reading the steps backwards gives i = (2 + 3i) - (1 + i) * 2 and 2 = (11 + 7i) - (3 - i)(2 + 3i). So 1 = -i * i is an explicit combination of the two generators.

applications.conclusion: The ideal (11 + 7i, 2 + 3i) equals (1), the whole ring Z[i]. The two numbers have no common non-unit divisor.

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: (1) implies (2). Let p be irreducible. Since p is not a unit, 1 is not in (p), so (p) != R. Let J be an ideal with (p) contained in J. Since R is a PID, J = (d) for some d.
Since p is in (d), p = d e for some e. By irreducibility, d is a unit or e is a unit. If d is a unit, then J = R. If e is a unit, then d = e^(-1) p lies in (p), so J = (p). So (p) is maximal.

(2) implies (3). If (p) is maximal, the quotient R/(p) is a field. A field has no zero divisors. If p | a b, then the classes of a and b satisfy a * b = 0 in R/(p). So one of the classes is 0, which means p | a or p | b. Also p is not a unit because (p) != R.
(3) implies (1). Let p be prime and p = a b. Then p | a b, so p | a or p | b. Say a = p c. Then p = p c b, so p (1 - c b) = 0.
Since R is an integral domain and p != 0, we get 1 = c b. So b is a unit. The case p | b is the same with the roles of a and b exchanged. Since p is not a unit, p is irreducible.
The three implications form a cycle (1) to (2) to (3) to (1), so the three statements are equivalent.

applications.title: In Z[i], if 3 divides a^2 + b^2 then 3 divides a and b
applications.inputs: R = Z[i] with norm N(a + b i) = a^2 + b^2. The element is p = 3. Z[i] is a PID because it is a Euclidean domain.
applications.hypotheses: 3 is nonzero in Z[i]. It is irreducible, as the steps below show, so the theorem applies.

steps.text: N is multiplicative and N(3) = 9. Suppose 3 = alpha beta with neither factor a unit. Then N(alpha) N(beta) = 9 and both norms are larger than 1, so N(alpha) = 3.
But a^2 + b^2 = 3 has no integer solution. If |a| >= 2 or |b| >= 2, the sum is at least 4. If |a| <= 1 and |b| <= 1, the sum is at most 2.
So 3 is irreducible in Z[i]. By the theorem, 3 is prime in Z[i].

Now suppose 3 divides a^2 + b^2 in Z. Then 3 divides (a + b i)(a - b i) in Z[i]. By primality, 3 divides a + b i or a - b i, so 3 divides both a and b. For example 45 = 3^2 + 6^2 and 3 divides 3 and 6.
Without the theorem one can check the converse by residues. Squares modulo 3 are 0 or 1, so a^2 + b^2 is 0 modulo 3 only when both squares are 0. A sum of two nonzero squares gives 2, never 0.

applications.conclusion: The prime 3 stays prime in Z[i]. So 3 divides a^2 + b^2 only if 3 divides a and 3 divides b.
