results.name: Equality case of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
results.statement: Let E be an inner product space over K = R or K = C. Let x and y be nonzero vectors in E. Then |<x,y>| = ||x|| ||y|| if and only if y = r x for some scalar r in K with r != 0. For every x and y the defect ||x||^2 ||y||^2 - |<x,y>|^2 equals ||x||^2 ||y - t x||^2 with t = <x,y>/<x,x>, when x != 0.
hypotheses: E is an inner product space over R or C. The inner product is linear in the second argument and conjugate-linear in the first.
The vectors x and y are both nonzero. If x = 0 or y = 0, both sides of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality are 0 and the two vectors are trivially dependent.
E can have any dimension. E need not be complete.

steps.text: Direction (if). Let y = r x. Then <x,y> = r <x,x> = r ||x||^2, so |<x,y>| = |r| ||x||^2. Also ||y|| = |r| ||x||, so ||x|| ||y|| = |r| ||x||^2. The two values are equal.
Direction (only if). Let x != 0. Put t = <x,y>/<x,x> and z = y - t x. By linearity in the second argument, <x,z> = <x,y> - t <x,x> = 0. So z is orthogonal to x, and also to t x.

Since y = t x + z with t x orthogonal to z, the Pythagorean expansion gives ||y||^2 = |t|^2 ||x||^2 + ||z||^2. Now |t|^2 ||x||^2 = |<x,y>|^2 / ||x||^2. Multiply by ||x||^2: ||x||^2 ||y||^2 = |<x,y>|^2 + ||x||^2 ||z||^2.
This identity is the defect formula. It also proves the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, because ||x||^2 ||z||^2 >= 0.
Assume |<x,y>| = ||x|| ||y||. The defect is 0, so ||x||^2 ||z||^2 = 0. Since x != 0, we get z = 0 and y = t x. Because y != 0, the scalar t is not 0. Take r = t.

applications.title: Maximum of a linear form on the unit sphere in R^3
applications.inputs: Take E = R^3 with the dot product and a = (2,3,6). Find the maximum of <a,v> over all unit vectors v, and find every maximizer.
applications.hypotheses: The inner product on R^3 is real, and a is nonzero. A unit vector v is nonzero, so the equality theorem applies to the pair (a,v).

steps.text: By Cauchy-Schwarz, <a,v> <= |<a,v>| <= ||a|| ||v|| = 7 for every unit vector v.
The bound 7 is reached. For another maximizer v we need <a,v> = 7 = ||a|| ||v||. By the equality theorem, v = r a. The condition <a,v> = 7 gives r ||a||^2 = 7, so r = 1/7.
As a contrast, take v = (1,0,0). Then <a,v> = 2, which is far below 7, and v is not a multiple of a.

applications.conclusion: The maximum of <a,v> over unit vectors is 7. The only maximizer is v = a/7.

results.name: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for positive semidefinite Hermitian forms
results.statement: Let V be a vector space over K = R or K = C. Let B: V x V -> K be Hermitian (B(y,x) = conj B(x,y)), linear in the second argument, and positive semidefinite (B(x,x) >= 0 for all x). Then |B(x,y)|^2 <= B(x,x) B(y,y) for all x and y in V. If B(x,x) = 0, then B(x,y) = 0 for every y. The set N of vectors x with B(x,x) = 0 is a subspace, and q(x) = sqrt(B(x,x)) satisfies q(x+y) <= q(x) + q(y).
hypotheses: V is a vector space over R or C. B is linear in the second argument and conjugate-linear in the first.
B is Hermitian: B(y,x) = conj B(x,y). In particular B(x,x) is real.
B is positive semidefinite, not necessarily definite. B(x,x) = 0 is allowed for x != 0.
No dimension or completeness assumption is made.

definitions.name: radical of B
definitions.text: The radical of a positive semidefinite form B is the set N of vectors x with B(x,x) = 0. The theorem shows that B(x,y) = 0 for all y when x is in N.

steps.text: Expand for x, y in V and lambda in K: 0 <= B(x + lambda y, x + lambda y) = B(x,x) + lambda B(x,y) + conj(lambda) B(y,x) + |lambda|^2 B(y,y). Put beta = B(x,y). Then B(y,x) = conj(beta).

Assume beta != 0. For a real number t, choose lambda = -t conj(beta)/|beta|. Then lambda beta = -t |beta| and conj(lambda) conj(beta) = -t |beta|, and |lambda|^2 = t^2. The expansion gives 0 <= B(x,x) - 2 t |beta| + t^2 B(y,y) for every real t.

Case B(y,y) = 0. Then B(x,x) - 2 t |beta| >= 0 for all real t. Letting t grow gives a contradiction because |beta| > 0. So beta = 0. Hence B(y,y) = 0 implies B(x,y) = 0 for every x, and the inequality holds.

Case B(y,y) > 0. The quadratic in t is nonnegative for every real t. Take t = |beta|/B(y,y). It gives B(x,x) - |beta|^2/B(y,y) >= 0. So |beta|^2 <= B(x,x) B(y,y). If beta = 0, the inequality is clear.
Radical. If B(x,x) = 0, the inequality gives |B(x,y)|^2 <= 0, so B(x,y) = 0 for all y. Then for x, x' in N and a scalar a: B(x+x',x+x') = 0 and B(ax,ax) = |a|^2 B(x,x) = 0. So N is a subspace.
Triangle inequality. B(x+y,x+y) = B(x,x) + 2 Re B(x,y) + B(y,y). Now Re B(x,y) <= |B(x,y)| <= q(x) q(y). So B(x+y,x+y) <= (q(x) + q(y))^2, and taking square roots gives q(x+y) <= q(x) + q(y).

applications.title: A nondegenerate and a degenerate form on R^2
applications.inputs: Take V = R^2 and B(x,y) = x^T A y with A = [[4,2],[2,3]]. Take also B0(x,y) = x^T A0 y with A0 = [[1,1],[1,1]]. Use x = (1,1) and y = (1,-2).
applications.hypotheses: Both matrices are symmetric. B is positive definite because 4 > 0 and det A = 12 - 4 = 8 > 0. B0 is positive semidefinite because B0(x,x) = (x1+x2)^2 >= 0, and it is not definite.

steps.text: Compute A y with y = (1,-2). The first entry is 4*1 + 2*(-2).
The second entry of A y is 2*1 + 3*(-2).
Compute B(x,x) = x . (A x) with A x = (6,5).
Compare the two sides of the inequality: B(x,y)^2 = 16 and B(x,x) B(y,y) = 88.

The inequality 16 <= 88 holds. Now use the degenerate form B0 with u = (1,-1). Then B0(u,u) = (1-1)^2 = 0, so u is in the radical. The theorem predicts B0(u,w) = 0 for every w. For w = (3,5), A0 w = (8,8), and u . (8,8) is 8 - 8.

applications.conclusion: For the definite form the inequality holds with room to spare. For the degenerate form, the vector u = (1,-1) with B0(u,u) = 0 is orthogonal to every vector, as the theorem states.

results.name: Gram determinant criterion for linear independence
results.statement: Let E be an inner product space over K = R or K = C. Let v_1, ..., v_k be vectors in E. Let G be the k x k matrix with entries G_ij = <v_i,v_j>. Then G is Hermitian and positive semidefinite, and det G is a real number with det G >= 0. Moreover det G != 0 if and only if v_1, ..., v_k are linearly independent. In that case det G > 0.
hypotheses: E is an inner product space over R or C. The inner product is linear in the second argument and conjugate-linear in the first.
k is a positive integer. The vectors v_1, ..., v_k can be any vectors of E, repeated or dependent.
E can have any dimension. Only the span of the k vectors matters.

prerequisites.reason: The proof of det G >= 0 diagonalizes the Hermitian matrix G and reads det G as the product of its real eigenvalues.

definitions.name: Gram matrix
definitions.text: The Gram matrix of v_1, ..., v_k is the k x k matrix G with G_ij = <v_i,v_j>.

definitions.name: positive semidefinite matrix
definitions.text: A Hermitian k x k matrix G is positive semidefinite if x* G x >= 0 for all x in K^k. Here x* is the conjugate transpose of x.

steps.text: Hermitian. G_ji = <v_j,v_i> = conj <v_i,v_j> = conj G_ij. So G equals its conjugate transpose.
Key identity. For x in K^k put w_x = sum_j x_j v_j. Then (G x)_i = sum_j <v_i,v_j> x_j = <v_i, w_x>. Also x* G x = sum_i conj(x_i) <v_i, w_x> = <w_x, w_x> = ||w_x||^2. In particular x* G x >= 0.

Eigenvalues. By the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, G has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues, and det G is the product of these eigenvalues. If G x = lambda x with x != 0, then lambda ||x||^2 = x* G x >= 0. So lambda >= 0. Hence det G is real and det G >= 0.
Dependent case. Let v_1, ..., v_k be linearly dependent. Then there is x != 0 with w_x = 0. By the key identity, (G x)_i = <v_i, 0> = 0 for all i. So G x = 0, G is singular and det G = 0.
Independent case. Let G x = 0. Then x* G x = 0, so ||w_x||^2 = 0 and w_x = 0. Linear independence forces x = 0. So G is injective, therefore invertible, and det G != 0.

Combine the two cases: det G != 0 if and only if the vectors are independent. In the independent case, det G is a nonzero product of nonnegative eigenvalues, so every eigenvalue is positive and det G > 0.

applications.title: Gram determinants of three vectors in R^3
applications.inputs: Take E = R^3 with the dot product. Take v1 = (1,2,0), v2 = (0,1,1) and v3 = (1,3,1) = v1 + v2.
applications.hypotheses: The vectors are in R^3, so the real inner product applies. The pair (v1,v2) is independent. The triple (v1,v2,v3) is dependent because v3 = v1 + v2.

steps.text: The Gram matrix of (v1,v2) is [[5,2],[2,2]], since <v1,v1> = 5, <v1,v2> = 2 and <v2,v2> = 2. Its determinant is 5*2 - 2*2.
The determinant 6 is positive, as the criterion predicts for an independent pair. Check with the cross product v1 x v2 = (2,-1,1). Its squared length is the area of the parallelogram squared.
For the triple, the extra entries are <v1,v3> = 1+6+0 = 7, <v2,v3> = 0+3+1 = 4 and <v3,v3> = 1+9+1 = 11. The Gram matrix is [[5,2,7],[2,2,4],[7,4,11]].
Expand det G along the first row: 5*(2*11-4*4) - 2*(2*11-4*7) + 7*(2*4-2*7).

applications.conclusion: The Gram determinant of the independent pair is 6, which equals the squared area of their parallelogram. The Gram determinant of the dependent triple is 0, as the criterion states.

results.name: Orthogonal decomposition and double orthogonal complement
results.statement: Let E be an inner product space over K = R or K = C. Let W be a complete linear subspace of E. For example, W can be finite-dimensional, or W can be a closed subspace of a Hilbert space. Let W-perp be the set of vectors orthogonal to every vector of W. Then every x in E is x = w + u in exactly one way with w in W and u in W-perp. The map x -> w is linear, and ||x||^2 = ||w||^2 + ||u||^2. Also (W-perp)-perp = W. If E is finite-dimensional, then dim W + dim W-perp = dim E.
hypotheses: E is an inner product space over R or C. The inner product is linear in the second argument and conjugate-linear in the first.
W is a linear subspace that is complete in the norm of E. Every finite-dimensional subspace is complete. A closed subspace of a complete space is complete.
The dimension formula needs E finite-dimensional. The other claims need no dimension hypothesis.
For a subspace that is not complete (for example a dense proper subspace of a Hilbert space), the decomposition and the double complement formula can fail.

prerequisites.reason: The Hilbert projection theorem gives, for each x, a point w of W with x - w orthogonal to W. This is the existence step of the decomposition.
The identity of Bessel's inequality shows that x minus its expansion along an orthonormal basis of W is orthogonal to W, which gives an explicit w in the finite-dimensional case.
Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation gives an orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional W.

definitions.name: orthogonal complement
definitions.text: For a subset W of E, W-perp is the set of u in E with <w,u> = 0 for all w in W. It is a closed linear subspace.

    intro hv

      simpa [inner_add_right, hyz] using hv z hz
    simp [hy, hz']
  · intro hv w hw
    rw [inner_eq_zero_symm]
    exact hw v hv

source.alignment: The Lean statement is for a subspace with an orthogonal projection (HasOrthogonalProjection), which holds for complete subspaces. The authored statement adds the direct sum and the dimension formula, which Lean states separately as Submodule.isCompl_orthogonal.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Uniqueness and directness. If x lies in W and in W-perp, then <x,x> = 0, so x = 0. Hence W and W-perp meet only in 0. Then x = w + u = w' + u' gives w - w' = u' - u in both spaces, so w = w' and u = u'.

Existence. If W is finite-dimensional, Gram-Schmidt gives an orthonormal basis e_1, ..., e_m of W. Put w = sum_i <e_i,x> e_i. By the identity in Bessel's inequality, x - w is orthogonal to every e_j, hence to W. In the general complete case, the Hilbert projection theorem gives w in W with ||x - w|| minimal over W. Then x - w is orthogonal to W. To see this, take v in W with ||v|| = 1 and put t = <v, x - w>. Then w + t v lies in W, and ||x - w - t v||^2 = ||x - w||^2 - |t|^2. Minimality gives |t|^2 <= 0, so t = 0. Put u = x - w, which lies in W-perp.

Linearity and Pythagoras. For x, x' and scalars a, b, the vector (a w + b w') + (a u + b u') is a decomposition of a x + b x'. By uniqueness it is the decomposition. So x -> w is linear. Since <w,u> = 0, ||x||^2 = ||w||^2 + ||u||^2.
Double complement, first inclusion. Every w in W is orthogonal to every u in W-perp, because <u,w> = conj <w,u> = 0. So W is contained in (W-perp)-perp.

Double complement, second inclusion. Let x be in (W-perp)-perp. Write x = w + u. Then u = x - w lies in (W-perp)-perp, because w is in W and W is contained in (W-perp)-perp, and (W-perp)-perp is a subspace. Also u lies in W-perp. So <u,u> = 0 and u = 0. Hence x = w is in W.
Dimension. If E is finite-dimensional, the decomposition makes E the direct sum of W and W-perp. So dim E = dim W + dim W-perp.

applications.title: Decompose a vector of R^3 along a plane and its normal
applications.inputs: Take E = R^3 with the dot product. Take W = span{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)} and x = (2,0,1).
applications.hypotheses: W is finite-dimensional, so it is complete. The vector n = (1,-1,1) is a candidate spanning vector of W-perp.

steps.text: Check that n is orthogonal to the first basis vector of W.
Check that n is orthogonal to the second basis vector of W.
Since dim W = 2 and dim R^3 = 3, W-perp has dimension 1. So W-perp = span{n}.
The component of x along n is (<n,x>/<n,n>) n. First compute <n,x>.
Next compute <n,n>. The ratio is 3/3 = 1, so u = n = (1,-1,1) and w = x - u = (1,1,0), which lies in W.
Check Pythagoras: ||w||^2 + ||u||^2 = 2 + 3.
Compare with the squared length of x itself, ||x||^2 = 4+0+1.

applications.conclusion: The vector x = (2,0,1) splits as w + u with w = (1,1,0) in W and u = (1,-1,1) in W-perp. The squared lengths 2 and 3 add up to ||x||^2 = 5.

results.name: Kernel and range of an adjoint operator are orthogonal complements
aliases: fundamental theorem of linear algebra for adjoints
results.statement: Let E and F be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over K = R or K = C. Let T: E -> F be linear and let T* : F -> E be its adjoint, defined by <Tx,y> = <x,T*y>. Then ker T* = (ran T)-perp and ker T = (ran T*)-perp. Also ran T* = (ker T)-perp and ran T = (ker T*)-perp. Hence F = ran T + ker T* and E = ran T* + ker T are orthogonal direct sums, and rank T = rank T*.
hypotheses: E and F are inner product spaces over R or C, with inner products linear in the second argument.

E and F are finite-dimensional. The two identities ker T* = (ran T)-perp and ker T = (ran T*)-perp hold for bounded operators between Hilbert spaces without this hypothesis, but the identities for the ranges need closed ranges.
T* exists and is unique because E and F are finite-dimensional. Its matrix in orthonormal bases is the conjugate transpose of the matrix of T.

prerequisites.reason: The proof of ran T* = (ker T)-perp uses (W-perp)-perp = W and dim W + dim W-perp = dim E for subspaces W of a finite-dimensional space.

definitions.name: adjoint
definitions.text: The adjoint of T: E -> F is the unique linear map T*: F -> E with <Tx,y>_F = <x,T*y>_E for all x in E and y in F.

definitions.name: rank
definitions.text: The rank of T is dim ran T.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration is T.rangeᗮ = T†.ker for bounded operators between complete inner product spaces. The authored statement adds the three companion identities in the finite-dimensional case.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: First inclusion. Let y be in ker T*. For every x in E, <Tx,y> = <x,T*y> = <x,0> = 0. So y is orthogonal to every vector Tx of ran T. Hence ker T* is contained in (ran T)-perp.

Second inclusion. Let y be orthogonal to ran T. For every x in E, <x,T*y> = <Tx,y> = conj <y,Tx> = 0. Take x = T*y. Then <T*y,T*y> = 0, so T*y = 0. Hence (ran T)-perp is contained in ker T*. This proves ker T* = (ran T)-perp.
Double adjoint. For all x and y, <T*y,x> = conj <x,T*y> = conj <Tx,y> = <y,Tx>. So T is the adjoint of T*, that is T** = T. Apply the first identity to T* in place of T: ker T = (ran T*)-perp.
Ranges. In a finite-dimensional space, (W-perp)-perp = W for every subspace W. Take W = ran T*. Then (ker T)-perp = ((ran T*)-perp)-perp = ran T*. In the same way ran T = (ker T*)-perp.
Decompositions. A subspace and its orthogonal complement give an orthogonal direct sum of the whole space. So E = ran T* + ker T and F = ran T + ker T*, each sum being direct and orthogonal.

Rank. By rank-nullity, dim E = dim ker T + rank T. By the decomposition and the dimension formula, dim E = dim ker T + dim (ker T)-perp = dim ker T + dim ran T*. Comparing the two gives rank T = rank T*.

applications.title: The four subspaces of a rank-one 3 x 2 matrix
applications.inputs: Take E = R^2, F = R^3 and T given by the matrix A = [[1,2],[2,4],[3,6]]. Over the reals, T* has the matrix A^T = [[1,2,3],[2,4,6]].
applications.hypotheses: The spaces are finite-dimensional real inner product spaces with the dot product. In orthonormal bases the adjoint of A is the transpose A^T.

steps.text: The columns of A are (1,2,3) and (2,4,6) = 2*(1,2,3). So ran T = span{(1,2,3)} and rank T = 1.
The kernel of A^T is the set of y with y1 + 2 y2 + 3 y3 = 0, because the second row of A^T is twice the first. This is a plane, so dim ker T* = 2 = 3 - 1.
Check that two kernel vectors are orthogonal to the column space. First (2,-1,0) against (1,2,3).
Check the second kernel vector (3,0,-1) against (1,2,3). These two vectors are independent, so they span ker T* = (ran T)-perp.

The kernel of A is the set of x with x1 + 2 x2 = 0, so ker T = span{(2,-1)}. The range of A^T is spanned by the columns (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) of A^T, so ran T* = span{(1,2)}. Check (2,-1) against (1,2).
Rank count: dim ker T + rank T* = 1 + 1 = 2 = dim E, and rank T = rank T* = 1.

applications.conclusion: In this example ker T* = (ran T)-perp is a plane, ran T* = (ker T)-perp is a line, and rank T = rank T* = 1, as the theorem states.

results.name: Norm criterion and eigenvector properties of normal operators
results.statement: Let E be a finite-dimensional inner product space over K = R or K = C. Let T: E -> E be linear with adjoint T*. Then T*T = TT* if and only if ||Tx|| = ||T*x|| for all x in E. Suppose T is normal (T*T = TT*). Then ker T* = ker T = (ran T)-perp. If Tx = lambda x, then T*x = conj(lambda) x. If Tx = lambda x and Ty = mu y with lambda != mu, then <x,y> = 0.
hypotheses: E is a finite-dimensional inner product space over R or C. The inner product is linear in the second argument.
T is normal if T*T = TT*. Self-adjoint, skew-adjoint and unitary operators are normal. A normal operator need not be self-adjoint.
For the eigenvector statements, lambda and mu are scalars in K. Over R, conj(lambda) = lambda.

prerequisites.reason: The statement ker T* = (ran T)-perp is used to turn ker T* = ker T into ker T = (ran T)-perp.

definitions.name: normal operator
definitions.text: A linear operator T on an inner product space is normal if T*T = TT*.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration is the equivalence of normality with ||Tv|| = ||T*v|| for bounded operators on a Hilbert space. The authored statement adds the kernel and eigenvector consequences, which Lean states as separate lemmas.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Normal implies equal norms. For every x, ||Tx||^2 = <Tx,Tx> = <x,T*Tx> and ||T*x||^2 = <T*x,T*x> = <x,TT*x>. If T*T = TT*, the two right-hand sides are equal. So ||Tx|| = ||T*x||.

Equal norms imply normal. Put S = T*T - TT*. Then S is self-adjoint, and <Sx,x> = ||Tx||^2 - ||T*x||^2 = 0 for all x. Expand <S(x+y),x+y> - <S(x-y),x-y> = 2<Sx,y> + 2<Sy,x> = 2<Sx,y> + 2 conj <Sx,y>, using <Sy,x> = <y,Sx>. This is 4 Re <Sx,y>, and the left side is 0. So Re <Sx,y> = 0 for all x, y.
Take y = Sx in the last result. Then Re <Sx,Sx> = ||Sx||^2 = 0 for every x. So S = 0, and T*T = TT*.

Kernel. For normal T, ||Tx|| = ||T*x||, so Tx = 0 if and only if T*x = 0. Hence ker T = ker T*. By the orthogonality of kernel and range of the adjoint, ker T* = (ran T)-perp. So ker T = (ran T)-perp.

Eigenvectors. For a scalar lambda, (T - lambda I)* = T* - conj(lambda) I. Expanding both products shows that (T - lambda I) and its adjoint commute, because both products equal TT* - conj(lambda) T - lambda T* + |lambda|^2 I when T*T = TT*. So T - lambda I is normal. If Tx = lambda x, then ||(T* - conj(lambda)I)x|| = ||(T - lambda I)x|| = 0, hence T*x = conj(lambda) x.

Orthogonality. Let Tx = lambda x and Ty = mu y with lambda != mu. Then <x,Ty> = mu <x,y>. Also <x,Ty> = <T*x,y> = <conj(lambda) x,y> = lambda <x,y>, because the inner product is conjugate-linear in the first argument. So (mu - lambda) <x,y> = 0. Since mu != lambda, <x,y> = 0.

applications.title: A normal matrix that is not self-adjoint
applications.inputs: Take E = C^2 with <u,v> = conj(u1) v1 + conj(u2) v2. Take N = [[1,-1],[1,1]], x = (1,-i) and y = (1,i).
applications.hypotheses: N has real entries, so N* = N^T = [[1,1],[-1,1]]. N is not self-adjoint because N differs from N^T. N is normal, as the first step shows.

steps.text: Compute the (1,1) entry of N N^T. It is 1*1 + (-1)*(-1).
The (1,2) entry of N N^T is 1*1 + (-1)*1. By the same pattern the other products give N N^T = N^T N = 2I, so N is normal.
Compute N x = (1 + i, 1 - i). This equals (1+i) x, because (1+i)(-i) = -i + 1. So x is an eigenvector with lambda = 1 + i. In the same way N y = (1 - i) y.
Check the adjoint statement N* x = conj(lambda) x = (1 - i) x. Directly, N^T x = (1 - i, -1 - i), and (1 - i)(1,-i) = (1 - i, -i + i^2) = (1 - i, -1 - i). The two vectors agree.
Compute the norm test. ||N x||^2 = |1+i|^2 + |1-i|^2 and ||N* x||^2 = |1-i|^2 + |-1-i|^2. Each modulus squared is 2.
Check orthogonality of the eigenvectors with different eigenvalues. <x,y> = conj(1)*1 + conj(-i)*i = 1 + i*i.

applications.conclusion: The matrix N is normal but not self-adjoint. Its eigenvectors x and y for the different eigenvalues 1 + i and 1 - i are orthogonal, and N* acts on x by the conjugate eigenvalue 1 - i.

results.name: Characterization of orthogonal projections
aliases: idempotent self-adjoint operators are orthogonal projections
results.statement: Let E be a finite-dimensional inner product space over K = R or K = C. Let P: E -> E be linear with P^2 = P. Then the following are equivalent. (a) P* = P. (b) ker P is orthogonal to ran P. (c) ||Px|| <= ||x|| for all x in E. (d) x - Px is orthogonal to ran P for all x in E, that is P is the orthogonal projection onto ran P.
hypotheses: E is a finite-dimensional inner product space over R or C. The inner product is linear in the second argument.
P is idempotent: P(Px) = Px for all x. An idempotent operator need not be orthogonal. The oblique projection [[1,1],[0,0]] on R^2 is a counterexample.
The adjoint P* is the unique linear map with <Px,y> = <x,P*y>.

definitions.name: idempotent operator
definitions.text: A linear map P is idempotent if P^2 = P. Then Pw = w for every w in ran P, and E = ker P + ran P as a direct sum of subspaces.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: (a) implies (b). Let z be in ker P and let w = Pu be in ran P. Then <z,Pu> = <Pz,u> = <0,u> = 0, because P* = P. So ker P is orthogonal to ran P.
(b) implies (d). For any x, P(x - Px) = Px - P^2 x = 0. So x - Px lies in ker P, and by (b) it is orthogonal to ran P. This is (d).

(d) implies (a). Let x and y be in E. Then <Px,y> = <Px,Py> + <Px,y - Py> = <Px,Py>, because y - Py is orthogonal to ran P. In the same way <x,Py> = <Px,Py> + <x - Px,Py> = <Px,Py>. So <Px,y> = <x,Py> for all x and y, which means P* = P.
(d) implies (c). Write x = Px + (x - Px). The two terms are orthogonal, so ||x||^2 = ||Px||^2 + ||x - Px||^2 >= ||Px||^2.

(c) implies (b). Let z be in ker P and let w be in ran P, so Pw = w. For any scalar t, P(w + t z) = w. By (c), ||w|| <= ||w + t z||. Expanding, ||w||^2 <= ||w||^2 + 2 Re(t c) + |t|^2 ||z||^2 with c = <w,z>. So 2 Re(t c) + |t|^2 ||z||^2 >= 0 for all scalars t.

Take t = -s conj(c) with real s > 0. Then t c = -s |c|^2 and the inequality reads -2 s |c|^2 + s^2 |c|^2 ||z||^2 >= 0. Divide by s: -2 |c|^2 + s |c|^2 ||z||^2 >= 0. Let s tend to 0 from above to get |c|^2 <= 0. So <w,z> = 0, which is (b).
The implications (a) to (b) to (d) to (a) and (d) to (c) to (b) connect all four statements, so they are equivalent.

applications.title: A symmetric and an oblique projection on R^2 and R^3
applications.inputs: Take u = (1,2,2) in R^3 and P x = (<u,x>/9) u. Take also the oblique projection Q = [[1,1],[0,0]] on R^2.
applications.hypotheses: Both operators are idempotent. P is the matrix u u^T / 9, and <u,u> = 9, so P^2 = P. Q^2 = Q is shown in the steps.

steps.text: Check that <u,u> = 9. Then P(Px) = (<u,Px>/9) u = (<u,x>/9) u = Px.
The matrix u u^T / 9 is symmetric, so P* = P. By the theorem, P is an orthogonal projection. Test (c) with x = (3,0,0). The coefficient is <u,x>/9.
So Px = (1/3,2/3,2/3). Its squared length is below ||x||^2 = 9.

Now Q^2 = Q, because the (1,1) entry of Q^2 is 1*1 + 1*0 = 1 and the (1,2) entry is 1*1 + 1*0 = 1. Q is not symmetric. The theorem predicts that Q fails (c). Take x = (1,1). Then Qx = (2,0) and ||Qx||^2 exceeds ||x||^2.
The squared length of x = (1,1) is only 2, and 4 > 2, so (c) fails.
Check (b) for Q. The kernel of Q is span{(1,-1)} and the range is span{(1,0)}. Their inner product is nonzero, so ker Q is not orthogonal to ran Q.

applications.conclusion: The symmetric idempotent P is an orthogonal projection and never lengthens a vector. The oblique projection Q fails all of (a), (b) and (c), as the theorem predicts.

results.name: Normal equations of linear least squares
results.statement: Let A be an m x n matrix over K = R or K = C and let b be in K^m. Use the standard inner product on K^m and K^n. For x in K^n the following are equivalent. (a) ||Ax - b|| <= ||Ay - b|| for every y in K^n. (b) A*(Ax - b) = 0, that is A*A x = A*b. (c) Ax is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space ran A. The normal equations A*A x = A*b always have a solution. The solution is unique if and only if the columns of A are linearly independent. In that case A*A is invertible and x = (A*A)^(-1) A*b. For every solution, the minimum value satisfies ||b - Ax||^2 = ||b||^2 - ||Ax||^2.
hypotheses: A is an m x n matrix over R or C, and b is a vector of K^m. No relation between m and n is assumed.
A* is the conjugate transpose of A. Over R, A* = A^T.
The inner product on K^m is <u,v> = sum conj(u_i) v_i. The norm is the Euclidean norm.

prerequisites.reason: The existence of a solution uses the splitting b = w + u with w in ran A and u in (ran A)-perp.
The equivalence of b - Ax orthogonal to ran A and A*(b - Ax) = 0 is the identity ker A* = (ran A)-perp.

definitions.name: column space
definitions.text: The column space ran A is the set of all vectors Ay with y in K^n. It is a subspace of K^m.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration states that a point v of a subspace K minimizes the distance to u if and only if u - v is orthogonal to K. The authored statement applies it to K = ran A and rewrites orthogonality as the normal equations.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Set W = ran A and w = Ax. Then (a) says that w is a point of W nearest to b. Let r = b - w. First suppose r is orthogonal to W. For any z in W, b - z = r + (w - z) with w - z in W. So ||b - z||^2 = ||r||^2 + ||w - z||^2 >= ||r||^2. Hence w is nearest.

Conversely, let w be nearest and let z be in W and t a scalar. Then w + t z is in W, so ||r||^2 <= ||r - t z||^2 = ||r||^2 - 2 Re(t <r,z>) + |t|^2 ||z||^2. Take t = s conj(<r,z>) with real s > 0. This gives 0 <= -2 s |<r,z>|^2 + s^2 |<r,z>|^2 ||z||^2, then let s tend to 0. So <r,z> = 0. Hence (a) is equivalent to r orthogonal to W, which is (c).

Orthogonality is the normal equation. The vector r is orthogonal to ran A if and only if <Ay,r> = <y,A*r> = 0 for every y in K^n. Take y = A*r to see that this holds if and only if A*r = 0. So (c) is equivalent to A*(b - Ax) = 0, which is (b).
Existence. By the orthogonal decomposition, b = w + u with w in ran A and u in (ran A)-perp. Choose x with Ax = w. Then b - Ax = u is orthogonal to ran A, so x satisfies the normal equations.

Uniqueness. Let x and x' both solve the normal equations and put d = x - x'. Then A*A d = 0, so ||Ad||^2 = <Ad,Ad> = <d,A*A d> = 0 and Ad = 0. So d = 0 whenever A is injective. Conversely, if Ad = 0 with d != 0, then x + d is another solution. Hence the solution is unique if and only if the columns of A are independent.

Invertibility and value. If A is injective, A*A is injective by the same computation, and A*A is a square matrix, so it is invertible and x = (A*A)^(-1) A*b. Finally b = Ax + r with Ax in ran A and r orthogonal to ran A, so ||b||^2 = ||Ax||^2 + ||r||^2.

applications.title: Least-squares line through three points
applications.inputs: Fit y = c0 + c1 t to the data (t,y) = (0,1), (1,2), (2,2). The matrix is A = [[1,0],[1,1],[1,2]] and b = (1,2,2). Work over R.
applications.hypotheses: The columns (1,1,1) and (0,1,2) of A are linearly independent. So the normal equations have exactly one solution.

steps.text: Compute A^T A. Its entries are 3 = 1+1+1, 3 = 0+1+2 and 5 = 0+1+4, so A^T A = [[3,3],[3,5]]. Its determinant is 3*5 - 3*3.
Compute A^T b = (1+2+2, 0*1+1*2+2*2) = (5,6). The second entry is shown here.
Solve with the inverse (1/6) [[5,-3],[-3,3]]. The first coefficient is (5*5 - 3*6)/6.
The second coefficient is (-3*5 + 3*6)/6.
So A x = (7/6, 5/3, 13/6) and the residual is r = b - Ax = (-1/6, 1/3, -1/6). Check that r is orthogonal to the column (0,1,2) of A.

applications.conclusion: The least-squares line is y = 7/6 + t/2. The residual is orthogonal to both columns of A, and the minimum squared error is 1/6.

results.name: Existence and properties of the adjoint of a bounded operator
results.statement: Let H and K be Hilbert spaces over K0 = R or C. Let T: H -> K be a bounded linear operator. Then there is exactly one map T*: K -> H with <Tx,y> = <x,T*y> for all x in H and y in K. This T* is linear and bounded, and ||T*|| = ||T||. Also T** = T, (ST)* = T*S*, and (aT + S)* = conj(a) T* + S* for bounded S and scalars a. If H and K are finite-dimensional with orthonormal bases, the matrix of T* is the conjugate transpose of the matrix of T.
hypotheses: H and K are complete inner product spaces over R or C. Completeness is needed for the Riesz representation theorem. The inner product is linear in the second argument.
T is bounded: there is C >= 0 with ||Tx|| <= C ||x|| for all x. The operator norm ||T|| is the least such C.
In the composition rule (ST)* = T*S*, S is a bounded operator from K to a third Hilbert space.

prerequisites.reason: The Riesz representation theorem produces the vector T*y that represents the bounded functional x -> <y,Tx>.

definitions.name: bounded operator norm
definitions.text: For bounded T, ||T|| = sup of ||Tx|| over ||x|| <= 1.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration states the defining identity <(T†) y, x> = <y, T x> for the adjoint T† built from the Riesz isomorphism. The authored statement adds uniqueness, boundedness, the norm equality and the algebraic rules.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Existence. Fix y in K. The map f(x) = <y,Tx> is linear in x, and |f(x)| <= ||y|| ||Tx|| <= ||y|| ||T|| ||x|| by Cauchy-Schwarz. So f is a bounded linear functional on H. By the Riesz representation theorem there is a unique vector z = T*y in H with <z,x> = <y,Tx> for all x.

Then <Tx,y> = conj <y,Tx> = conj <T*y,x> = <x,T*y>, so T* satisfies the defining identity. Uniqueness. If B also satisfies it, then <x,(T* - B)y> = 0 for all x. Take x = (T* - B)y to get (T* - B)y = 0.

Linearity. For y, y' in K and scalars a, b: <Tx,ay + by'> = a<Tx,y> + b<Tx,y'> = <x,aT*y + bT*y'>. So aT*y + bT*y' also satisfies the identity for a y + b y'. By uniqueness, T*(ay + by') = aT*y + bT*y'.

Boundedness. For y in K, ||T*y||^2 = <T*y,T*y> = <TT*y,y> <= ||TT*y|| ||y|| <= ||T|| ||T*y|| ||y||. If T*y != 0, divide by ||T*y|| to get ||T*y|| <= ||T|| ||y||. This also holds if T*y = 0. So T* is bounded and ||T*|| <= ||T||.

Double adjoint and norm. For all x and y, <T*y,x> = conj <x,T*y> = conj <Tx,y> = <y,Tx>. So T is the adjoint of T*. By uniqueness, T** = T. Apply the bound of the last step to T*: ||T|| = ||T**|| <= ||T*||. Hence ||T*|| = ||T||.

Algebra. For bounded S from K to L, <STx,w> = <Tx,S*w> = <x,T*S*w>, so (ST)* = T*S*. For scalars, <aTx,y> = conj(a)<Tx,y> = <x,conj(a)T*y>, so the adjoint of aT is conj(a)T*. For sums, <(T+S)x,y> = <x,(T*+S*)y>. Uniqueness gives (aT + S)* = conj(a)T* + S*.

Matrices. Let (e_i) and (f_j) be orthonormal bases. The entry of T is T_ji = <f_j,Te_i>. The entry of T* is (T*)_ij = <e_i,T*f_j> = <Te_i,f_j> = conj <f_j,Te_i> = conj(T_ji). This is the conjugate transpose.

applications.title: The adjoint of a 3 x 2 real matrix
applications.inputs: Take H = R^2, K = R^3 and T given by the matrix [[1,2],[0,3],[4,0]]. Take x = (1,-1) and y = (2,1,3).
applications.hypotheses: Finite-dimensional real inner product spaces are complete. The standard bases are orthonormal, so T* has the matrix T^T = [[1,0,4],[2,3,0]].

steps.text: Compute T^T y. Its first entry is 1*2 + 0*1 + 4*3 and its second entry is 2*2 + 3*1 + 0*3.
The second entry of T^T y is 2*2 + 3*1 + 0*3.
Compute <x,T*y> = 1*14 + (-1)*7. It equals <Tx,y> = 7, as the defining identity requires.
Norm check. The operator norm of T is at least ||Te1|| for the unit vector e1 = (1,0), and ||Te1||^2 = 1 + 0 + 16 = 17. By ||T*|| = ||T||, the same lower bound holds for T*.

applications.conclusion: The transpose T^T satisfies <Tx,y> = <x,T^T y> for the test vectors, so it is the adjoint of T. The identity cannot hold with any other matrix, by uniqueness.

results.name: C*-identity for bounded Hilbert space operators
results.statement: Let H and K be Hilbert spaces over K0 = R or C and let T: H -> K be a bounded linear operator with adjoint T*. Then ||T*T|| = ||T||^2. Consequently ||TT*|| = ||T||^2 = ||T*||^2.
hypotheses: H and K are complete inner product spaces over R or C. T is bounded, so T* exists and ||T*|| = ||T||.
The norm is the operator norm: ||T|| = sup of ||Tx|| over ||x|| <= 1. It is not the Hilbert-Schmidt norm.
The identity fails for the operator norm on Banach spaces without an inner product, and fails for the Frobenius norm of a matrix.

prerequisites.reason: The upper bound uses ||T*|| = ||T||, and the second claim uses T** = T.
The lower bound uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality |<x,T*Tx>| <= ||x|| ||T*Tx||.

definitions.name: operator norm
definitions.text: For a bounded operator S, ||S|| is the least C >= 0 with ||Sx|| <= C ||x|| for all x. It satisfies ||SR|| <= ||S|| ||R||.

steps.text: Upper bound. The operator norm is submultiplicative, so ||T*T|| <= ||T*|| ||T||. By the adjoint theorem, ||T*|| = ||T||. So ||T*T|| <= ||T||^2.
Lower bound, first step. Let x be in H. Then ||Tx||^2 = <Tx,Tx> = <x,T*Tx>, by the definition of the adjoint.

Lower bound, second step. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, <x,T*Tx> <= |<x,T*Tx>| <= ||x|| ||T*Tx||. By the definition of the operator norm, ||T*Tx|| <= ||T*T|| ||x||. Together, ||Tx||^2 <= ||T*T|| ||x||^2 for every x.
Lower bound, conclusion. For ||x|| <= 1 this gives ||Tx||^2 <= ||T*T||. Take the supremum over x. Then ||T||^2 <= ||T*T||. With the upper bound, ||T*T|| = ||T||^2.
Second identity. Apply the first identity to the operator T* from K to H. Since T** = T, it gives ||TT*|| = ||T**T*|| = ||T*||^2. By ||T*|| = ||T||, this equals ||T||^2.

applications.title: Check the identity for a rank-one matrix
applications.inputs: Take H = K = R^2 with the dot product and T = [[1,1],[0,0]]. Then T* = T^T = [[1,0],[1,0]].
applications.hypotheses: R^2 is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. The matrix T is a bounded operator, and its adjoint is the transpose.

steps.text: Compute T^T T. Its (1,1) entry is 1*1 + 0*0 and its (1,2) entry is 1*1 + 0*0. The (2,2) entry is 1*1 + 0*0. So T^T T = [[1,1],[1,1]].

The matrix [[1,1],[1,1]] maps (1,1) to (2,2), so 2 is an eigenvalue. Its trace is 2, so the other eigenvalue is 0. For a symmetric matrix the operator norm is the largest absolute eigenvalue. So ||T^T T|| = 2.
Now compute ||T||^2 directly. For x = (x1,x2), ||Tx||^2 = (x1+x2)^2 <= 2(x1^2 + x2^2) by Cauchy-Schwarz. Equality holds for x = (1,1).
So ||T||^2 = 2. Compute T T^T. Its (1,1) entry is 1*1 + 1*1, and the other entries are 0. So T T^T = [[2,0],[0,0]], whose norm is 2.

applications.conclusion: The numbers ||T^T T||, ||T T^T|| and ||T||^2 all equal 2, as the C*-identity states.

results.statement: Let E be an inner product space over K = R or K = C. Let T: E -> E be a bounded linear operator that is symmetric: <Tx,y> = <x,Ty> for all x, y in E. Then <Tx,x> is real for every x, and ||T|| = sup over x != 0 of |<Tx,x>|/||x||^2.
hypotheses: E is an inner product space over R or C. The inner product is linear in the second argument. E need not be complete.
T is bounded and symmetric. Symmetry is essential. A rotation of R^2 by 90 degrees has <Jx,x> = 0 for all x and norm 1.
The supremum is over nonzero x. If E = {0}, both sides are 0.

prerequisites.reason: The easy inequality |<Tx,x>| <= ||Tx|| ||x|| <= ||T|| ||x||^2 is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
The hard inequality uses the parallelogram identity ||x+y||^2 + ||x-y||^2 = 2||x||^2 + 2||y||^2.

definitions.name: numerical radius
definitions.text: For a bounded operator T, the numerical radius is the supremum of |<Tx,x>| over unit vectors x. For a symmetric T the quantity <Tx,x>/||x||^2 is the Rayleigh quotient.

theorem norm_eq_iSup_rayleighQuotient (hT : T.IsSymmetric) :
    ‖T‖ = ⨆ x, |T.rayleighQuotient x| := by
  set M := ⨆ x, |T.rayleighQuotient x|
  have nonneg : 0 ≤ M := le_ciSup_of_le T.bddAbove_rayleighQuotient 0 (abs_nonneg _)
  have hM x : |re ⟪T x, x⟫| ≤ M * ‖x‖ ^ 2 := by
    have hM : |T.rayleighQuotient x| ≤ M := le_ciSup T.bddAbove_rayleighQuotient x
    by_cases hx : 0 < ‖x‖ ^ 2
    · rwa [rayleighQuotient, abs_div, abs_sq, reApplyInnerSelf, div_le_iff₀ hx] at hM
    · simp_all
  refine le_antisymm ?_ (ciSup_le T.rayleighQuotient_le_norm)
  refine opNorm_le_of_re_inner_le nonneg fun x y hx hy ↦ ?_
  transitivity M * (‖x + y‖ ^ 2 + ‖x - y‖ ^ 2) / 4
  · have key := congrArg re (add_conj ⟪T x, y⟫)
    rw [map_add, conj_inner_symm, ← coe_coe, ← hT, coe_coe, re_mul_ofReal, ofNat_re] at key
    grind [inner_add_left, inner_add_right, inner_sub_left, inner_sub_right]

source.alignment: The Lean statement is the equality ||T|| = sup_x |rayleighQuotient T x| for a symmetric T, where the Rayleigh quotient is Re<Tx,x>/||x||^2. For symmetric T, <Tx,x> is real, so the real part is not needed in the authored statement.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Real values. For symmetric T, <Tx,x> = <x,Tx> = conj <Tx,x>. So <Tx,x> is real. Put M = sup over x != 0 of |<Tx,x>|/||x||^2.
Easy inequality. By Cauchy-Schwarz and boundedness, |<Tx,x>| <= ||Tx|| ||x|| <= ||T|| ||x||^2. So M <= ||T||.
Polarization. For all x, y, expand <T(x+y),x+y> - <T(x-y),x-y> = 2<Tx,y> + 2<Ty,x>. By symmetry, <Ty,x> = <y,Tx> = conj <Tx,y>. So the difference equals 4 Re <Tx,y>.

Bound the difference. By the definition of M, |<Tz,z>| <= M ||z||^2 for all z. So 4 |Re <Tx,y>| <= M (||x+y||^2 + ||x-y||^2). The parallelogram identity turns the right side into 2M(||x||^2 + ||y||^2).
Choice of y. Let ||x|| = 1 and Tx != 0. Put y = Tx/||Tx||, which has norm 1. Then Re <Tx,y> = ||Tx||^2/||Tx|| = ||Tx||. The last step gives 4 ||Tx|| <= 2M(1 + 1) = 4M.
Conclusion. So ||Tx|| <= M for every unit vector x, which is trivial if Tx = 0. Hence ||T|| <= M. With the easy inequality, ||T|| = M.

applications.title: Norm of a symmetric matrix and a rotation
applications.inputs: Take E = R^2 with the dot product. Take A = [[2,1],[1,2]] and the rotation J = [[0,-1],[1,0]].
applications.hypotheses: The matrix A is symmetric, so the theorem applies. The matrix J is not symmetric, so the theorem does not apply to it.

steps.text: For A, the quadratic form is <Ax,x> = 2 x1^2 + 2 x1 x2 + 2 x2^2. At x = (1,1) it equals 2+1+1+2, and ||x||^2 = 2.
So the Rayleigh quotient at x = (1,1) is 6/2. This is a lower bound for the norm.
On a unit vector x = (cos t, sin t), the form is 2 + 2 cos t sin t = 2 + sin 2t, which is at most 3. So the supremum M equals 3.

Check the norm directly. A(1,1) = (3,3) = 3(1,1), so ||A|| >= 3. The theorem gives ||A|| = M = 3, with no further computation. The other eigenvector (1,-1) gives the form value 2 and the quotient 2/2 = 1, which is below 3.
For the rotation J, <Jx,x> = -x1 x2 + x2 x1 = 0 for all x, so the supremum of the quotient is 0. But J(1,0) = (0,1) has norm 1, so ||J|| = 1. The theorem fails for J because J is not symmetric.

applications.conclusion: For the symmetric matrix A, the norm equals the supremum 3 of its Rayleigh quotient. For the non-symmetric rotation J, the supremum is 0 while the norm is 1, so the symmetry hypothesis is needed.

source.alignment: The Lean statement is the equivalence of (a) and (d). The authored statement adds (b) and (c).

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check

steps.text: (c) implies (a). If M = B*B, then M* = B*B** = B*B = M, so M is Hermitian. For every x, x*Mx = (Bx)*(Bx) = ||Bx||^2 >= 0.
(a) implies (b). Let Mx = lambda x with x != 0. Then x*Mx = lambda x*x = lambda ||x||^2. The left side is >= 0 and ||x||^2 > 0, so lambda >= 0. The eigenvalue lambda is real because M is Hermitian.

(b) implies (c). By the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, there is an orthonormal basis u_1, ..., u_n of K^n with M u_i = lambda_i u_i, and all lambda_i >= 0. Let U be the matrix with columns u_i and D = diag(lambda_i). Then M = U D U*, because U*U = I.
Put B = D^(1/2) U*, where D^(1/2) = diag(sqrt(lambda_i)) is well defined since lambda_i >= 0. Then B*B = U D^(1/2) D^(1/2) U* = U D U* = M. This is (c) with B square.

(c) is equivalent to (d). Let b_1, ..., b_m be the rows of B, and put v_i = b_i*. The matrix product B*B is the sum over the rows of b_i* b_i = v_i v_i*. So B*B = sum v_i v_i*. Conversely, given such v_i, let B be the matrix with rows v_i*.
The chain (c) to (a) to (b) to (c) shows that (a), (b) and (c) are equivalent. With the last step, (d) is equivalent too.

applications.title: Factor and test two symmetric 2 x 2 matrices
applications.hypotheses: A and C are symmetric. For A we exhibit B with B^T B = A. For C we exhibit a vector with a negative quadratic form.

steps.text: Compute B^T B. Its (1,1) entry is 1*1 + 1*1 and its (1,2) entry is 1*2 + 1*1.
The (1,2) entry of B^T B is 1*2 + 1*1.
The (2,2) entry of B^T B is 2*2 + 1*1. So B^T B = [[2,3],[3,5]] = A, and A is positive semidefinite by (c).
Check with (b). The trace of A is 7 and its determinant is 2*5 - 3*3 = 1. Both eigenvalues are real with sum 7 and product 1, so both are positive.

Check the form (d). The rows of B are (1,2) and (1,1). The sum of the outer products v v^T has (1,2) entry 1*2 + 1*1, and it equals A. Test the form at x = (1,-1): x^T A x = ||Bx||^2 with Bx = (-1,0).

Now C. Its determinant is 1*1 - 2*2 = -3 < 0, so the eigenvalues have opposite signs. At x = (1,-1), x^T C x = 1 - 2 - 2 + 1 is negative, so C is not positive semidefinite and has no factorization B^T B.

applications.conclusion: The matrix A = B^T B with B = [[1,2],[1,1]] is positive semidefinite, and its eigenvalues are positive. The matrix C has x^T C x = -2 < 0 at x = (1,-1), so no real matrix B gives C = B^T B.

aliases: isometries of finite-dimensional inner product spaces
results.statement: Let E be a finite-dimensional inner product space over K = R or K = C. Let U: E -> E be linear. The following are equivalent. (a) U*U = I. (b) <Ux,Uy> = <x,y> for all x, y. (c) ||Ux|| = ||x|| for all x. (d) U maps some orthonormal basis of E to an orthonormal basis. (e) U is invertible and U^(-1) = U*, that is U*U = UU* = I. The operators with these properties are the unitary operators for K = C and the orthogonal operators for K = R.
hypotheses: E is a finite-dimensional inner product space over R or C. The inner product is linear in the second argument.
U maps E to itself. In infinite dimensions, (a) to (c) are equivalent for operators between Hilbert spaces, but an isometry need not be invertible, as the shift on l^2 shows.
U* is the adjoint of U. In an orthonormal basis, U* is the conjugate transpose of U.

prerequisites.reason: The step from (c) to (b) recovers the inner product from norms by the polarization identity.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration is the equivalence of (a) and (b) for bounded operators between Hilbert spaces. The Lean lemma norm_map_iff_adjoint_comp_self gives (c). The authored statement adds (d) and (e) in finite dimension.

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: (a) implies (b). <Ux,Uy> = <x,U*Uy> = <x,y>, by the definition of the adjoint and U*U = I.
(b) implies (a). For all x, y: <x,(U*U - I)y> = <Ux,Uy> - <x,y> = 0. Take x = (U*U - I)y to get (U*U - I)y = 0 for every y. So U*U = I.

(b) implies (c) by taking y = x. (c) implies (b): the polarization identity expresses <x,y> through the norms of x + c y, with c running over the fourth roots of unity (c = ±1 for K = R). Since U is linear, ||U(x + cy)|| = ||x + cy||, so <Ux,Uy> = <x,y>.

(a) implies (e). If Ux = 0, then x = U*Ux = 0. So U is injective. In finite dimension an injective endomorphism is bijective by rank-nullity. Then U* = U*(UU^(-1)) = (U*U)U^(-1) = U^(-1), so UU* = I too. The converse (e) to (a) is clear.
(b) implies (d). Let (e_i) be any orthonormal basis. Then <Ue_i,Ue_j> = <e_i,e_j> = delta_ij. So (Ue_i) is orthonormal. It has n = dim E elements, so it is a basis.

(d) implies (b). Let (e_i) and (Ue_i) both be orthonormal bases. For x = sum x_i e_i and y = sum y_j e_j, sesquilinearity gives <Ux,Uy> = sum_{i,j} conj(x_i) y_j <Ue_i,Ue_j> = sum_i conj(x_i) y_i = <x,y>.

applications.title: A rotation matrix with rational entries
applications.inputs: Take E = R^2 with the dot product and R = [[3/5,-4/5],[4/5,3/5]]. Take x = (5,12).
applications.hypotheses: E is a finite-dimensional real inner product space, and R is a linear map. The adjoint of R in the standard basis is R^T.

steps.text: The first column of R has squared length (3/5)^2 + (4/5)^2.
The inner product of the two columns (3/5,4/5) and (-4/5,3/5) is the (1,2) entry of R^T R.
The second column has squared length (-4/5)^2 + (3/5)^2 = 1 in the same way. So R^T R = I, and by (a) and (e) R is orthogonal with R^(-1) = R^T.
Test (c) with x = (5,12). First entry of Rx is 3/5*5 - 4/5*12.
The second entry of Rx is 4/5*5 + 3/5*12.
The squared length of Rx is (-33/5)^2 + (56/5)^2.
The squared length of x is 5^2 + 12^2, which is also 169. So ||Rx|| = ||x|| = 13.

applications.conclusion: The matrix R has orthonormal columns, so R^T R = I and R preserves lengths. Here ||Rx|| = ||x|| = 13 for x = (5,12).

results.name: Monotone convergence theorem for bounded real sequences
results.statement: Let (x_n) be a sequence of real numbers. If (x_n) is non-decreasing and bounded above, then (x_n) converges, and its limit is sup_n x_n. If (x_n) is non-increasing and bounded below, then (x_n) converges, and its limit is inf_n x_n.
hypotheses: x_n is a real number for every natural number n >= 1.
Case 1: x_n <= x_{n+1} for every n, and there is a real number B with x_n <= B for every n.
Case 2: x_{n+1} <= x_n for every n, and there is a real number A with A <= x_n for every n.
The real numbers are complete: every non-empty set of reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

definitions.name: limit of a sequence
definitions.text: x_n -> L means: for every e > 0 there is N such that |x_n - L| < e for every n >= N.

definitions.name: supremum
definitions.text: sup S is the least upper bound of a non-empty set S that is bounded above. It is an upper bound of S, and no smaller real number is an upper bound of S.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration is for a monotone family in a conditionally complete order with the sup-convergence property. The authored statement is the case of the real numbers. Case 2 follows from Case 1 and is not a separate Lean declaration here.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Case 1. The set S = {x_n : n >= 1} is non-empty and bounded above by B. By the least upper bound property, L = sup S exists. Since L is an upper bound of S, x_n <= L for every n.
Let e > 0. The number L - e is smaller than L, so it is not an upper bound of S. Hence there is an index N with x_N > L - e.
Let n >= N. The sequence is non-decreasing, so x_n >= x_N > L - e. Also x_n <= L. Hence L - e < x_n <= L, so |x_n - L| < e for every n >= N.
Because e > 0 was arbitrary, x_n -> L = sup S. This proves Case 1.

Case 2. Put y_n = -x_n. Then (y_n) is non-decreasing and bounded above by -A. By Case 1, y_n -> sup y_n. Also sup_n y_n = -inf_n x_n, because a number is a lower bound of the x_n if and only if its negative is an upper bound of the y_n.
Hence x_n = -y_n -> -sup y_n = inf x_n, since the limit of a negated sequence is the negated limit. This proves Case 2.

applications.title: Newton iteration for the square root of 2 converges to a positive root
applications.inputs: Put x_1 = 2 and x_{n+1} = (x_n + 2/x_n)/2 for n >= 1. The first terms are 2, 3/2, 17/12, 577/408.
applications.hypotheses: Every x_n is positive and x_n^2 >= 2, shown by induction below. This gives a non-increasing sequence that is bounded below by 0, so Case 2 applies.

steps.text: For x_n > 0: x_{n+1}^2 - 2 = (x_n - 2/x_n)^2 / 4 >= 0, and x_{n+1} > 0. Also x_1^2 = 4 >= 2. So x_n > 0 and x_n^2 >= 2 for every n.
x_n^2 >= 2 gives 2/x_n <= x_n, so x_{n+1} = (x_n + 2/x_n)/2 <= x_n. The sequence is non-increasing and bounded below by 0. By Case 2, it converges to some L >= 0.
The second term is x_2 = (2 + 2/2)/2.
The third term is x_3 = (3/2 + 2/(3/2))/2.
The fourth term is x_4 = (17/12 + 2/(17/12))/2.
The error of x_4^2 against 2 is already below 10^-5, as the exact value shows.
Since x_n^2 >= 2, the limit satisfies L^2 >= 2, so L > 0. Pass to the limit in the recursion: L = (L + 2/L)/2. This gives L^2 = 2, so L = sqrt(2).

applications.conclusion: The monotone bounded sequence of Newton iterates converges, and its limit is the positive solution of L^2 = 2, which is sqrt(2). The existence of the limit comes from the theorem, not from a formula for x_n.

steps.text: Let L = inf_{n>=1} u(n)/n. It is a real number because the set is non-empty and bounded below by A. By definition, u(n)/n >= L for every n >= 1.
Fix e > 0. By the definition of the infimum, there is k >= 1 with u(k)/k < L + e.
Claim: u(qk + r) <= q u(k) + u(r) for all q, r >= 0. For q = 0 this is an equality. If it holds for q, then subadditivity gives u((q+1)k + r) <= u(k) + u(qk + r) <= (q+1) u(k) + u(r).
Let B = max{|u(r)| : 0 <= r < k}, a finite maximum. Write n = qk + r with 0 <= r < k. Then u(n) <= q u(k) + B. Divide by n and use qk = n - r: u(n)/n <= (u(k)/k)(1 - r/n) + B/n.

Since 0 <= r < k, the term (u(k)/k)(r/n) has absolute value at most |u(k)/k| k/n, and B/n is at most B/n. Both bounds tend to 0 as n -> infinity. So there is N1 such that u(n)/n < u(k)/k + e < L + 2e for every n >= N1.
Together with u(n)/n >= L, we get L <= u(n)/n < L + 2e for every n >= N1. Since e is arbitrary, u(n)/n -> L.

steps.text: Let S = sum a_n. It exists because sum |a_n| converges.
Let e > 0. Choose N such that sum_{n>N} |a_n| < e. Then |S - S_N| <= sum_{n>N} |a_n| < e, where S_N = a_0 + ... + a_N.
Since sigma is a bijection, the numbers sigma^{-1}(0), ..., sigma^{-1}(N) are N+1 natural numbers. Let M be their maximum. Then {0, ..., N} is contained in sigma({0, ..., m}) for every m >= M.

Let m >= M and T_m = a_{sigma(0)} + ... + a_{sigma(m)}. The index set sigma({0..m}) has m+1 distinct elements and contains {0..N}. So T_m - S_N is the sum of a_j over the distinct indices j in sigma({0..m}) with j > N.
A finite sum over distinct indices j > N is bounded in absolute value by sum_{j>N} |a_j| < e. So |T_m - S_N| < e for every m >= M.
Hence |T_m - S| <= |T_m - S_N| + |S_N - S| < 2e for every m >= M. As e is arbitrary, T_m -> S, so sum a_{sigma(n)} = S.
The same argument applied to |a_n| (which has the same absolute values) shows that sum |a_{sigma(n)}| converges to sum |a_n|. So the rearranged series converges absolutely.

steps.text: Fix x in X. Since 0 <= |f_n(x)| <= M_n and sum M_n converges, the comparison test shows that sum |f_n(x)| converges.
Absolute convergence implies convergence in R, so F(x) = sum f_n(x) is a well-defined real number.
For N >= 0, F(x) - sum_{n<N} f_n(x) = sum_{n>=N} f_n(x), the tail of a convergent series.
By the triangle inequality for finite sums and passage to the limit, |sum_{n>=N} f_n(x)| <= sum_{n>=N} |f_n(x)| <= sum_{n>=N} M_n =: R_N.
The number R_N does not depend on x. Hence sup_{x in X} |F(x) - sum_{n<N} f_n(x)| <= R_N.
R_N = sum_n M_n - sum_{n<N} M_n tends to 0, because the partial sums of a convergent series tend to its sum. So the partial sums converge to F uniformly on X.

steps.text: Compute the ratio of consecutive terms: s_n / s_{n+1} = ((n+1)/n)^(n+1/2) / e. So b_n := log(s_n) - log(s_{n+1}) = (n + 1/2) log(1 + 1/n) - 1.

The series log((1+x)/(1-x)) = 2 sum_{k>=0} x^(2k+1)/(2k+1) holds for |x| < 1. It comes from integrating 1/(1-t^2) = sum t^(2k) termwise on [0, x], and 1/(1-t^2) = (1/2)(1/(1-t) + 1/(1+t)). Hence b_n = sum_{k>=1} x^(2k)/(2k+1).
All terms are positive, so b_n > 0. For k >= 1, x^(2k)/(2k+1) <= x^(2k)/3, with strict inequality for k >= 2. So b_n < (1/3) sum_{k>=1} x^(2k) = (1/3) x^2/(1-x^2).

From b_n > 0, (s_n) is strictly decreasing. Summing b_n over n, m-1 gives 0 < log s_n - log s_m < (1/12)(1/n - 1/m) for m > n. In particular log s_m > log s_1 - 1/12 = 11/12 - (1/2) log 2 > 11/12 - 1/2 > 0, because log 2 < 1.

The sequence (s_n) is decreasing and bounded below by e^(5/12) > 0. By the monotone convergence theorem, s_n -> a, with log a >= log s_1 - 1/12 > 0, so a > 0. Also a < s_n for every n, because s_n > s_{n+1} >= a.

Upper bound: let m -> infinity in the bound of step 6 for log s_{n+1}: log s_{n+1} - log a <= 1/(12(n+1)). Add b_n < 1/(12 n (n+1)). Since 1/(12 n (n+1)) + 1/(12 (n+1)) = 1/(12 n), we get log s_n - log a < 1/(12 n).

steps.text: Let n >= 2 and h = n^(1/n) - 1. Since n > 1, n^(1/n) > 1, because b <= 1 would give b^n <= 1 < n. So h > 0.
By definition (1+h)^n = n. The binomial theorem gives (1+h)^n = sum_{k=0}^n C(n,k) h^k. All terms are positive, so (1+h)^n >= C(n,2) h^2.
Hence n >= C(n,2) h^2 = n(n-1)/2 * h^2. Divide by n(n-1)/2 > 0 to get h^2 <= 2/(n-1).

As n -> infinity, sqrt(2/(n-1)) -> 0, because 2/(n-1) -> 0 and the square root is continuous at 0. By the squeeze theorem, h -> 0, so n^(1/n) -> 1.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Define h(x) = (g(b) - g(a)) f(x) - (f(b) - f(a)) g(x). The function h is a linear combination of f and g with constant coefficients. So h is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with h'(x) = (g(b) - g(a)) f'(x) - (f(b) - f(a)) g'(x).
Compute h(a). It equals (g(b) - g(a)) f(a) - (f(b) - f(a)) g(a) = g(b) f(a) - g(a) f(a) - f(b) g(a) + f(a) g(a) = g(b) f(a) - f(b) g(a).
Compute h(b). It equals (g(b) - g(a)) f(b) - (f(b) - f(a)) g(b) = g(b) f(b) - g(a) f(b) - f(b) g(b) + f(a) g(b) = f(a) g(b) - g(a) f(b). Hence h(a) = h(b).
Apply Rolle's theorem to h on [a,b]. It gives c in (a,b) with h'(c) = 0. This says (g(b) - g(a)) f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) g'(c), which is the product form.

Now assume g'(x) is not zero on (a,b). If g(b) = g(a), Rolle's theorem applied to g gives a point where g' is zero. This is a contradiction, so g(b) - g(a) is not zero. Divide the product form by (g(b) - g(a)) g'(c), which is not zero, to get the quotient form.

steps.text: Fix x in I with x not equal to x0. The function f has continuous derivatives up to order n on the closed interval between x0 and x. So f^(n-1) is continuous there and differentiable in the open interval between x0 and x.
Apply Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder of order n - 1. There is xi_x strictly between x0 and x with f(x) = T_{n-1}(x) + f^(n)(xi_x) (x - x0)^n / n!.
Subtract the last term of T_n. We have T_n(x) = T_{n-1}(x) + f^(n)(x0)(x - x0)^n / n!. Hence f(x) - T_n(x) = (f^(n)(xi_x) - f^(n)(x0)) (x - x0)^n / n!.
Divide by (x - x0)^n. This gives (f(x) - T_n(x)) / (x - x0)^n = (f^(n)(xi_x) - f^(n)(x0)) / n!.

Since xi_x lies between x0 and x, |xi_x - x0| <= |x - x0|. So xi_x tends to x0 as x tends to x0. The function f^(n) is continuous at x0, so f^(n)(xi_x) tends to f^(n)(x0). The quotient in the previous step therefore tends to 0.

At x = 1/100 the quotient x / (1 - x) is smaller. It equals 1/99.
In general the quotient is x / (1 - x). It tends to 0 as x tends to 0, as the theorem predicts for n = 3.

steps.text: Claim: f maps Cauchy sequences in D to Cauchy sequences. Let (x_n) in D be Cauchy and let eps > 0. Take delta from uniform continuity. Take N with |x_m - x_n| < delta for m, n >= N. Then |f(x_m) - f(x_n)| < eps for m, n >= N.
Let p be in D_bar. Choose x_n in D with x_n -> p. A convergent sequence is Cauchy, so (f(x_n)) is Cauchy by step 1. R is complete, so f(x_n) converges to some real number L.

The limit L does not depend on the sequence. Let y_n in D also tend to p. The interleaved sequence x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2, ... tends to p, so its image under f converges by step 2. The subsequences (f(x_n)) and (f(y_n)) of a convergent sequence have the same limit. Define F(p) = L.
F extends f. For p in D use the constant sequence x_n = p. Then F(p) = lim f(p) = f(p).

F is uniformly continuous. Let eps > 0 and take delta from uniform continuity of f. Let p, q in D_bar with |p - q| < delta. Take x_n -> p and y_n -> q in D. For large n, |x_n - y_n| < delta, so |f(x_n) - f(y_n)| < eps. Letting n tend to infinity gives |F(p) - F(q)| <= eps. In particular F is continuous.
Uniqueness. Let G be continuous on D_bar with G = f on D. For p in D_bar and x_n -> p with x_n in D, continuity gives G(p) = lim G(x_n) = lim f(x_n) = F(p).

steps.text: Take u < v in [a,b]. Since f is injective, f(u) is not equal to f(v). So the pair (u,v) is either increasing or decreasing.
Suppose, for contradiction, that (u,v) is increasing and (u',v') is decreasing, with u < v and u' < v' in [a,b].
For t in [0,1] put p(t) = (1 - t) u + t u' and q(t) = (1 - t) v + t v'. Then p(t) < q(t), because (1 - t)(v - u) + t(v' - u') > 0. Both points lie in [a,b], since [a,b] is convex.
Define g(t) = f(q(t)) - f(p(t)). Then g is continuous on [0,1], as a composition of continuous functions. We have g(0) = f(v) - f(u) > 0 and g(1) = f(v') - f(u') < 0.
By the intermediate value theorem there is t* in (0,1) with g(t*) = 0. So f(q(t*)) = f(p(t*)). But p(t*) < q(t*), which contradicts injectivity.
Hence the pairs cannot be of both types. If some pair is increasing, all pairs are increasing, so f is strictly increasing. Otherwise all pairs are decreasing and f is strictly decreasing.

steps.text: Chord slope inequality. Let x < y < z in I. Write y = (1 - t) x + t z with t = (y - x)/(z - x). Convexity gives f(y) <= (1 - t) f(x) + t f(z). Rearranging gives s(x,y) <= s(x,z) <= s(y,z).
Fix x0 in I and choose p < x0 < q in I. Put S1 = s(p,x0) and S2 = s(x0,q). By the chord inequality for p < x0 < q, S1 <= S2. Put M = max(|S1|, |S2|).

Right side. Let x0 < x < q. The chord inequality for x0 < x < q gives s(x0,x) <= s(x0,q) = S2. The chord inequality for p < x0 < x gives S1 = s(p,x0) <= s(x0,x). So S1 <= s(x0,x) <= S2, and |s(x0,x)| <= M.
Left side. Let p < x < x0. The chord inequality for x < x0 < q gives s(x,x0) <= s(x0,q) = S2. The chord inequality for p < x < x0 gives s(p,x0) <= s(x,x0), that is S1 <= s(x,x0). So |s(x,x0)| <= M.

In both cases |f(x) - f(x0)| = |s| |x - x0| <= M |x - x0| for x in (p,q). Given eps > 0, the choice delta = min(x0 - p, q - x0, eps / (M + 1)) gives |f(x) - f(x0)| < eps for |x - x0| < delta. Hence f is continuous at x0.

steps.text: The function f' is differentiable on the interior of I. So it is continuous there. Since (f')' = f'' >= 0 on the interior of I, the derivative sign criterion shows that f' is non-decreasing on the interior of I.
Let x < z be points of I. Let y = (1 - t) x + t z with 0 < t < 1, so x < y < z. The cases t = 0 and t = 1 are trivial.
On [x,y] the function f is continuous, and on (x,y) it is differentiable, because (x,y) lies in the interior of I. The mean value theorem gives c1 in (x,y) with f(y) - f(x) = f'(c1)(y - x).
In the same way the mean value theorem on [y,z] gives c2 in (y,z) with f(z) - f(y) = f'(c2)(z - y). Since c1 < y < c2 and f' is non-decreasing on the interior of I, f'(c1) <= f'(c2).
Therefore (f(y) - f(x))/(y - x) <= (f(z) - f(y))/(z - y). Multiply by (y - x)(z - y), which is positive: (z - y)(f(y) - f(x)) <= (y - x)(f(z) - f(y)).

Collect the terms in f(y). We get (z - x) f(y) <= (z - y) f(x) + (y - x) f(z). Divide by z - x and use (z - y)/(z - x) = 1 - t and (y - x)/(z - x) = t. This gives f(y) <= (1 - t) f(x) + t f(z), which is convexity.

steps.text: Set x = y = 0 in the equation: f(0) = 2 f(0), so f(0) = 0. Set y = -x: 0 = f(x) + f(-x), so f(-x) = -f(x).

For every natural number n and every real x we have f(n x) = n f(x). Induction: the case n = 0 is f(0) = 0. If f(n x) = n f(x), then f((n + 1) x) = f(n x) + f(x) = (n + 1) f(x). With step 1 this extends to every integer n.
Let m be an integer and n a positive integer. Put q = m/n. By step 2, n f(q) = f(n q) = f(m) = f(m * 1) = m f(1). Hence f(q) = (m/n) f(1) = c q.
Let x be real. Choose rational numbers q_k with q_k -> x, which is possible because the rational numbers are dense in R.
By continuity of f, f(x) = lim f(q_k). By step 3, f(q_k) = c q_k. Hence f(x) = lim c q_k = c x.
The continuity cannot be dropped. A Hamel basis of R over Q gives an additive function that is Q-linear but not R-linear. Such a function is not continuous, by the result above.

steps.text: A non-zero polynomial has at most deg p real roots, so N(p) is finite. Let r_1 < r_2 < ... < r_k be the distinct real roots of p. If k <= 1, then N(p) = k <= 1 <= N(p') + 1, and the claim holds. If p' is the zero polynomial, then p is a non-zero constant, so k = 0 and the claim holds.
Let k >= 2. For each i < k the polynomial p is continuous on [r_i, r_{i+1}] and differentiable there. Also p(r_i) = 0 = p(r_{i+1}).
Rolle's theorem gives a point c_i in the open interval (r_i, r_{i+1}) with p'(c_i) = 0.
The open intervals (r_i, r_{i+1}) are pairwise disjoint. So the points c_1, ..., c_{k-1} are pairwise distinct. All of them are real roots of p'.
Hence p' has at least k - 1 distinct real roots. So N(p') >= k - 1 = N(p) - 1, which is the claim.

applications.title: Count the real roots of x^3 - 3x + 1
applications.hypotheses: p is a non-zero real polynomial. Its derivative has the two distinct real roots 1 and -1, and no others.

steps.text: The derivative has N(p') = 2 distinct real roots. The theorem gives N(p) <= 2 + 1.
Evaluate p at -2. The value is negative.
Evaluate p at 0. The value is positive.
Evaluate p at 1. The value is negative.
Evaluate p at 2. The value is positive.

The sign changes on [-2,0], [0,1] and [1,2] give three roots by the intermediate value theorem. They are distinct since the intervals meet only at points where p is not zero. So N(p) = 3, which equals the bound.

applications.conclusion: The polynomial x^3 - 3x + 1 has exactly three distinct real roots, one in each of the intervals (-2,0), (0,1) and (1,2).

Also g(x) > 0 for x > 0. Hence the Taylor series of g at 0 is the zero series, but g is not equal to the zero function on any neighborhood of 0. So g is not analytic at 0.
hypotheses: g is defined by exp(-1/x) for x > 0 and by 0 for x <= 0.

Analytic at 0 means that g equals the sum of its Taylor series at 0 on some open interval around 0.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Derivative formula for x > 0. If h(x) = P(1/x) exp(-1/x) for a polynomial P, then h'(x) = (-P'(1/x)/x^2) exp(-1/x) + P(1/x) (1/x^2) exp(-1/x) = (1/x^2)(P - P')(1/x) exp(-1/x). So the recursion P_{k+1}(y) = y^2 (P_k(y) - P_k'(y)) gives the next derivative.

Growth bound. For y > 0 and an integer m >= 0, exp(y) >= y^(m+1)/(m+1)! because all terms of the exponential series are positive. So 0 < y^m exp(-y) <= (m+1)!/y, which tends to 0 as y -> infinity. Hence Q(1/x) exp(-1/x) -> 0 as x -> 0+ for every polynomial Q.
Induction claim: g^(k)(x) exists for all x. It equals P_k(1/x) exp(-1/x) for x > 0 and 0 for x <= 0. For k = 0 this is the definition of g.
Induction step at x not equal to 0. For x > 0 use step 1 on the formula for g^(k). For x < 0 the function g^(k) is 0 on a neighborhood of x. So g^(k+1)(x) exists and has the claimed form.

Induction step at x = 0. The left difference quotient (g^(k)(h) - 0)/h is 0 for h < 0. For h > 0 it equals (1/h) P_k(1/h) exp(-1/h) = Q(1/h) exp(-1/h) with Q(y) = y P_k(y), which tends to 0 by step 2. So g^(k+1)(0) exists and equals 0.

Therefore g has derivatives of all orders at every point, so each g^(k) is differentiable and hence continuous. So g is C-infinity and g^(k)(0) = 0 for all k. The Taylor series of g at 0 is the zero series.
Since g(x) = exp(-1/x) > 0 for x > 0, g is not zero on any neighborhood of 0. If g were analytic at 0, it would equal its Taylor series, the zero series, near 0. This is a contradiction.

steps.text: Compute P_2(1) from P_2(y) = y^4 - 2 y^3. So g''(1) = P_2(1) exp(-1).

steps.text: Define G(u) as the integral of g(s) ds from f(a) to u. Since g is continuous, the first part of the fundamental theorem of calculus says that G is differentiable at every u with G'(u) = g(u).
Let H(x) = G(f(x)). For x in [[a, b]], f has derivative f'(x) at x and G has derivative g(f(x)) at f(x). The chain rule gives H'(x) = g(f(x)) f'(x).

The function x -> g(f(x)) f'(x) is continuous on [[a, b]]. This is true because f is continuous (it is differentiable there), g is continuous, and f' is continuous. A continuous function on a compact interval is integrable, so H' is integrable on [[a, b]].
The second part of the fundamental theorem of calculus applies to H. It says that the integral of H'(x) dx from a to b equals H(b) - H(a).

By definition G(f(a)) = 0, so H(a) = 0. Also H(b) = G(f(b)), which is the integral of g from f(a) to f(b). Hence the integral of g(f(x)) f'(x) from a to b equals the integral of g(u) du from f(a) to f(b).

steps.text: Replace f by a measurable function equal to f almost everywhere and nonnegative everywhere. This changes neither side of the formula. For every x, f(x) = the integral over t in (0, infinity) of 1{t < f(x)} dt, because the integrand is 1 exactly on the interval (0, f(x)).
The set {(x, t) : 0 < t < f(x)} is measurable in the product X x (0, infinity), because it is {(x, t) : f(x) - t > 0} and both (x, t) -> f(x) and (x, t) -> t are measurable.

The set {f > 0} is the union over n of {f > 1/n}. By Markov's inequality, mu({f > 1/n}) is at most n times the integral of f, so it is finite. Hence mu is sigma-finite on {f > 0}, and Tonelli's theorem can be applied there.

By Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative function 1{t < f(x)}, the integral over x of the integral over t equals the integral over t of the integral over x. The inner integral over x is the measure of {x : f(x) > t}.
Therefore the integral of f d mu equals the integral over t > 0 of mu({f > t}) dt. Both sides are finite, since the left side is finite. This gives the formula with real-valued measures.

steps.text: The truncations f_N are measurable and increase pointwise to f. By the monotone convergence theorem, the integral of f_N tends to the integral of f, which is finite.
Because the integral of f is finite, choose N so that the integral of f minus the integral of f_N is less than epsilon/2. Both integrals are finite, so the difference is the integral of f - f_N.
For any measurable set A, split f = f_N + (f - f_N) on A. Then the integral of f over A is at most the integral of f_N over A plus the integral of f - f_N over X.
Since f_N <= N, the integral of f_N over A is at most N mu(A). The integral of f - f_N over X is less than epsilon/2 by the choice of N.
Put delta = epsilon / (2N) (take N >= 1). If mu(A) < delta, then the integral of f over A is less than N delta + epsilon/2 = epsilon. This proves the claim.

steps.text: Suppose f = 0 almost everywhere. Then f and the zero function have the same integral, because changing a function on a null set does not change its integral. So the integral of f is 0.
Now suppose the integral of f is 0. Fix eps > 0. Markov's inequality for the almost everywhere nonnegative function f gives eps mu({f >= eps}) <= the integral of f = 0.
Since eps > 0, the last inequality gives mu({f >= eps}) = 0. Apply this with eps = 1/n for every natural number n >= 1.
Almost everywhere f >= 0, so up to a null set {f != 0} = {f > 0} = the union over n >= 1 of {f >= 1/n}. This is a countable union of null sets.
By countable subadditivity, the measure of the union is at most the sum of the measures, which is 0. So f = 0 outside a null set. This proves f = 0 almost everywhere.

applications.title: Two functions with the same values almost everywhere, and a Markov bound for the difference
applications.inputs: On [0, 1] with Lebesgue measure, let g(x) = x^2 and h(x) = x^2 + (1/10) 1_[0, 1/100](x). Put d = |g - h|.
applications.hypotheses: d is bounded and measurable on a set of finite measure, so it is integrable. It is nonnegative.

steps.text: The function d equals 1/10 on [0, 1/100] and 0 elsewhere. Its integral is the height times the length of the interval.
The integral is not 0, so the theorem says that d is not 0 almost everywhere. Markov's inequality with eps = 1/20 gives an upper bound on the measure of the set where d >= 1/20.
The exact measure of {d >= 1/20} is 1/100, which is below the Markov bound 1/50 and above 0. This agrees with the theorem.

applications.conclusion: Since the integral of |g - h| is 1/1000 and not 0, g and h differ on a set of positive measure. By contrast, if h differed from g at one point only, the integral would be 0 and g = h almost everywhere.

steps.text: Choose measurable sets E_n of finite measure with union X. It is enough to show that f = 0 almost everywhere on each E_n, because a countable union of null sets is null.
Fix n. Let P = {f > 0} intersect E_n. P is measurable, because f is measurable, and mu(P) <= mu(E_n) < infinity. By hypothesis the integral of f over P is 0.
The function f 1_P is nonnegative and integrable, and its integral is the integral of f over P, which is 0. By the vanishing criterion, f 1_P = 0 almost everywhere.
On P we have f > 0, so f 1_P = 0 almost everywhere forces mu(P) = 0. The same argument for -f on Q = {f < 0} intersect E_n gives mu(Q) = 0, because the integral of -f over Q is also 0.
Hence f = 0 on E_n outside the null set P union Q. Taking the union over n, the set {f != 0} is contained in a countable union of null sets. So f = 0 almost everywhere.

steps.text: On the whole space the integral is 0, because the integral of 2x - 1 over [0, 1] is 1 - 1. The whole space is therefore not a witness.
The negative set of f is s = [0, 1/2). The integral of 2x - 1 over it is (1/2)^2 - 1/2, using the antiderivative x^2 - x.
The integral over s is -1/4, which is not 0. This is what the contrapositive of the lemma predicts, because f is not zero almost everywhere.

steps.text: Choose n_1 < n_2 < ... recursively. For k >= 1, choose n_k larger than n_{k-1} such that mu(A_k) <= 2^(-k), where A_k = {x : |f_{n_k}(x) - g(x)| >= 2^(-k)}. This is possible because convergence in measure applies with eps = 2^(-k).
The sum of mu(A_k) over k >= 1 is at most the sum of 2^(-k), which is 1. So the sum is finite.
By the first Borel-Cantelli lemma, the set N of points that lie in A_k for infinitely many k has measure 0.
Let x be outside N. Then there is K such that x is not in A_k for all k >= K. For these k we have |f_{n_k}(x) - g(x)| < 2^(-k).
Since 2^(-k) tends to 0, f_{n_k}(x) tends to g(x). This holds for every x outside the null set N, so f_{n_k} converges to g almost everywhere.

applications.title: The typewriter sequence converges in measure and has an almost everywhere convergent subsequence
applications.inputs: On [0, 1] with Lebesgue measure, list the indicators of the intervals [i 2^(-j), (i+1) 2^(-j)] for j = 0, 1, 2, ... and i = 0, ..., 2^j - 1. Call the list f_1, f_2, .... The limit is g = 0.
applications.hypotheses: For eps in (0, 1], the set {f_n >= eps} is the n-th interval, with measure 2^(-j) for n in block j. This tends to 0 as n goes to infinity, so f_n tends to 0 in measure.

steps.text: Every x in [0, 1] lies in one interval of each block j. So f_n(x) = 1 for infinitely many n. Also f_n(x) = 0 for infinitely many n. The full sequence converges at no point.
Take the subsequence of intervals [0, 2^(-k)], one for each block k. This subsequence has mu(A_k) = 2^(-k). The sum of the first six measures is below 1.
For x > 0 the point x is outside [0, 2^(-k)] when 2^(-k) < x. So the subsequence is 0 at x for all large k. It converges to 0 at every x in (0, 1]. Only the null set {0} is exceptional.

applications.conclusion: The typewriter sequence converges to 0 in measure and at no point, yet its subsequence of intervals [0, 2^(-k)] converges to 0 almost everywhere, as the theorem states.

steps.text: For part (a), disjointify: D_1 = A_1 and D_n = A_n minus A_(n-1). The D_n are measurable and disjoint, and the union of all D_n equals the union of all A_n.
By countable additivity, mu(union of A_n) = sum over n of mu(D_n). By finite additivity, the partial sum of the first N terms equals mu(A_N), because D_1, ..., D_N are disjoint with union A_N.
The partial sums mu(A_N) are non-decreasing. A series of nonnegative terms equals the limit of its partial sums, which is also the supremum. This proves part (a).

For part (b), assume mu(B_1) < infinity (otherwise drop the first sets, as the sequence starts at a set of finite measure). Put C_n = B_1 minus B_n. The C_n are measurable and increasing, and their union is B_1 minus the intersection of all B_n.
Apply part (a) to C_n. We get mu(B_1 minus the intersection) = lim of mu(C_n) = lim of (mu(B_1) - mu(B_n)). The subtraction is valid because B_n is contained in B_1 and mu(B_1) is finite.

Also mu(B_1 minus the intersection) = mu(B_1) - mu(intersection), since the intersection is contained in B_1 and has finite measure. Subtract the finite number mu(B_1) from both sides. This gives mu(intersection) = lim of mu(B_n), which is also the infimum because mu(B_n) is non-increasing.

steps.text: Let S(x) = sum over n of |f_n(x)|, a measurable function with values in [0, infinity]. The partial sums of S increase to S. By the monotone convergence theorem, the integral of S equals the sum of the integrals of |f_n|, which is finite.

A function with finite integral is finite almost everywhere. So S(x) < infinity for almost every x, and S is integrable. For such x the series of f_n(x) converges absolutely, so F(x) is defined there.
At those x we have |F(x)| <= S(x) and |F_N(x)| <= S(x) for all N, by the triangle inequality. So F is measurable (a pointwise limit of measurable functions) and integrable.
F_N(x) tends to F(x) almost everywhere, and |F_N| <= S where S is integrable. The dominated convergence theorem gives that the integral of F_N tends to the integral of F.

By linearity, the integral of F_N is the finite sum of the integrals of f_0, ..., f_N. The limit of these partial sums is the sum of the series of integrals. Hence the integral of F equals the sum of the integrals of f_n.
