steps.text: Fix b > a. The function f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b). Its derivative f' is integrable on (a, b), because it is integrable on (a, infinity). The fundamental theorem of calculus gives the integral of f' over (a, b] equals f(b) - f(a).
Take b = a + k for k = 1, 2, 3, ... and let g_k = f' times the indicator function of (a, a + k]. For every x > a we have g_k(x) = f'(x) once k >= x - a. So g_k tends to f' 1_(a, infinity) pointwise.
The functions g_k satisfy |g_k| <= |f'|, and |f'| is integrable on (a, infinity). The dominated convergence theorem gives that the integral of g_k tends to the integral of f' over (a, infinity).
By step 1, the integral of g_k equals f(a + k) - f(a). Since f(a + k) tends to m, this number tends to m - f(a).
A sequence of real numbers has at most one limit. So the integral of f' over (a, infinity), which is the limit from step 3, equals m - f(a), which is the limit from step 4.

applications.title: The integral of 1/x^2 over (1, infinity)
applications.inputs: Take a = 1, f(x) = -1/x and f'(x) = 1/x^2 for x > 1.
applications.hypotheses: f is continuous on [1, infinity) and differentiable on (1, infinity) with derivative 1/x^2. The limit of f at infinity is m = 0. The integral of f' over (1, b] is 1 - 1/b <= 1 for every b, so by monotone convergence the integral of f' over (1, infinity) is finite.

steps.text: On (1, b] the fundamental theorem gives f(b) - f(1) = -1/b + 1. At b = 10 this value is 9/10.
At b = 100 the same formula gives 99/100. The values increase towards 1 and stay below 1.
The theorem gives the full integral as m - f(a) with m = 0 and f(1) = -1.

applications.conclusion: The Lebesgue integral of 1/x^2 over (1, infinity) is 1, equal to the limit of the partial integrals 1 - 1/b.

results.name: Monotone functions are integrable on bounded intervals
results.statement: Let u: R -> R be monotone (non-decreasing or non-increasing) and let a < b. Then u is Lebesgue integrable on [a, b]. It is also Riemann integrable on [a, b], and the two integrals are equal. For every n, the upper and lower Darboux sums of the uniform partition with n parts differ by (b - a)(|u(b) - u(a)|)/n.
hypotheses: u is defined on R (or on [a, b]) and is monotone. It may have jump discontinuities, at most countably many.
a < b are real numbers. The interval [a, b] is bounded and has finite Lebesgue measure.
The measure in the cited declaration is any locally finite measure on R. The authored statement uses Lebesgue measure.

definitions.name: Darboux sums
definitions.text: For a partition a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b, the lower sum L is the sum of (inf of u on [x_(i-1), x_i]) (x_i - x_(i-1)). The upper sum U uses the supremum. The Darboux criterion says that u is Riemann integrable if and only if, for every eps > 0, some partition has U - L < eps.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Assume u is non-decreasing. The non-increasing case follows by applying the result to -u. For x in [a, b] we have u(a) <= u(x) <= u(b). So u is bounded on [a, b] by M = max(|u(a)|, |u(b)|).

For every real c, the set {x : u(x) > c} is closed upwards: if x is in it and y >= x, then y is in it. A subset of R that is closed upwards is a ray (t, infinity) or [t, infinity) or empty or all of R. Each of these sets is a Borel set, so u is Borel measurable.

u restricted to [a, b] is measurable and satisfies |u| <= M. The interval has measure b - a. So the integral of |u| over [a, b] is at most M (b - a), which is finite. Therefore u is Lebesgue integrable on [a, b].

Take the uniform partition x_i = a + i h with h = (b - a)/n. Since u is non-decreasing, the infimum on [x_(i-1), x_i] is u(x_(i-1)) and the supremum is u(x_i). So U - L = h times the sum over i of (u(x_i) - u(x_(i-1))).
The sum telescopes to u(b) - u(a). Hence U - L = (b - a)(u(b) - u(a))/n, which tends to 0 as n goes to infinity. By the Darboux criterion, u is Riemann integrable.
Both the Riemann integral and the Lebesgue integral lie between L and U for every partition. Their difference is at most U - L, which can be made as small as we like. So the two integrals are equal.

applications.title: Darboux sums of the floor function on [0, 4]
applications.inputs: Take u(x) = floor(x), a = 0, b = 4 and the partition with n = 8 equal parts of length h = 1/2. The function u is non-decreasing with jumps at the integers.
applications.hypotheses: u is monotone, so the theorem applies even though u has discontinuities at 1, 2, 3 and 4.

steps.text: The values of u at the right end points x_1, ..., x_8 = 1/2, 1, ..., 4 are 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4. The upper sum is h times their total.
The values at the left end points x_0, ..., x_7 = 0, 1/2, ..., 7/2 are 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3. The lower sum is h times their total.
The difference U - L must equal (b - a)(u(b) - u(a))/n = 4 * 4 / 8.
The integral lies between 6 and 8. The exact value is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3, because u equals k on [k, k+1). The value 6 equals the lower sum.

applications.conclusion: The floor function is integrable on [0, 4] with integral 6. The Darboux sums 6 and 8 bracket it, and their gap 2 equals (b - a)(u(b) - u(a))/n.

results.name: Comparison of Lp norms on a finite measure space
aliases: L^q is contained in L^p on a finite measure space
results.statement: Let (X, mu) be a measure space with mu(X) < infinity. Let 0 < p <= q <= infinity and let f: X -> R be measurable. Then the L^p norm satisfies ||f||_p <= ||f||_q mu(X)^(1/p - 1/q), with the convention 1/infinity = 0. In particular L^q(mu) is contained in L^p(mu).
hypotheses: mu(X) is finite. The result fails for infinite measure: on R with Lebesgue measure, the function 1/(1 + |x|) is in L^2 and not in L^1.
0 < p <= q <= infinity.
f is measurable. The norm ||f||_p is (integral |f|^p d mu)^(1/p) for p < infinity and the essential supremum of |f| for p = infinity. Both sides may be infinite.

prerequisites.reason: The proof applies Hölder's inequality to |f|^p and the constant function 1 with the exponent q/p and its conjugate exponent.

definitions.name: conjugate exponent
definitions.text: For r with 1 < r < infinity, the conjugate exponent r' satisfies 1/r + 1/r' = 1. In the proof, r = q/p and 1/r' = 1 - p/q.

theorem eLpNorm_le_eLpNorm_mul_rpow_measure_univ {p q : ℝ≥0∞} (hpq : p ≤ q)
    (hf : AEStronglyMeasurable f μ) :
    eLpNorm f p μ ≤ eLpNorm f q μ * μ Set.univ ^ (1 / p.toReal - 1 / q.toReal) := by
  obtain rfl | hp0 := eq_or_ne p 0
  · simp [hf]
  have hq0_lt : 0 < q := hp0.pos.trans_le hpq
  obtain rfl | hq_top := eq_or_ne q ∞
  · simp only [_root_.div_zero, one_div, ENNReal.toReal_top, sub_zero]
    obtain rfl | hp_top := eq_or_ne p ∞
    · simp [hf]
    rw [eLpNorm_eq_eLpNorm' hp0 hp_top hf]
    have hp_pos : 0 < p.toReal := ENNReal.toReal_pos hp0 hp_top
    refine (eLpNorm'_le_eLpNormEssSup_mul_rpow_measure_univ hp_pos).trans (le_of_eq ?_)
    congr
    · rw [eLpNorm_exponent_top hf]
    · exact one_div _
  have hp_lt_top : p < ∞ := hpq.trans_lt (lt_top_iff_ne_top.mpr hq_top)
  have hp_pos : 0 < p.toReal := ENNReal.toReal_pos hp0 hp_lt_top.ne
  rw [eLpNorm_eq_eLpNorm' hp0 hp_lt_top.ne hf,
    eLpNorm_eq_eLpNorm' hq0_lt.ne.symm hq_top hf]
  have hpq_real : p.toReal ≤ q.toReal := ENNReal.toReal_mono hq_top hpq
  exact eLpNorm'_le_eLpNorm'_mul_rpow_measure_univ hp_pos hpq_real hf

steps.text: Treat the case q = infinity first. Then |f| <= ||f||_infinity almost everywhere. So the integral of |f|^p is at most ||f||_infinity^p mu(X). Taking the 1/p power gives ||f||_p <= ||f||_infinity mu(X)^(1/p).
Now let q < infinity. If p = q, the claim is an equality, because mu(X)^0 = 1. So assume p < q and put r = q/p > 1 with conjugate exponent r' = q/(q - p).
Apply Hölder's inequality to the functions |f|^p and 1 with exponents r and r'. This gives the integral of |f|^p * 1 at most (the integral of |f|^(pr))^(1/r) times (the integral of 1)^(1/r').
Now pr = q, 1/r = p/q and the integral of 1 is mu(X). So the integral of |f|^p is at most (the integral of |f|^q)^(p/q) mu(X)^(1 - p/q).
Take the 1/p power on both sides. The left side becomes ||f||_p. The right side becomes ||f||_q mu(X)^(1/p - 1/q), since (p/q)(1/p) = 1/q and (1 - p/q)(1/p) = 1/p - 1/q.

The approximation by an open set from outside is the companion declaration MeasurableSet.exists_isOpen_sdiff_lt in the same module.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let C be a closed set, and for n >= 1 let G_n = {x : d(x, C) < 1/n}. Each G_n is open, they decrease, and the intersection of all G_n is C because C is closed. Since mu is finite, continuity from above gives mu(G_n) -> mu(C). So mu(G_n minus C) < eps for large n, and C is good with F = C.

The family of good sets is closed under complements. If F is contained in A and A is contained in G, then the complement of G is closed and contained in the complement of A, which is contained in the open complement of F. The difference of these two sets is G minus F.

The family is closed under countable unions. Let A be the union of good sets A_i, i >= 1. Choose closed F_i and open G_i with F_i contained in A_i, A_i contained in G_i and mu(G_i minus F_i) < eps / 2^(i+1). Put G = the union of G_i. It is open and contains A.
The set G minus the union of F_i is contained in the union of the sets G_i minus F_i. By countable subadditivity its measure is less than the sum of eps / 2^(i+1), which equals eps / 2.

Let H_N = F_1 union ... union F_N. It is closed, contained in A, and increasing in N. By continuity from below, mu(H_N) -> mu(the union of F_i). Since mu is finite, choose N so that mu(the union of F_i minus H_N) < eps / 2.

With F = H_N, the set G minus F is contained in (G minus the union of F_i) union (the union of F_i minus H_N). So mu(G minus F) < eps / 2 + eps / 2 = eps. The good sets form a sigma-algebra containing all closed sets, hence all open sets (complements), hence all Borel sets.

applications.title: Cover the rationals in [0, 1] by an open set of small measure
applications.inputs: Let X = [0, 1] with Lebesgue measure. Let A be the set of rational numbers q_1, q_2, ... in [0, 1]. Put eps = 1/10.
applications.hypotheses: A is countable, so it is a Borel set. Lebesgue measure on [0, 1] is finite. A is neither open nor closed in [0, 1], so the theorem is not trivial.

steps.text: Every closed subset of A is countable, so it has measure 0. The empty set F is a closed subset of A with mu(F) = mu(A) = 0.
Take the open set G_i = the interval around q_i with radius r_i = eps 2^(-i-2). Its length is 2 r_i = eps 2^(-i-1). The first five lengths add up to a number below eps/2.
All lengths together have the sum eps/2 = 1/20, which is 32/640. The partial sum 31/640 is below it, and the full sum is the limit.
G is the union of the G_i, so mu(G) <= eps/2 < eps. Hence mu(G minus F) < eps. The theorem guarantees such F and G for every eps, and here they are explicit.

applications.conclusion: The rationals in [0, 1] lie in an open set of measure at most 1/20, although the rationals are dense. The closed set F = empty set and the open set G satisfy mu(G minus F) < 1/10.

For N >= 1 put h = (b - a)/N and T_N = h * ((f(a) + f(b))/2 + the sum for k = 1, ..., N - 1 of f(a + k h)). Then |T_N - the integral of f from a to b| <= (b - a)^3 Z / (12 N^2).
hypotheses: f is C^2 on the closed interval [a, b]: f, f' and f'' exist and f'' is continuous.

    (N_nonzero : 0 < N) : |trapezoidal_error f N a b| ≤ |b - a| ^ 3 * ζ / (12 * N ^ 2) := by
  -- This use of rcases slightly duplicates effort from the proof of trapezoidal_error_le, but doing
  -- it any other way that I can think of would be worse.
  rcases eq_or_ne a b with h_eq | h_ne
  · simp [h_eq]
  -- Once we have a ≠ b, all the necessary assumptions on f follow pretty quickly from its being
  -- C^2.
  have h_ddf : DifferentiableOn ℝ (derivWithin f [[a, b]]) [[a, b]] := by
    rw [← iteratedDerivWithin_one]
    exact h_f_c2.differentiableOn_iteratedDerivWithin (by norm_cast) (uniqueDiffOn_uIcc h_ne)
  exact trapezoidal_error_le (h_f_c2.differentiableOn two_ne_zero) h_ddf fpp_bound N_nonzero

steps.text: Fix a sub-interval [x, x + h] and define K(t) = (t - x)(t - x - h)/2. Then K(x) = K(x + h) = 0, K'(t) = t - x - h/2 and K''(t) = 1. In particular K'(x + h) = h/2 and K'(x) = -h/2.
Integrate by parts with K and f'. The integral of K f'' over [x, x + h] equals [K f'] minus the integral of K' f'. The boundary term [K f'] is 0 because K vanishes at both end points.

Integrate by parts again. The integral of K' f' equals [K' f] minus the integral of f, and [K' f] = (h/2) f(x + h) + (h/2) f(x). So the integral of K f'' = the integral of f minus (h/2)(f(x) + f(x + h)).
Hence the error E = (h/2)(f(x) + f(x + h)) minus the integral of f over the sub-interval equals minus the integral of K f''. On the sub-interval K <= 0, and |K(t)| = (t - x)(x + h - t)/2.
Compute the integral of |K| over the sub-interval. With s = t - x it is the integral of s(h - s)/2 over [0, h], which equals (1/2)(h^3/2 - h^3/3) = h^3/12.

Since |f''| <= Z, we get |E| <= Z times the integral of |K|, which is Z h^3/12. Sum over the N sub-intervals. The sum of the trapezoids is T_N because every interior point is counted twice with weight h/2, and the sum of the integrals is the integral over [a, b].
Therefore |T_N - the integral of f| <= N Z h^3 / 12. Since h = (b - a)/N, we have N h^3 = (b - a)^3 / N^2. This gives the bound (b - a)^3 Z / (12 N^2).

applications.title: Trapezoidal rule for x^2 on [0, 1] with N = 4
applications.inputs: Take f(x) = x^2, a = 0, b = 1, N = 4 and h = 1/4. Then f''(x) = 2, so Z = 2.
applications.hypotheses: f is a polynomial, so it is C^2. The bound |f''| <= 2 holds everywhere.

steps.text: The interior values f(1/4), f(1/2), f(3/4) are 1/16, 4/16, 9/16. Their sum is 14/16.
The end point average is (0 + 1)/2. Then T_4 = h times (1/2 + 7/8).
The exact integral of x^2 over [0, 1] is 1/3. The error T_4 minus the integral is 11/32 - 1/3.
The theorem bounds the error by (b - a)^3 Z / (12 N^2) = 2 / (12 * 16).

applications.conclusion: The error 1/96 equals the bound 1/96. The bound is sharp for f(x) = x^2, because f'' is constant and equal to Z.

results.name: Compactness of a metric space as completeness plus total boundedness
aliases: compact metric space is complete and totally bounded
results.statement: Let (X, d) be a metric space. Then X is compact if and only if X is complete and totally bounded.
hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space. Compact means that every open cover of X has a finite subcover.
Complete means that every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X.
Totally bounded means that for every e > 0 there is a finite set F of X such that every point of X is at distance less than e from some point of F.

prerequisites.reason: The proof uses that compactness and sequential compactness are equivalent for a metric space.

definitions.name: Cauchy sequence
definitions.text: A sequence (x_n) in X is Cauchy if for every e > 0 there is N such that d(x_m, x_n) < e for all m, n >= N.

definitions.name: subsequence
definitions.text: A sequence (x_(n_k)) with n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < ... is a subsequence of (x_n).

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Assume X is compact. Fix e > 0. The open balls B(x, e) for x in X cover X. A finite subcover gives a finite set F with every point within distance e of F. So X is totally bounded.

Assume X is compact and let (x_n) be Cauchy. By sequential compactness, a subsequence (x_(n_k)) converges to some x in X. Given e > 0, choose N with d(x_m, x_n) < e/2 for m, n >= N. Choose k with n_k >= N and d(x_(n_k), x) < e/2.
For every n >= N, d(x_n, x) <= d(x_n, x_(n_k)) + d(x_(n_k), x) < e/2 + e/2 = e. So x_n converges to x, and X is complete. This proves the direction from compact to complete and totally bounded.

Now assume X is complete and totally bounded. Let (x_n) be any sequence. Cover X by finitely many balls of radius 1. One ball contains x_n for infinitely many n. Keep these terms as a subsequence S_1. Cover X by finitely many balls of radius 1/2. One ball contains infinitely many terms of S_1. Keep them as S_2. Continue with radius 1/j to obtain S_j inside S_(j-1).

Let y_k be the k-th term of S_k. The sequence S_k is a subsequence of S_j for k >= j, and the indices of y_k grow strictly. So (y_k) is a subsequence of (x_n). For k, l >= j, both y_k and y_l lie in one ball of radius 1/j, so d(y_k, y_l) < 2/j. Hence (y_k) is Cauchy.

X is complete, so (y_k) converges. Every sequence in X has a convergent subsequence, so X is sequentially compact. By the equivalence of sequential compactness and compactness for metric spaces, X is compact.

applications.title: The interval (0, 1] is not compact
applications.inputs: Take X = (0, 1] with the metric d(x, y) = |x - y|. Test the two conditions of the criterion.
applications.hypotheses: (0, 1] is a metric space with the induced metric of the real line, so the criterion applies.

steps.text: X is totally bounded. For e = 1/10, take the 10 points j/10 for j = 1, ..., 10. A point x with (j-1)/10 < x <= j/10 has distance less than 1/10 to j/10. So 10 balls of radius 1/10 cover X.
X is not complete. The sequence x_n = 1/n lies in X. For m > n >= 100, |1/n - 1/m| < 1/n <= 1/100, so it is Cauchy. For example, the two terms n = 100 and m = 200 differ by 1/200.
The Cauchy sequence 1/n tends to 0, and 0 is not in X. If it converged to a point of X, the limit would be 0 by uniqueness of limits in R. So X is not complete.
By the criterion, a compact space is complete. X is not complete, so X is not compact. The cover by the sets (1/n, 2] for n >= 1 has no finite subcover, which agrees with this result.

applications.conclusion: The set (0, 1] is totally bounded but not complete, so it is not compact. Total boundedness alone is not enough.

steps.text: If K or L is empty, take U = X and V = empty, or the reverse. So assume K and L are nonempty. First fix a point x in K and separate x from L.
For each y in L, x is not equal to y because K and L are disjoint. The Hausdorff axiom gives disjoint open sets U_y containing x and V_y containing y. The sets V_y for y in L form an open cover of L.

L is compact, so finitely many sets V_(y_1), ..., V_(y_m) cover L. Put U^x = the intersection of U_(y_1), ..., U_(y_m) and V^x = the union of V_(y_1), ..., V_(y_m). U^x is open because it is a finite intersection. It contains x. V^x is open and contains L.
U^x and V^x are disjoint. A point z in both lies in V_(y_i) for some i, and also in U_(y_i). This contradicts U_(y_i) and V_(y_i) being disjoint.

Now vary x. The sets U^x for x in K form an open cover of K. K is compact, so finitely many sets U^(x_1), ..., U^(x_n) cover K. Put U = the union of the U^(x_j) and V = the intersection of the V^(x_j). U is open and contains K. V is open (finite intersection) and contains L.
U and V are disjoint. A point z in both lies in U^(x_j) for some j. It also lies in V^(x_j) because V is contained in V^(x_j). This contradicts U^(x_j) and V^(x_j) being disjoint.

For the closedness of a compact set K, take a point p outside K and L = {p}. The result gives an open set V containing p and disjoint from K. So the complement of K is open. A closed subset of a compact space is compact, so two disjoint closed sets of a compact Hausdorff space are compact and can be separated. This gives normality.

applications.title: Separate the intervals [0, 1] and [2, 3] with the proof construction
applications.inputs: Take X = R with the usual topology. Take the compact sets K = [0, 1] and L = [2, 3]. Run the construction of the proof for the point x = 1 in K.
applications.hypotheses: R is Hausdorff, and K and L are closed and bounded, so they are compact. They are disjoint because 1 < 2.

steps.text: For y = 2 in L, the Hausdorff separation of x = 1 and y = 2 uses balls of radius (2 - 1)/2. This gives U_2 = (1/2, 3/2) and V_2 = (3/2, 5/2).
For y = 3 in L, the separation uses balls of radius (3 - 1)/2. This gives U_3 = (0, 2) and V_3 = (2, 4).
The two sets V_2 = (3/2, 5/2) and V_3 = (2, 4) cover L = [2, 3]. So U^1 = U_2 intersect U_3 = (1/2, 3/2) and V^1 = V_2 union V_3 = (3/2, 4).
The sets U^1 and V^1 are disjoint open sets. Their boundary point 3/2 is the midpoint of 1 and 2, which gives the gap.

applications.conclusion: The construction gives disjoint open neighbourhoods of the point 1 and of [2, 3]. Repeating it for each x in [0, 1] and taking a finite subcover gives U and V for the full intervals.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let F be a closed subset of X. A closed subset of a compact space is compact. Indeed, take an open cover of F by open sets O_i of X. Adding the open set X minus F gives an open cover of X. A finite subcover of X gives a finite subfamily of the O_i that covers F.

The image f(F) is compact. Take an open cover of f(F) by open sets W_j of Y. The sets f^(-1)(W_j) are open in X because f is continuous. They cover F. A finite subfamily covers F, and the matching W_j cover f(F).
f(F) is a compact subset of the Hausdorff space Y, so f(F) is closed. This follows from the separation of a compact set from a point outside it.
So f is a closed map. Now let f be bijective. The inverse g = f^(-1) is a map from Y to X. For a closed set F of X, the preimage g^(-1)(F) equals f(F) because f is bijective.

The set f(F) is closed by the first part. So the preimage under g of every closed set is closed. Hence g is continuous. Since f and g are continuous bijections that invert each other, f is a homeomorphism.

applications.title: The map t -> t^2 + t is a homeomorphism from [0, 1] onto [0, 2]
applications.inputs: Take f(t) = t^2 + t from X = [0, 1] to Y = [0, 2]. The space X is compact. The space Y is Hausdorff as a subspace of R.
applications.hypotheses: f is continuous as a polynomial. f is strictly increasing on [0, 1] because its derivative 2t + 1 is positive, so f is injective. f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 2, so by the intermediate value theorem f is onto [0, 2].

steps.text: Compute the end values. At t = 1 the value is f(1) = 1 + 1.
Compute an inner value to check the order. At t = 1/2 the value is f(1/2) = 1/4 + 1/2.
The values 0 < 3/4 < 2 are in the same order as the inputs 0 < 1/2 < 1, which agrees with strict increase. So f is a continuous bijection from [0, 1] onto [0, 2].
By the theorem, f is a homeomorphism. The inverse is continuous, with no formula for it needed. The inverse sends 3/4 to 1/2.

applications.conclusion: The inverse of t -> t^2 + t is continuous on [0, 2] by the theorem. Compactness of the domain is essential: the map t -> (cos t, sin t) from [0, 2 pi) to the circle is a continuous bijection that is not a homeomorphism.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: A space is connected exactly when every continuous map to {0, 1} is constant. Indeed, a nonconstant continuous map h gives the disjoint nonempty open sets h^(-1)(0) and h^(-1)(1), and a separation into two open sets A and B gives such a map. So take a continuous map f: X x Y -> {0, 1}. We show that f is constant.

Fix a base point (x0, y0) in X x Y. Each slice map j_x: Y -> X x Y is continuous, because its components are a constant map and the identity. So f composed with j_x is a continuous map from Y to {0, 1}.
Y is connected, so f(x, y) = f(x, y0) for every y in Y. This holds for every x in X.
The slice map i_(y0): X -> X x Y is continuous, so f composed with i_(y0) is a continuous map from X to {0, 1}. X is connected, so f(x, y0) = f(x0, y0) for every x in X.
Combine the two equalities: f(x, y) = f(x, y0) = f(x0, y0) for all x, y. So f is constant. Hence X x Y is connected.
For n spaces, apply the result to X_1 x ... x X_(n-1) and X_n. This space is homeomorphic to the product of n spaces. Induction on n completes the proof.

applications.title: A continuous function on the unit square takes every value between two of its values
applications.inputs: Take the function g(x, y) = x^2 + 2xy on the square [0, 1] x [0, 1]. We have g(0, 0) = 0 and g(1, 1) = 3.
applications.hypotheses: [0, 1] is connected, so the square [0, 1] x [0, 1] is connected by the theorem. The function g is continuous as a polynomial.

steps.text: The image of a connected space under a continuous map is connected. So g([0,1]^2) is a connected subset of R, which is an interval. It contains g(0, 0) = 0 and g(1, 1).
An interval that contains 0 and 3 contains all numbers between them, so it contains 2. This proves that g takes the value 2 at some point of the square.
A point where g takes the value 2 is (1, 1/2). We check g(1, 1/2) = 1 + 1.

applications.conclusion: The connectedness of the square forces the value 2 to be taken by g. The point (1, 1/2) is one such point.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: A space is connected exactly when every continuous map h: X -> {0, 1}, with the discrete topology on {0, 1}, is constant. Let h be such a map. We show that h is constant.
Fix a point x0 in X and let x be any point of X. Choose a path gamma: [0, 1] -> X from x0 to x. The composition h o gamma is a continuous map from [0, 1] to {0, 1}.
The interval [0, 1] is connected. So every continuous map from [0, 1] to {0, 1} is constant. Hence (h o gamma)(0) = (h o gamma)(1).
This says h(x0) = h(x). The point x was arbitrary, so h is constant on X. Hence X is connected.

The converse fails. The topologist's sine curve is the closure of the graph {(x, sin(1/x)) : 0 < x <= 1} in the plane. It is connected as the closure of a connected set, but no path joins a point on the vertical segment {0} x [-1, 1] to a point of the graph. So connected does not imply path connected.

applications.title: The unit circle without the point (-1, 0) is connected
applications.inputs: Take the circle S = {(u, v): u^2 + v^2 = 1} without the point (-1, 0). Use the rational parametrization phi(t) = ((1 - t^2)/(1 + t^2), 2t/(1 + t^2)) for t in R.
applications.hypotheses: phi is continuous on R because the denominator 1 + t^2 is never zero. Its image lies on the circle and misses (-1, 0). Every point of the circle except (-1, 0) is phi(t) for one real t.

steps.text: At t = 2 the first coordinate of phi(2) is (1 - 4)/(1 + 4).
At t = 2 the second coordinate of phi(2) is 4/5.
The point phi(2) lies on the circle, since the squares of its coordinates add to 1.

The restriction of phi to the parameter interval [0, 2] is a path from phi(0) = (1, 0) to phi(2) = (-3/5, 4/5). In the same way, phi restricted to the interval between the parameters s and t joins phi(s) to phi(t). So any two points of the circle without (-1, 0) are joined by a path in it.
By the theorem, the circle without the point (-1, 0) is connected.

applications.conclusion: The circle with one point removed is connected, because it is path connected through the parametrization phi.

source.alignment: The Lean statement is for any locally path connected space. The authored statement is the special case of a normed real vector space, where balls are convex and hence path connected.

steps.text: If U is path connected, then U is connected by the previous result. So assume U is open and connected. Fix a point a in U. Let A be the set of points x in U that can be joined to a by a path inside U. A contains a (constant path), so A is nonempty.

A is open. Let x be in A. Since U is open, there is a ball B(x, r) contained in U. For y in the ball, the segment path from x to y stays in the ball, hence in U. Join a to x by a path in U and then x to y by the segment. The result is a path in U from a to y. So B(x, r) is contained in A.

The set U minus A is open. Let x be in U minus A. Choose a ball B(x, r) contained in U. Suppose some y in the ball were in A. Then a path in U from a to y followed by the segment from y to x would join a to x in U, so x would be in A. This is false. Hence B(x, r) is contained in U minus A.
So U is the union of the two disjoint open sets A and U minus A, and A is nonempty. Since U is connected, U minus A must be empty. Hence A = U.
Now let p, q be in U. Both are joined to a by paths in U. Reverse the path from a to p and follow it with the path from a to q. This path lies in U and joins p to q. So U is path connected.

applications.title: Two overlapping open disks form a path connected set

applications.hypotheses: U is open as a union of open disks. D1 and D2 are convex, so each is connected. The point m = (3/4, 0) lies in both disks, so U is a union of two connected sets with a common point and U is connected.

steps.text: Check that m is in D2. The distance from m to the center (3/2, 0) is 3/2 - 3/4, which is less than 1.
Check that q is in D2. The distance from q to the center (3/2, 0) is 12/5 - 3/2, which is less than 1.
The point p has distance 9/10 from the center (0, 0) of D1, and m has distance 3/4 from it. Both are less than 1, so p and m are in D1.

U is open and connected, so the theorem says that U is path connected. The proof gives the path explicitly: the segment from p to m inside D1, followed by the segment from m to q inside D2. Each segment stays in one disk because a disk is convex.

applications.conclusion: The union U of the two disks is path connected. The path from p to q goes through the common point m = (3/4, 0).

results.name: Nonempty perfect sets in complete metric spaces are uncountable
aliases: perfect set theorem for closed sets without isolated points
results.statement: Let (X, d) be a complete metric space and let P be a nonempty closed subset of X with no isolated points. Then P is uncountable.
hypotheses: (X, d) is a complete metric space.
P is a nonempty closed subset of X.
P has no isolated points: every point p of P is a limit of points of P different from p. A closed set with this property is called perfect.

prerequisites.reason: The proof applies the Baire category theorem to the complete metric space P.

definitions.name: Baire category theorem
definitions.text: A nonempty complete metric space is not the union of countably many closed sets that each have empty interior.

definitions.name: interior in P
definitions.text: The interior of a subset A of P relative to P is the largest set open in P that is contained in A.

theorem Perfect.exists_nat_bool_injection
    (hC : Perfect C) (hnonempty : C.Nonempty) [CompleteSpace α] :
    ∃ f : (ℕ → Bool) → α, range f ⊆ C ∧ Continuous f ∧ Injective f := by
  obtain ⟨u, -, upos', hu⟩ := exists_seq_strictAnti_tendsto' (zero_lt_one' ℝ≥0∞)
  have upos := fun n => (upos' n).1
  let P := Subtype fun E : Set α => Perfect E ∧ E.Nonempty
  choose C0 C1 h0 h1 hdisj using
    fun {C : Set α} (hC : Perfect C) (hnonempty : C.Nonempty) {ε : ℝ≥0∞} (hε : 0 < ε) =>
    hC.small_diam_splitting hnonempty hε
  let DP : List Bool → P := fun l => by
    induction l with
    | nil => exact ⟨C, ⟨hC, hnonempty⟩⟩
    | cons a l ih =>
      cases a
      · use C0 ih.property.1 ih.property.2 (upos (l.length + 1))
        exact ⟨(h0 _ _ _).1, (h0 _ _ _).2.1⟩
      use C1 ih.property.1 ih.property.2 (upos (l.length + 1))
      exact ⟨(h1 _ _ _).1, (h1 _ _ _).2.1⟩
  let D : List Bool → Set α := fun l => (DP l).val
  have hanti : ClosureAntitone D := by
    refine Antitone.closureAntitone ?_ fun l => (DP l).property.1.closed
    intro l a
    cases a
    · exact (h0 _ _ _).2.2.1
    exact (h1 _ _ _).2.2.1
  have hdiam : VanishingDiam D := by
    intro x
    apply tendsto_of_tendsto_of_tendsto_of_le_of_le' tendsto_const_nhds hu
    · simp
    rw [eventually_atTop]
    refine ⟨1, fun m (hm : 1 ≤ m) => ?_⟩
    rw [Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero] at hm
    rcases Nat.exists_eq_succ_of_ne_zero hm with ⟨n, rfl⟩
    dsimp
    cases x n
    · convert (h0 _ _ _).2.2.2
      rw [PiNat.res_length]
    convert (h1 _ _ _).2.2.2
    rw [PiNat.res_length]
  have hdisj' : CantorScheme.Disjoint D := by
    rintro l (a | a) (b | b) hab <;> try contradiction
    · exact hdisj _ _ _
    exact (hdisj _ _ _).symm
  have hdom : ∀ {x : ℕ → Bool}, x ∈ (inducedMap D).1 := fun {x} => by
    rw [hanti.map_of_vanishingDiam hdiam fun l => (DP l).property.2]
    apply mem_univ
  refine ⟨fun x => (inducedMap D).2 ⟨x, hdom⟩, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · rintro y ⟨x, rfl⟩
    exact map_mem ⟨_, hdom⟩ 0
  · apply hdiam.map_continuous.comp
    fun_prop
  intro x y hxy
  simpa only [← Subtype.val_inj] using hdisj'.map_injective hxy

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: P is closed in the complete space X, so P with the metric d is complete. Every Cauchy sequence in P converges in X, and the limit is in P because P is closed.
Suppose that P is countable. P is nonempty, so list its points as p_1, p_2, p_3, ... (repeats allowed). Then P is the union of the singletons {p_n}.
Each singleton {p_n} is closed in P, because points are closed in a metric space.

Each singleton {p_n} has empty interior relative to P. If {p_n} were open in P, there would be a radius r > 0 with no point of P other than p_n in the ball B(p_n, r). Then p_n would be an isolated point of P. This contradicts the hypothesis.

So the nonempty complete metric space P is a countable union of closed sets with empty interior. By the Baire category theorem, this is impossible, because the union is all of P and P has nonempty interior in itself.
The assumption that P is countable is false. Hence P is uncountable.

applications.title: The Cantor ternary set is uncountable
applications.inputs: Let C_0 = [0, 1]. Let C_(n+1) be C_n with the open middle third removed from each of its intervals. Then C = the intersection of all C_n, a subset of the complete space R.
applications.hypotheses: C is closed as an intersection of closed sets. C is nonempty because 0 belongs to every C_n. C has no isolated points, as the steps show.

steps.text: C_n is the union of 2^n closed intervals, each of length 3^(-n). For n = 4 there are 16 intervals of length 1/81.
The total length of C_4 is 16/81, which is (2/3)^4. The total length goes to 0, but every endpoint of every interval stays in C.

Take x in C and n >= 1. Then x lies in an interval I of C_n with length 3^(-n). Both endpoints of I belong to C. At least one endpoint differs from x. So there is a point of C, different from x, at distance at most 3^(-n) from x.
For n = 4 this distance is at most 1/81. The distance bound 3^(-n) goes to 0, so x is a limit of other points of C. Hence C has no isolated points.
C is a nonempty closed subset of the complete space R with no isolated points. By the theorem, C is uncountable.

applications.conclusion: The Cantor set is uncountable, although it has total length zero. The same argument shows that R itself is uncountable, since R is perfect.

results.name: McShane extension of real Lipschitz functions
results.statement: Let (X, d) be a metric space, let A be a subset of X, let K >= 0, and let f: A -> R satisfy |f(a) - f(b)| <= K d(a, b) for all a, b in A. Then there is a function g: X -> R with |g(x) - g(y)| <= K d(x, y) for all x, y in X and g(a) = f(a) for all a in A. One choice is g(x) = inf over a in A of ( f(a) + K d(x, a) ).
hypotheses: (X, d) is a metric space.
A is a nonempty subset of X. For empty A, take g = 0.
K is a real number with K >= 0.
f: A -> R is K-Lipschitz on A. The target is the real line, not a general metric space.

definitions.name: K-Lipschitz
definitions.text: A function h is K-Lipschitz on a set S if |h(x) - h(y)| <= K d(x, y) for all x, y in S.

theorem LipschitzOnWith.extend_real {f : α → ℝ} {s : Set α} {K : ℝ≥0} (hf : LipschitzOnWith K f s) :
    ∃ g : α → ℝ, LipschitzWith K g ∧ EqOn f g s := by
  /- An extension is given by `g y = Inf {f x + K * dist y x | x ∈ s}`. Taking `x = y`, one has
    `g y ≤ f y` for `y ∈ s`, and the other inequality holds because `f` is `K`-Lipschitz, so that it
    cannot counterbalance the growth of `K * dist y x`. One readily checks from the formula that
    the extended function is also `K`-Lipschitz. -/
  rcases eq_empty_or_nonempty s with (rfl | hs)
  · exact ⟨fun _ => 0, (LipschitzWith.const _).weaken zero_le, eqOn_empty _ _⟩
  have : Nonempty s := by simp only [hs, nonempty_coe_sort]
  let g := fun y : α => iInf fun x : s => f x + K * dist y x
  have B : ∀ y : α, BddBelow (range fun x : s => f x + K * dist y x) := fun y => by
    rcases hs with ⟨z, hz⟩
    refine ⟨f z - K * dist y z, ?_⟩
    rintro w ⟨t, rfl⟩
    dsimp
    rw [sub_le_iff_le_add, add_assoc, ← mul_add, add_comm (dist y t)]
    calc
      f z ≤ f t + K * dist z t := hf.le_add_mul hz t.2
      _ ≤ f t + K * (dist y z + dist y t) := by gcongr; apply dist_triangle_left
  have E : EqOn f g s := fun x hx => by
    refine le_antisymm (le_ciInf fun y => hf.le_add_mul hx y.2) ?_
    simpa only [add_zero, Subtype.coe_mk, mul_zero, dist_self] using ciInf_le (B x) ⟨x, hx⟩
  refine ⟨g, LipschitzWith.of_le_add_mul K fun x y => ?_, E⟩
  rw [← sub_le_iff_le_add]
  refine le_ciInf fun z => ?_
  rw [sub_le_iff_le_add]
  calc
    g x ≤ f z + K * dist x z := ciInf_le (B x) _
    _ ≤ f z + K * dist y z + K * dist x y := by
      rw [add_assoc, ← mul_add, add_comm (dist y z)]
      gcongr
      apply dist_triangle

steps.text: Define g(x) = inf over a in A of ( f(a) + K d(x, a) ). First we show that this infimum is a real number. Fix a0 in A and x in X. For every a in A, the Lipschitz inequality gives f(a) >= f(a0) - K d(a, a0).

The triangle inequality gives d(a, a0) <= d(a, x) + d(x, a0). So f(a) + K d(x, a) >= f(a0) - K d(a, x) - K d(x, a0) + K d(x, a) = f(a0) - K d(x, a0). The set of values is bounded below, so the infimum is a real number.
Show that g = f on A. Let b be in A. Taking a = b gives g(b) <= f(b) + K d(b, b) = f(b).
For every a in A, the Lipschitz inequality gives f(b) <= f(a) + K d(a, b) = f(a) + K d(b, a). So f(b) is a lower bound of all the values, and g(b) >= f(b). Hence g(b) = f(b).
Show that g is K-Lipschitz. Let x, y be in X. For every a in A, g(x) <= f(a) + K d(x, a) <= f(a) + K d(y, a) + K d(x, y), by the triangle inequality d(x, a) <= d(x, y) + d(y, a).
Take the infimum over a in A on the right side. This gives g(x) <= g(y) + K d(x, y). Exchange x and y to get g(y) <= g(x) + K d(x, y). So |g(x) - g(y)| <= K d(x, y).

applications.title: Extend a 2-Lipschitz function from two points to the real line
applications.inputs: Take X = R, A = {0, 1}, f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 2, and K = 2.
applications.hypotheses: |f(0) - f(1)| = 2 and K d(0, 1) = 2, so 2 <= 2 and f is 2-Lipschitz on A.

steps.text: The extension is g(x) = min( 0 + 2|x|, 2 + 2|x - 1| ). At x = 1/2 the first value is 2 times 1/2 and the second value is 2 + 2 times 1/2.
Compare the two values at x = 1/2. The first value is 1 and the second value is 3, so g(1/2) = 1.
At x = 3 the first value is 6 and the second value is 2 + 2 times 2 = 6. So g(3) = 6.
Check the Lipschitz bound between x = 1/2 and x = 3. The difference of values is 6 - 1 = 5. The bound is K |3 - 1/2| = 2 times 5/2.
The difference 5 is at most the bound 5, so the inequality holds. At the points of A we have g(0) = 0 and g(1) = min(2, 2) = 2, which agree with f.

applications.conclusion: The function g(x) = min(2|x|, 2 + 2|x - 1|) is 2-Lipschitz on R and agrees with f at 0 and 1.

results.statement: Let (X, d) be a metric space, let D be a dense subset of X, let (Y, e) be a complete metric space, and let f: D -> Y be uniformly continuous. Then there is exactly one continuous function F: X -> Y with F(x) = f(x) for all x in D. This F is uniformly continuous.

f is uniformly continuous: for every eps > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(a, b) < delta implies e(f(a), f(b)) < eps for a, b in D.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: A uniformly continuous map sends Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences. If (a_n) is Cauchy in D and eps > 0, take delta from uniform continuity. For large m, n we have d(a_m, a_n) < delta, so e(f(a_m), f(a_n)) < eps.
Define F. Let x be in X. Choose a sequence (a_n) in D with a_n -> x. It is Cauchy in X, hence in D, so (f(a_n)) is Cauchy in Y. Y is complete, so f(a_n) converges. Put F(x) = lim f(a_n).

F(x) does not depend on the sequence. Let (b_n) be another sequence in D with b_n -> x. Then d(a_n, b_n) -> 0, so by uniform continuity e(f(a_n), f(b_n)) -> 0. The two limits are equal. If x is in D, the constant sequence gives F(x) = f(x).
F is uniformly continuous. Let eps > 0 and choose delta for eps/2 in the uniform continuity of f. Let x, y in X with d(x, y) < delta. Choose a_n -> x and b_n -> y in D.

Since d(a_n, b_n) <= d(a_n, x) + d(x, y) + d(y, b_n) and the first and last terms go to 0, we have d(a_n, b_n) < delta for large n. So e(f(a_n), f(b_n)) < eps/2 for large n. The metric e is continuous, so passing to the limit gives e(F(x), F(y)) <= eps/2 < eps.
Uniqueness. Let G be a continuous function on X with G = f on D. For x in X and a_n -> x with a_n in D, G(x) = lim G(a_n) = lim f(a_n) = F(x), by continuity of G. So G = F.

applications.title: Extend the squaring map from the rationals of [0, 1] to the real interval [0, 1]
applications.inputs: Take X = [0, 1], D = the rational numbers in [0, 1], Y = R and f(q) = q^2. Approximate the irrational point x = sqrt(2)/2 by rationals 7/10 and 707/1000.
applications.hypotheses: D is dense in [0, 1]. R is complete. For p, q in [0, 1], |p^2 - q^2| = |p - q| (p + q) <= 2 |p - q|, so f is uniformly continuous with delta = eps/2.

steps.text: The first approximation gives f(7/10) = 49/100. The second gives f(707/1000) = 499849/1000000.
The two rationals differ by 7/1000. The uniform continuity bound says that the values differ by at most 2 times 7/1000.
The actual difference of values is 499849/1000000 - 49/100 = 9849/1000000, which is below the bound 7/500 = 14000/1000000. So the Cauchy estimate holds.
As the rationals tend to sqrt(2)/2, the values f(a_n) are Cauchy and converge to 1/2. So F(sqrt(2)/2) = 1/2, which is the square of sqrt(2)/2.

applications.conclusion: The unique continuous extension of q -> q^2 from the rationals of [0, 1] to [0, 1] is x -> x^2. It is uniformly continuous with the same constant 2.

(Y, e) is a complete metric space.
A function f: X -> Y is bounded if its image has finite diameter. Then d(f, g) is finite for f, g in C_b(X, Y).

instance instCompleteSpace [CompleteSpace β] : CompleteSpace (α →ᵇ β) :=
  complete_of_cauchySeq_tendsto fun (f : ℕ → α →ᵇ β) (hf : CauchySeq f) => by
    /- We have to show that `f n` converges to a bounded continuous function.
      For this, we prove pointwise convergence to define the limit, then check
      it is a continuous bounded function, and then check the norm convergence. -/
    rcases cauchySeq_iff_le_tendsto_0.1 hf with ⟨b, b0, b_bound, b_lim⟩
    have f_bdd := fun x n m N hn hm => le_trans (dist_coe_le_dist x) (b_bound n m N hn hm)
    have fx_cau : ∀ x, CauchySeq fun n => f n x :=
      fun x => cauchySeq_iff_le_tendsto_0.2 ⟨b, b0, f_bdd x, b_lim⟩
    choose F hF using fun x => cauchySeq_tendsto_of_complete (fx_cau x)
    /- `F : α → β`, `hF : ∀ (x : α), Tendsto (fun n ↦ ↑(f n) x) atTop (𝓝 (F x))`
      `F` is the desired limit function. Check that it is uniformly approximated by `f N`. -/
    have fF_bdd : ∀ x N, dist (f N x) (F x) ≤ b N :=
      fun x N => le_of_tendsto (tendsto_const_nhds.dist (hF x))
        (Filter.eventually_atTop.2 ⟨N, fun n hn => f_bdd x N n N (le_refl N) hn⟩)
    refine ⟨⟨⟨F, ?_⟩, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
    · -- Check that `F` is continuous, as a uniform limit of continuous functions
      have : TendstoUniformly (fun n x => f n x) F atTop := by
        refine Metric.tendstoUniformly_iff.2 fun ε ε0 => ?_
        refine ((tendsto_order.1 b_lim).2 ε ε0).mono fun n hn x => ?_

steps.text: Let (f_n) be a Cauchy sequence in C_b(X, Y). For each x in X, e(f_n(x), f_m(x)) <= d(f_n, f_m). So (f_n(x)) is a Cauchy sequence in Y. Y is complete, so it converges. Define f(x) = lim f_n(x).

Show uniform convergence. Let eps > 0 and choose N with d(f_n, f_m) < eps for n, m >= N. For fixed x and n >= N, e(f_n(x), f_m(x)) < eps for all m >= N. Let m tend to infinity. By continuity of e, e(f_n(x), f(x)) <= eps.
This holds for every x, so sup_x e(f_n(x), f(x)) <= eps for all n >= N. Hence f_n converges to f uniformly.
f is continuous. It is the uniform limit of the continuous functions f_n.

f is bounded. Take eps = 1 and the index N from step 2. For x, x0 in X, e(f(x), f(x0)) <= e(f(x), f_N(x)) + e(f_N(x), f_N(x0)) + e(f_N(x0), f(x0)) <= 1 + diam(f_N(X)) + 1. The bound does not depend on x.
So f is in C_b(X, Y). Step 3 gives d(f_n, f) <= eps for n >= N. Hence f_n converges to f in C_b(X, Y). Every Cauchy sequence converges, so the space is complete.

applications.title: The partial sums of the exponential series converge in C_b([0, 1], R)
applications.inputs: Take X = [0, 1], Y = R, and f_n(x) = the sum of x^k / k! for k = 0, ..., n. These are polynomials, so they are bounded continuous functions on [0, 1].
applications.hypotheses: R is complete. For m > n and x in [0, 1], |f_m(x) - f_n(x)| <= the sum of 1/k! for k from n+1 to m, so d(f_m, f_n) is at most the tail of the series for e, which is small for large n.

steps.text: The next term is 1/4! = 1/24. So f_4(1) - f_3(1) = 1/24, and d(f_4, f_3) = 1/24 because the terms x^k / k! are largest at x = 1.
The tail after n = 3 is at most (1/4!) times 1/(1 - 1/4) = 1/24 times 4/3. Each later term is at most one fourth of the one before it.

So d(f_m, f_3) <= 1/18 for all m >= 3, and the same tail estimate shows that (f_n) is Cauchy. By the theorem, f_n converges uniformly to a bounded continuous function f on [0, 1]. This f is x -> exp(x).

applications.conclusion: The sequence of partial sums is Cauchy in C_b([0, 1], R), so its limit exp is continuous on [0, 1], and its sup distance from f_3 is at most 1/18.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: It is enough to show that every norm N on V satisfies m |x|_1 <= N(x) <= M |x|_1 for constants 0 < m <= M. Then c N_1 <= N_2 <= C N_1 follows by comparing both norms with |.|_1: take c = m_2 / M_1 and C = M_2 / m_1.
Upper bound. Put M = max over i of N(e_i). By the triangle inequality and homogeneity, N(x) <= sum |x_i| N(e_i) <= M |x|_1. M > 0 because the basis vectors are nonzero.

N is continuous for |.|_1. By the triangle inequality, |N(x) - N(y)| <= N(x - y) <= M |x - y|_1. In coordinates, the set S is closed and bounded in R^n, so S is compact by the Heine-Borel theorem. S is nonempty because e_1 is in S.
N is continuous on the nonempty compact set S, so it attains a minimum m at some point x* of S. The point x* is nonzero because |x*|_1 = 1. Since N is positive definite, m = N(x*) > 0.
Lower bound. Let x be nonzero. The vector x / |x|_1 lies in S. By homogeneity, N(x) = |x|_1 N(x / |x|_1) >= m |x|_1. For x = 0 both sides are 0. So m |x|_1 <= N(x) <= M |x|_1.

Apply this to N_1 and N_2. Then N_2(x) <= M_2 |x|_1 <= (M_2 / m_1) N_1(x), and N_2(x) >= m_2 |x|_1 >= (m_2 / M_1) N_1(x). Equivalent norms have the same open balls up to scaling, so they give the same topology and the same Cauchy sequences.

applications.title: The maximum norm and the l1 norm on R^2
applications.inputs: Take V = R^2 with the standard basis e_1, e_2. Take N(x) = max(|x_1|, |x_2|) and compare it with |x|_1 = |x_1| + |x_2|. Test the point x = (3, -1).
applications.hypotheses: N is a norm on R^2. N(e_1) = N(e_2) = 1, so M = 1. On S, |x_1| + |x_2| = 1, so the larger of the two coordinates is at least 1/2.

steps.text: On S the minimum of N is attained at (1/2, 1/2), where |x_1| + |x_2| = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 and N = 1/2. So m = 1/2.
The lower bound at x = (3, -1): |x|_1 = 3 + 1 = 4.
Then m |x|_1 = (1/2) times 4 = 2, and N(x) = 3 and M |x|_1 = 4. The inequality 2 <= 3 <= 4 holds.
So (1/2) |x|_1 <= N(x) <= |x|_1 for all x in R^2. This is the equivalence of the maximum norm and the l1 norm with constants 1/2 and 1.

applications.conclusion: The two norms satisfy (1/2)|x|_1 <= max(|x_1|, |x_2|) <= |x|_1. The compactness argument also proves this for norms with no explicit formula.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: For each integer n >= 1, total boundedness gives a finite set F_n in X such that every point of X is within distance less than 1/n of a point of F_n.
Let D be the union of the sets F_n for n >= 1. A countable union of finite sets is countable, so D is countable.
D is dense. Let x be in X and e > 0. Choose n with 1/n < e. There is a point q in F_n with d(x, q) < 1/n < e. So every ball around x meets D.
Now the base. Let U be open and let x be in U. Choose r > 0 with B(x, r) in U. Choose m with 2/m < r. By density, there is q in D with d(q, x) < 1/m.

Then x is in B(q, 1/m). For z in B(q, 1/m), d(z, x) <= d(z, q) + d(q, x) < 2/m < r. So B(q, 1/m) is contained in B(x, r), hence in U. The balls B(q, 1/m) with q in D and m >= 1 form a base. There are countably many of them.
A compact metric space is totally bounded by the compactness criterion. So the result applies to every compact metric space.

steps.text: The grid F_10 has 11 values for each coordinate. The number of grid points is 11 times 11.
The point x = (37/100, 13/25) has nearest grid point (2/5, 1/2). The squared distance is (2/5 - 37/100)^2 + (1/2 - 13/25)^2.
We compare with the squared radius 1/n^2 = 1/100 = 100/10000. Since 13/10000 < 100/10000, the point x is within 1/10 of F_10.

The union D of all F_n is the set of points of the square with rational coordinates and denominators dividing some n. It is countable and dense. The balls of rational center and radius 1/m form a countable base of the square.

applications.conclusion: The unit square is separable and second countable. The countable dense set is the set of points of the square with rational coordinates.

results.name: Classification of linear isometries of the complex plane
results.statement: Let f: C -> C be a bijective R-linear map with |f(z)| = |z| for every z in C. Then there is a complex number a with |a| = 1 such that f(z) = a z for every z, or f(z) = a conj(z) for every z. Conversely, each of these two maps is a bijective R-linear isometry. The first kind are the rotations about 0. The second kind are the reflections in lines through 0 (followed by a rotation).
hypotheses: C is regarded as the real vector space R^2 with the Euclidean norm |x + iy| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
f is R-linear: f(s z + t w) = s f(z) + t f(w) for real s, t and complex z, w. It is not assumed to be C-linear.
f preserves the norm: |f(z)| = |z| for every z in C. Bijectivity follows from this in dimension 2, and it is assumed here to match the formal statement.

source.alignment: The formal statement uses a linear isometric equivalence of C over R and a unit-circle element a. The conjugate case is written there as conjLIE followed by a rotation, which is the map z -> a conj(z).

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Polarization: for all z, w, Re(z conj(w)) = (|z + w|^2 - |z|^2 - |w|^2) / 2. Since f is linear and preserves the norm, |f(z) + f(w)|^2 = |f(z + w)|^2 = |z + w|^2. Hence Re(f(z) conj(f(w))) = Re(z conj(w)) for all z, w.
Put a = f(1). Then |a| = |1| = 1. Define g(z) = conj(a) f(z). The map g is R-linear, it preserves the modulus because |conj(a)| = 1, and g(1) = conj(a) a = |a|^2 = 1.
Apply step 1 to g with w = 1. Since g(1) = 1, Re(g(z)) = Re(g(z) conj(g(1))) = Re(z conj(1)) = Re(z) for every z. So g does not change the real part of any number.
Take z = i. Then Re(g(i)) = Re(i) = 0, and |g(i)| = |i| = 1. So g(i) = ti with t real and |t| = 1. Hence g(i) = i or g(i) = -i.
Every z is x + i y with x, y real. By R-linearity and g(1) = 1, g(x + i y) = x + y g(i). If g(i) = i, then g(z) = z for all z. If g(i) = -i, then g(z) = x - i y = conj(z) for all z.

Since a conj(a) = 1, f(z) = a g(z). So f(z) = a z in the first case and f(z) = a conj(z) in the second case. For the converse, |a z| = |a||z| = |z| and |a conj(z)| = |z|. The map z -> a z has the inverse z -> conj(a) z, because conj(a) a = 1. The map z -> a conj(z) is its own inverse: if w = a conj(z), then conj(w) = conj(a) z, so a conj(w) = a conj(a) z = z. So both maps are bijective.

applications.title: Identify an isometry from two data
applications.inputs: Let f be an R-linear norm-preserving bijection of C with f(1) = (3 + 4i)/5 and Re f(i) = 4/5. Decide whether f is a rotation or a reflection, and find a fixed line.
applications.hypotheses: f is R-linear and preserves |z|, so the classification applies. The value a = f(1) = 3/5 + (4/5) i is given.

steps.text: Check |a| = 1 as the theorem requires. The squared modulus is (3/5)^2 + (4/5)^2.
If f were the rotation z -> a z, then Re f(i) = Re(i a) = (3/5)(0) - (4/5)(1). This is the real part of a product (x + iy)(u + iv) = xu - yv with i = (0, 1).
This value -4/5 is not the given value 4/5, so f is not a rotation. By the classification f(z) = a conj(z). Then f(i) = -i a = (4 - 3i)/5, whose real part is 4/5 as given.
Find a fixed vector. The image of 2 + i is a conj(2 + i) = a (2 - i) = (3 + 4i)(2 - i)/5. The real part is (3*2 + 4*1)/5.
The imaginary part of (3 + 4i)(2 - i)/5 is (4*2 - 3*1)/5.

applications.conclusion: The map f is the reflection z -> ((3 + 4i)/5) conj(z). It fixes 2 + i, so it is the reflection in the line through 0 and 2 + i.

results.name: Conformal linear maps of the plane and holomorphic conformality
aliases: holomorphic maps with nonzero derivative are conformal
results.statement: Let L: C -> C be a nonzero R-linear map. Then L is conformal, which means L = c U with a real number c > 0 and a norm-preserving R-linear map U, if and only if there is a nonzero complex number alpha such that L(z) = alpha z for all z, or L(z) = alpha conj(z) for all z. Consequently, if f is complex differentiable at z0 and f'(z0) is not 0, then the real derivative Df(z0) is the map h -> f'(z0) h. It is conformal: it multiplies all lengths by |f'(z0)| and rotates all directions by arg f'(z0).
hypotheses: C is regarded as the real vector space R^2 with the Euclidean norm.
L is R-linear and L is not the zero map.
For the consequence, f is defined on a neighbourhood of z0 and is complex differentiable at z0 with f'(z0) not equal to 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step 2 writes the isometry part U of a conformal map as a rotation or as a reflection followed by a rotation.

definitions.name: conformal linear map
definitions.text: A nonzero R-linear map L: C -> C is conformal if L = c U with c > 0 and U a linear isometry. Then L multiplies every length by c and keeps every angle between nonzero vectors.

definitions.name: real derivative
definitions.text: A map f is real differentiable at z0 if f(z0 + h) = f(z0) + Df(z0)(h) + o(|h|) for an R-linear map Df(z0).

steps.text: Suppose L(z) = alpha z with alpha not 0. Write alpha = |alpha| u with |u| = 1. Then L = c U with c = |alpha| and U(z) = u z. Also |u z| = |z|, so U is a linear isometry. The case L(z) = alpha conj(z) is the same with U(z) = u conj(z).
Suppose L = c U with c > 0 and U a norm-preserving R-linear map. U is injective because |U(z)| = |z|. An injective linear map of R^2 into R^2 is bijective. Hence U is a bijective isometry.

By the classification of linear isometries, there is u with |u| = 1 such that U(z) = u z for all z, or U(z) = u conj(z) for all z. So L(z) = (c u) z or L(z) = (c u) conj(z). Put alpha = c u. Then alpha is not 0 because c > 0.

Matrix form. Let alpha = p + iq and z = x + iy. Then alpha z = (px - qy) + i(qx + py), with matrix [[p, -q], [q, p]] and determinant p^2 + q^2 > 0. Also alpha conj(z) = (px + qy) + i(qx - py), with matrix [[p, q], [q, -p]] and determinant -(p^2 + q^2) < 0. The first kind keeps orientation. The second reverses it. The first kind is the Cauchy-Riemann form: the entries satisfy A = D and B = -C.

Now let f be complex differentiable at z0. Then f(z0 + h) = f(z0) + f'(z0) h + o(|h|). The map h -> f'(z0) h is R-linear, so it is the real derivative Df(z0). It has the form L(z) = alpha z with alpha = f'(z0), which is not 0.

By the first step with alpha = f'(z0), Df(z0) is conformal with c = |f'(z0)|. Every length at z0 is multiplied by |f'(z0)|. Every direction is rotated by arg f'(z0). So the angle between two curves through z0 is equal to the angle between their images, with orientation kept.

applications.title: Angle preservation for z^2 at 1 + i
applications.inputs: Let f(z) = z^2 and z0 = 1 + i. Check that Df(z0) multiplies lengths by the same factor in two orthogonal directions and keeps them orthogonal.
applications.hypotheses: f is a polynomial, so it is complex differentiable at every point. Its derivative f'(z) = 2z gives f'(1 + i) = 2 + 2i, which is not 0.

steps.text: Df(z0) is multiplication by alpha = 2 + 2i, with matrix [[2, -2], [2, 2]]. Its determinant is 2*2 - (-2)*2 and it must equal |alpha|^2.
The squared modulus of alpha is 2^2 + 2^2.
The image of the unit vector 1 is alpha = (2, 2). The image of the unit vector i is i alpha = (-2, 2). Their dot product is 2*(-2) + 2*2, so the images stay orthogonal.
The squared length of the image of i is (-2)^2 + 2^2, which equals the squared length of the image of 1. So both directions are scaled by sqrt(8).

applications.conclusion: At 1 + i the map z^2 scales all lengths by 2 sqrt(2) and rotates by arg(2 + 2i) = 45 degrees. Two orthogonal curves through 1 + i have orthogonal images.

steps.text: The denominator is not 0. Write z = x + iy with y > 0. Then Im(cz + d) = c y. If c is not 0, this is not 0, so cz + d is not 0. If c = 0, then ad > 0 gives d not 0, so cz + d = d is not 0.
Multiply numerator and denominator by conj(cz + d) = c conj(z) + d. Then g.z = (az + b)(c conj(z) + d) / |cz + d|^2. Expand the numerator: (az + b)(c conj(z) + d) = ac|z|^2 + ad z + bc conj(z) + bd.
The terms ac|z|^2 and bd are real. Also Im(ad z) = ad y and Im(bc conj(z)) = -bc y. So the imaginary part of the numerator is (ad - bc) y. Hence Im(g.z) = (det g) y / |cz + d|^2.
Since det g > 0, y > 0 and |cz + d|^2 > 0, we have Im(g.z) > 0. So g.z is in H. Taking a = d = 1 and b = c = 0 gives 1.z = z.

Cocycle identity. Let h = [[a', b'], [c', d']] and w = h.z, so w (c' z + d') = a' z + b'. The matrix g h has bottom row (c a' + d c', c b' + d d'). So j(g h, z) = c(a' z + b') + d(c' z + d') = c w (c' z + d') + d (c' z + d') = (c w + d) j(h, z).

In the same way the top row of g h gives a(a' z + b') + b(c' z + d') = (a w + b) j(h, z). Dividing, (g h).z = (a w + b)/(c w + d) = g.(h.z). A scalar matrix t I gives (t z)/t = z, so it acts as the identity.

applications.title: Compute an action and check the cocycle
applications.inputs: Let g = [[2, 1], [1, 1]], h = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and z = i. Compute Im(g.i) with the formula, and check Im((g h).i).
applications.hypotheses: det g = 2*1 - 1*1 = 1 > 0 and det h = 1 > 0. Also i is in H.

steps.text: Compute the determinant of the matrix g, which must be positive.
With c = 1 and d = 1, the denominator is i + 1 and |i + 1|^2 = 1^2 + 1^2.
The formula gives Im(g.i) = 1 * 1 / 2. The direct value is g.i = (2i + 1)/(i + 1) = (3 + i)/2.
The real part of g.i is (ac|z|^2 + (ad + bc) x + bd)/|cz + d|^2 with x = 0, which is (2*1*1 + 1*1)/2. This matches (3 + i)/2.
Now g h = [[2, 3], [1, 2]] has determinant 2*2 - 3*1.
For g h, the denominator at i is 1*i + 2 and its squared modulus is 1^2 + 2^2. So Im((g h).i) = 1 * 1 / 5.

Check by composition. h.i = i + 1, and g.(1 + i) = (3 + 2i)/(2 + i) = (8 + i)/5, whose imaginary part is 1/5. This equals the value above. The cocycle sums agree: j(g, h.i) j(h, i) = (1*(1 + i) + 1)(0*i + 1) = 2 + i = j(g h, i).

applications.conclusion: g.i = (3 + i)/2 with imaginary part 1/2, and (g h).i = (8 + i)/5 with imaginary part 1/5. Both agree with the formula, and (g h).i = g.(h.i).

steps.text: For z in H the denominator cz + d is not 0. So g.z = z holds if and only if az + b = z (cz + d), that is, if c z^2 + (d - a) z - b = 0.

Case c = 0. The equation becomes (d - a) z = b. Take imaginary parts: (d - a) Im z = 0, so a = d because Im z > 0. Then b = 0. So g = a I is scalar. Hence a non-scalar g with c = 0 has no fixed point in H. Also D = (a - d)^2 >= 0 when c = 0, so this case is consistent with the statement.
Case c not 0. The equation is a quadratic with real coefficients c, d - a, -b. Its discriminant is (d - a)^2 + 4bc. We have (d - a)^2 + 4bc = a^2 + d^2 - 2ad + 4bc = (a + d)^2 - 4(ad - bc) = D.
If D >= 0, both roots ((a - d) + sqrt(D))/(2c) and ((a - d) - sqrt(D))/(2c) are real. A real number is not in H. So g has no fixed point in H.

If D < 0, the roots are ((a - d) + i sqrt(-D))/(2c) and ((a - d) - i sqrt(-D))/(2c). They are complex conjugates with imaginary parts of opposite sign, because sqrt(-D) > 0. Exactly one has positive imaginary part. Its imaginary part is sqrt(-D)/(2|c|). So the fixed point is z* = (a - d)/(2c) + i sqrt(-D)/(2|c|), and it is the only one.
If g = t I is scalar, then g.z = tz/t = z for all z. So g fixes every point of H. This completes the three cases.

steps.text: The map q(z) = exp(2 pi i z/h) sends the half-plane {Im z > A} onto the punctured disc D*(r) with r = exp(-2 pi A/h). It is onto because exp maps C onto the nonzero complex numbers: for 0 < |q| < r pick z = (h/(2 pi i)) log q for any value of log q. Its modulus is exp(-2 pi Im z/h) < r exactly when Im z > A.

Define F(q) = f(z) for any z in the half-plane with q(z) = q. This is well defined. If q(z) = q(w), then z - w = m h for an integer m, since exp(u) = 1 exactly when u is in 2 pi i Z. Then f(z) = f(w) by h-periodicity.

F is holomorphic on D*(r). Fix q0 = q(z0). The derivative q'(z0) = (2 pi i/h) q0 is not 0. So q has a holomorphic local inverse phi near q0 with phi(q0) = z0, given by phi(q) = z0 + (h/(2 pi i)) Log(q/q0) for the principal logarithm. Near q0 we have F = f o phi, which is holomorphic as a composition.
F is bounded by M on D*(r). By Riemann's theorem on removable singularities, F extends to a holomorphic function on the full disc |q| < r. Put c = F(0).
Because F is holomorphic at 0, F(q) - F(0) = q G(q) with G holomorphic near 0. So there are rho in (0, r) and K with |G(q)| <= K for |q| <= rho. Hence |F(q) - c| <= K |q| for |q| <= rho.

Translate back. For z with |q(z)| <= rho, that is, Im z >= B = -(h/(2 pi)) ln(rho) (with B also at least A), |f(z) - c| = |F(q(z)) - c| <= K |q(z)| = K exp(-2 pi Im z/h). In particular f(z) -> c as Im z -> infinity.

steps.text: Beta identity. For real s, t > 0, Gamma(s) Gamma(t) = integral over x, y > 0 of x^(s-1) y^(t-1) e^(-(x+y)) dx dy by Fubini. Substitute x = u v and y = u (1 - v) with u > 0 and 0 < v < 1. The Jacobian is u. This gives Gamma(s) Gamma(t) = Gamma(s + t) B(s, t).

Take s = a and t = 1 - a with 0 < a < 1. Since Gamma(1) = 1, Gamma(a) Gamma(1 - a) = B(a, 1 - a) = integral_0^1 x^(a-1) (1 - x)^(-a) dx. Substitute x = u/(1 + u). Then dx = du/(1 + u)^2, x^(a-1) = u^(a-1) (1 + u)^(1-a) and (1 - x)^(-a) = (1 + u)^a. The product of the powers of (1 + u) is (1 + u)^(1-a+a-2) = (1 + u)^(-1). So Gamma(a) Gamma(1 - a) = I(a), with I(a) = integral_0^infinity u^(a-1)/(1 + u) du.

Keyhole contour. Let the function h(w) = w^(a-1)/(1 + w) use the branch of the argument in (0, 2 pi) on the plane cut along [0, infinity). Integrate h over the contour that follows the upper edge from r to R, then a big circle, then the lower edge back, then a small circle. The only pole is w = -1 = e^(i pi), with residue e^(i pi (a-1)). The two edges give (1 - e^(2 pi i (a-1))) I(a). The circle integrals tend to 0 as r -> 0 and R -> infinity because 0 < a < 1.

By the residue theorem, (1 - e^(2 pi i a)) I(a) = 2 pi i e^(i pi (a-1)) = -2 pi i e^(i pi a). Divide by e^(i pi a): I(a) (e^(-i pi a) - e^(i pi a)) = -2 pi i. So I(a) (-2 i sin(pi a)) = -2 pi i. Hence I(a) = pi / sin(pi a), and Gamma(a) Gamma(1 - a) = pi / sin(pi a) for 0 < a < 1.

Extension. The function z -> Gamma(z) Gamma(1 - z) is holomorphic on C minus Z, because Gamma(z) is holomorphic off P and Gamma(1 - z) is holomorphic off {1, 2, ...}. The function pi / sin(pi z) is holomorphic on C minus Z. The set C minus Z is open and connected. The two functions agree on (0, 1), which has an accumulation point in the set. By the identity theorem they agree on all of C minus Z.
Special value. Put z = 1/2. Then 1 - z = 1/2 and sin(pi/2) = 1. So Gamma(1/2)^2 = pi. Since Gamma(1/2) is an integral of a positive function, it is positive, so Gamma(1/2) = sqrt(pi).

steps.text: Let Re s > 0. By the Beta identity B(s, t) = Gamma(s) Gamma(t)/Gamma(s + t), which holds for complex s and t with positive real part, B(s, s) = Gamma(s)^2/Gamma(2s) = integral_0^1 (x (1 - x))^(s-1) dx. The integrand is symmetric under x -> 1 - x, so B(s, s) = 2 integral_0^(1/2) (x (1 - x))^(s-1) dx.

Substitute u = 4 x (1 - x) on (0, 1/2). It increases from 0 to 1. Then du = 4 (1 - 2x) dx and 1 - 2x = sqrt(1 - u), because (1 - 2x)^2 = 1 - 4x(1 - x). Also x(1 - x) = u/4. So dx = du/(4 sqrt(1 - u)).

Write both Beta values with Gamma: Gamma(s)^2/Gamma(2s) = 2^(1-2s) Gamma(s) Gamma(1/2)/Gamma(s + 1/2). For Re s > 0, Gamma(s) is not 0 by the result on the zeros of Gamma, so divide by Gamma(s) and rearrange: Gamma(s) Gamma(s + 1/2) = 2^(1-2s) Gamma(1/2) Gamma(2s). The reflection formula at z = 1/2 gives Gamma(1/2) = sqrt(pi).

Extension. Both sides are holomorphic on U = C minus {0, -1/2, -1, ...}. The set U is open and connected. The sides agree on the half-plane Re s > 0, which is a non-empty open subset of U. By the identity theorem they agree on U.

source.alignment: The formal statement says that z -> (Gamma z)^(-1) is differentiable on all of C, with the convention that it is 0 at the poles of Gamma. The zero set and the derivative at -n come from the proof below.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Non-integers. If z is not an integer, then pi/sin(pi z) is a finite number that is not 0. By the reflection formula Gamma(z) Gamma(1 - z) is not 0, so Gamma(z) is not 0.

Positive integers. For an integer n >= 1, the functional equation and Gamma(1) = 1 give Gamma(n) = (n - 1)! by induction, because Gamma(k + 1) = k Gamma(k). This is not 0. Together with step 1, Gamma has no zero on C minus {0, -1, -2, ...}.

Formula near a pole. For n >= 0, repeat the functional equation n + 1 times: Gamma(z + n + 1) = (z + n)(z + n - 1) ... z Gamma(z). So 1/Gamma(z) = z (z + 1) ... (z + n) / Gamma(z + n + 1), for z not in {0, ..., -n}.

The right side of step 3 is holomorphic on the disc |z + n| < 1/2. The factor Gamma(z + n + 1) is holomorphic there, because Re(z + n + 1) > 1/2, and it is not 0 by step 1 and step 2. So the right side defines a holomorphic function that equals 1/Gamma(z) off the poles. This is the removable extension of 1/Gamma, with value 0 at z = -k for k <= n.

Every point z0 of C is of one of two kinds. If z0 is not in {0, -1, -2, ...}, then Gamma is holomorphic and not 0 near z0 by step 2, so 1/Gamma is holomorphic near z0. If z0 = -n with n >= 0, then z0 lies in the disc |z + n| < 1/2 of step 4, where the extension is holomorphic. The extensions agree where the discs overlap, because they all equal 1/Gamma off the poles. So 1/Gamma is entire. At z = -n, the factor z + n is the only vanishing factor in step 3, so the zero is simple. The derivative is (-n)(-n + 1) ... (-1) / Gamma(1) = (-1)^n n!, which is not 0.

applications.title: Derivative of 1/Gamma at -3 and -2

applications.hypotheses: Both points are poles of Gamma, so 1/Gamma has a zero there. The product formula of step 3 holds near each point, and Gamma(1) = 1.

steps.text: For n = 3, 1/Gamma(z) = z (z+1) (z+2) (z+3)/Gamma(z+4). Only the factor (z + 3) vanishes at -3. The derivative equals the product of the other factors at -3, divided by Gamma(1) = 1.
This value equals (-1)^3 times 3!.
For n = 2, 1/Gamma(z) = z (z+1) (z+2)/Gamma(z+3). The derivative at -2 is the product of the other factors at -2, divided by Gamma(1).

applications.conclusion: The derivative of 1/Gamma is -6 at -3 and 2 at -2. Both are not 0, so the zeros are simple, and they match (-1)^n n!.

results.name: Non-emptiness of the spectrum in a complex Banach algebra
results.statement: Let A be a complex Banach algebra with unit 1 and with 1 not equal to 0. Then for every a in A the spectrum sigma(a) = {lambda in C : lambda 1 - a is not invertible in A} is not empty.
hypotheses: A is a complex vector space with an associative multiplication, a unit 1, and a complete norm with ||xy|| <= ||x|| ||y||.
A is nontrivial: 1 is not 0, so A is not the zero algebra.
The scalar field is C. The statement is false over R.

prerequisites.reason: Step 4 applies Liouville's theorem to the bounded entire function phi composed with the resolvent.

Step 3 bounds the norm of the inverse by comparing the Neumann series with the scalar geometric series.

protected theorem nonempty (a : A) : (spectrum ℂ a).Nonempty := by
  /- Suppose `σ a = ∅`, then resolvent set is `ℂ`, any `(z • 1 - a)` is a unit, and `resolvent a`
    is differentiable on `ℂ`. -/
  by_contra! h
  have H₀ : resolventSet ℂ a = Set.univ := by rwa [spectrum, Set.compl_empty_iff] at h
  have H₁ : Differentiable ℂ fun z : ℂ => resolvent a z := fun z =>
    hasDerivAt_resolvent_const_left (H₀.symm ▸ Set.mem_univ z : z ∈ resolventSet ℂ a)
      |>.differentiableAt
  /- Since `resolvent a` tends to zero at infinity, by Liouville's theorem `resolvent a = 0`,
  which contradicts that `resolvent a z` is invertible. -/
  have H₃ := H₁.apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact 0 <| by
    simpa [Metric.cobounded_eq_cocompact] using resolvent_tendsto_cobounded a (𝕜 := ℂ)
  exact not_isUnit_zero <| H₃ ▸ (isUnit_resolvent.mp <| H₀.symm ▸ Set.mem_univ 0)

steps.text: Suppose sigma(a) is empty. Then lambda 1 - a is invertible for every lambda in C, and R(lambda) = (lambda 1 - a)^(-1) is defined on all of C.

R is holomorphic. The set of units is open and inversion is continuous on it in a Banach algebra. For lambda and mu, (lambda 1 - a) - (mu 1 - a) = (lambda - mu) 1, so R(mu) - R(lambda) = (lambda - mu) R(mu) R(lambda). Divide by mu - lambda and let mu -> lambda. Then R'(lambda) = -R(lambda)^2, so R is complex differentiable at every point.

Bound at infinity. Let r = 2 ||a|| + 1 and let |lambda| >= r. Then lambda is not 0 and ||a||/|lambda| <= 1/2, also when a = 0. Then R(lambda) = lambda^(-1) sum_{n>=0} (a/lambda)^n, which converges in norm. Compare with the scalar geometric series: ||R(lambda)|| <= |lambda|^(-1) sum (||a||/|lambda|)^n <= |lambda|^(-1) sum 2^(-n) = 2/|lambda|. So R(lambda) -> 0 as |lambda| -> infinity.

Let phi be any bounded linear functional on A. Then f = phi o R is entire. By the bound of step 3 and continuity of R, f is bounded on the compact disc |lambda| <= r and on its complement |lambda| >= r. So f is bounded and entire, hence constant by Liouville's theorem. The bound of step 3 shows f(lambda) -> 0 as |lambda| -> infinity, so the constant is 0.

Since phi(R(0)) = 0 for every phi in A*, the Hahn-Banach theorem gives R(0) = 0, because for a non-zero element x there is phi with phi(x) = ||x||. But R(0) = (-a)^(-1) is invertible, so it is not 0, because A is nontrivial. This contradicts the assumption. Hence sigma(a) is not empty.

source.alignment: The formal statement says that a harmonic function on a ball is the real part of a function that is analytic on the ball. Analytic and holomorphic are equivalent in one complex variable.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Define g = f_x - i f_y on D. Write g = u + i v with u = f_x and v = -f_y. These are C^1 functions because f is C^2.

Cauchy-Riemann equations for g. First, u_x = f_xx and v_y = -f_yy, and f_xx + f_yy = 0 gives u_x = v_y. Second, u_y = f_xy and v_x = -f_yx. Equality of mixed partials of a C^2 function gives u_y = -v_x. A C^1 function with these two equations is holomorphic, so g is holomorphic on D.
A holomorphic function on a disc has a primitive. So there is a holomorphic G on D with G' = g.
Compute the gradient of Re G. Since G' = g, d(Re G)/dx = Re(G') = Re g = f_x. Also d(Re G)/dy = Re(i G') = -Im(g) = f_y, because Im g = -f_y. So the gradient of Re G - f is 0 on D.
D is connected, so Re G - f is a constant c. Put F = G + c. Then F is holomorphic and Re F = f on D, and F' = G' = f_x - i f_y.

Uniqueness. If F1 and F2 both have real part f, then F1 - F2 is holomorphic with zero real part. By the Cauchy-Riemann equations all its partial derivatives vanish, so it is a constant, and this constant is imaginary.

steps.text: Let f(z) = exp(a Log(1 + z)) on the disc |z| < 1. The map z -> 1 + z sends the disc into the right half-plane, where Log is holomorphic. So f is holomorphic, f(0) = exp(0) = 1, and f'(z) = a f(z)/(1 + z).
A holomorphic function on a disc equals its Taylor series at the centre on the whole disc. So f(z) = sum c_n z^n for |z| < 1, with c_n = f^(n)(0)/n!. The series can be differentiated term by term.

Differential equation. From f'(z) = a f(z)/(1 + z), (1 + z) f'(z) = a f(z). Insert the series: sum (n+1) c_(n+1) z^n + sum n c_n z^n = a sum c_n z^n. Compare coefficients of z^n, which are unique for a power series: (n + 1) c_(n+1) = (a - n) c_n.
Induction. We have c_0 = f(0) = 1 = C(a, 0). If c_n = C(a, n), then c_(n+1) = (a - n) C(a, n)/(n + 1) = a (a - 1) ... (a - n)/(n + 1)! = C(a, n + 1). So c_n = C(a, n) for all n.
Therefore (1 + z)^a = sum C(a, n) z^n for |z| < 1. For natural a, C(a, n) = 0 for n > a, and the series is the finite binomial theorem.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Lemma 1 (rigidity). Let W be a well-order and g: W -> W strictly increasing. Then g(x) >= x for all x. Otherwise the set of x with g(x) < x is nonempty and has a least element x0. Then g(g(x0)) < g(x0) because g is increasing, so g(x0) is a smaller element of the set. This contradicts the choice of x0.

Consequences of Lemma 1. A well-order W is not isomorphic to a proper initial segment W_b of itself. An isomorphism g: W -> W_b would give g(b) < b, which contradicts g(b) >= b. Also, two isomorphisms from W onto the same ordered set are equal, since g = h^(-1) h' is an automorphism of W. Both g and g^(-1) satisfy g(x) >= x, so g(x) = x.

Define D as the set of a in A such that A_a is isomorphic to B_b for some b in B. For a in D the element b is unique, because B_b is isomorphic to B_b' with b < b' would give an isomorphism from B_b' onto a proper initial segment of itself. Write f(a) = b. Let phi_a be the isomorphism A_a -> B_f(a).

The map f is strictly increasing and D is an initial segment of A. If a' < a and a in D, then phi_a restricted to A_a' is an isomorphism onto the initial segment of B_f(a) below phi_a(a'), which is B_phi_a(a'). So a' is in D and f(a') = phi_a(a') < f(a). The image E = f(D) is an initial segment of B, since every c < f(a) equals phi_a(a') for some a' < a.

Case D = A. Then f is an isomorphism from A onto the initial segment E of B. Case D is not A. Let a0 be the least element of A minus D. Then D = A_a0, because D is an initial segment and a0 is not in D. If E were not B, let b0 be the least element of B minus E. Then E = B_b0 and f would be an isomorphism A_a0 -> B_b0. This puts a0 in D, which is false. So E = B, and f^(-1) is an isomorphism from B onto the initial segment A_a0 of A.

In both cases one of the two sets is isomorphic to an initial segment of the other. Uniqueness follows from Lemma 1. Let f, f' be isomorphisms from A onto initial segments L, L' of B. If L differs from L', one is a proper initial segment of the other, say L' inside L. Then L is isomorphic to its proper initial segment L', which Lemma 1 forbids. So L = L', and f^(-1) f' is an automorphism of A, which is the identity.

steps.text: By the well-ordering theorem, choose a well-order on A and a well-order on B.

By the comparability of well-orders, one of the two well-ordered sets is isomorphic to an initial segment of the other. Say A is isomorphic to an initial segment L of B by an isomorphism f: A -> L. The other case is symmetric.
The map f followed by the inclusion L -> B is an injection A -> B. In the symmetric case, the same argument gives an injection B -> A. Hence the relation <= on cardinals is total.

Reflexivity holds by the identity map and transitivity by composition of injections. Antisymmetry holds by the Cantor-Schroeder-Bernstein theorem: injections both ways give a bijection. So <= is a total order.

Trichotomy follows. At least one of |A| <= |B| and |B| <= |A| holds. If both hold, then |A| = |B| by antisymmetry. If only one holds, say |A| <= |B| but not |B| <= |A|, then no bijection exists, because a bijection would give an injection B -> A. So exactly one of the three cases holds.

Count the injections B -> A. The first element a needs one of 3 values, b needs one of 2 values, c needs one of 1 value, and d has no value left.

applications.conclusion: There are 60 injections A -> B and none B -> A, so |A| < |B|. This is the one case of the trichotomy that the data satisfy.

theorem mul_eq_self {c : Cardinal} (hc : ℵ₀ ≤ c) : c * c = c := by
  -- The only nontrivial part is `c * c ≤ c`. We prove it inductively.
  induction c using WellFoundedLT.induction with | ind c IH
  refine le_antisymm ?_ (by simpa using mul_le_mul_right (one_le_aleph0.trans hc) c)
  -- Consider the minimal well-order on `α` (a type with cardinality `c`).
  induction c using Cardinal.inductionOn with | mk α
  obtain ⟨_, _, hα⟩ := exists_ord_eq_type_lt α
  have : NoMaxOrder α := by
    rw [← isSuccPrelimit_type_lt_iff, ← hα]
    exact (isSuccLimit_ord hc).isSuccPrelimit
  -- We embed `α × α` into `α ×ₗ α ×ₗ α` by sending `(x, y)` to `(max x y, x, y)`.
  -- Every initial segment of the embedding is contained in `β × β` for some `#β < c`.
  -- By the inductive hypothesis, this means `#(β × β) < c`, and thus `#(α × α) ≤ c`.
  apply mk_le_of_forall_mk_setOfPred_lt (β := α ×ₗ (α ×ₗ α))
    (fun p ↦ toLex (uncurry max p, toLex p)) (fun _ _ ↦ congrArg Prod.snd)
  intro ⟨a, b⟩
  obtain ⟨q, hq'⟩ := exists_gt (max a b)
  apply lt_of_le_of_lt (b := #(Iio q) * #(Iio q))
  · rw [← mk_setProd]
    apply (Set.embeddingOfSubset ..).cardinal_le
    simp [Prod.Lex.lt_iff, subset_def]
    grind
  rcases lt_or_ge #(Iio q) ℵ₀ with hq | hq
  · exact (mul_lt_aleph0 hq hq).trans_le hc
  · have := mk_Iio_lt q hα
    rwa [IH _ this hq]
