proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Reduction. By the well-ordering theorem every infinite set is in bijection with an infinite initial ordinal. By Cantor-Schroeder-Bernstein, it is enough to find an injection from k x k into k for every infinite initial ordinal k, because the map a -> (a, a0) injects k into k x k.
Case k = omega. The map (m, n) -> 2^m (2n+1) - 1 from N x N to N is a bijection. Each positive integer is 2^m times an odd number 2n+1 in exactly one way, by taking out all factors of 2.

Minimal counterexample. Suppose the claim is false. Since ordinals are well-ordered, there is a least infinite initial ordinal k such that no injection k x k -> k exists. By step 2, k is larger than omega. Every infinite initial ordinal below k has the property that its square injects into it.

Order the set P = k x k by the pair order. This is a well-order, because it is the order induced on P by the lexicographic order of the triples (max(x,y), x, y) in k x k x k, and the lexicographic order of well-orders is a well-order. For p = (x,y), let m = max(x,y). Every predecessor (u,v) of p has max(u,v) <= m, so the set of predecessors lies in B x B with B = {z : z <= m}.

Every proper initial segment of P has cardinality below k. Here m < k. The ordinal k is a limit ordinal, since k is infinite and initial, so B = m+1 < k and |B| < k. If B is finite, B x B is finite. If B is infinite, then |B x B| = |B| < k by the choice of k. Either way the initial segment has size below k.

Apply the comparability of well-orders to (P, before) and (k, <). If P is isomorphic to an initial segment of k, then P injects into k and we have a contradiction. Otherwise k is isomorphic to an initial segment of P. That segment is proper or equal to P. A proper segment has size below k by the previous step, but its size is k. A segment equal to P gives a bijection P -> k, which again gives an injection.

So no least counterexample exists, and k x k injects into k for all infinite initial ordinals. For the corollary, 2 <= k, so k <= k + k <= k * 2 <= k * k = k. Here k + k is the union of two disjoint copies of k, which is in bijection with k x {0, 1}, and k x {0, 1} injects into k x k because 2 <= k.

Invert the pairing. The number 39 + 1 = 40 factors as 2^3 * 5, so m = 3 and 2n+1 = 5, which gives n = 2. This recovers the pair (3, 2).

A polynomial of degree at most d is a tuple of d+1 integers. Since |Z| = ALEPH0, the theorem gives |Z^(d+1)| = ALEPH0 by induction on d, because Z^(d+1) = Z^d x Z has the size of Z x Z, which is that of Z.

Z[x] is the union of a countable family of countable sets, with the sets indexed by d. A union of this kind injects into N x N by (d, tuple) -> (d, index of the tuple), and N x N has size ALEPH0 by the theorem.

steps.text: Lower bound. The map a -> (a) from A into A* is injective, so |A| <= |A*|. Fix an element a0 of A. The sequences (a0, ..., a0) of length 0, 1, 2, ... are distinct, so ALEPH0 <= |A*|. Hence max(ALEPH0, |A|) <= |A*|.

Finite A with k elements, k >= 1. Number the elements 0, ..., k-1. The map (a_1, ..., a_n) -> sum of (a_i + 1)(k+1)^(i-1) is injective on A*, because the digits a_i + 1 lie in 1..k, and an integer has a unique expansion in base k+1 with digits in 1..k. So A* injects into N, and |A*| <= ALEPH0.

Infinite A. Show |A^n| = |A| for n >= 1 by induction. For n = 1 this is clear. If |A^n| = |A|, then A^(n+1) is in bijection with A^n x A, which is in bijection with A x A by the induction hypothesis, and A x A is in bijection with A by the Hessenberg theorem.

For each n >= 1 choose, with the axiom of choice, an injection g_n: A^n -> A. Define h: A* minus the empty sequence -> N x A by h(s) = (length of s, g_length(s)(s)). The map h is injective because the length and the value of g_length(s) determine s.
Hence |A*| <= 1 + |N x A|. By the Hessenberg theorem with ALEPH0 <= |A|, we get |N x A| <= |A x A| = |A|. Adding the single empty sequence does not change an infinite cardinal, so |A*| <= |A|.
Combine the bounds with Cantor-Schroeder-Bernstein. In the finite case, |A*| = ALEPH0 = max(ALEPH0, |A|). In the infinite case, |A*| = |A| = max(ALEPH0, |A|).

steps.text: Suppose, for a contradiction, that X is a cofinal subset of k+ with |X| < k+. Since k+ is the least cardinal above k, |X| <= k.
Each x in X is an ordinal below k+, so x + 1 is also below k+ (k+ is a limit ordinal), and |x + 1| <= k. By the axiom of choice, choose for each x in X an injection g_x: x + 1 -> k.
For each ordinal e < k+, let s(e) be the least x in X with e <= x. This exists because X is cofinal and the ordinals are well-ordered. No further choice is used here.
Define F(e) = (s(e), g_s(e)(e)) in X x k. The map F is injective: if F(e) = F(e'), then s(e) = s(e') =: x, so e and e' are both in x + 1, and g_x(e) = g_x(e') gives e = e' because g_x is injective.
Thus k+ injects into X x k. By the Hessenberg theorem, |X x k| <= k * k = k. So |k+| <= k, which contradicts the definition of k+. Hence every cofinal subset has size k+.

The equivalent form follows. If k+ were the union of at most k sets of size at most k, then a bijection of the index set with a subset of k would give a bound |k+| <= k * k = k, again a contradiction. So a union of at most k sets of size at most k has size at most k.

applications.title: A countable set of countable ordinals is bounded in omega_1
applications.inputs: k = ALEPH0, k+ = omega_1, and the countable family of ordinals a_n = omega^n for n = 1, 2, 3, ...
applications.hypotheses: ALEPH0 is infinite, so the theorem applies. Each omega^n is a countable ordinal, so a_n < omega_1.

steps.text: The set X = {a_n : n >= 1} is countable, so |X| <= ALEPH0 < ALEPH1. By regularity of omega_1, X is not cofinal in omega_1.
Hence some ordinal e < omega_1 lies above every a_n. In fact the supremum of X, which is omega^omega, is itself countable and gives such a bound.

Check with a count of the pieces. The ordinal omega^omega is the union of the sets of ordinals below a_n. Each piece is countable, and there are ALEPH0 pieces. The union of ALEPH0 sets of size ALEPH0 has size ALEPH0 by the equivalent form of the theorem, so omega^omega is countable.

applications.conclusion: Every countable subset of omega_1 is bounded below omega_1, and sup omega^n = omega^omega is a countable ordinal. This is the regularity of omega_1 at work.

results.name: Solution of constant-coefficient linear ODE systems by the matrix exponential
results.statement: Let A be a real n x n matrix and let x0 be in R^n. Define exp(tA) = sum_{k>=0} t^k A^k / k!. Then t -> exp(tA) is differentiable on R with derivative A exp(tA) = exp(tA) A. The curve x(t) = exp(tA) x0 solves x' = A x with x(0) = x0. If I is an open interval containing 0 and y: I -> R^n is a differentiable curve with y' = A y and y(0) = x0, then y(t) = exp(tA) x0 for all t in I.
hypotheses: A is a real n x n matrix with n >= 1, and x0 is a vector in R^n.
The matrix norm is the operator norm of a norm on R^n. It satisfies ||XY|| <= ||X|| ||Y||.
The series for exp(tA) converges absolutely for every real t, because ||t^k A^k / k!|| <= (|t| ||A||)^k / k!.

prerequisites.reason: The identity exp((s+t)A) = exp(sA) exp(tA) follows from the binomial theorem for the commuting matrices sA and tA.
The uniqueness proof shows that a differentiable curve with zero derivative on an interval is constant, using the mean value theorem on each coordinate.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Convergence. ||t^k A^k / k!|| <= (|t| ||A||)^k / k!, and the series of these bounds converges to exp(|t| ||A||). So the series for exp(tA) converges absolutely, and ||exp(tA)|| <= exp(|t| ||A||).

Addition law. The matrices sA and tA commute. The Cauchy product of the two absolutely convergent series and the binomial theorem give exp(sA) exp(tA) = sum_m (s+t)^m A^m / m! = exp((s+t)A). With s = -t this gives exp(tA) exp(-tA) = exp(0) = I. So exp(tA) is invertible, with inverse exp(-tA).
Remainder bound. Let y0 = |s| ||A||. Since k! >= 2 (k-2)! for k >= 2, we get ||exp(sA) - I - sA|| <= sum_{k>=2} y0^k / k! <= (y0^2 / 2) sum_{j>=0} y0^j / j! = (y0^2 / 2) exp(y0).

Derivative. By the addition law, (exp((t+s)A) - exp(tA))/s - exp(tA) A = exp(tA) [ (exp(sA) - I)/s - A ] for s != 0. Its norm is at most ||exp(tA)|| |s| ||A||^2 exp(|s| ||A||) / 2, which tends to 0 as s tends to 0. Hence d/dt exp(tA) = exp(tA) A. Every power of A commutes with A, so exp(tA) A = A exp(tA).
Existence. Put x(t) = exp(tA) x0. Then x is differentiable with x'(t) = A exp(tA) x0 = A x(t), and x(0) = exp(0) x0 = x0 because exp(0) = I.

Uniqueness. Let y solve y' = A y on I with y(0) = x0. Put z(t) = exp(-tA) y(t). By the derivative step applied to -A, d/dt exp(-tA) = -A exp(-tA). The product rule gives z'(t) = -A exp(-tA) y(t) + exp(-tA) A y(t).

The matrices A and exp(-tA) commute, so the two terms cancel and z'(t) = 0 on the interval I. By the mean value theorem on each coordinate, z is constant on I, so z(t) = z(0) = x0. Multiplying by exp(tA), which inverts exp(-tA), gives y(t) = exp(tA) x0 for all t in I.

steps.text: Because A^3 = 0, exp(tA) = I + tA + t^2 A^2 / 2. Applied to x0 = (1,2,3), the first coordinate is 1 + 2t + 3 t^2 / 2. At t = 2 this is 1 + 4 + 6.
The second coordinate is x0_2 + t x0_3 = 2 + 3t. At t = 2 it equals 8.
The third coordinate is constant, x3(t) = 3. So x(2) = (11, 8, 3).

Check the equation x' = A x at t = 2. The derivative of the first coordinate is 2 + 3t = 8, which equals x2(2) = 8. The derivative of the second coordinate is 3, which equals x3(2) = 3. The third derivative is 0.

applications.conclusion: The solution is x(t) = (1 + 2t + 3t^2/2, 2 + 3t, 3), and it is the only solution with x(0) = (1,2,3) by the uniqueness part of the theorem.

results.name: A priori and a posteriori error estimates for contraction iteration
results.statement: Let (X,d) be a nonempty complete metric space. Let T: X -> X satisfy d(Tx,Ty) <= K d(x,y) for all x, y, with 0 <= K < 1. Let p be the unique fixed point of T. T is a contraction: d(Tx,Ty) <= K d(x,y) for all x, y in X, with a constant 0 <= K < 1.
p is the fixed point of T. It exists and is unique by the Banach fixed-point theorem.
x0 is any starting point in X, and T^n denotes the n-th iterate, with T^0 the identity.

prerequisites.reason: The Banach fixed-point theorem gives the existence and uniqueness of the fixed point p used in all estimates.

steps.text: Point estimate. Let x be any point. Since Tp = p, the triangle inequality gives d(x,p) <= d(x,Tx) + d(Tx,Tp) <= d(x,Tx) + K d(x,p).
Because K < 1, collect the terms with d(x,p): (1 - K) d(x,p) <= d(x,Tx). Divide by 1 - K > 0 to get d(x,p) <= d(x,Tx)/(1 - K).
A posteriori bound. Apply the point estimate to x = T^n x0. Since T(T^n x0) = T^(n+1) x0, we get d(T^n x0, p) <= d(T^n x0, T^(n+1) x0)/(1 - K).

Step sizes. By induction, d(T^n x0, T^(n+1) x0) <= K^n d(x0, T x0). The case n = 0 is an equality. If it holds for n, then d(T^(n+1) x0, T^(n+2) x0) = d(T(T^n x0), T(T^(n+1) x0)) <= K d(T^n x0, T^(n+1) x0) <= K^(n+1) d(x0, T x0).
A priori bound. Insert the step-size bound into the a posteriori bound. This gives d(T^n x0, p) <= K^n d(x0, T x0)/(1 - K). The right-hand side tends to 0, so T^n x0 converges to p.

Also T'(x) = 1/2 - 1/x^2 lies in [-1/2, 1/4], so |T'| <= 1/2 and T is a contraction with K = 1/2 by the mean value theorem. The space [1,2] is complete.

steps.text: Compute the iterates exactly. T(1) = 1/2 + 1 = 3/2, and T(3/2) = 3/4 + 2/3.
The next iterate is T(17/12) = 17/24 + 12/17.

A posteriori bound for n = 2. Here x2 = 17/12 and x3 = 577/408, so d(x2,x3) = 17/12 - 577/408 = 1/408. Divide this distance by 1 - K.

steps.text: Apply the Banach fixed-point theorem to the contraction T^m on the complete space X. It gives a unique point p with T^m p = p.
The point Tp is also a fixed point of T^m, because T^m(Tp) = T(T^m p) = Tp. By uniqueness of the fixed point of T^m, Tp = p. So p is a fixed point of T.
Uniqueness. If q satisfies Tq = q, then T^m q = q, so q is a fixed point of T^m. By uniqueness for T^m, q = p.

Convergence. Fix x in X. For n = q m + r with 0 <= r < m, write T^n x = (T^m)^q (T^r x). For each r, the a priori estimate for T^m with start y_r = T^r x gives d((T^m)^q y_r, p) <= K^q d(y_r, T^m y_r)/(1 - K).

Let C = max over r in {0,...,m-1} of d(y_r, T^m y_r)/(1 - K). It is a finite maximum of finite numbers. Then d(T^n x, p) <= C K^q, and q tends to infinity as n does. Since 0 <= K < 1, K^q tends to 0, so T^n x converges to p.

applications.title: A map on R^2 that is not a contraction while its square is
applications.inputs: Take X = R^2 with the sup norm ||(x,y)|| = max(|x|,|y|) and T(x,y) = (2y + 1, x/4 + 1/2). Start at the origin.
applications.hypotheses: The space (R^2, sup norm) is complete. T is not a contraction in this norm, because T(0,1) - T(0,0) = (2,0), which has norm 2, while (0,1) - (0,0) has norm 1. The square T^2 satisfies T^2(x,y) = (x/2 + 2, y/2 + 3/4), which is a contraction with K = 1/2.

steps.text: Compute T^2 from the formula for T: T(T(x,y)) = (2(x/4 + 1/2) + 1, (2y + 1)/4 + 1/2) = (x/2 + 2, y/2 + 3/4). The first coordinate has the constant 2(1/2) + 1.
The second coordinate has the constant 1/4 + 1/2.
The fixed point of T^2 solves x = x/2 + 2 and y = y/2 + 3/4. So x = 4 and y = 3/2.
Check that (4, 3/2) is a fixed point of T. The first coordinate of T(4, 3/2) is 2*(3/2) + 1.
The second coordinate of T(4, 3/2) is 4/4 + 1/2.

applications.conclusion: T has the unique fixed point (4, 3/2), and the iterates T^n(0,0) converge to it, although T itself has Lipschitz constant 2 in the sup norm.

results.name: Factorial contraction estimate for Picard iterates
aliases: Weissinger estimate for the Picard operator
results.statement: Let E be a Banach space, let [a,b] be a compact interval, let t0 be in [a,b] and let x0 be in E. Let v: [a,b] x E -> E be continuous such that x -> v(t,x) is Lipschitz with constant K >= 0 for each t. For a continuous phi: [a,b] -> E define (P phi)(t) = x0 + integral from t0 to t of v(s, phi(s)) ds. Then for all continuous phi, psi, all n >= 0 and all t in [a,b], ||(P^n phi)(t) - (P^n psi)(t)|| <= (K |t - t0|)^n / n! * D, where D = sup over [a,b] of ||phi - psi||. Hence sup ||P^n phi - P^n psi|| <= (K T)^n / n! * D with T = max(b - t0, t0 - a).
hypotheses: E is a Banach space, so the integrals of continuous curves exist.

phi and psi are continuous maps [a,b] -> E. Then P phi and P psi are continuous, so P maps C([a,b],E) to itself.

steps.text: Induction on n. For n = 0 the claim is ||phi(t) - psi(t)|| <= D, which is the definition of D. The factor (K|t - t0|)^0/0! equals 1.
Induction step. The constants x0 cancel, so (P^(n+1) phi)(t) - (P^(n+1) psi)(t) = integral from t0 to t of [ v(s,(P^n phi)(s)) - v(s,(P^n psi)(s)) ] ds.
The Lipschitz bound in the second variable and the induction hypothesis give ||v(s,(P^n phi)(s)) - v(s,(P^n psi)(s))|| <= K ||(P^n phi)(s) - (P^n psi)(s)|| <= K (K|s - t0|)^n D / n!.
Use ||integral of F|| <= |integral of ||F|| |. The norm is at most K^(n+1) D / n! times |integral from t0 to t of |s - t0|^n ds|. This integral equals |t - t0|^(n+1)/(n+1) for t on either side of t0.
Therefore the norm is at most K^(n+1) |t - t0|^(n+1) D / (n! (n+1)) = (K|t - t0|)^(n+1) D / (n+1)!. This is the claim for n + 1.

Take the supremum over t in [a,b]. Since |t - t0| <= T, the sup norm satisfies sup ||P^n phi - P^n psi|| <= (K T)^n D / n!. The terms (KT)^n/n! are those of the convergent series for exp(KT), so they tend to 0. For large n, P^n is a contraction.

applications.title: Picard operator for x' = 2x, x(0) = 1 on [0,2]
applications.inputs: Take E = R, v(t,x) = 2x, K = 2, t0 = 0, x0 = 1 and [a,b] = [0,2], so T = 2 and K T = 4. The operator is (P phi)(t) = 1 + 2 times the integral of phi from 0 to t.
applications.hypotheses: The map v is continuous and Lipschitz with K = 2 in x. The operator P itself is not a contraction in the sup norm: for phi = 1 and psi = 0 we get (P phi - P psi)(t) = 2t, with sup norm 4 > 1 = sup norm of phi - psi.

steps.text: For n = 1 the theorem gives the constant (K T)^1/1! = 4. This agrees with the example, where the sup norm of P phi - P psi is exactly 4.
For n = 8 the constant is 4^8/8!, which is still larger than 1.
For n = 9 the constant is 4^9/9!, which is less than 1. So P^9 is a contraction with this constant K9 on C([0,2],R).
By the Banach fixed-point theorem for a contracting iterate, P has a unique fixed point. It solves the integral equation x(t) = 1 + 2 times the integral of x, which is x' = 2x, x(0) = 1.

applications.conclusion: On [0,2], the Picard operator for x' = 2x has the 9-th iterate as a contraction with constant 2048/2835 < 1, which proves a unique solution on the whole interval without shrinking it.

steps.text: Fix x, y in s. If x = y the claim is 0 <= 0. Otherwise define g(t) = x + t(y - x) for t in [0,1] and G(t) = f(g(t)) - f(x). Since s is convex, g(t) is in s for each t, so f is differentiable at g(t).
The chain rule gives G'(t) = Df(g(t))(y - x) for t in [0,1]. A differentiable map is continuous, so G is continuous on [0,1] and has a right derivative at each t in [0,1).
The operator norm bound gives ||G'(t)|| <= ||Df(g(t))|| ||y - x|| <= C ||y - x||. Put eps = C ||y - x||. Then ||G'(t)|| <= 0 * ||G(t)|| + eps for all t in [0,1).

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Choose constants. Put eps = 1/(2M). By strict differentiability there is r > 0 such that ||f(x) - f(x') - L(x - x')|| <= eps ||x - x'|| for x, x' in the open ball B = B(a,r).

Lower bound. For x, x' in B, ||x - x'|| = ||L^(-1) L(x - x')|| <= M ||L(x - x')||. So ||f(x) - f(x')|| >= ||L(x - x')|| - eps ||x - x'|| >= ||x - x'||/M - ||x - x'||/(2M) = ||x - x'||/(2M). Hence f is injective on B, and a local inverse is 2M-Lipschitz. Also ||f(x) - f(x')|| <= (||L|| + eps)||x - x'||, so f is continuous on B.

Fix rho with 0 < rho < r and put s = rho/(2M). For y in F with ||y - f(a)|| < s, define T(x) = x + L^(-1)(y - f(x)) on the closed ball closedB = { x : ||x - a|| <= rho }. Then T(x) = x if and only if f(x) = y, because L^(-1) is injective.
T is a contraction. For x, x' in closedB, T(x) - T(x') = (x - x') - L^(-1)(f(x) - f(x')) = -L^(-1)[ f(x) - f(x') - L(x - x') ]. Its norm is at most M eps ||x - x'|| = ||x - x'||/2.

T maps closedB into the open ball B(a,rho). Indeed T(a) - a = L^(-1)(y - f(a)) has norm at most M ||y - f(a)|| < rho/2, and ||T(x) - T(a)|| <= ||x - a||/2 <= rho/2. The triangle inequality gives ||T(x) - a|| < rho.

The closed ball closedB is a closed subset of the Banach space E, so it is complete. The Banach fixed-point theorem gives a point x in closedB with T(x) = x, so f(x) = y. Since x = T(x), the previous step gives ||x - a|| < rho.

Define V = { y : ||y - f(a)|| < s } and U = B(a,rho) intersected with f^(-1)(V). Since f is continuous on B, U is open, and a is in U. For y in V the fixed point x above lies in B(a,rho) and satisfies f(x) = y in V, so x is in U. Hence f(U) = V, and V is open.
f is injective on U by the lower bound, so f: U -> V is a bijection. Its inverse is 2M-Lipschitz by the lower bound, so it is continuous.

applications.inputs: Take E = F = R^2 with the sup norm, f(x,y) = (x + y^2, y + x^2), a = (0,0), L = identity (so M = 1). Solve f(x,y) = (1/20, 0).

steps.text: T has two different vertices, and T is connected. So T has an edge, and T has a path of length at least 1. T is finite, so only finitely many paths exist. Choose a path P = v0, v1, ..., vk of maximal length. Here k >= 1.
Look at the end v0. The vertex v1 is a neighbour of v0. Let w be any neighbour of v0 with w different from v1. We show that this case is impossible.
Case 1: w is not on P. Then w, v0, v1, ..., vk is a path of length k+1. This contradicts the choice of P as a longest path.
Case 2: w = vi for some i >= 2. The vertices v0, v1, ..., vi are all different, vi is adjacent to v0, and i >= 2. So v0, v1, ..., vi, v0 is a cycle. This contradicts that T has no cycle.
The vertex w cannot be v0, because T has no loops. The case w = v1 is excluded by choice. Hence v1 is the only neighbour of v0, and the degree of v0 is 1.
The reversed path vk, ..., v0 is also a longest path. The same argument shows that vk has degree 1. The vertices v0 and vk are different because k >= 1. So T has two leaves.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Direction (i) implies (ii). We prove by induction on n that a tree with n vertices has n - 1 edges. For n = 1 the graph has one vertex. It has no loop, so it has 0 = n - 1 edges.
Let n >= 2 and let G be a tree on n vertices. By the leaf lemma, G has a leaf v. Let u be the only neighbour of v. Let G' be G with v and the edge vu deleted.

G' is connected. Take two vertices x and y of G'. G has a path from x to y. A path has no repeated vertex. If v were on this path, v would not be an end, because x and y differ from v. So v would have two different neighbours on the path. But v has degree 1. Hence the path avoids v and is a path of G'.
G' has no cycle, because every cycle of G' is a cycle of G. So G' is a tree on n - 1 vertices. By the induction hypothesis G' has n - 2 edges. G has exactly one more edge, vu. So G has n - 1 edges.

Direction (ii) implies (i). First we show that deleting one edge e = xy of a cycle C keeps a connected graph connected. Take a walk W between two vertices. Replace each use of e in W by the rest of C, which joins x to y without e. The new walk avoids e.

Let G be connected with n - 1 edges. Suppose G has a cycle. Delete an edge of a cycle. By the claim G stays connected. Repeat while a cycle exists. Each step removes an edge and keeps connectivity, so the process stops after finitely many steps.

The result T is a connected spanning subgraph with no cycle. So T is a tree on n vertices. By direction (i) implies (ii), T has n - 1 edges. But T lost at least one edge, so T has at most n - 2 edges. This is a contradiction. Hence G has no cycle, and G is a tree.

applications.title: Count the leaves of a tree from its degrees
applications.inputs: A tree T has exactly 4 vertices of degree 3. Every other vertex is a leaf. Let L be the number of leaves.
applications.hypotheses: T is a finite tree, so it is connected with n = 4 + L vertices. The edge count theorem gives m = n - 1 edges. The degree sum equals 2m.

steps.text: The degree sum is 3 times 4 plus L times 1. With L = 6 this sum is 12 + 6 = 18.
The number of vertices is n = 4 + 6 = 10. By the theorem the tree has n - 1 = 9 edges. Twice this number is the degree sum.
The equation 12 + L = 2(3 + L) gives L = 6. So the two sides agree for L = 6 only. Every such tree has exactly 6 leaves.

applications.conclusion: A tree with 4 vertices of degree 3 and no other non-leaf vertex has exactly 6 leaves. In general a tree with a vertices of degree 3 and no other non-leaf vertex has a + 2 leaves.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Step 1: D_n satisfies the Catalan recurrence. D_0 = 1 (the empty sequence). Let n >= 0. A Dyck sequence of length 2n+2 starts with +1, because the first partial sum is at least 0 and the terms are +1 or -1.
The total sum is 0, so the partial sums return to 0 at some first index 2i+2, with 0 <= i <= n. Write the sequence as (+1) A (-1) B. Here A has length 2i and B has length 2(n-i).

Between index 1 and index 2i+1 the partial sums are at least 1. So the partial sums of A are at least 0, and A has total 0. This means A is a Dyck sequence. After index 2i+2 the partial sums are those of B. So B is a Dyck sequence.

Conversely, any i, any Dyck sequence A of length 2i and any Dyck sequence B of length 2(n-i) give a Dyck sequence (+1) A (-1) B whose first return to 0 is at 2i+2. The two maps are inverse. Hence D_(n+1) = D_0 D_n + ... + D_n D_0. By induction D_n = C_n for all n.

Step 2: the cycle lemma. Let N = 2n+1. Let w = (e_1, ..., e_N) have n+1 terms +1 and n terms -1. The total sum is 1. Extend w with period N and let S_k be the partial sums, so S_0 = 0 and S_(k+N) = S_k + 1. The rotation by j has partial sums S_(j+m) - S_j for m = 1..N.

Existence: let mu be the minimum of S_0, ..., S_(N-1). Let j be the largest index in 0..N-1 with S_j = mu. For j+m <= N-1, S_(j+m) > mu because S_(j+m) >= mu and j is the largest index with value mu. For N <= j+m <= j+N, S_(j+m) = S_(j+m-N) + 1 >= mu + 1. So the rotation by j is positive.

Uniqueness: suppose j < j' in 0..N-1 both give positive rotations. Then S_j' > S_j, using m = j'-j in 1..N-1. Also S_(j+N) > S_j', using m = j+N-j' in 1..N. But S_(j+N) = S_j + 1. So S_j < S_j' < S_j + 1 for integers, which is impossible. So each w has exactly one rotation index with a positive rotation.

Step 3: count. Let W be the set of all such w, so |W| = binom(2n+1, n). Let P be the set of positive sequences in W. The map (p, j) -> rotation of p by j from P x {0..N-1} to W is onto, by existence, and one-to-one, by uniqueness. Hence |W| = (2n+1) |P|.

A sequence is positive in W if and only if it is (+1) followed by a Dyck sequence of length 2n. Indeed, the first term must be +1, and removing it lowers all later partial sums by 1, so they are at least 0 and end at 0. So |P| = D_n.

Hence binom(2n+1, n) = (2n+1) D_n. Now binom(2n+1, n) = (2n+1)! / (n! (n+1)!) = (2n+1) (2n)! / (n! (n+1)!). Divide by 2n+1: D_n = (2n)! / (n! (n+1)!). Multiply by n+1: (n+1) D_n = (2n)! / (n! n!) = binom(2n, n). Since D_n = C_n, the formula holds.

theorem pow_eq_sum_stirlingSecond_mul_descFactorial (n k : ℕ) :
    n ^ k = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), stirlingSecond k j * n.descFactorial j := by
  induction k with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih =>
    have : ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1), stirlingSecond k j * (j * n.descFactorial j)
        = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (k + 1),
            (j + 1) * (stirlingSecond k (j + 1) * n.descFactorial (j + 1)) := by
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ' (fun j ↦ stirlingSecond k j * (j * n.descFactorial j)) k,

    rw [pow_succ, ih, Finset.sum_mul,

steps.text: Key identity: x * x^(k) = x^(k+1) + k * x^(k) for natural x and k. If k <= x, then x^(k+1) = x^(k) (x-k), so x^(k+1) + k x^(k) = x^(k) (x-k+k) = x x^(k). If k > x, then x^(k) = 0 and x^(k+1) = 0, so both sides are 0.
Base case n = 0: x^0 = 1, and the sum has the single term S(0,0) x^(0) = 1. So the formula holds.
Induction step. Assume x^n = sum_k S(n,k) x^(k). Multiply by x and use the key identity: x^(n+1) = sum_k S(n,k) (x^(k+1) + k x^(k)), with k from 0 to n.

Collect the coefficient of x^(j) for 1 <= j <= n+1. The first part gives S(n, j-1). The second part gives j S(n, j). Their sum is j S(n,j) + S(n,j-1), which is S(n+1, j) by the recurrence (with k = j-1).

The coefficient of x^(0) is S(n,0) * 0 from the second part, and the first part has no x^(0) term. So it is 0, and S(n+1, 0) = 0 for n+1 >= 1. Also S(n, n+1) = 0 and S(n+1, k) = 0 for k > n+1, so the sum can run over k = 0..n+1.
Hence x^(n+1) = sum_{j=0}^{n+1} S(n+1, j) x^(j). This closes the induction.

steps.text: Define the map F from compositions of n to subsets of {1,...,n-1}. F sends (a_1,...,a_k) to the set of partial sums s_i = a_1 + ... + a_i for 1 <= i <= k-1.

F is well defined. The parts are positive, so the sums s_1 < s_2 < ... < s_(k-1) are strictly increasing. Also s_1 >= 1 and s_(k-1) = n - a_k <= n - 1. So F(c) is a subset of {1,...,n-1} with k - 1 elements.

Define the map G in the other direction. Given a subset T = {t_1 < ... < t_r} of {1,...,n-1}, put t_0 = 0 and t_(r+1) = n. Let G(T) be the list of differences (t_1 - t_0, t_2 - t_1, ..., t_(r+1) - t_r). All differences are positive because the t_i increase strictly, and they sum to n. So G(T) is a composition with r + 1 parts.

G and F are inverse. The partial sums of the differences of T are t_1, ..., t_r, so F(G(T)) = T. The differences of the partial sums of a composition, with s_0 = 0 and s_k = n, are the parts a_i, so G(F(c)) = c. Hence F is a bijection.
A set with n - 1 elements has 2^(n-1) subsets. So there are 2^(n-1) compositions of n.
The bijection sends a composition with k parts to a subset with k - 1 elements. The number of such subsets is binom(n-1, k-1). So exactly binom(n-1, k-1) compositions have k parts.

steps.text: k = 1: only the composition (5). The count is binom(4,0).
k = 2: the subsets of size 1 are {1},{2},{3},{4}. They give (1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1). The count is binom(4,1).
k = 3, 4, 5 give binom(4,2) = 4*3/2 = 6, binom(4,3) = 4 and binom(4,4) = 1 compositions. The total is the sum over all k.
The total equals 2 to the power n - 1.

applications.conclusion: The integer 5 has 16 = 2^4 compositions. The two counts agree: 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16.

results.name: Double counting principle for a finite relation
results.statement: Let A and B be finite sets and let R be a subset of A x B. For a in A let d(a) be the number of b in B with (a,b) in R. For b in B let d(b) be the number of a in A with (a,b) in R. Then the sum of d(a) over a in A equals |R|, and equals the sum of d(b) over b in B. If d(a) >= m for all a in A and d(b) <= n for all b in B, then |A| m <= |B| n. If d(a) = m for all a and d(b) = n for all b, then |A| m = |B| n.
hypotheses: A and B are finite sets.
R is any relation between A and B. It is a set of ordered pairs.
m and n are natural numbers (or real numbers with the same order).
For the inequality, d(a) >= m holds for every a in A and d(b) <= n holds for every b in B.

steps.text: Split R by the first coordinate. The sets {a} x R(a) for a in A are pairwise disjoint and their union is R. By the sum rule |R| is the sum over a of |R(a)|, which is the sum of d(a).

Split R by the second coordinate. The sets R'(b) x {b} for b in B are pairwise disjoint and their union is R. By the sum rule |R| is the sum over b of |R'(b)|, which is the sum of d(b). So the two sums are equal.
Assume d(a) >= m for every a in A. A sum of |A| terms, each at least m, is at least |A| m. So |A| m is at most the sum of d(a), which is |R|.
Assume d(b) <= n for every b in B. A sum of |B| terms, each at most n, is at most |B| n. So |R| is at most |B| n. Together with the last step, |A| m <= |R| <= |B| n.

Assume d(a) = m for all a and d(b) = n for all b. Then both inequalities hold in both directions: d(a) >= m and d(a) <= m, and the same for n. The chain |A| m <= |B| n and |B| n <= |A| m gives |A| m = |B| n.

steps.text: Let uv be an edge. The sets N(u) and N(v) are disjoint. If w were in both, then u, v, w would be three distinct, pairwise adjacent vertices, which is a triangle. Both sets lie in the vertex set, so d(u) + d(v) <= n.

Add this inequality over all e edges. The right side gives n e. On the left side, a vertex v occurs in d(v) edges, and each time it contributes d(v). So the left side equals the sum over all vertices of d(v)^2. Hence the sum of d(v)^2 is at most n e.

The sum of all degrees is 2e by the degree-sum formula. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the all-ones vector and the degree vector gives (sum of d(v))^2 <= n times (sum of d(v)^2). So 4 e^2 <= n times the sum of d(v)^2 <= n^2 e.
If e = 0, then e <= n^2/4 is clear. If e > 0, divide 4 e^2 <= n^2 e by 4 e to get e <= n^2/4. Because e is an integer, e <= floor(n^2/4).

Sharpness: take the complete bipartite graph with parts X and Y of sizes floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2). Among any three vertices, two are in the same part, and they are not adjacent. So there is no triangle. The number of edges is |X||Y|, which is m^2 for n = 2m and m(m+1) for n = 2m+1. Both equal floor(n^2/4).

steps.text: Fix a vertex v. Let N be the set of neighbours of v, so |N| = k. Let M be the set of vertices other than v that are not adjacent to v. The sets {v}, N and M partition the vertex set, so |M| = n - k - 1.

Let R be the set of pairs (w, x) with w in N, x in M and w adjacent to x. We count R from the side of N. Take w in N. The neighbours of w are v itself, the vertices of N adjacent to w, and the vertices of M adjacent to w. The vertices of N adjacent to w are exactly the common neighbours of v and w, so there are l of them.
So w has k - 1 - l neighbours in M, because w has degree k and one neighbour is v. Hence every w in N has exactly k - 1 - l partners in M.

Now count from the side of M. Take x in M. Then x differs from v and is not adjacent to v, so x and v have exactly mu common neighbours. Common neighbours of x and v are the neighbours of x that lie in N. So x has exactly mu partners in N.
Apply the equality form of the double counting principle with A = N, B = M, m = k - 1 - l and n' = mu. It gives |N| (k - 1 - l) = |M| mu. This is k (k - l - 1) = (n - k - 1) mu.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: We prove by induction on k that (A^k)(u,v) = W_k(u,v) for all u and v. For k = 0, A^0 is the identity. The only walk of length 0 from u is the one-vertex walk, and it ends at u. So W_0(u,v) is 1 if u = v and 0 otherwise. This is the identity matrix.

Induction step. Write A^(k+1) = A A^k. By the definition of the matrix product, (A^(k+1))(u,v) is the sum over w in V of A(u,w) (A^k)(w,v). The factor A(u,w) is 1 if w is a neighbour of u and 0 otherwise. So the entry is the sum over neighbours w of u of (A^k)(w,v).

Count the walks of length k+1 from u to v by their second vertex w. The first step goes from u to a neighbour w. The rest is a walk of length k from w to v. Deleting the first edge is a bijection between walks of length k+1 from u to v with second vertex w and walks of length k from w to v. So W_(k+1)(u,v) is the sum over neighbours w of u of W_k(w,v).
By the induction hypothesis (A^k)(w,v) = W_k(w,v) for every w. The two sums in the last two steps are therefore equal, so (A^(k+1))(u,v) = W_(k+1)(u,v). This closes the induction.

The trace of A^3 is the sum over u of W_3(u,u), the number of closed walks u, x, y, u. Adjacent vertices are different, so u, x, y are three distinct vertices that are pairwise adjacent: a triangle. Conversely a triangle gives 3 choices of start vertex and 2 directions, so 6 closed walks of length 3. Hence the trace of A^3 is 6 times the number of triangles.

applications.title: Count the triangles of the complete graph K4
applications.inputs: G = K4 has 4 vertices, every two adjacent. Its adjacency matrix A is J - I, where J is the all-ones matrix. Its eigenvalues are 3 once and -1 three times.
applications.hypotheses: K4 is a finite simple graph, so the walk-counting theorem and its trace corollary apply.

steps.text: The trace of A^3 counts ordered closed walks u, x, y, u. Choose u, then x different from u, then y different from both: 4 times 3 times 2 choices.
Cross-check with the eigenvalues. The trace of A^3 is the sum of the cubes of the eigenvalues 3, -1, -1, -1.
The trace of A^3 is 6 times the number of triangles. Divide 24 by 6.

applications.conclusion: K4 has exactly 4 triangles. This agrees with binom(4,3) = 4 and shows how the trace of A^3 counts triangles without listing them.

results.name: The kernel of the graph Laplacian counts connected components
aliases: multiplicity of the eigenvalue 0 of the Laplacian
results.statement: Let G be a finite simple graph with vertex set V. Let L = D - A be its Laplacian matrix, where D is the diagonal matrix of degrees and A is the adjacency matrix. Then the dimension of the kernel of L, acting on real vectors in R^V, equals the number of connected components of G. The kernel is the space of vectors that are constant on each component.
hypotheses: G is a finite simple graph.
L has real entries and acts on R^V.
A connected component is a maximal set of vertices that are pairwise joined by walks. An isolated vertex is a component.

definitions.text: The vector 1_C with entry 1 at the vertices of C and entry 0 elsewhere.

steps.text: Quadratic form. For x in R^V, x^T D x is the sum over v of d(v) x_v^2. Each vertex v lies in d(v) edges, so this equals the sum over edges {u,v} of (x_u^2 + x_v^2). Also x^T A x is the sum over ordered adjacent pairs (u,v) of x_u x_v, which equals 2 times the sum over edges of x_u x_v. Subtracting gives x^T L x = sum over edges {u,v} of (x_u - x_v)^2.
Suppose L x = 0. Then x^T L x = 0. The right side of the formula is a sum of real squares, so every term is 0. Hence x_u = x_v for every edge {u,v}.
If x_u = x_v for every edge, then x is constant along every walk. Vertices in the same component are joined by a walk, so x is constant on each component.

Conversely, let x be constant on every component. The formula (Lx)_v = d(v) x_v - sum of x_w over neighbours w equals the sum over neighbours w of (x_v - x_w). Every neighbour of v is in the component of v, so every term is 0. Thus L x = 0.

So the kernel is the set of vectors constant on components. This set is spanned by the indicator vectors 1_C of the components C, because such a vector x equals the sum over C of (value of x on C) times 1_C. These indicators have disjoint, non-empty supports, so they are linearly independent. They form a basis. The dimension is the number of components.

steps.text: By the theorem the kernel of L has dimension 3. By the rank-nullity theorem the rank of L is the number of vertices minus 3.

Check by matrices. First x^T D x, the sum of d(v) x_v^2 for the degrees 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0.
Next x^T A x is twice the sum of x_u x_v over the edges 12, 23, 45.
The difference of the two values is x^T L x. It matches the sum over edges.

applications.conclusion: The graph has 3 components, so L has a 3-dimensional kernel and rank 3. Both ways to compute x^T L x give 14.

results.name: Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz
results.statement: Let R be an integral domain. Let f be a polynomial in R[x_1, ..., x_n] of total degree t_1 + ... + t_n, where the coefficient of the monomial x_1^t_1 ... x_n^t_n in f is non-zero. Let S_1, ..., S_n be finite subsets of R with |S_i| > t_i for each i. Then there is a point s = (s_1, ..., s_n) with s_i in S_i for each i such that f(s) is not zero.
hypotheses: R is an integral domain: commutative, with 1 different from 0, and no zero divisors. A field is an example.
The total degree of f is exactly t_1 + ... + t_n, and the coefficient of x_1^t_1 ... x_n^t_n is non-zero.
Each S_i is a finite subset of R with strictly more than t_i elements.

definitions.name: total degree
definitions.text: The largest sum a_1 + ... + a_n over the monomials x_1^a_1 ... x_n^a_n that occur in f with non-zero coefficient.

definitions.name: grid
definitions.text: The set S_1 x ... x S_n of all points whose i-th coordinate lies in S_i.

theorem combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_eval_nonzero [IsDomain R]
    (f : MvPolynomial σ R)
    (t : σ →₀ ℕ) (ht : f.coeff t ≠ 0) (ht' : f.totalDegree = t.degree)
    (S : σ → Finset R) (htS : ∀ i, t i < #(S i)) :
    ∃ s : σ → R, (∀ i, s i ∈ S i) ∧ eval s f ≠ 0 := by
  let _ : LinearOrder σ := WellOrderingRel.isWellOrder.linearOrder
  by_contra! Heval
  apply ht
  obtain ⟨h, hh, hf⟩ := combinatorial_nullstellensatz_exists_linearCombination S
    (fun i ↦ by rw [← Finset.card_pos]; exact Nat.zero_lt_of_lt (htS i)) f Heval
  rw [hf]
  rw [linearCombination_apply, Finsupp.sum, coeff_sum]
  apply Finset.sum_eq_zero
  intro i _
  set g := h i * Alon.P (S i) i with hg
  by_cases hi : h i = 0
  · simp [hi]
  have : g.totalDegree ≤ f.totalDegree := by
    rw [hg, mul_comm]
    exact hh i
  -- one could simplify this by proving `totalDegree_mul_eq` (at least in a domain)
  rw [hg, ← degree_degLexDegree,
    degree_mul_of_isRegular_right hi (by simp only [(Alon.monic_P ..).leadingCoeff_eq_one,
      isRegular_one]),
    Alon.degree_P, map_add, degree_degLexDegree, degree_single, ht'] at this
  rw [smul_eq_mul, coeff_mul, Finset.sum_eq_zero]
  rintro ⟨p, q⟩ hpq
  simp only [Finset.mem_antidiagonal] at hpq
  simp only [mul_eq_zero, Classical.or_iff_not_imp_right]
  rw [← ne_eq, ← mem_support_iff]
  intro hq
  obtain ⟨e, hq', hq⟩ := Alon.of_mem_P_support _ _ _ hq
  apply coeff_eq_zero_of_totalDegree_lt
  rw [← Finsupp.degree_apply]
  apply lt_of_add_lt_add_right (lt_of_le_of_lt this _)
  rw [← hpq, map_add, add_lt_add_iff_left, hq, degree_single]
  apply lt_of_le_of_lt _ (htS i)
  simp [← hpq, hq]

steps.text: Grid lemma. Let r be a polynomial in R[x_1..x_n] with degree in x_i at most |S_i| - 1 for each i. If r vanishes at every point of the grid S_1 x ... x S_n, then r = 0. Proof by induction on n. For n = 1, r is a one-variable polynomial of degree less than |S_1| with |S_1| roots, so r = 0 in an integral domain.

For n >= 2 write r = sum over j of r_j(x_1..x_(n-1)) x_n^j with j <= |S_n| - 1. Fix a point s' of the smaller grid. The one-variable polynomial in x_n with coefficients r_j(s') vanishes on S_n and has degree below |S_n|, so all r_j(s') are 0. Thus each r_j vanishes on the smaller grid and r_j = 0 by induction. So r = 0.

Main proof by contradiction. Suppose f vanishes on the grid. Shrink each S_i to a subset S_i' of size exactly t_i + 1. The polynomial f still vanishes on the smaller grid. Put g_i = the product of (x_i - s) over s in S_i'. It is monic of degree t_i + 1 in x_i, and it vanishes whenever x_i is in S_i'.

Reduce f. Take a monomial of f whose x_i-exponent is at least t_i + 1. Replace x_i^(t_i+1) by g_i + (x_i^(t_i+1) - g_i). The second part has x_i-degree at most t_i. Each replacement gives monomials of no larger total degree and with a smaller exponent of x_i. By repetition we get f = h_1 g_1 + ... + h_n g_n + r, where the total degree of each h_i g_i is at most deg f = t_1 + ... + t_n and the degree of r in x_i is at most t_i.

The monomial coefficient. The top-degree part (total degree t = t_1 + ... + t_n) of h_i g_i is a multiple of x_i^(t_i+1), because the top part of g_i is x_i^(t_i+1). The monomial x_1^t_1 ... x_n^t_n has x_i-exponent t_i, so it does not occur in h_i g_i. Because the total degree of h_i g_i is at most t, the coefficient of this monomial in h_i g_i is 0. So r has the same non-zero coefficient as f.

On the grid S_1' x ... x S_n' we have f = 0 and every g_i = 0. So r = f - sum h_i g_i vanishes there. The degree of r in x_i is at most t_i = |S_i'| - 1. By the grid lemma r = 0. But r has a non-zero coefficient. This is a contradiction. So f does not vanish on the grid: some point s has f(s) not zero.

applications.inputs: The cycle C4 has vertices 1,2,3,4 and edges 12, 23, 34, 41. Take the graph polynomial f = (x1 - x2)(x2 - x3)(x3 - x4)(x4 - x1) over the real numbers. Each vertex has a list of 2 allowed colours, for example L1 = {1,2}, L2 = {1,2}, L3 = {1,3}, L4 = {2,3}.

steps.text: Expand f and find all ways to choose one variable from each factor so that each of x1, x2, x3, x4 is chosen once. f(c) is not zero if and only if the colours of adjacent vertices differ. For example c = (1, 2, 1, 3) lies in the lists. Its value is:
The value 4 is not zero, so c is a proper colouring: 1 differs from 2, 2 from 1, 1 from 3, and 3 from 1.

results.name: Characterization of trees by unique paths
aliases: a graph is a tree iff any two vertices are joined by exactly one path
results.statement: Let G be a simple graph with a non-empty vertex set. Then G is a tree (connected and without cycles) if and only if for every two vertices u and v there is exactly one path from u to v. A path is a walk with no repeated vertex.
hypotheses: G is a simple graph: no loops and no multiple edges.
The vertex set of G is not empty.
A cycle is a closed walk of length at least 3 with no repeated vertex except that the end equals the start.

definitions.name: tree
definitions.text: A connected graph that has no cycle.

definitions.name: path
definitions.text: A walk v_0, v_1, ..., v_k in which the vertices are pairwise distinct.

source.excerpt:
theorem isTree_iff_existsUnique_path :
    G.IsTree ↔ Nonempty V ∧ ∀ v w : V, ∃! p : G.Walk v w, p.IsPath := by
  classical
  simp_rw [isTree_iff, isAcyclic_iff_subsingleton_path, subsingleton_iff]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hc, hu⟩
    refine ⟨hc.nonempty, ?_⟩
    intro v w
    let q := (hc v w).some.toPath
    use q
    simp only [true_and, Path.isPath]
    intro p hp
    specialize hu v w ⟨p, hp⟩ q
    exact Subtype.ext_iff.mp hu
  · rintro ⟨hV, h⟩
    refine ⟨Connected.mk ?_, ?_⟩
    · intro v w
      obtain ⟨p, _⟩ := h v w
      exact p.reachable
    · rintro v w ⟨p, hp⟩ ⟨q, hq⟩
      simp only [ExistsUnique.unique (h v w) hp hq]

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Assume G is a tree. Existence of a path: G is connected, so a walk from u to v exists. Take a shortest such walk. If it repeated a vertex, we could delete the part between the two visits and get a shorter walk. So the shortest walk has no repeated vertex and is a path.

Uniqueness, set-up. Suppose P = (u = p_0, ..., p_a = v) and Q = (u = q_0, ..., q_b = v) are two different paths from u to v. Let i be the first index with p_(i+1) different from q_(i+1) (one path may end earlier, but then the other path would revisit v, which a path cannot do, so both continue at index i). Then p_i = q_i = w.

From w, the path P leaves by the vertex p_(i+1) and the path Q leaves by q_(i+1). These differ. Follow P after w until the first vertex x, with index j > i, that also lies on Q after w. Such an x exists because v lies on both. Let the vertex x be q_m with m > i.

Build a closed walk: go along P from w to x, then back along Q from x to w. The P-part has no repeated vertex, and its interior vertices avoid Q after w by the choice of x. The Q-part has no repeated vertex. Both parts are disjoint except at w and x. The P-part and the Q-part start with different edges at w, so the closed walk has length at least 3 and is a cycle.
A cycle contradicts that G is a tree. So P = Q, and the path is unique. This proves the forward direction.

Assume now that every two vertices are joined by exactly one path. Then G is connected, because a path is a walk. Suppose G had a cycle c_0, c_1, ..., c_(k-1), c_0 with k >= 3. The vertices c_0 and c_1 are adjacent, so the one-edge walk c_0, c_1 is a path.

The walk c_0, c_(k-1), c_(k-2), ..., c_1 goes around the other way. It has k - 1 >= 2 edges and no repeated vertex, so it is a path from c_0 to c_1. It differs from the one-edge path because its length is at least 2. This gives two paths between c_0 and c_1, a contradiction. So G has no cycle and is a tree.

applications.title: Test the path graph P7 and the cycle C4 for the unique path property
applications.inputs: P7 has vertices 1,...,7 and edges {i, i+1} for i = 1,...,6. C4 has vertices 1,2,3,4 and edges 12, 23, 34, 41.
applications.hypotheses: Both graphs are simple graphs with non-empty vertex sets. P7 is connected and has no cycle, so it is a tree. C4 is connected but is itself a cycle.

steps.text: In P7 each pair i < j has the unique path i, i+1, ..., j of length j - i. There is one such path for each unordered pair of vertices.
The sum of the path lengths j - i over all pairs is n(n^2 - 1)/6 for n = 7. Check: pairs at distance d number 7 - d, so the sum is 6*1+5*2+4*3+3*4+2*5+1*6.
The closed formula gives the same total.

In C4 the vertices 1 and 3 are joined by the two paths 1,2,3 and 1,4,3. There are two paths, so the unique path property fails. By the theorem C4 is not a tree. This agrees with the fact that C4 is a cycle.

applications.conclusion: P7 has exactly one path between any two vertices, with total length 56 over its 21 pairs. C4 has two paths between vertices 1 and 3, so it is not a tree.

results.name: Every connected graph has a spanning tree
results.statement: Let G be a finite connected simple graph with n vertices. Then G has a spanning tree: a subgraph T with the same vertex set as G, whose edges are edges of G, and which is a tree. Such a T has exactly n - 1 edges, so G has at least n - 1 edges.
hypotheses: G is a finite simple graph with n >= 1 vertices.
G is connected: any two vertices are joined by a walk.
A spanning subgraph keeps all vertices and keeps some of the edges.

prerequisites.reason: The edge count n - 1 of a spanning tree comes from the edge-count theorem for trees.

steps.text: The set of connected spanning subgraphs of G is not empty, because G itself is in it. The set is finite since G is finite. Choose H in this set with the smallest number of edges.
Claim: H has no cycle. Suppose H has a cycle, and let e = {a, b} be an edge of that cycle. The rest of the cycle is a walk from a to b that does not use e.

Delete e from H to get H'. Take two vertices x and y. Since H is connected, there is a walk from x to y in H. Replace each use of e in this walk by the walk around the rest of the cycle. The result is a walk from x to y in H'. So H' is connected.
H' is a connected spanning subgraph of G with one edge fewer than H. This contradicts the choice of H. So H has no cycle.
H is connected and has no cycle, so H is a tree. It uses all n vertices and only edges of G. So H is a spanning tree of G.
By the edge-count theorem for trees, H has n - 1 edges. H is a subgraph of G, so G has at least n - 1 edges. The number of edges of G that are not in H is |E(G)| - (n - 1), which is the cycle rank.

results.name: Equivalent forms of well-foundedness
results.statement: Let R be a binary relation on a set X. Write R(y, x) for 'y is R-below x'. The following are equivalent. (a) Induction: for every property P of elements of X, if P(x) holds whenever P(y) holds for all y with R(y, x), then P(x) holds for all x. (b) Minimal elements: every nonempty subset S of X has an element m such that no s in S satisfies R(s, m). (c) No descent: there is no sequence x_0, x_1, x_2, ... in X with R(x_(n+1), x_n) for all n. The implications (a) <=> (b) and (b) => (c) hold in ZF. The implication (c) => (b) uses the axiom of dependent choice.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary binary relation on a set X. It need not be transitive or total.
A property P of elements of X is the same as a subset of X, namely {x : P(x)}.
The implication (c) => (b) needs the axiom of dependent choice. Without it, (c) can hold while (b) fails.

definitions.name: well-founded relation
definitions.text: A relation R on X is well-founded if it satisfies condition (b), or equivalently (a).

definitions.name: dependent choice
definitions.text: If T is a relation on a nonempty set S and every s in S has some t in S with T(t, s), then there is a sequence s_0, s_1, ... in S with T(s_(n+1), s_n) for all n.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration states that R is well-founded if and only if every nonempty set has an R-minimal element. Well-founded in Lean means that every element is accessible, which is equivalent to the induction principle (a). The authored statement adds the descent form (c).

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: (a) => (b). Let S be nonempty. Suppose S has no R-minimal element. Take P(x) to be the property 'x is not in S'. If every y below x satisfies P(y) but x is in S, then x is R-minimal in S, because no element of S is below x. That is excluded, so P(x) holds. By (a), P(x) holds for all x. Then S is empty, which is a contradiction.

(b) => (a). Assume the induction hypothesis of (a) for a property P. Suppose P(x0) fails for some x0. The set S = {x : not P(x)} is nonempty. By (b), S has an R-minimal element m. Every y below m is outside S, so P(y) holds for all y below m. The hypothesis of (a) now gives P(m), which contradicts m in S.

(b) => (c). Suppose x_0, x_1, ... is a sequence with R(x_(n+1), x_n) for all n. The set S = {x_n : n >= 0} is nonempty. An element x_n of S is not minimal, because x_(n+1) is in S and below x_n. So S has no minimal element, which contradicts (b).

(c) => (b), with dependent choice. Suppose a nonempty S has no minimal element. Then each s in S has some t in S with R(t, s). Apply dependent choice to the relation T(t, s) = R(t, s) on S. This gives a sequence s_0, s_1, ... in S with R(s_(n+1), s_n) for all n, which contradicts (c).
The four implications give (a) <=> (b) <=> (c), with the use of dependent choice only in the last one. So the three conditions are equivalent.

applications.inputs: States (a, b) in N x N. A step goes from (a, b) to (a, b-1) if b > 0. If b = 0 and a > 0, a step goes to (a-1, 5). The start state is (2, 3).

steps.text: Show that the lexicographic order is well-founded by condition (b). In a nonempty S, take the least first coordinate a0 in S. Among the pairs of S with first coordinate a0, take one with the least second coordinate b0. The pair (a0, b0) is minimal in S.

Since each step is a step down in the lexicographic order, a sequence of states with R(x_(n+1), x_n) is an infinite descending chain. By (c), no such chain exists, so the loop stops after finitely many steps from every start state.
Count the steps from (2, 3). First 3 steps reach (2, 0). One step reaches (1, 5), 5 steps reach (1, 0), one step reaches (0, 5), and 5 steps reach (0, 0).
General formula for refill 5: from (a, b) the loop makes b + a * 6 steps. For (2, 3) this equals the count above.

applications.conclusion: The loop stops from (2, 3) after exactly 15 steps. The well-foundedness of the lexicographic order proves that this loop stops from every start state.

results.statement: Let L be a complete lattice and f: L -> L a monotone map. Define x_a for every ordinal a by x_a = join of f(x_d) over all d < a. So x_0 = bottom. f is monotone: x <= y implies f(x) <= f(y).

The Hartogs ordinal of L is the least ordinal that has no injection into L. It is defined without choice.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration states that lfp f is in the range of the approximation sequence started at bottom. The authored statement adds the monotonicity of the sequence, the bound by prefixed points, and the stabilization at a stage below the Hartogs ordinal.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Claim (i). Prove by strong induction on b: (A_b) x_c <= x_b for every c < b, and (B_b) x_b <= f(x_b). Assume (B_c) for all c < b. For c < b, x_c <= f(x_c) by (B_c), and f(x_c) <= x_b by the definition of x_b as a join. So x_c <= x_b, which is (A_b).

Now (B_b). For every d < b we have x_d <= x_b by (A_b), so f(x_d) <= f(x_b) by monotonicity of f. The join over d < b of f(x_d) is then at most f(x_b), so x_b <= f(x_b). This completes the induction and shows x_c <= x_d for c <= d.

Claim (ii). Let p satisfy f(p) <= p. Prove x_a <= p by strong induction on a. For d < a, x_d <= p by the induction hypothesis, so f(x_d) <= f(p) <= p. The join of these elements is at most p. Hence x_a <= p. Every fixed point q satisfies f(q) <= q, so x_a <= lfp(f).

Claim (iii). Let H be the Hartogs ordinal of L. Suppose x_a is not a fixed point for all a < H. By (i), x_a <= f(x_a), so x_a < f(x_a) strictly. For a < b < H we have f(x_a) <= x_b by definition of x_b, so x_a < f(x_a) <= x_b. Thus a -> x_a is strictly increasing, hence injective from H into L, which contradicts the definition of H.

So some a < H has x_a = f(x_a). Let a be any ordinal with this property. Then x_a is a fixed point, so lfp(f) <= x_a by the definition of lfp(f) as a meet of the prefixed points. By (ii), x_a <= lfp(f). Therefore x_a = lfp(f).

applications.title: Iterating f(S) = {0} union (S + 1) on the subsets of N reaches the least fixed point only after omega steps

steps.text: Compute the finite stages. x_0 is the empty set. If x_n = {0, ..., n-1}, then x_(n+1) = f(x_n) = {0} union {1, ..., n} = {0, ..., n}. So the size of x_n is n.
Size of x_5 from five applications of f, each adding one element.
Compute the stage omega. It is the join of f(x_n) over all n, which is the union of all {0, ..., n}. This is N. Then f(N) = {0} union {1, 2, ...} = N, so x_omega is a fixed point.
By part (iii), x_omega = lfp(f) = N. For every finite stage n, x_n is a finite set and differs from N, so the finite stages never reach lfp(f). The index omega is necessary.

applications.conclusion: The least fixed point of f is N, and the transfinite iteration reaches it at stage omega, not at any finite stage.

hypotheses: f maps ordinals to ordinals and a < b implies f(a) < f(b).
Continuity: f(l) = sup {f(b) : b < l} for every limit ordinal l.
a is an arbitrary ordinal. For a limit ordinal l, 'the supremum of a family' means the least ordinal that is at least every member.

source.alignment: In the Lean file, nfp f a is the supremum of the iterates of f from a. The declaration says that f applied to it gives itself for a normal f. The authored statement adds that the supremum is at least a and is the least fixed point at least a.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: First, x <= f(x) for every ordinal x. Suppose some x has f(x) < x. Let x0 be the least such x. Then f(f(x0)) < f(x0) because f is strictly increasing, so f(x0) is a smaller counterexample. This contradicts the choice of x0.
The sequence a_n is non-decreasing. Indeed a_0 = a <= f(a) = a_1 by the first step. If a_n <= a_(n+1), then a_(n+1) = f(a_n) <= f(a_(n+1)) = a_(n+2), since f is increasing.
Let b = sup of the a_n, so b >= a. Case 1: a_n = a_(n+1) for some n. Then a_n is a fixed point, the sequence is constant from n on, and b = a_n. So f(b) = b.

Case 2: a_n < a_(n+1) for all n. Then b is a limit ordinal. It is above every a_n, and if b were c + 1, then c < b would give some a_n > c, so a_n >= c + 1 = b, which is false. The a_n are cofinal in b. For d < b there is n with d <= a_n, so f(d) <= f(a_n).
By continuity at the limit b, f(b) is the supremum of f(d) for d < b. By the cofinality, this equals the supremum of the f(a_n) = a_(n+1), which is b. So f(b) = b.

Least fixed point. Let c >= a with f(c) = c. By induction, a_n <= c for all n: a_0 = a <= c, and a_n <= c implies a_(n+1) = f(a_n) <= f(c) = c. Hence b <= c. So b is the least fixed point above a, and the fixed points are unbounded because a was arbitrary.

steps.text: Compute the iterates. a_0 = 0 and a_1 = omega + 0 = omega. If a_n = omega * n, then a_(n+1) = omega + omega * n = omega * (1 + n) = omega * (n + 1), because 1 + n = n + 1 for a natural number n.
Check the coefficient for n = 4: the next iterate after omega * 4 has coefficient 1 + 4.
The supremum of omega * n over n is omega * omega = omega squared. The lemma says that b = omega squared is a fixed point of f.
Verify directly. f(omega * omega) = omega + omega * omega = omega * (1 + omega) = omega * omega, because 1 + omega = omega.

applications.conclusion: The least fixed point of x -> omega + x above 0 is omega squared, and the iteration from 0 needs omega many steps to reach it.

results.name: Compactness theorem for propositional logic
aliases: finite satisfiability implies satisfiability for propositional formulas
results.statement: Let P be a set of propositional variables, of any size. Let Gamma be a set of propositional formulas built from the variables of P with the connectives not and and. If every finite subset of Gamma is satisfiable, then Gamma is satisfiable. That is, if every finite subset has a truth assignment v: P -> {true, false} that makes all its formulas true, then one assignment makes all formulas of Gamma true.
hypotheses: Formulas are variables p in P, negations (not f), and conjunctions (f and g) for formulas f and g. Other connectives are abbreviations built from these.
A truth assignment v: P -> {true, false} extends to all formulas in the usual way. (not f) is true iff f is false. (f and g) is true iff both are true.
Gamma can be infinite, and P can be uncountable. The proof uses Zorn's lemma.

prerequisites.reason: Step 1 applies Zorn's lemma to the family of finitely satisfiable extensions of Gamma.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration is the compactness theorem for first-order theories over any language. Propositional logic is the special case of a language that has only relation symbols of arity zero. The authored proof is the direct Zorn argument for this case, not the ultraproduct proof of mathlib.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let F be the set of all finitely satisfiable sets D of formulas with Gamma inside D, ordered by inclusion. F contains Gamma. A nonempty chain in F has its union in F: a finite subset of the union lies in one member of the chain (take the largest of finitely many members), and so it is satisfiable. By Zorn's lemma, F has a maximal element D.

Dichotomy. For every formula f, f is in D or (not f) is in D. Suppose neither D plus f nor D plus (not f) is finitely satisfiable. Then there are finite sets D1 and D2 inside D such that D1 plus f and D2 plus (not f) are unsatisfiable. The finite set D1 union D2 is satisfied by some v. Under v, f is true or false. If f is true, v satisfies D1 plus f. If f is false, v satisfies D2 plus (not f). Both cases are impossible. So one of the two sets is finitely satisfiable, and by maximality f or (not f) is in D.
Exclusion. D never contains both f and (not f), because the finite set {f, (not f)} has no satisfying assignment. So exactly one of f and (not f) is in D.

Conjunction. If (f and g) is in D, then f is in D: otherwise (not f) is in D, and the finite set {(f and g), (not f)} is unsatisfiable. In the same way g is in D. Conversely, if f and g are in D but (f and g) is not, then (not (f and g)) is in D by the dichotomy, and the finite set {f, g, (not (f and g))} is unsatisfiable.

Define v(p) = true iff p is in D. Show by induction on formulas that f is true under v iff f is in D. For a variable this is the definition. For (not f) it follows from the exclusion and the dichotomy. For (f and g) it follows from the previous step and the induction hypotheses.
Gamma is inside D, so every formula of Gamma is true under v. Thus Gamma is satisfiable.

applications.title: A sequence of variables with each neighbouring pair different has a satisfying assignment
applications.inputs: Variables p_0, p_1, p_2, ... and the formulas g_n saying 'exactly one of p_n and p_(n+1) is true', that is g_n = (not (p_n and p_(n+1))) and (not ((not p_n) and (not p_(n+1)))). Gamma = {g_n : n >= 0}.
applications.hypotheses: Any finite subset of Gamma mentions the formulas g_n for n up to some m. All these formulas are satisfied by the assignment with p_j true iff j is even.

steps.text: Check the formulas g_0, g_1, g_2 on four variables p_0..p_3. There are 2^4 truth assignments to the four variables.
g_0, g_1, g_2 force p_1 = not p_0, p_2 = not p_1, p_3 = not p_2. Only the value of p_0 is free, so the number of satisfying assignments is a power of 2.
The alternating assignment (true, false, true, false) is one of them, so the finite subset {g_0, g_1, g_2} is satisfiable. The same argument works for g_0..g_m with any m.
Each finite subset of Gamma is satisfiable, so by the theorem Gamma is satisfiable by one assignment of all the variables p_n.

applications.conclusion: Gamma has a model. Here the model alternates truth values, and the theorem gives it without constructing it, which also works for sets of formulas that have no pattern.

results.name: Rado selection lemma
results.statement: Let A be a set. For each a in A let B_a be a finite set. Suppose that for every finite subset s of A we are given a function g(s) in the product of the sets B_a, that is, g(s)(a) is in B_a for all a in A. Then there is a function chi in the product of the B_a such that for every finite s there is a finite t with s inside t and chi(x) = g(t)(x) for all x in s.
hypotheses: A is any set, finite or infinite. Each B_a is finite.
If some B_a is empty then no function g(s) exists, so the hypothesis already says that every B_a is nonempty.
The proof uses the Tychonoff theorem for a product of finite discrete spaces. That form needs a weak form of the axiom of choice. The ultrafilter lemma is enough.

prerequisites.reason: Step 1 uses that a product of finite discrete spaces is compact, which is the Tychonoff theorem for finite factors.

definitions.name: compactness by closed sets

theorem Finset.rado_selection (g : Finset α → (a : α) → β a) :
    ∃ χ : (a : α) → β a, ∀ s : Finset α, ∃ t : Finset α, s ⊆ t ∧ ∀ x ∈ s, χ x = g t x := by
  classical
  let instTop (a : α) : TopologicalSpace (β a) := ⊥
  have instDiscr (a : α) : DiscreteTopology (β a) := discreteTopology_bot _
  let e (s : Finset α) : Set ((a : α) → β a) := {f | ∃ t, s ⊆ t ∧ ∀ x ∈ s, f x = g t x}
  have (s : Finset α) : s.restrict ⁻¹' {f | ∃ t, s ⊆ t ∧ ∀ x, f x = g t x} = e s := by simp [e]
  have he' (s : Finset α) : IsClosed (e s) := by
    rw [← this]
    exact (isClosed_discrete _).preimage (by fun_prop)
  have he'' (B : Finset (Finset α)) : (⋂ i ∈ B, e i).Nonempty := by
    refine ⟨g (B.biUnion id), ?_⟩
    simp only [Set.mem_iInter, Set.mem_ofPred_eq, e]
    intro i hi
    exact ⟨_, subset_biUnion_of_mem id hi, by simp⟩
  simpa using! CompactSpace.iInter_nonempty he' he''

source.alignment: The Lean declaration uses a family of types and the product of finite types. The authored statement is the same with sets B_a. The authored proof gives the topological argument in detail.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Give each B_a the discrete topology. Since each B_a is finite, the product space X of the B_a is compact by Tychonoff's theorem. Each g(s) is a point of X.
For each finite s, let C_s be the closure in X of the set G_s = {g(t) : t finite, s inside t}. C_s is closed. C_s is nonempty because g(s) is in G_s.

The family has the finite intersection property. If s_1, ..., s_n are finite sets, then u = s_1 union ... union s_n is finite. Every t containing u contains each s_i, so G_u is inside each G_(s_i), and C_u is inside each C_(s_i). The point g(u) is in all of them, so the intersection of C_(s_1), ..., C_(s_n) is nonempty.
By compactness, the intersection of all C_s is nonempty. Choose chi in it. For a finite s, consider the basic open set U = {psi in X : psi(x) = chi(x) for all x in s}. It contains chi.

Because chi lies in the closure C_s of G_s, every open set that contains chi meets G_s. So U contains some g(t) with t finite and s inside t. For this t, g(t)(x) = chi(x) for all x in s. This is the claim.

applications.title: A proper 3-colouring of the infinite graph on N where i and j are adjacent when 0 < |i - j| <= 2
applications.inputs: A = N, B_i = {0, 1, 2} for every i. For a finite set s, g(s) is the greedy colouring: vertices of s in increasing order get the least colour not used by an earlier neighbour in s, and vertices outside s get colour 0.
applications.hypotheses: Each B_i is finite. For every finite s the map g(s) gives different colours to adjacent vertices of s, because the greedy rule avoids the colours of earlier neighbours, and each vertex has at most 2 earlier neighbours, so a free colour exists among 3.

steps.text: Check the greedy rule on s = {0,...,5}. Vertex 0 gets colour 0 and vertex 1 gets colour 1. Vertex i with i >= 2 has earlier neighbours i-1 and i-2 with two different colours, so exactly one colour of the three is left.
The colours are therefore 0,1,2,0,1,2 on s. The colour of vertex 5 equals 5 minus 3 times 1.

Apply the lemma to get chi: N -> {0, 1, 2}. Take an edge {i, j}. Let s = {i, j}. There is a finite t with s inside t and chi = g(t) on s. The colouring g(t) is proper on t, so chi(i) differs from chi(j).
Every edge of the infinite graph is of this kind, so chi is a proper 3-colouring of the whole graph.

applications.conclusion: The lemma turns a family of finite proper colourings into one proper colouring chi of the infinite graph with 3 colours.

results.name: Euclidean division of ordinals
results.statement: Let b be a nonzero ordinal. For every ordinal a there are unique ordinals q and r such that a = b * q + r and r < b. Here * and + are ordinal multiplication and addition.
hypotheses: b is an ordinal with b > 0. For b = 0 the statement is false.
Ordinal multiplication x -> b * x is strictly increasing and continuous for b > 0. Ordinal addition is strictly increasing in its right argument.
If x <= y then there is a unique ordinal z with x + z = y (subtraction on the left).

steps.text: Let S = {c : b * c <= a}. S contains 0. Every c in S satisfies c <= b * c <= a, because x -> b * x is strictly increasing and b >= 1. So S is a set of ordinals bounded by a. Let q be its supremum.

Claim q is in S. If q is the largest element of S, this is clear. Otherwise q is a limit ordinal and each c < q lies below some element of S, so b * c <= a. By continuity, b * q is the supremum of the b * c with c < q, so b * q <= a.
Since q is the maximum of S, q + 1 is not in S. So b * (q + 1) = b * q + b > a. Because b * q <= a, subtraction gives r with b * q + r = a.
Show r < b. If r >= b, then a = b * q + r >= b * q + b = b * (q + 1), which contradicts b * (q + 1) > a. Hence a = b * q + r with r < b. This is existence.

Uniqueness. Suppose b * q + r = b * q' + r' with r, r' < b and q < q'. Then b * q' >= b * (q + 1) = b * q + b > b * q + r, so b * q' + r' > b * q + r, which contradicts equality. So q = q'. Then b * q + r = b * q + r' gives r = r' because addition is strictly increasing in the right argument.

results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only standard properties of ordinal addition and multiplication, which are listed in the hypotheses. It needs no named result from the catalog.

results.name: Cantor normal form of ordinals
aliases: Cantor normal form for ordinals to the base omega
results.statement: Let b > 1 be an ordinal. Every ordinal a > 0 can be written in exactly one way as a = b^(e_1) * c_1 + b^(e_2) * c_2 + ... + b^(e_k) * c_k with k >= 1, ordinals e_1 > e_2 > ... > e_k, and ordinals c_i with 0 < c_i < b. The ordinal 0 is the empty sum, with k = 0. With b = omega, the c_i are positive natural numbers.
hypotheses: b is an ordinal with b >= 2. Powers and products are ordinal powers and products. The order of the factors matters.
a is any ordinal. The exponents e_i are ordinals and they strictly decrease.
The coefficients c_i are ordinals with 0 < c_i < b. If b = omega, the coefficients are the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ...

prerequisites.reason: Steps 2 and 5 divide a by b^(e_1) with remainder and use the uniqueness of the quotient and the remainder.

definitions.name: ordinal power
definitions.text: b^0 = 1, b^(e+1) = b^e * b, and b^l is the supremum of b^e for e < l when l is a limit ordinal. For b > 1 the map e -> b^e is strictly increasing and continuous, so e <= b^e.

steps.text: Leading exponent. For a > 0, the set S = {e : b^e <= a} contains 0 and is bounded by a, since e <= b^e. Its supremum e_1 is in S: either S has a largest element, or the supremum is a limit ordinal l and b^l is the supremum of the b^e below it, so b^l <= a by continuity. So e_1 is the largest element of S, and b^(e_1) <= a < b^(e_1 + 1) = b^(e_1) * b.

Existence by induction on a. Divide a by b^(e_1) to get a = b^(e_1) * c_1 + r with r < b^(e_1). If c_1 = 0 then a = r < b^(e_1) <= a, which is false, so c_1 >= 1. If c_1 >= b then a >= b^(e_1) * b, which contradicts a < b^(e_1) * b. So 0 < c_1 < b.

If r = 0 we are done with k = 1. Otherwise r < b^(e_1) <= a, so r < a, and the induction hypothesis writes r = b^(e_2) * c_2 + ... with e_2 the largest e with b^e <= r. Since b^(e_2) <= r < b^(e_1) and e -> b^e is increasing, e_2 < e_1. This gives the form for a.

Size bound for uniqueness. If a = b^(e_1) * c_1 + T with T the tail sum of the later terms, then b^(e_1) <= a < b^(e_1 + 1). The lower bound holds because c_1 >= 1. For the upper bound, T < b^(e_2 + 1) <= b^(e_1) by induction on the length of the sum and e_2 + 1 <= e_1. Then a < b^(e_1) * c_1 + b^(e_1) = b^(e_1) * (c_1 + 1) <= b^(e_1) * b, since c_1 + 1 <= b.

Uniqueness. By the size bound, e_1 is the largest e with b^e <= a, so e_1 depends only on a. Also T < b^(e_1), so a = b^(e_1) * c_1 + T is the division of a by b^(e_1) with remainder. By the uniqueness of that division, c_1 and T depend only on a. Since T < b^(e_1) <= a, T is smaller than a, and induction on a shows that the rest of the expansion is unique.

applications.title: Add two ordinals in Cantor normal form to the base omega
applications.inputs: a = omega^2 * 3 + omega * 5 + 7 and c = omega * 2 + 4. The base is b = omega, and a base-10 check with the number 2026.
applications.hypotheses: Both ordinals are sums of terms omega^e * n with exponents 2 > 1 > 0 and coefficients that are positive natural numbers, so they are in Cantor normal form with b = omega.

steps.text: First a base-10 check on a finite number. The number 2026 has Cantor normal form 10^3 * 2 + 10^1 * 2 + 10^0 * 6 with exponents 3 > 1 > 0 and coefficients below 10. The term 10^2 * 0 is left out.
Compute a + c = omega^2 * 3 + omega * 5 + 7 + omega * 2 + 4. The tail 7 + omega * 2 equals omega * 2, because 7 + omega = omega.
Then omega * 5 + omega * 2 = omega * (5 + 2) by left distributivity. Add the coefficients.
So a + c = omega^2 * 3 + omega * 7 + 4. This is in Cantor normal form: exponents 2 > 1 > 0 and coefficients 3, 7, 4 are positive and below omega. By uniqueness, this is the only such form of a + c.

applications.conclusion: The sum is omega^2 * 3 + omega * 7 + 4. The term 7 of a is absorbed by omega * 2, and Cantor normal form shows which terms survive.

results.name: Embedding of countable linear orders into dense orders
aliases: every countable linear order embeds in the rationals
Cantor embedding theorem for countable orders
results.statement: Let A be a countable set with a strict total order. Let B be a densely ordered set with a strict total order and at least two elements. Then there is a map f: A -> B such that a < a' if and only if f(a) < f(a'). In particular every countable linear order embeds in the rational numbers.
hypotheses: A is countable, finite or countably infinite, with a total order <.
B is totally ordered and dense: for x < y in B there is z in B with x < z < y.
B has two elements x < y. B can have endpoints. The embedding takes values in the open interval from x to y.
The choices of the elements z use the axiom of dependent choice. For B = Q they can be made explicit.

definitions.name: order embedding
definitions.text: A map f with a < a' iff f(a) < f(a'). It is injective because the order on A is total.

definitions.name: dense order
definitions.text: A total order in which every pair x < y has some z with x < z < y.

theorem embedding_from_countable_to_dense [Countable α] [DenselyOrdered β] [Nontrivial β] :
    Nonempty (α ↪o β) := by
  cases nonempty_encodable α
  rcases exists_pair_lt β with ⟨x, y, hxy⟩
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := exists_between hxy
  have : Nonempty (Set.Ioo x y) := ⟨⟨a, ha⟩⟩
  let our_ideal : Ideal (PartialIso α _) :=
    idealOfCofinals default (definedAtLeft (Set.Ioo x y))
  let F a := funOfIdeal a our_ideal (cofinal_meets_idealOfCofinals _ _ a)
  refine
    ⟨RelEmbedding.trans (OrderEmbedding.ofStrictMono (fun a ↦ (F a).val) fun a₁ a₂ ↦ ?_)
        (OrderEmbedding.subtype _)⟩
  rcases (F a₁).prop with ⟨f, hf, ha₁⟩
  rcases (F a₂).prop with ⟨g, hg, ha₂⟩
  rcases our_ideal.directed _ hf _ hg with ⟨m, _hm, fm, gm⟩
  exact (lt_iff_lt_of_cmp_eq_cmp <| m.prop (a₁, _) (fm ha₁) (a₂, _) (gm ha₂)).mp

steps.text: Enumerate A as a_0, a_1, a_2, ... (finite or infinite). Fix x < y in B. We define f(a_0), f(a_1), ... one after another so that after n steps the map f on F_n = {a_0, ..., a_(n-1)} is order preserving in both directions and takes values in the open interval (x, y).

Step n. Let L be the set of elements of F_n below a_n and U the set of elements of F_n above a_n. By totality, F_n is the disjoint union of L and U. Put l = f(max L) if L is nonempty, otherwise l = x. Put u = f(min U) if U is nonempty, otherwise u = y.

Show l < u. If L and U are both nonempty, max L < min U in A, so f(max L) < f(min U) by the invariant. If only one is nonempty, the value of f lies in (x, y), so x < f(min U) or f(max L) < y. If both are empty, x < y. By density, choose f(a_n) with l < f(a_n) < u.

The invariant holds for F_(n+1). The value f(a_n) is in (x, y). For a_i in L, f(a_i) <= f(max L) < f(a_n). For a_i in U, f(a_n) < f(min U) <= f(a_i). So f is order preserving in both directions on F_(n+1).
Two elements a_i and a_j of A with i < j are both in F_(j+1), so f compares them as the order of A does. Hence a < a' iff f(a) < f(a') for all a, a' in A, and f is an order embedding.

applications.title: Place four points of a countable order in the rationals between 0 and 1
applications.inputs: A = {a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3} with a_1 < a_3 < a_0 < a_2, enumerated in this index order, and B = Q with x = 0, y = 1.
applications.hypotheses: A is finite, hence countable. Q is dense and has the two elements 0 < 1.

steps.text: Step 0. F_0 is empty, so l = 0 and u = 1. Choose the midpoint for f(a_0).
Step 1. The element a_1 is below a_0, so L is empty and U = {a_0}. Then l = 0 and u = 1/2. Choose the midpoint for f(a_1).
Step 2. The element a_2 is above a_0 and above a_1. So L = {a_0, a_1} with max L = a_0, and U is empty. Then l = 1/2 and u = 1. Choose the midpoint.
Step 3. The element a_3 is above a_1 and below a_0. So max L = a_1 and min U = a_0, with l = 1/4 and u = 1/2. Choose the midpoint.

applications.conclusion: The values f(a_1) = 1/4 < f(a_3) = 3/8 < f(a_0) = 1/2 < f(a_2) = 3/4 follow the order a_1 < a_3 < a_0 < a_2, so f is an order embedding of A into Q.

results.name: Equivalence of all norms on a finite-dimensional space
aliases: all norms on a finite-dimensional vector space are equivalent
results.statement: Let E be a finite-dimensional vector space over K = R or K = C. Let N_a and N_b be two norms on E. Then there are constants 0 < c <= C < infinity such that c N_a(x) <= N_b(x) <= C N_a(x) for every x in E. Hence the identity map between (E, N_a) and (E, N_b) is a homeomorphism, and both norms give the same open sets, the same Cauchy sequences and the same bounded sets.
hypotheses: The scalar field K is R or C. The field must be complete for its absolute value. The result is false over Q with the usual absolute value.
E is a vector space over K of finite dimension n >= 0.
N_a and N_b are norms on E: they are positive definite, absolutely homogeneous and satisfy the triangle inequality.

prerequisites.reason: The proof needs the Heine-Borel theorem: the l^1 unit sphere in K^n is closed and bounded, so it is compact.

definitions.name: l^1 norm of a basis
definitions.text: Let e_1, ..., e_n be a basis of E. For x = x_1 e_1 + ... + x_n e_n define ||x||_1 = |x_1| + ... + |x_n|. This is a norm on E. The coordinate map x -> (x_1, ..., x_n) is a linear isometry from (E, ||.||_1) onto K^n with the l^1 norm.

definitions.name: equivalent norms
definitions.text: Two norms N_a and N_b on E are equivalent if there are constants c, C > 0 with c N_a <= N_b <= C N_a on E.
