source.alignment: Mathlib proves that every linear equivalence between finite-dimensional Hausdorff topological vector spaces over a complete field is a homeomorphism. The authored statement applies this to the identity map from (E, N_a) to (E, N_b), and then converts continuity of the map and of its inverse into the two inequalities.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Fix a basis e_1, ..., e_n of E with n >= 1. The case n = 0 is trivial because E = {0}. Let N be any norm on E, and let C_N = max_i N(e_i). For x = sum x_i e_i the triangle inequality and homogeneity give N(x) <= sum |x_i| N(e_i) <= C_N ||x||_1.
The norm N is continuous on (E, ||.||_1). By the reverse triangle inequality, |N(x) - N(y)| <= N(x - y) <= C_N ||x - y||_1. So N is Lipschitz for ||.||_1.

Let S = {x in E : ||x||_1 = 1}. Under the coordinate isometry S corresponds to {z in K^n : |z_1| + ... + |z_n| = 1}. This set is closed and bounded in K^n, which is R^n or R^(2n). By the Heine-Borel theorem it is compact. Also S is not empty.

A continuous real function on a non-empty compact set attains its minimum. So there is x_0 in S with N(x_0) = m_N = min over S of N. Since ||x_0||_1 = 1, x_0 is not 0. Because N is positive definite, m_N = N(x_0) > 0.

Let x in E with x not 0. Then x / ||x||_1 lies in S, so N(x / ||x||_1) >= m_N. Homogeneity of N gives N(x) >= m_N ||x||_1. The inequality is trivial for x = 0. So for every norm N we have m_N ||x||_1 <= N(x) <= C_N ||x||_1.

Apply Step 5 to N_a and N_b. Then N_b(x) <= C_b ||x||_1 <= (C_b / m_a) N_a(x), and N_a(x) <= C_a ||x||_1 <= (C_a / m_b) N_b(x). So c = m_b / C_a and C = C_b / m_a satisfy c N_a <= N_b <= C N_a, and c <= C follows by taking x not 0. The identity map and its inverse are Lipschitz, so they are homeomorphisms.

applications.title: Explicit equivalence constants for a norm on R^2
applications.inputs: Let E = R^2 with basis e_1 = (1, 0), e_2 = (0, 1). Let N(x) = |x_1 + x_2| + |x_2|. Compare N with the l^1 norm ||x||_1 = |x_1| + |x_2|.
applications.hypotheses: N is a norm on R^2: it is the sum of two seminorms, and N(x) = 0 forces x_2 = 0 and then x_1 = 0. The space R^2 is finite-dimensional over R, so the theorem applies.

steps.text: Compute N on the basis. N(e_1) = |1 + 0| + |0| = 1.
N(e_2) = |0 + 1| + |1| = 2. So C_N = max(1, 2) = 2 and the upper bound is N(x) <= 2 ||x||_1.
For the lower bound, use x_1 = (x_1 + x_2) - x_2 and the triangle inequality. Then |x_1| <= N(x) and |x_2| <= N(x), so ||x||_1 <= 2 N(x). Thus m_N >= 1/2.
The constant 1/2 is attained at x_0 = (1/2, -1/2). Here ||x_0||_1 = 1 and N(x_0) = |0| + 1/2 = 1/2.
Check the sharp lower bound ||x_0||_1 <= 2 N(x_0): the left side is 1 and the right side is 1.

applications.conclusion: On R^2 the norms N and ||.||_1 satisfy (1/2) ||x||_1 <= N(x) <= 2 ||x||_1, with both constants sharp. The proof of the theorem gives these constants by one compactness argument.

results.name: A linear map between normed spaces is continuous if and only if it is bounded
results.statement: Let X and Y be normed spaces over K = R or K = C. Let T: X -> Y be a linear map. The following four statements are equivalent. (a) T is continuous. (b) T is continuous at 0. (c) There is M >= 0 with ||Tx|| <= M ||x|| for every x in X. (d) T is bounded on the closed unit ball: sup of ||Tx|| over ||x|| <= 1 is finite. In this case T is Lipschitz with constant M.
hypotheses: X and Y are normed spaces over the same field K = R or K = C. Completeness is not needed.
T is linear: T(x + y) = Tx + Ty and T(ax) = aTx for all x, y in X and a in K.
The statement is false for non-linear T and for non-normed topological vector spaces in general.

definitions.name: operator norm
definitions.text: For a bounded linear map T, ||T|| is the smallest M with ||Tx|| <= M ||x|| for all x. It equals sup of ||Tx|| over ||x|| <= 1.

source.alignment: Mathlib states the equivalence between continuity of a linear map and the existence of a bound ||f x|| <= M ||x|| (IsBoundedLinearMap). The authored statement adds the two extra equivalent forms (b) and (d).

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: (a) implies (b): continuity at every point includes continuity at 0. (c) implies (d): if ||x|| <= 1 then ||Tx|| <= M ||x|| <= M. (d) implies (c): let M = sup over the unit ball. For x not 0, ||x / ||x|| || = 1, so ||T(x / ||x||)|| <= M. By linearity ||Tx|| <= M ||x||, and the case x = 0 is trivial.

(b) implies (c): continuity at 0 with T(0) = 0 gives delta > 0 such that ||u|| < delta implies ||Tu|| < 1. Let x not 0 and put u = (delta / 2) x / ||x||. Then ||u|| = delta / 2 < delta, so ||Tu|| < 1.
By homogeneity ||Tu|| = (delta / (2 ||x||)) ||Tx||. Hence ||Tx|| < (2 / delta) ||x||. So (c) holds with M = 2 / delta. The case x = 0 is trivial.

(c) implies (a): for x, y in X linearity gives ||Tx - Ty|| = ||T(x - y)|| <= M ||x - y||. So T is Lipschitz with constant M. Given epsilon > 0, take delta = epsilon / (M + 1). Then ||x - y|| < delta implies ||Tx - Ty|| < epsilon.
The implications (a) -> (b) -> (c) -> (a) and (c) <-> (d) show that the four statements are equivalent.

applications.title: Differentiation is not continuous on polynomials with the sup norm
applications.inputs: Let P be the space of real polynomials on [0, 1] with the sup norm ||p|| = max |p(t)|. Let D: P -> P be the derivative, D p = p'. D is linear. Take p_n(t) = t^n / n for n >= 1.
applications.hypotheses: P is a normed space and D is linear, so the theorem applies. P is not complete, but completeness is not needed.

steps.text: Compute the norm of p_n. The maximum of t^n / n on [0, 1] is at t = 1, so ||p_n|| = 1/n. For n = 10 this value is 1/10.
Compute D p_n = t^(n-1). Its sup norm is 1 for every n. In particular ||D p_10|| = 1, and the ratio ||D p_10|| / ||p_10|| equals 10.
The ratio ||D p_n|| / ||p_n|| equals n for every n. No finite M satisfies ||Dp|| <= M ||p|| on P, so statement (c) fails.
By the theorem, (a) and (c) are equivalent. So D is not continuous. Directly: p_n -> 0 uniformly because ||p_n|| = 1/n, but ||D p_n|| = 1 does not tend to 0.

applications.conclusion: The derivative is an unbounded linear operator on (P, sup norm), and the theorem shows that it is discontinuous. The sequence p_n shows the discontinuity at 0.

results.name: Finite-dimensional subspaces of a normed space are closed
results.statement: Let X be a normed space over K = R or K = C and let M be a linear subspace of X with finite dimension. Then M is a closed subset of X. Consequently, if x is not in M, then dist(x, M) = inf over m in M of ||x - m|| is strictly positive.
hypotheses: X is a normed space over K = R or K = C. X need not be complete.

steps.text: The subspace M with the norm of X is a finite-dimensional normed space over K. Since K is complete, M is a complete metric space.
Let (m_k) be a sequence in M that converges in X to a point x. We show x is in M.
A convergent sequence in X is a Cauchy sequence. Since M has the same metric as X, (m_k) is Cauchy in M. By completeness of M there is y in M with m_k -> y in M, hence in X.
Limits in the metric space X are unique, so x = y. So x is in M. Thus M contains the limits of all its convergent sequences, and M is closed.
For the distance consequence, let x not in M. The complement of M is open, so a ball B(x, r) with r > 0 does not meet M. Hence ||x - m|| >= r for all m in M, and dist(x, M) >= r > 0.

applications.title: The monomial t^3 stays at positive distance from quadratic polynomials in C[-1, 1]
applications.inputs: Let X = C[-1, 1] with the sup norm and M = P_2, the space of real polynomials of degree at most 2. dim M = 3. Let x(t) = t^3. Use the functional phi(f) = -f(-1) + 3 f(-1/3) - 3 f(1/3) + f(1).
applications.hypotheses: X is a normed space, M is a subspace of dimension 3, and t^3 is not in M. So the theorem applies and says dist(t^3, M) > 0.

steps.text: The functional phi kills the quadratics. For f = 1 the weights sum to zero.
For f(t) = t, phi(t) = 1 - 1 - 1 + 1 = 0. For f(t) = t^2, phi(t^2) = -1 + 3/9 - 3/9 + 1 = 0. So phi vanishes on P_2.
The weights have absolute sum 8, so |phi(f)| <= 8 ||f||. For q in M, phi(t^3 - q) = phi(t^3) = 16/9 and so ||t^3 - q|| >= (16/9) / 8.

applications.conclusion: The distance from t^3 to P_2 is at least 2/9. The theorem gives dist(t^3, P_2) > 0 without any computation; the functional phi gives the explicit lower bound 2/9.

source.alignment: Mathlib states the equivalence for topological vector spaces over a nontrivially normed field. The authored statement is the special case of a normed space, and the authored proof uses a distance argument.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Continuous implies closed kernel: ker f is the preimage f^{-1}({0}) of the closed set {0} in K. The preimage of a closed set under a continuous map is closed.
Now let ker f be closed. If f = 0 then f is continuous. Otherwise choose x_0 with f(x_0) = 1, by scaling a vector with f not 0. Then x_0 is not in ker f.
The complement of ker f is open and contains x_0. So there is r > 0 such that the ball B(x_0, r) does not meet ker f. Equivalently, ||x_0 - z|| >= r for every z in ker f.
Let y in X with f(y) not 0. Define z = x_0 - y / f(y). Then f(z) = 1 - 1 = 0, so z is in ker f. Therefore r <= ||x_0 - z|| = ||y|| / |f(y)|, so |f(y)| <= ||y|| / r.
If f(y) = 0 the inequality |f(y)| <= ||y|| / r is trivial. So f is bounded with constant 1/r. By the bounded-operator criterion, f is continuous.

applications.title: The derivative at 1 is a discontinuous functional on polynomials
applications.inputs: Let P be the space of real polynomials on [0, 1] with the sup norm. Let f(p) = p'(1). It is linear. Take p_n(t) = t - t^n / n.
applications.hypotheses: P is a normed space and f is a nonzero linear functional (f(t) = 1). So the theorem applies: f is continuous iff ker f is closed.

steps.text: p_n is in ker f. Indeed p_n'(t) = 1 - t^(n-1), so p_n'(1) = 1 - 1 = 0. For n = 7 the value is 1 - 7 * 1^6 / 7.
Compare p_n with q(t) = t. The difference is t^n / n with sup norm 1/n. For n = 7 the distance is 1/7.
So p_n -> q in P as n -> infinity, because 1/n -> 0. All p_n are in ker f, but f(q) = q'(1) = 1, which is not 0. So q is a limit of points of ker f that is not in ker f.
Therefore ker f is not closed. By the theorem, f is not continuous.

applications.conclusion: The functional p -> p'(1) is not continuous on (P, sup norm). The theorem turns the check into a search for one sequence in the kernel with a limit outside it.

theorem tendsto_of_tendsto_pointwise_of_cauchySeq {f : ℕ → E' →SL[σ₁₂] F} {g : E' →SL[σ₁₂] F}
    (hg : Tendsto (fun n x => f n x) atTop (𝓝 g)) (hf : CauchySeq f) : Tendsto f atTop (𝓝 g) := by
  /- Since `f` is a Cauchy sequence, there exists `b → 0` such that `‖f n - f m‖ ≤ b N` for any
    `m, n ≥ N`. -/
  rcases cauchySeq_iff_le_tendsto_0.1 hf with ⟨b, hb₀, hfb, hb_lim⟩
  simp_rw [dist_eq_norm] at hfb
  -- Since `b → 0`, it suffices to show that `‖f n x - g x‖ ≤ b n * ‖x‖` for all `n` and `x`.
  suffices ∀ n x, ‖f n x - g x‖ ≤ b n * ‖x‖ from
    tendsto_iff_norm_sub_tendsto_zero.2
    (squeeze_zero (fun n => norm_nonneg _) (fun n => opNorm_le_bound _ (hb₀ n) (this n)) hb_lim)
  intro n x
  -- Note that `f m x → g x`, hence `‖f n x - f m x‖ → ‖f n x - g x‖` as `m → ∞`
  have : Tendsto (fun m => ‖f n x - f m x‖) atTop (𝓝 ‖f n x - g x‖) :=
    (tendsto_const_nhds.sub <| tendsto_pi_nhds.1 hg _).norm
  -- Thus it suffices to verify `‖f n x - f m x‖ ≤ b n * ‖x‖` for `m ≥ n`.
  refine le_of_tendsto this (eventually_atTop.2 ⟨n, fun m hm => ?_⟩)
  -- This inequality follows from `‖f n - f m‖ ≤ b n`.
  exact (f n - f m).le_of_opNorm_le (hfb _ _ _ le_rfl hm) _

source.alignment: Mathlib gives the key lemma: if a Cauchy sequence of operators converges pointwise to an operator g, then it converges to g in the operator norm. The authored proof also constructs the pointwise limit and proves that it is a bounded linear operator; mathlib states the completeness itself as an instance in another module.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let (T_n) be a Cauchy sequence in B(X, Y). For each x, ||T_n x - T_m x|| <= ||T_n - T_m|| ||x||. So (T_n x) is a Cauchy sequence in Y. Since Y is complete, it converges. Define Tx = lim T_n x.
T is linear: T(ax + by) = lim T_n(ax + by) = lim (a T_n x + b T_n y) = a Tx + b Ty. Limits respect sums and scalar multiples.
T is bounded. A Cauchy sequence is bounded, so there is M with ||T_n|| <= M for all n. Then ||Tx|| = lim ||T_n x|| <= M ||x||, because the norm is continuous. So T is in B(X, Y).
Let epsilon > 0. Choose N with ||T_n - T_m|| < epsilon for n, m >= N. For x with ||x|| <= 1 and n >= N we have ||T_n x - T_m x|| <= epsilon. Let m -> infinity: ||T_n x - Tx|| <= epsilon.

Take the supremum over ||x|| <= 1: ||T_n - T|| <= epsilon for all n >= N. So T_n -> T in operator norm, and every Cauchy sequence in B(X, Y) converges. The dual X* is the case Y = K, which is complete.

applications.title: The matrix exponential series converges in operator norm
applications.inputs: Let X = R^2 with the Euclidean norm. Let J = [[0, -1], [1, 0]] be the rotation by 90 degrees. Let S_n = sum_{k=0}^{n} J^k / k! in B(X, X).
applications.hypotheses: B(R^2, R^2) is a Banach space by the theorem (R^2 is complete). J is orthogonal, so ||J^k|| = 1 for every k. Hence ||S_n - S_m|| <= sum_{k=m+1}^{n} 1/k!.

steps.text: Since J^2 = -I and J^4 = I, the (1,1) entry of S_5 is 1 - 1/2 + 1/24, because the entries of J^k/k! at (1,1) are 1, 0, -1/2, 0, 1/24, 0.
For the tail, use 1/k! <= (1/6!)(1/7)^(k-6) for k >= 6. So the sum over k >= 6 of 1/k! is at most (1/720) times the geometric sum 1 + 1/7 + 1/49 + ... = 7/6.
So the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence in B(R^2, R^2). The theorem gives a limit operator exp(J) in operator norm, and ||exp(J) - S_5|| <= 7/4320.
Each entry of exp(J) - S_5 is bounded by the operator norm. So the (1,1) entry of exp(J) lies within 7/4320 of 13/24.

applications.conclusion: The series for exp(J) converges in operator norm, with an explicit tail bound 7/4320 after five terms. The existence of the limit uses the completeness of B(R^2, R^2).

source.alignment: Mathlib proves completeness of M-quotients for a normed group M quotient by a subgroup S. The authored statement is the vector-space case and also records the quotient norm.

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let (xi_n) be a Cauchy sequence in X/M. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges, so it suffices to find a convergent subsequence. Choose indices n_1 < n_2 < ... with ||xi_{n_{k+1}} - xi_{n_k}|| < 2^{-k}.

Build lifts. Pick x_1 in X with pi(x_1) = xi_{n_1}. Suppose x_k is chosen with pi(x_k) = xi_{n_k}. The coset xi_{n_{k+1}} - xi_{n_k} has norm below 2^{-k}, so by the definition of the infimum it contains a vector y_k with ||y_k|| < 2^{-k}. Put x_{k+1} = x_k + y_k. Then pi(x_{k+1}) = xi_{n_{k+1}}.
(x_k) is Cauchy in X. For l > k, ||x_l - x_k|| <= sum_{j=k}^{l-1} ||y_j|| < sum_{j>=k} 2^{-j} = 2^{1-k}. This tends to 0 as k -> infinity.
X is complete, so x_k -> x for some x in X. The map pi is linear and ||pi(z)|| <= ||z||, because z belongs to its own coset. So pi is continuous, and pi(x_k) -> pi(x).
Since pi(x_k) = xi_{n_k}, the subsequence (xi_{n_k}) converges to pi(x). The Cauchy sequence (xi_n) has a convergent subsequence, so it converges to pi(x). Hence X/M is complete.

applications.title: The quotient of (R^2, l^1) by the diagonal is isometric to R
applications.inputs: Let X = R^2 with the l^1 norm ||(a, b)|| = |a| + |b|. Let M = { (t, t) : t in R }, the diagonal. M is closed. Take the coset of (5, 2).
applications.hypotheses: X is complete and M is a closed subspace, so X/M is a Banach space. Here we compute the quotient norm explicitly.

steps.text: For a coset of (a, b), ||(a, b) + M|| = inf over t of |a + t| + |b + t|. The triangle inequality gives |a + t| + |b + t| >= |(a + t) - (b + t)| = |a - b|.
The bound is attained at t = -3. Then |5 - 3| + |2 - 3| = 2 + 1.
So ||(a, b) + M|| = |a - b| for all (a, b). The map (a, b) + M -> a - b is a linear isometry from X/M onto R.
R is complete, which agrees with the theorem. The coset of (5, 2) has norm 3 in X/M, although the vector (5, 2) has norm 7 in X.

applications.conclusion: X/M is a one-dimensional Banach space isometric to (R, |.|), and the coset of (5, 2) has quotient norm 3. The theorem guarantees completeness for the general case.

steps.text: Let (x^(n)) be a Cauchy sequence in l^p. For each coordinate i, |x^(n)_i - x^(m)_i| <= ||x^(n) - x^(m)||_p. So (x^(n)_i)_n is a Cauchy sequence in K. Since K is complete, it converges to a limit x_i. Let x = (x_i).
Let epsilon > 0 and choose N with ||x^(n) - x^(m)||_p < epsilon for n, m >= N. For any finite index set J and n, m >= N, sum_{i in J} |x^(n)_i - x^(m)_i|^p <= epsilon^p.

Let m -> infinity. The sum over J is finite, so the limit can be taken termwise: sum_{i in J} |x^(n)_i - x_i|^p <= epsilon^p for n >= N. Take the supremum over finite J: sum_i |x^(n)_i - x_i|^p <= epsilon^p for n >= N.
So x^(N) - x is in l^p. Since l^p is closed under sums by Minkowski's inequality, x = x^(N) - (x^(N) - x) is in l^p.
From Step 3, ||x^(n) - x||_p <= epsilon for all n >= N. So x^(n) -> x in l^p. Every Cauchy sequence converges, and l^p is complete.

applications.title: Truncated harmonic sequences converge in l^2
applications.inputs: Let p = 2 and x^(n) = (1, 1/2, ..., 1/n, 0, 0, ...) for n >= 1. The expected limit is x = (1/i)_{i>=1}.
applications.hypotheses: Each x^(n) has finite support, so it is in l^2. For n > m, ||x^(n) - x^(m)||_2^2 = sum_{i=m+1}^{n} 1/i^2. The theorem applies because l^2 is complete.

steps.text: Estimate the tail by telescoping: for i >= 2, 1/i^2 <= 1/(i(i-1)) = 1/(i-1) - 1/i. So sum_{i=m+1}^{n} 1/i^2 <= 1/m - 1/n < 1/m.
So (x^(n)) is a Cauchy sequence in l^2. The theorem gives a limit in l^2, and its coordinates are the pointwise limits 1/i. The limit is x = (1/i).
Compute the partial sum of ||x||_2^2 for i <= 4: 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16.
The distance from x^(4) to the limit satisfies ||x - x^(4)||_2^2 = sum_{i>=5} 1/i^2 <= sum_{i>=5} (1/(i-1) - 1/i) = 1/(5-1).

applications.conclusion: The sequence x = (1/i) is in l^2, and x^(4) is within 1/2 of x in l^2 norm, because the squared distance is at most 1/4. Completeness of l^2 gives the limit without a closed formula.

def continuousLinearMapOfTendsto
    [T2Space F] {l : Filter α} [l.IsCountablyGenerated]
    [l.NeBot] (g : α → E →SL[σ₁₂] F) {f : E → F} (h : Tendsto (fun n x ↦ g n x) l (𝓝 f)) :
    E →SL[σ₁₂] F where
  toLinearMap := linearMapOfTendsto _ _ h
  cont := by
    -- Since the filter `l` is countably generated and nontrivial, we can find a sequence
    -- `u : ℕ → α` that tends to `l`. By considering `g ∘ u` instead of `g`, we can thus assume
    -- that `α = ℕ` and `l = atTop`
    rcases l.exists_seq_tendsto with ⟨u, hu⟩
    -- We claim that the limit is continuous because it's a limit of an equicontinuous family.
    -- By the Banach-Steinhaus theorem, this equicontinuity will follow from pointwise boundedness.
    refine (h.comp hu).continuous_of_equicontinuous
      (PolynormableSpace.banach_steinhaus ?_).equicontinuous
    -- For `x` fixed, we need to show that the range of `(i : ℕ) ↦ g i x` is bounded.
    intro x
    -- This follows from the fact that this sequence converges (to `f x`) by hypothesis.
    rw [tendsto_pi_nhds] at h
    exact ((h x).comp hu).isVonNBounded_range 𝕜₂

theorem exists_dual_vector (x : E) (h : ‖x‖ ≠ 0) : ∃ g : StrongDual 𝕜 E, ‖g‖ = 1 ∧ g x = ‖x‖ := by
  have hhomothety := LinearEquiv.toSpanNonzeroSingleton_homothety 𝕜 x (ne_zero_of_norm_ne_zero h)
  let coord : span 𝕜 {x} →L[𝕜] 𝕜 := (ofHomothety _ _ (by positivity) hhomothety).symm
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ := exists_extension_norm_eq (span 𝕜 {x}) ((‖x‖ : 𝕜) • coord)
  have hval : g x = ‖x‖ := by
    have hgx : g x = g (⟨x, by simp⟩ : span 𝕜 {x}) := by rw [Submodule.coe_mk]
    have hcx : coord ⟨x, _⟩ = 1 := LinearEquiv.coord_self 𝕜 E x (ne_zero_of_norm_ne_zero h)
    simp [-algebraMap_smul, hgx, ↓hg.left, hcx]
  refine ⟨g, le_antisymm ?_ ?_, hval⟩
  · simp only [hg.right, norm_smul, norm_algebraMap', norm_norm]
    grw [coord.opNorm_le_bound (by positivity)
      (fun y ↦ (homothety_inverse _ (by positivity) _ hhomothety y).le), mul_inv_cancel₀ h]
  · have hle := g.le_opNorm x
    simp only [hval, norm_algebraMap', norm_norm] at hle
    exact one_le_of_le_mul_right₀ (by positivity) hle

steps.text: Let M = K x be the span of x. Since x is not 0, every element of M is written uniquely as a x with a in K. Define g on M by g(a x) = a ||x||. This is a well-defined linear functional.
Compute its norm on M. |g(a x)| = |a| ||x|| = ||a x||. So |g(m)| = ||m|| for all m in M. Hence ||g|| = 1, because the supremum over the unit ball of M is attained at m = x / ||x||.
By the Hahn-Banach theorem g extends to a linear functional f on X with ||f|| = ||g|| = 1.
Since x lies in M, f(x) = g(x) = ||x||. This proves the existence of f.

steps.text: For fixed x, the map f -> f(x) is linear in f. It is bounded: |(Jx)(f)| = |f(x)| <= ||f|| ||x||. So Jx is a continuous linear functional on X*, and ||Jx|| <= ||x||.
J is linear in x: (J(ax + by))(f) = f(ax + by) = a f(x) + b f(y) = (a Jx + b Jy)(f), because every f is linear.
Let x not 0. By the norming functional theorem there is f_0 in X* with ||f_0|| = 1 and f_0(x) = ||x||. Then ||Jx|| >= |(Jx)(f_0)| / ||f_0|| = ||x||.
Together ||Jx|| = ||x|| for x not 0, and for x = 0 both sides are 0. So J is a linear isometry. In particular J is injective.

X** is the dual of the normed space X*, so it is a Banach space. The closure of J(X) in X** is complete because it is closed in a complete space, and it contains J(X) densely. So it is a completion of X.

applications.title: The right shift is bounded below; the diagonal operator 1/k is not
applications.inputs: On l^2 let S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) and D(x_1, x_2, ...) = (x_1, x_2/2, x_3/3, ...). Both are bounded linear operators on the Banach space l^2.
applications.hypotheses: l^2 is a Banach space and S and D are bounded, so the theorem applies. S preserves the norm. The standard unit vector e_k has D e_k = e_k / k.

steps.text: S is an isometry: ||Sx||_2^2 = 0 + sum |x_i|^2 = ||x||_2^2. So S is bounded below with c = 1, and the theorem says S is injective with closed range. The range is { y : y_1 = 0 }.
For D: ||D e_k|| = 1/k and ||e_k|| = 1. If D were bounded below by c = 1/100 we would need 1/k >= 1/100 for every k. At k = 101 the difference is positive, so the inequality fails.
No c > 0 works, because 1/k tends to 0. So D is not bounded below. D is injective (D x = 0 forces every x_i = 0), so by the theorem the range of D is not closed.

The range of D contains every finite sequence, which is dense in l^2, and does not contain the sequence (1/k), because D^{-1}(1/k) = (1, 1, 1, ...) is not in l^2. So the range is dense and proper, hence not closed.

applications.conclusion: The right shift has closed range and is bounded below with c = 1. The diagonal operator D is injective with dense proper range, so it is not bounded below. The theorem separates the two cases.

steps.text: If p = 1, both sides equal 1 + s, so the inequality holds with equality. From now on assume p > 1. Define g(s) = (1+s)^p - 1 - p*s on [-1, infinity). We must show g(s) >= 0, and g(s) > 0 for s != 0.

The function g is continuous on [-1, infinity) because x -> x^p is continuous on [0, infinity) for p > 0. On (-1, infinity) the function g is differentiable and g'(s) = p*(1+s)^(p-1) - p = p*((1+s)^(p-1) - 1), by the power rule for the positive base 1+s.
Determine the sign of g'. Here p > 1 gives p - 1 > 0. If s > 0, then 1+s > 1, so (1+s)^(p-1) > 1 and g'(s) > 0. If -1 < s < 0, then 0 < 1+s < 1, so (1+s)^(p-1) < 1 and g'(s) < 0. Also g'(0) = 0.

Let 0 <= a < b. The function g is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), where g' > 0. The mean value theorem gives g(b) - g(a) = g'(c)(b - a) for some c in (a, b), so g(b) - g(a) > 0. Hence g is strictly increasing on [0, infinity).

Let -1 <= a < b <= 0. Again g is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b) where g' < 0. The mean value theorem gives g(b) - g(a) < 0. Hence g is strictly decreasing on [-1, 0]. The endpoint -1 needs only continuity, because the mean value theorem uses differentiability on the open interval.

Since g(0) = 1 - 1 - 0 = 0, step 4 gives g(s) > 0 for s > 0, and step 5 gives g(s) > 0 for -1 <= s < 0. So g(s) >= 0 for every s >= -1, with equality only at s = 0. This is the claim 1 + p*s <= (1+s)^p, strict for s != 0 when p > 1.

The square of the left bound is (11/8)^2.

  have ha : 0 ≤ (z - y) / (z - x) := by positivity
  have hb : 0 ≤ (y - x) / (z - x) := by positivity
  have key := hf.2 hx hz ha hb (by field)
  simp only [smul_eq_mul] at key
  ring_nf at key
  field_simp at key ⊢
  linarith

steps.text: Put P = p/r and Q = q/r. Then 1/P + 1/Q = r(1/p + 1/q) = r * (1/r) = 1.

Both P and Q exceed 1. Indeed 1/P = r/p = r * (1/p) and 1/p = 1/r - 1/q < 1/r because 1/q > 0, so 1/P < 1. The same argument gives 1/Q < 1. Together with 1/P + 1/Q = 1 and P, Q > 0, the numbers P and Q are conjugate exponents.
Define u_i = f(i)^r >= 0 and v_i = g(i)^r >= 0. Then (f(i) g(i))^r = u_i v_i for nonnegative numbers, by the rule (xy)^r = x^r y^r.
Apply Hölder's inequality with the conjugate pair (P, Q): sum u_i v_i <= (sum u_i^P)^(1/P) (sum v_i^Q)^(1/Q).

Rewrite the powers. Since u_i^P = (f(i)^r)^(p/r) = f(i)^p and 1/P = r/p, the first factor is (sum f(i)^p)^(r/p). In the same way v_i^Q = g(i)^q and 1/Q = r/q, so the second factor is (sum g(i)^q)^(r/q). Combined with step 3, this is the claim.

steps.text: Consider the double sum D = sum_{i=1}^n sum_{j=1}^n (x_i - x_j)^2. It is a sum of squares of real numbers, so D >= 0.
Expand each term: (x_i - x_j)^2 = x_i^2 - 2 x_i x_j + x_j^2.

Sum over j and then over i. The term x_i^2 occurs n times for each i, so the first part gives n sum x_i^2. The term x_j^2 gives the same, n sum x_j^2. The cross term gives -2 sum_i sum_j x_i x_j = -2 (sum x_i)^2.
Hence D = 2n sum x_i^2 - 2 (sum x_i)^2. Together with D >= 0 this gives (sum x_i)^2 <= n sum x_i^2.
Equality case. D = 0 holds if and only if every term (x_i - x_j)^2 is 0, that is, if and only if all x_i are equal. So equality holds exactly when x_1 = ... = x_n.

steps.text: Case a = 0. Then a*b = 0 and a^p = 0. The right side is 0 + b^q/q, which is 0 if and only if b = 0. And a^p = b^q means 0 = b^q, which is also true if and only if b = 0. So the equivalence holds. The case b = 0 is symmetric. In both cases the inequality is clear since a^p/p + b^q/q >= 0.
Now let a, b > 0. Put x = a^p > 0 and y = b^q > 0. Then a = x^(1/p) and b = y^(1/q), so a*b = x^(1/p) y^(1/q) = exp((1/p) ln x + (1/q) ln y).

The weights 1/p and 1/q are positive and add to 1. Apply Jensen's inequality to the concave function ln: (1/p) ln x + (1/q) ln y <= ln(x/p + y/q). The strict form of Jensen says this is an equality if and only if x = y, because ln is strictly concave and the weights are positive.
Apply the increasing function exp to both sides of step 3. This gives a*b <= x/p + y/q = a^p/p + b^q/q. This is Young's inequality, and it is an equality if and only if x = y.
Since x = a^p and y = b^q, the condition x = y is the condition a^p = b^q. So a*b = a^p/p + b^q/q if and only if a^p = b^q. With the cases of step 1, this proves the theorem.

steps.text: Put N = (sum f(i)^p)^(1/p). Upper bound. Let g >= 0 with sum g(i)^q <= 1. By Hölder's inequality, sum f(i) g(i) <= N * (sum g(i)^q)^(1/q).
Since 0 <= sum g(i)^q <= 1 and 1/q > 0, we have (sum g(i)^q)^(1/q) <= 1. Hence sum f(i) g(i) <= N. So N is an upper bound of the set.
Attainment, case N = 0. Then every f(i)^p = 0, so f = 0. The choice g = 0 is in the unit ball, and sum f g = 0 = N.
Attainment, case N > 0. Define g(i) = f(i)^(p-1) / N^(p-1). Since 1/p + 1/q = 1, we have q = p/(p-1), so (p-1) q = p. Then g(i)^q = f(i)^((p-1)q) / N^((p-1)q) = f(i)^p / N^p.
Sum over i: sum g(i)^q = (sum f(i)^p)/N^p = N^p/N^p = 1. So g lies in the unit ball.
Compute the pairing: sum f(i) g(i) = sum f(i)^p / N^(p-1) = N^p / N^(p-1) = N. So the value N is reached by this g. Together with steps 1 and 2, N is the greatest element of the set.

steps.text: We prove by induction on n the claim: every nonzero p in D[x] of degree n has at most n distinct roots in D.
Base case n = 0. Then p is a nonzero constant c. Every value p(a) equals c ≠ 0, so p has no root and 0 ≤ 0 holds.
Induction step, n ≥ 1. If p has no root, there is nothing to show. Otherwise let a be a root. The factor theorem gives p = (x - a) q with q in D[x].
The leading coefficient of (x - a) q is the leading coefficient of q, because x - a is monic. So q ≠ 0, and deg q = n - 1. The ring D need not have inverses here.
Let b be a root of p with b ≠ a. Then 0 = p(b) = (b - a) q(b). Since b - a ≠ 0 and D has no zero divisors, q(b) = 0. Hence every root of p is a or a root of q.
By the induction hypothesis q has at most n - 1 distinct roots. So p has at most 1 + (n - 1) = n distinct roots. This completes the induction.

The same argument with multiplicities: the multiplicity of a in p is 1 plus the multiplicity of a in q, and the other roots of p are roots of q with equal multiplicity. So the count with multiplicity is also at most n.

applications.title: Square roots of 1 modulo a prime and modulo 15
applications.inputs: The polynomial p = x^2 - 1 over the field Z/13 and over the ring Z/15. Here n = 2.
applications.hypotheses: Z/13 is a field because 13 is prime, so it is an integral domain. Z/15 is not an integral domain because 3 * 5 = 15 = 0 in Z/15.

steps.text: In Z/13 the elements 1 and 12 are roots. We check 12^2 - 1 = 143 and 143 = 11 * 13.
The quotient 143 / 13 is an integer, so 13 divides 143.
The theorem says p has at most 2 roots in Z/13. Hence 1 and 12 are the only square roots of 1 modulo 13.
In Z/15 the element 4 is a root, because 4^2 - 1 = 15 = 0 modulo 15.
The element 11 is also a root, because 11^2 - 1 = 120 = 8 * 15.
So x^2 - 1 has the 4 roots 1, 4, 11, 14 in Z/15. This is more than the degree 2. The hypothesis of no zero divisors cannot be dropped.

applications.conclusion: Modulo the prime 13 the equation x^2 = 1 has exactly the two solutions 1 and 12. Modulo 15 it has 4 solutions, so the bound fails in a ring with zero divisors.

results.name: Lagrange interpolation theorem
results.statement: Let F be a field. Let x_0, ..., x_n be n + 1 distinct elements of F, and let y_0, ..., y_n be any elements of F. Then there is exactly one polynomial P in F[x] of degree at most n with P(x_i) = y_i for all i. It is P = sum_i y_i L_i, where L_i(x) = prod_{j ≠ i} (x - x_j)/(x_i - x_j). If P has degree at most n, then the coefficient of x^n in P equals sum_i P(x_i) / prod_{j ≠ i} (x_i - x_j).
hypotheses: F is a field.
The nodes x_0, ..., x_n are pairwise distinct. Then every denominator x_i - x_j with i ≠ j is not 0.
The number of nodes is n + 1 and the degree bound is n. A polynomial of degree at most n means the zero polynomial or a polynomial of degree ≤ n.

prerequisites.reason: Uniqueness uses that a nonzero polynomial of degree at most n has at most n roots.

steps.text: Because the nodes are distinct, each denominator x_i - x_j with j ≠ i is a nonzero element of F. So L_i is a well defined polynomial of degree exactly n, as a product of n linear factors.
The value L_i(x_k) is 1 if k = i, because every factor then equals (x_i - x_j)/(x_i - x_j) = 1. The value L_i(x_k) is 0 if k ≠ i, because the factor with j = k contains (x_k - x_k) = 0.
Set P = sum_i y_i L_i. It has degree at most n as a sum of polynomials of degree n. Then P(x_k) = sum_i y_i L_i(x_k) = y_k by step 2. This proves existence.
For uniqueness let Q be another polynomial of degree at most n with Q(x_i) = y_i. Then P - Q has degree at most n and has the n + 1 distinct roots x_0, ..., x_n.
A nonzero polynomial of degree at most n has at most n roots. So P - Q = 0, and P = Q. Thus P is the only solution.

For the coefficient formula, take P of degree at most n. Then P is the unique interpolant of its own values, so P = sum_i P(x_i) L_i. The coefficient of x^n in L_i is 1 / prod_{j ≠ i} (x_i - x_j), because the numerator is monic of degree n. Summing gives the formula.

results.name: Division with remainder for polynomials
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring. Let g be a monic polynomial in R[x] of degree d. For every f in R[x] there are unique polynomials q and r in R[x] with f = g q + r and deg r < d (r = 0 is allowed). If R is a field, the same holds for every nonzero g.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with 1.
g is monic, which means the leading coefficient of g is 1. In particular g ≠ 0.
The zero polynomial has degree -infinity, so deg r < d includes r = 0.
For a field R, g is any nonzero polynomial and the quotient is found after division by the leading coefficient of g.

theorem div_modByMonic_unique {f g} (q r : R[X]) (hg : Monic g)
    (h : r + g * q = f ∧ degree r < degree g) : f /ₘ g = q ∧ f %ₘ g = r := by
  nontriviality R
  have h₁ : r - f %ₘ g = -g * (q - f /ₘ g) :=
    eq_of_sub_eq_zero
      (by
        rw [← sub_eq_zero_of_eq (h.1.trans (modByMonic_add_div f g).symm)]
        simp [mul_add, sub_eq_add_neg, add_comm, add_left_comm, add_assoc])
  have h₂ : degree (r - f %ₘ g) = degree (g * (q - f /ₘ g)) := by simp [h₁]
  have h₄ : degree (r - f %ₘ g) < degree g :=
    calc
      degree (r - f %ₘ g) ≤ max (degree r) (degree (f %ₘ g)) := degree_sub_le _ _
      _ < degree g := max_lt_iff.2 ⟨h.2, degree_modByMonic_lt _ hg⟩
  have h₅ : q - f /ₘ g = 0 :=
    _root_.by_contradiction fun hqf =>
      not_le_of_gt h₄ <|
        calc
          degree g ≤ degree g + degree (q - f /ₘ g) := by
            rw [degree_eq_natDegree hg.ne_zero, degree_eq_natDegree hqf]
            norm_cast
            exact Nat.le_add_right _ _
          _ = degree (r - f %ₘ g) := by rw [h₂, degree_mul']; simpa [Monic.def.1 hg]
  exact ⟨Eq.symm <| eq_of_sub_eq_zero h₅, Eq.symm <| eq_of_sub_eq_zero <| by simpa [h₅] using h₁⟩

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Existence, by strong induction on deg f. If f = 0 or deg f < d, take q = 0 and r = f. These satisfy f = g * 0 + r and deg r < d.
Now let m = deg f ≥ d and let c be the leading coefficient of f. Define f_1 = f - c x^(m-d) g. Because g is monic, c x^(m-d) g has leading term c x^m. So the x^m terms cancel and deg f_1 < m.
By the induction hypothesis f_1 = g q_1 + r with deg r < d. Then f = g (q_1 + c x^(m-d)) + r, so the pair (q_1 + c x^(m-d), r) works. This proves existence.
Uniqueness. Suppose g q + r = g q' + r' with deg r < d and deg r' < d. Then g (q - q') = r' - r. The right side has degree less than d.

Assume q ≠ q'. Let e be the leading coefficient of q - q'. The leading coefficient of g (q - q') is 1 * e = e ≠ 0, because g is monic. So deg g (q - q') = d + deg (q - q') ≥ d. This contradicts step 4.
Hence q = q', and then r = r'. For a field R and nonzero g with leading coefficient c, apply the monic case to g/c: f = (g/c) q + r gives f = g (q/c) + r with the same remainder.

applications.title: Divide x^4 + 2x^3 - x + 5 by x^2 + x - 1 over Z
applications.inputs: f = x^4 + 2x^3 + 0x^2 - x + 5 and the monic divisor g = x^2 + x - 1 with d = 2, over the integers Z.
applications.hypotheses: g is monic because its leading coefficient is 1, and Z is a commutative ring. So the theorem gives a unique pair (q, r) with deg r < 2.

steps.text: Step 1: the leading term x^4 of f is cancelled by x^2 * g = x^4 + x^3 - x^2. The difference is f_1 = x^3 + x^2 - x + 5.
Step 2: the leading term x^3 of f_1 is cancelled by x * g = x^3 + x^2 - x. The difference is the constant 5, with degree 0 < 2. So q = x^2 + x and r = 5.
The two values agree, as the identity f = g q + r requires. By uniqueness no other pair with deg r < 2 exists.

applications.conclusion: The quotient is x^2 + x and the remainder is 5. The remainder is the only polynomial of degree less than 2 that completes the identity.

results.name: Derivative criterion for multiple roots
aliases: a is a repeated root iff p(a) = p'(a) = 0
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, let p be a polynomial in R[x] and let a be an element of R. Then (x - a)^2 divides p if and only if p(a) = 0 and p'(a) = 0, where p' is the formal derivative. For p ≠ 0 this says that a is a root of multiplicity at least 2 if and only if p(a) = p'(a) = 0.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with 1.
p' is the formal derivative of p. It is defined by (sum c_k x^k)' = sum k c_k x^(k-1) and needs no limits.
The multiplicity of a root a of p ≠ 0 is the largest m with (x - a)^m dividing p.

prerequisites.reason: The proof factors p = (x - a) q when p(a) = 0, and again q = (x - a) s when q(a) = 0.

definitions.name: formal derivative
definitions.text: The map p ↦ p' that is additive, sends x^k to k x^(k-1), and obeys the product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv'.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Suppose p(a) = 0 and p'(a) = 0. By the factor theorem p = (x - a) q for some q in R[x].
The product rule gives p' = q + (x - a) q'. Evaluate at a: p'(a) = q(a) + 0 = q(a). So q(a) = p'(a) = 0.
By the factor theorem again q = (x - a) s. Then p = (x - a)^2 s, so (x - a)^2 divides p.
Conversely suppose p = (x - a)^2 s. Then p(a) = 0. The product rule gives p' = 2 (x - a) s + (x - a)^2 s', and p'(a) = 0.
For p ≠ 0 the multiplicity of a is at least 2 exactly when (x - a)^2 divides p. So the criterion gives the statement on multiplicity.

applications.title: Find the double root of x^3 - 3x + 2
applications.inputs: The polynomial p = x^3 - 3x + 2 over Q, with p' = 3x^2 - 3. The candidates are a = 1 and a = -2.
applications.hypotheses: Q is a commutative ring. The polynomial p is not 0, so the criterion applies to every a in Q.

steps.text: Value of the polynomial at a = 1: p(1) = 1 - 3 + 2.
Derivative at a = 1: p'(1) = 3 - 3.
Both values vanish, so (x - 1)^2 divides p. The division p / (x - 1)^2 = x + 2 gives p = (x - 1)^2 (x + 2).
Derivative at a = -2: p'(-2) = 12 - 3.
Here p'(-2) = 9 ≠ 0, so -2 is a simple root. The criterion shows exactly which root repeats, with no factoring needed.

applications.conclusion: The root 1 has multiplicity at least 2, and the root -2 is simple. So x^3 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)^2 (x + 2).

results.name: Cauchy bound on the roots of a polynomial
results.statement: Let K be the field R or C. Let p(x) = a_n x^n + ... + a_1 x + a_0 be a polynomial over K with a_n ≠ 0 and n ≥ 1. Put M = max over 0 ≤ i < n of |a_i| / |a_n|. Then every root a in K of p satisfies |a| < 1 + M.
hypotheses: K is R or C with the usual absolute value. The proof works for any normed field.
The leading coefficient a_n is not 0, and the degree n is at least 1. A nonzero constant has no root.
M is the maximum of the n numbers |a_0|/|a_n|, ..., |a_(n-1)|/|a_n|.

prerequisites.reason: Step 5 sums 1 + |a| + ... + |a|^(n-1) in closed form for |a| > 1.

definitions.name: Cauchy bound
definitions.text: The number 1 + max_{i<n} |a_i|/|a_n| attached to a polynomial of degree n. Every root has absolute value below it.

theorem IsRoot.norm_lt_cauchyBound {p : K[X]} (hp : p ≠ 0) {a : K} (h : p.IsRoot a) :
    ‖a‖₊ < cauchyBound p := by
  rw [IsRoot.def, eval_eq_sum_range, range_add_one] at h
  simp only [mem_range, lt_self_iff_false, not_false_eq_true, sum_insert, coeff_natDegree,
    add_eq_zero_iff_eq_neg] at h
  apply_fun nnnorm at h
  simp only [nnnorm_mul, nnnorm_pow, nnnorm_neg] at h
  suffices ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree ≤ (cauchyBound p - 1) * ∑ x ∈ range p.natDegree, ‖a‖₊ ^ x by
    rcases eq_or_ne ‖a‖₊ 1 with ha | ha
    · simp only [ha, one_pow, sum_const, card_range, nsmul_eq_mul, mul_one, gt_iff_lt] at this ⊢
      apply lt_of_le_of_ne (by simp)
      intro nh
      simp [← nh, tsub_self] at this
    rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne ha with ha | ha
    · apply ha.trans_le
      simp
    · rw [geom_sum_of_one_lt ha] at this
      calc
        ‖a‖₊ = ‖a‖₊ - 1 + 1 := (tsub_add_cancel_of_le ha.le).symm
        _ = ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree * (‖a‖₊ - 1) / ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree + 1 := by field
        _ ≤ (cauchyBound p - 1) * ((‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree - 1) / (‖a‖₊ - 1)) * (‖a‖₊ - 1)
            / ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree + 1 := by gcongr
        _ = (cauchyBound p - 1) * (‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree - 1) / ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree + 1 := by
          congr 2
          have : ‖a‖₊ - 1 ≠ 0 := fun nh ↦ (ha.trans_le (tsub_eq_zero_iff_le.mp nh)).false
          field
        _ < (cauchyBound p - 1) * ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree / ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree + 1 := by
          gcongr
          · apply lt_of_le_of_ne (by simp)
            contrapose! this
            simp only [← this, zero_mul]
            apply pow_pos
            exact zero_lt_one.trans ha
          simp [zero_lt_one.trans ha]
        _ = cauchyBound p := by simp [field, tsub_add_cancel_of_le]
  apply le_of_eq at h
  have pld : ‖p.leadingCoeff‖₊ ≠ 0 := by simpa
  calc ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree
    _ = ‖p.leadingCoeff‖₊ * ‖a‖₊ ^ p.natDegree / ‖p.leadingCoeff‖₊ := by
      rw [mul_div_cancel_left₀]

    _ ≤ ‖∑ x ∈ range p.natDegree, p.coeff x * a ^ x‖₊ / ‖p.leadingCoeff‖₊ := by gcongr

      apply nnnorm_sum_le
    _ = (∑ x ∈ range p.natDegree, ‖p.coeff x‖₊ * ‖a‖₊ ^ x) / ‖p.leadingCoeff‖₊ := by simp

steps.text: Let a be a root. Since p(a) = 0 we have a_n a^n = -(a_(n-1) a^(n-1) + ... + a_0). All a_i with i < n satisfy |a_i| ≤ M |a_n| by the definition of M.
Take absolute values and use the triangle inequality: |a_n| |a|^n ≤ sum_{i<n} |a_i| |a|^i ≤ M |a_n| sum_{i<n} |a|^i. Divide by |a_n| > 0. Put s = sum_{i<n} |a|^i. Then |a|^n ≤ M s. (*)
Case M = 0. Then (*) gives |a|^n ≤ 0, so a = 0 because n ≥ 1. Hence |a| = 0 < 1 = 1 + M.
Case M > 0 and |a| ≤ 1. Then |a| ≤ 1 < 1 + M, and the claim holds.
Case M > 0 and |a| > 1. The geometric sum is s = (|a|^n - 1)/(|a| - 1), which is smaller than |a|^n/(|a| - 1). By (*) and M > 0 we get |a|^n < M |a|^n/(|a| - 1).
Divide by |a|^n > 0 to get 1 < M/(|a| - 1). Since |a| - 1 > 0, this gives |a| - 1 < M, so |a| < 1 + M. All cases are done.

results.name: Resultant criterion for a common factor of two polynomials
aliases: Sylvester resultant vanishes iff common root
results.statement: Let F be a field. Let f and g be nonzero polynomials in F[x] of degrees m and n. Let Res(f, g) be the determinant of the (m+n) x (m+n) Sylvester matrix of f and g. Then Res(f, g) = 0 if and only if f and g have a common factor of positive degree in F[x]. Equivalently, they have a common root in an algebraic closure of F.
hypotheses: F is a field and f, g are both nonzero. Degrees m and n are the true degrees, so the leading coefficients are not 0.
The Sylvester matrix has n rows built from f and m rows built from g, as defined below. If m = 0 or n = 0 it is a diagonal matrix.
The equivalent form with a common root uses that every positive degree factor has a root over an algebraic closure.

prerequisites.reason: Division with remainder makes F[x] a Euclidean domain. It gives gcds and the identity 1 = a f + b g for coprime f and g.

definitions.name: Sylvester map
definitions.text: The F-linear map Phi from pairs (u, v) with deg u < n and deg v < m to polynomials of degree below m + n, defined by Phi(u, v) = u f + v g. Both spaces have dimension m + n.

definitions.name: Sylvester matrix and resultant
definitions.text: The matrix of Phi in the monomial bases. Its rows list the coefficients of x^(n-1-i) f for i < n, then of x^(m-1-j) g for j < m. Res(f, g) is its determinant, up to a sign that depends on the basis order.

lemma resultant_eq_zero_iff {K : Type*} [Field K] {f g : K[X]} :
    resultant f g = 0 ↔ (f ≠ 0 ∨ g ≠ 0) ∧ ¬ IsCoprime f g := by
  obtain rfl | hf := eq_or_ne f 0
  · obtain rfl | hg := eq_or_ne g 0; · simp
    simpa [isCoprime_zero_left, isUnit_iff, hg, natDegree_eq_zero] using
      show (∀ x, C x ≠ g) ↔ ∀ x ≠ 0, C x ≠ g by aesop
  have H : (C f.leadingCoeff⁻¹ * f).Monic := by
    rw [Monic, ← coeff_natDegree, natDegree_C_mul (by simpa), coeff_C_mul]; simp [hf]
  have := isUnit_resultant_iff_isCoprime (f := C f.leadingCoeff⁻¹ * f) (g := g) H
  rw [resultant_C_mul_left, IsUnit.mul_iff, natDegree_C_mul (by simp [hf]),
    isCoprime_mul_unit_left_left (isUnit_C.mpr (by simp [hf]))] at this
  simp [← this, hf]

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: A square matrix has determinant 0 if and only if its map is not injective. The Sylvester matrix represents Phi between spaces of equal dimension m + n. So Res(f, g) = 0 if and only if some pair (u, v) ≠ (0, 0) has deg u < n, deg v < m and u f + v g = 0.

Assume Res = 0 and take such a pair. Neither u nor v is 0. If u = 0 then v g = 0 and g ≠ 0 force v = 0, a contradiction. If v = 0 then u f = 0 and f ≠ 0 force u = 0. So u f = -v g with u, v both nonzero.
Suppose for contradiction that f and g are coprime. Then 1 = a f + b g for some a, b in F[x]. Multiply by v and use v g = -u f: v = v a f + b v g = f (v a - b u).
So f divides v. Since v ≠ 0, deg v ≥ deg f = m. This contradicts deg v < m. Hence f and g are not coprime. They have a common factor of positive degree.
Conversely let h be a common factor of positive degree e. Put u = g/h and v = -f/h. Then deg u = n - e < n, deg v = m - e < m, and u, v ≠ 0.
Also u f + v g = g f / h - f g / h = 0. So Phi has a nonzero element in its kernel, and Res(f, g) = 0 by step 1.

Every factor of positive degree has a root in an algebraic closure. Conversely a common root a gives the common factor x - a over the closure, and the determinant does not change when the field grows. This gives the root form.

applications.title: Test x^2 - 3x + 2 against two quadratics
applications.inputs: f = x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2). Two partners: g_1 = x^2 + 1 and g_2 = x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3). Here m = n = 2 and the Sylvester matrices are 4 x 4.
applications.hypotheses: All three polynomials are nonzero over Q and have degree 2 with leading coefficient 1.

steps.text: For f and g_1 the rows are (1, -3, 2, 0), (0, 1, -3, 2), (1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1). Subtract row 3 from row 1 and row 4 from row 2. The rows become (0, -3, 1, 0), (0, 0, -3, 1), (1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1).
Expand along column 1. Only row 3 has an entry 1, in position (3, 1), with sign +. The minor is the determinant of rows (-3, 1, 0), (0, -3, 1), (1, 0, 1).
So Res(f, g_1) = 10 ≠ 0. The theorem shows that f and x^2 + 1 have no common factor of positive degree.
For f and g_2 the theorem predicts Res = 0 since both are divisible by x - 2. The kernel pair is u = g_2/(x - 2) = x - 3 and v = -f/(x - 2) = -(x - 1).
The pair is nonzero with deg u = 1 < 2 and deg v = 1 < 2, so Phi has a nonzero kernel and Res(f, g_2) = 0.

applications.conclusion: The resultant is 10 for x^2 - 3x + 2 and x^2 + 1, so they share no root. It is 0 for x^2 - 3x + 2 and x^2 - 5x + 6, which share the root 2.

results.name: Fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials
aliases: symmetric polynomials are polynomials in the elementary symmetric polynomials
results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring and let e_1, ..., e_n be the elementary symmetric polynomials in R[x_1, ..., x_n]. Every symmetric polynomial f in R[x_1, ..., x_n] equals g(e_1, ..., e_n) for exactly one polynomial g in R[y_1, ..., y_n]. Equivalently, the map g ↦ g(e_1, ..., e_n) is a bijection from R[y_1, ..., y_n] onto the ring of symmetric polynomials.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with 1. No division is needed.
f is symmetric: f(x_σ(1), ..., x_σ(n)) = f(x_1, ..., x_n) for every permutation σ.
The number of variables n equals the number of generators e_1, ..., e_n. With fewer generators the map is injective but not surjective.

definitions.name: elementary symmetric polynomial
definitions.text: e_k is the sum of all products x_(i_1) ... x_(i_k) with i_1 < ... < i_k. So e_1 = x_1 + ... + x_n and e_n = x_1 ... x_n.

definitions.name: lexicographic order
definitions.text: For exponent vectors α and β write α > β if the first index where they differ has α_i > β_i. The leading monomial of a nonzero polynomial is its largest monomial in this order.

source.alignment: The Lean lemma states bijectivity of the algebra map from R[y_1, ..., y_n] to the symmetric subalgebra of R[x_1, ..., x_n] (Fin n variables) given by y_i ↦ e_i.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: The lexicographic order is a total order on monomials and is compatible with products. If f and g have leading terms c x^α and d x^β with c d ≠ 0, then fg has leading term c d x^(α+β). The leading monomial of e_k is x_1 x_2 ... x_k with coefficient 1.

Let f ≠ 0 be symmetric with leading term c x^α. Then α_1 ≥ α_2 ≥ ... ≥ α_n. If α_i < α_(i+1) for some i, swapping x_i and x_(i+1) keeps f and gives the monomial x^α' in f with coefficient c ≠ 0. But α' > α, a contradiction.

Put t_i = α_i - α_(i+1) ≥ 0 for i < n and t_n = α_n. Then the product e_1^(t_1) ... e_n^(t_n) has leading term x^α with coefficient 1, because the exponent of x_j is t_j + ... + t_n = α_j, and leading terms multiply by step 1.

Then f_1 = f - c e_1^(t_1) ... e_n^(t_n) is symmetric and its monomials are smaller than x^α, or f_1 = 0. All its monomials have total degree at most deg f, since e^t has total degree α_1 + ... + α_n. Only finitely many monomials have degree at most deg f, so repeating the step ends. This proves f is a polynomial in e_1, ..., e_n (existence).
Uniqueness. The map t ↦ α with α_j = t_j + ... + t_n is injective, as t_j = α_j - α_(j+1). So distinct exponents t give distinct leading monomials of e^t.

Suppose sum over a finite nonempty set T of c_t e^t = 0 with all c_t ≠ 0. Pick t_0 in T whose e^(t_0) has the largest leading monomial. All other terms have smaller leading monomials. So the sum has leading term c_(t_0) x^α ≠ 0, a contradiction. Hence the e_i are algebraically independent, and g is unique.

applications.title: Write the sum of x_i^2 x_j over i ≠ j in terms of e_1, e_2, e_3
applications.inputs: f = sum over ordered pairs i ≠ j of x_i^2 x_j in R[x_1, x_2, x_3], with 6 terms. This f is symmetric.
applications.hypotheses: f is symmetric and has 3 variables, so n = 3 and the theorem applies over any commutative ring such as Z.

steps.text: The leading monomial of f is x_1^2 x_2 with coefficient 1. So α = (2, 1, 0) and t = (1, 1, 0). The theorem's recipe subtracts e_1 e_2.
In e_1 e_2 the monomial x_1 x_2 x_3 arises 3 ways: x_1 * x_2 x_3, x_2 * x_1 x_3 and x_3 * x_1 x_2. All other monomials are of the form x_i^2 x_j.
So e_1 e_2 = f + 3 e_3, and f - e_1 e_2 = -3 x_1 x_2 x_3 = -3 e_3. Thus f = e_1 e_2 - 3 e_3, with unique g(y) = y_1 y_2 - 3 y_3.
At the same point e_1 = 6, e_2 = 11, e_3 = 6, so e_1 e_2 - 3 e_3.

applications.conclusion: The symmetric polynomial sum of x_i^2 x_j equals e_1 e_2 - 3 e_3, and no other polynomial in e_1, e_2, e_3 gives the same function. For the cubic with roots 1, 2, 3 this sum equals 48.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Base cases. T_0(cos θ) = 1 = cos(0 * θ) and T_1(cos θ) = cos θ = cos(1 * θ).
The cosine addition formula gives cos((n+1)θ) = cos nθ cos θ - sin nθ sin θ and cos((n-1)θ) = cos nθ cos θ + sin nθ sin θ. Adding these gives cos((n+1)θ) + cos((n-1)θ) = 2 cos θ cos nθ.
Strong induction on n. Assume T_k(cos θ) = cos kθ for k = n and k = n - 1, with n ≥ 1. Then T_(n+1)(cos θ) = 2 cos θ T_n(cos θ) - T_(n-1)(cos θ) = 2 cos θ cos nθ - cos((n-1)θ).
By step 2 the last expression equals cos((n+1)θ). This completes the induction and proves the identity.

Degree and leading coefficient. T_1 = x has degree 1 and leading coefficient 1 = 2^0. If T_n has degree n and leading coefficient 2^(n-1), then 2x T_n has degree n + 1 and leading coefficient 2^n, while T_(n-1) has smaller degree. So T_(n+1) has degree n + 1 and leading coefficient 2^n.

Uniqueness. If Q(cos θ) = cos nθ for all θ, then Q - T_n vanishes at every point of [-1, 1] because cos maps R onto [-1, 1]. A polynomial with infinitely many roots is zero by the root count bound, so Q = T_n.

theorem T_mul (m n : ℤ) : T R (m * n) = (T R m).comp (T R n) := by
  induction m using Polynomial.Chebyshev.induct with
  | zero => simp
  | one => simp
  | add_two m ih1 ih2 =>
    have h₁ := T_mul_T R ((m + 1) * n) n
    have h₂ := congr(comp $(T_add_two R m) (T R n))
    simp only [sub_comp, mul_comp, ofNat_comp, X_comp] at h₂
    linear_combination (norm := ring_nf) -ih2 - h₂ - h₁ + 2 * T R n * ih1
  | neg_add_one m ih1 ih2 =>
    have h₁ := T_mul_T R ((-m) * n) n
    have h₂ := congr(comp $(T_add_two R (-m - 1)) (T R n))
    simp only [sub_comp, mul_comp, ofNat_comp, X_comp] at h₂
    linear_combination (norm := ring_nf) -ih2 - h₂ - h₁ + 2 * T R n * ih1

steps.text: Fix a real number θ and put x = cos θ. By the cosine identity, T_n(x) = cos(nθ).
Apply the cosine identity again, now with the angle nθ in place of θ: T_m(T_n(x)) = T_m(cos(nθ)) = cos(m n θ).
Apply the cosine identity with index mn and angle θ: T_(mn)(x) = cos(mnθ). So T_m(T_n(x)) = T_(mn)(x) for every x = cos θ in [-1, 1].
The polynomial D = T_m ∘ T_n - T_(mn) vanishes at every point of [-1, 1], because cos maps R onto [-1, 1]. So D has infinitely many roots.
A nonzero real polynomial has at most deg D roots. Hence D = 0, and T_(mn) = T_m ∘ T_n as polynomials. Exchanging m and n gives T_m ∘ T_n = T_(mn) = T_n ∘ T_m.

steps.text: Put x_i = cos(iπ/n) for 0 ≤ i ≤ n. Cosine is strictly decreasing on [0, π], so 1 = x_0 > x_1 > ... > x_n = -1 and the n + 1 nodes are distinct. Let w_i = prod over j ≠ i of (x_i - x_j).
By the coefficient formula of Lagrange interpolation, a polynomial P of degree at most n has coefficient of x^n equal to sum_i P(x_i)/w_i. This holds for P and for T_n.
The sign of w_i is (-1)^i. The i factors with j < i are negative, since x_j > x_i. The n - i factors with j > i are positive.
By the cosine identity T_n(x_i) = cos(iπ) = (-1)^i, so T_n(x_i)/w_i = 1/|w_i| > 0. Also the coefficient of x^n in T_n is 2^(n-1). Hence sum_i 1/|w_i| = 2^(n-1).

Now let P satisfy the hypotheses. Then |P(x_i)| ≤ 1, because each x_i lies in [-1, 1]. By step 2 and the triangle inequality, |coefficient of x^n| = |sum_i P(x_i)/w_i| ≤ sum_i |P(x_i)|/|w_i| ≤ sum_i 1/|w_i|.
By step 4 the last sum is 2^(n-1). So the coefficient has absolute value at most 2^(n-1). For T_n the bound is attained, and |T_n(cos θ)| = |cos nθ| ≤ 1 shows T_n is allowed.

applications.hypotheses: P = x^3 has degree 3 = n and |x^3| ≤ 1 on [-1, 1]. So the theorem bounds its leading coefficient by 2^(3-1) = 4.

steps.text: The signs are +, -, +, - as predicted. The sum of 1/|w_i| equals 2/3 + 4/3 + 4/3 + 2/3.
The coefficient formula for P = x^3 gives sum P(x_i)/w_i, which must equal the leading coefficient 1.

applications.conclusion: The sum of 1/|w_i| is 4 = 2^2, which is the leading coefficient of T_3 = 4x^3 - 3x. So no cubic bounded by 1 on [-1, 1] has a leading coefficient above 4 in absolute value. The cubic x^3 has leading coefficient 1 and obeys the bound.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: The map θ ↦ cos θ is a smooth, strictly decreasing bijection from (0, π) onto (-1, 1). For x = cos θ we have dx = -sin θ dθ and sqrt(1 - x^2) = sin θ > 0.

The change of variables gives the integral of f(x)/sqrt(1 - x^2) over (-1, 1) equal to the integral over (0, π) of f(cos θ) dθ. This also shows convergence, because the new integrand is bounded when f is a polynomial.
By the cosine identity T_n(cos θ) T_m(cos θ) = cos nθ cos mθ. So the integral equals I = integral over (0, π) of cos nθ cos mθ dθ.
Product-to-sum: cos nθ cos mθ = (1/2)[cos((n-m)θ) + cos((n+m)θ)]. For an integer k ≠ 0 the integral of cos kθ over (0, π) is sin(kπ)/k = 0. For k = 0 it is π.
Case n ≠ m. Both n - m and n + m are nonzero integers, since n + m ≥ 1. So I = (1/2)(0 + 0) = 0.
Case n = m = 0. Both k = 0, so I = (1/2)(π + π) = π. Case n = m ≥ 1. Then n - m = 0 and n + m ≠ 0, so I = (1/2)(π + 0) = π/2.

applications.title: Chebyshev coefficient of x^3 on T_3
applications.inputs: The function f(x) = x^3 on [-1, 1]. We use T_1 = x and T_3 = 4x^3 - 3x. The expansion has the form f = sum c_k T_k.
applications.hypotheses: The polynomials T_1 and T_3 are orthogonal for the weight 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) by the theorem, with <T_3, T_3> = π/2 and <T_1, T_3> = 0.

steps.text: From T_3 = 4x^3 - 3x we get x^3 = (3 T_1 + T_3)/4. This is a finite Chebyshev expansion, so f needs only T_1 and T_3.
Check the identity x^3 = (3x + (4x^3 - 3x))/4 at x = 2.
Compute <x^3, T_3> in units of π. Use <T_1, T_3> = 0 and <T_3, T_3> = 1/2.
The coefficient formula c_3 = <f, T_3> / <T_3, T_3> gives c_3 in the same units.
Likewise <x^3, T_1> = (3 <T_1, T_1> + <T_3, T_1>)/4 = (3 * 1/2 + 0)/4 in units of π, and c_1 = this divided by 1/2.
So x^3 = (3/4) T_1 + (1/4) T_3. The orthogonality relations alone give both coefficients, with no integral of x^3 computed.

applications.conclusion: The Chebyshev expansion of x^3 is (3/4) T_1 + (1/4) T_3. Both coefficients come from the orthogonality relations and the norm π/2.

source.alignment: The Lean lemma indexes the nodes by i = 0, ..., n - 1 as cos((2i+1)/(2n) π), which is k = i + 1 here.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Both sides are linear in P. The polynomials T_0, ..., T_(2n-1) have degrees 0, ..., 2n - 1 with nonzero leading coefficients, so they span the polynomials of degree < 2n. It is enough to prove the formula for P = T_m with 0 ≤ m ≤ 2n - 1.
Left side. By orthogonality with T_0 = 1, the integral of T_m against the weight is π if m = 0 and 0 if 1 ≤ m ≤ 2n - 1.
Right side. T_m(cos θ_k) = cos(m θ_k) by the cosine identity. So we need the sum s_m = sum_{k=1}^{n} cos(m θ_k). For m = 0 it is n, and the right side is (π/n) n = π, which matches.

Let 1 ≤ m ≤ 2n - 1. Put η = e^(i m π/(2n)) and ζ = η^2. Then e^(i m θ_k) = η ζ^(k-1), and s_m is the real part of η (1 + ζ + ... + ζ^(n-1)). Since 0 < mπ/n < 2π, ζ ≠ 1, so the geometric sum is (ζ^n - 1)/(ζ - 1).
Here ζ^n = e^(i m π) = (-1)^m. If m is even, ζ^n = 1, the geometric sum is 0, and s_m = 0.

If m is odd, ζ^n = -1 and the sum equals η (-2)/(η^2 - 1) = -2/(η - 1/η) = -2/(2i sin(mπ/(2n))) = i / sin(mπ/(2n)). Here sin(mπ/(2n)) ≠ 0 because 0 < mπ/(2n) < π. This number is purely imaginary, so s_m = 0.
So the right side is 0 for 1 ≤ m ≤ 2n - 1, which matches the left side. By linearity the formula holds for every P of degree < 2n. For P = x^(2n) the rule fails in general, see the example.

applications.title: Two-point rule for n = 2 on x^2 and x^4
applications.inputs: n = 2. The nodes are cos(π/4) = √2/2 and cos(3π/4) = -√2/2, with weight π/n = π/2 each. We test P = x^2 (degree 2 < 4) and P = x^4 (degree 4 = 2n).
applications.hypotheses: x^2 has degree 2 < 2n = 4, so the rule is exact. The polynomial x^4 has degree 4, which is outside the theorem.

steps.text: At both nodes x^2 = 1/2. The rule gives (π/2)(1/2 + 1/2) = (1/2) π. We record the number in units of π.
Exact value: x^2 = (T_0 + T_2)/2, because T_2 = 2x^2 - 1. By orthogonality the integral of T_0 is π and of T_2 is 0.
The exact integral of x^2 in units of π is (1 + 0)/2.
The two values agree: the rule is exact for x^2, as the theorem says.
For x^4 each node gives 1/4, so the rule gives (π/2)(1/4 + 1/4) in units of π.
Exact value: x^4 = (T_4 + 4 T_2 + 3 T_0)/8, so the integral in units of π is (0 + 4*0 + 3)/8.

applications.conclusion: The two-point rule gives π/2 for x^2, the exact value. For x^4 it gives π/4 but the exact value is 3π/8, so the degree bound 2n - 1 cannot be raised.

results.name: Equivalent conditions for a Noetherian module
results.statement: Let R be a ring and let M be a left R-module. The following three conditions are equivalent. (a) Every submodule of M is finitely generated. (b) Every ascending chain N_1 <= N_2 <= ... of submodules of M is eventually constant. (c) Every nonempty set S of submodules of M has a maximal element, that is, an element N0 in S such that no N in S satisfies N0 < N. A module with these properties is Noetherian.
hypotheses: R is a ring with identity. It need not be commutative.
M is a left R-module.
The inclusion order on submodules is used. N0 < N means N0 is contained in N and N0 differs from N.
The implication (b) implies (c) uses the axiom of dependent choice.

definitions.name: finitely generated submodule
definitions.text: A submodule N of M is finitely generated if N = R x_1 + ... + R x_k for finitely many elements x_1, ..., x_k of M.

definitions.name: eventually constant
definitions.text: A chain N_1 <= N_2 <= ... is eventually constant if there is n with N_i = N_n for all i >= n.

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: (a) implies (b). Let N_1 <= N_2 <= ... be a chain and let N be the union of the N_i. The union of a chain of submodules is a submodule, because two elements lie in a common N_i.
By (a), N is generated by finitely many elements x_1, ..., x_k. Each x_j lies in some N_{i_j}. Let n be the largest of i_1, ..., i_k. Because the chain is increasing, all x_j lie in N_n.
Then N is contained in N_n, so N_i is contained in N = N_n for all i >= n. Also N_n is contained in N_i. Hence N_i = N_n for every i >= n, and the chain is eventually constant.
(b) implies (c). Suppose a nonempty set S of submodules has no maximal element. Choose N_1 in S. Since N_1 is not maximal, there is N_2 in S with N_1 < N_2. Repeat this choice with dependent choice.
This builds a chain N_1 < N_2 < N_3 < ... in S in which every inclusion is strict. Such a chain is never eventually constant. This contradicts (b), so S has a maximal element.
(c) implies (a). Let N be a submodule of M. Let S be the set of finitely generated submodules of N. The set S is nonempty because it contains the zero submodule. By (c), S has a maximal element N0.

Suppose N0 differs from N. Choose x in N that is not in N0. The submodule N0 + R x is finitely generated, because N0 is, and it lies in N. So N0 + R x is in S and N0 < N0 + R x. This contradicts the maximality of N0.
Hence N = N0 and N is finitely generated. This proves (a). The three implications (a) to (b) to (c) to (a) show that the three conditions are equivalent.

applications.title: Find maximal proper ideals of Z that contain 12 Z
applications.inputs: Take R = Z and M = Z as a Z-module. Its submodules are the ideals d Z. Let S be the set of ideals d Z with d a divisor of 12 and d > 1.
applications.hypotheses: Every ideal of Z is principal, so it is finitely generated. Thus (a) holds for M = Z and the theorem gives (b) and (c). The set S contains 12 Z, so S is nonempty.

steps.text: The divisors of 12 that are greater than 1 are 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. So S has 5 elements. The count of divisors of 12 is (2+1)*(1+1) = 6, and we remove the divisor 1.
By (c), S has a maximal element. The inclusion d Z <= e Z holds exactly when e divides d. So d Z is maximal in S when no divisor e of d with 1 < e < d exists, that is, when d is prime.
The ideals 2 Z and 3 Z are maximal in S. For example, 2 Z is contained in e Z only for e = 1 or e = 2. Since e = 1 is not allowed in S, nothing in S lies strictly above 2 Z.
The chain 12 Z < 4 Z < 2 Z is strictly increasing. Its steps have index 3 and 2. These indices multiply to the index of 12 Z in 2 Z, which is 12/2.

applications.conclusion: The proper ideals of Z that contain 12 Z have maximal elements 2 Z and 3 Z. This agrees with the theorem, and every chain of such ideals stops after finitely many steps.

steps.text: Use condition (b). Let N_1 <= N_2 <= ... be an ascending chain of submodules of M. Put A_i = f^{-1}(N_i), a submodule of M', and B_i = g(N_i), a submodule of M''. Both A_i and B_i are ascending in i.
M' and M'' are Noetherian. So there is n such that A_i = A_n and B_i = B_n for all i >= n. Take the larger of the two stabilization indices.
Fix i >= n and take x in N_i. Then g(x) is in B_i = B_n. So there is y in N_n with g(y) = g(x).
The element x - y lies in the kernel of g. It also lies in N_i, because x is in N_i and y is in N_n, which is contained in N_i. Since kernel(g) = image(f), we have x - y = f(z) for some z in M'.
The element f(z) = x - y lies in N_i, so z is in f^{-1}(N_i) = A_i = A_n. Hence f(z) lies in N_n.

Therefore x = y + f(z) is a sum of two elements of N_n. So x is in N_n. This shows N_i is contained in N_n. The reverse inclusion holds because the chain is ascending, so N_i = N_n for all i >= n and M is Noetherian.

applications.inputs: Take R = Z, M' = Z, M = Z^2, M'' = Z. Let f(a) = (a, 0) and g(a, b) = b. Let N be the submodule of Z^2 of all (a, b) with 3a + 5b divisible by 7.

steps.text: The proof of the theorem shows how to build generators. Let A = f^{-1}(N). Then a is in A when 3a is divisible by 7. Since 3 and 7 are coprime, A = 7 Z, generated by 7. The lift is the vector (7, 0).

Let B = g(N), the set of b that occur as second coordinate. For every b there is a with 3a + 5b divisible by 7, because 3 is invertible modulo 7. So B = Z, generated by 1. We need a vector in N with second coordinate 1.
Try a = 3 and b = 1. The value 3a + 5b is 14, and 14 divided by 7 is 2. So (3, 1) is in N.
By the argument of the proof, N is generated by (7, 0) and (3, 1). The determinant of these two vectors equals the index of N in Z^2, which is 7.

applications.conclusion: The submodule N of Z^2 is generated by (7, 0) and (3, 1). It needs only two generators because the sequence has Noetherian ends.

steps.text: First show that R^n is Noetherian, by induction on n. For n = 0 the module is zero and has only one submodule, so every chain is constant.
Assume R^(n-1) is Noetherian. Define f: R^(n-1) -> R^n by f(r_1, ..., r_(n-1)) = (r_1, ..., r_(n-1), 0). Define g: R^n -> R by g(r_1, ..., r_n) = r_n. Both maps are R-linear.
The image of f is the set of tuples with last coordinate 0. This is exactly the kernel of g. The ends R^(n-1) and R are Noetherian, by the induction hypothesis and by the assumption on R.
By closure under extension, R^n is Noetherian. This completes the induction.
Now let M be generated by x_1, ..., x_n. The map p: R^n -> M with p(r_1, ..., r_n) = r_1 x_1 + ... + r_n x_n is R-linear and surjective.
Let N_1 <= N_2 <= ... be a chain of submodules of M. The preimages p^{-1}(N_i) form a chain in R^n. By condition (b) for R^n, there is n0 with p^{-1}(N_i) = p^{-1}(N_n0) for all i >= n0.
Because p is surjective, p(p^{-1}(N)) = N for every submodule N of M. Applying p gives N_i = N_n0 for all i >= n0. So every chain in M is eventually constant, and M is Noetherian by condition (b).

Then f^(n+1)(y) = f(f^n(y)) = f(x) = 0. So y is in K_(n+1) = K_n. Hence f^n(y) = 0.

steps.text: R is nontrivial and commutative by hypothesis. It remains to find an inverse for each nonzero x in R.
Consider the principal ideals (x) >= (x^2) >= (x^3) >= ... . Each is contained in the one before, because x^(k+1) = x * x^k is a multiple of x^k.
R is Artinian. So the chain is eventually constant. There is n >= 1 with (x^n) = (x^(n+1)).
Then x^n is in (x^(n+1)). So x^n = x^(n+1) y for some y in R.
Rewrite this as x^n (1 - x y) = 0.
R has no zero divisors and x is nonzero. So x^n is nonzero, as a product of nonzero elements. Therefore 1 - x y = 0, that is x y = 1. Every nonzero x is invertible, and R is a field.

applications.title: Inverses in Q[t]/(t^2 - 2)
applications.inputs: Take R = Q[t]/(t^2 - 2). Write t for the class of t. The ring R has dimension 2 over Q, with basis 1 and t.
applications.hypotheses: R is Artinian: an ideal of R is a Q-subspace, a strictly descending chain of subspaces of a 2-dimensional space has length at most 2, so every chain stops. R is a domain because t^2 - 2 is irreducible over Q, since 2 is not a square in Q.

steps.text: By the theorem, R is a field. So 1 + t has an inverse. We find it. Compute (1 + t)(t - 1) = t^2 - 1 and use t^2 = 2.
So the inverse of 1 + t is t - 1. Now find the inverse of 3 + t. Compute (3 + t)(3 - t) = 9 - t^2 = 9 - 2.
The product (3 + t)(3 - t) equals 7, which is a unit in Q. So the inverse of 3 + t is (3 - t)/7.
Check. The product (3 + t)(3 - t)/7 equals 7/7.

applications.conclusion: Q[t]/(t^2 - 2) is a field. The inverse of 1 + t is t - 1 and the inverse of 3 + t is (3 - t)/7.

steps.text: Let p be a prime ideal of R. The quotient ring R/p is a commutative ring with 1 differing from 0, because p is proper. It has no zero divisors, because p is prime: if (a + p)(b + p) = 0 then ab is in p, so a or b is in p.
R/p is Artinian. Let J_1 >= J_2 >= ... be ideals of R/p and let q: R -> R/p be the quotient map. The preimages q^{-1}(J_i) form a descending chain of ideals of R.
R is Artinian. So there is n with q^{-1}(J_i) = q^{-1}(J_n) for i >= n. The map q is surjective, so q(q^{-1}(J)) = J for each ideal J. Hence J_i = J_n for i >= n.
By the result for Artinian domains, R/p is a field.
A field has only two ideals, 0 and itself. Ideals of R/p correspond to ideals of R that contain p. So the only ideals that contain p are p and R.
Thus p is a proper ideal that is maximal. The converse also holds in every commutative ring: a maximal ideal m has R/m a field, so R/m has no zero divisors and m is prime.

applications.title: The prime ideals of Z/12
applications.inputs: Take R = Z/12. The ring is finite, so every chain of ideals stops. Thus R is Artinian. Its ideals are generated by the divisors of 12.
applications.hypotheses: R is commutative and finite. A finite ring has finitely many ideals, so a descending chain of ideals is eventually constant.

steps.text: The ideal (0) is not prime. Check: 3 and 4 are nonzero in Z/12 and their product is zero.
By the theorem, a prime ideal of R must be maximal. A quotient of Z/12 by the ideal (d) is Z/d. It is a field exactly when d is prime. The divisors of 12 that are prime are 2 and 3.
So the prime ideals are (2) and (3). The ideal (2) has 6 elements and the quotient has 2 elements, so (2) is maximal.
The ideal (3) has 4 elements and the quotient has 3 elements, so (3) is maximal too.
The ideal (4) is not prime, because 2*2 = 4 is in (4) but 2 is not in (4). It lies strictly inside (2), so it is not maximal either. This agrees with the theorem.

applications.conclusion: Z/12 has exactly two prime ideals, (2) and (3), and both are maximal.

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Surjectivity of g (x) 1. The module C (x) D is generated by pure tensors c (x) d. Since g is surjective, c = g(b) for some b in B. Then c (x) d = (g (x) 1)(b (x) d). So the image of g (x) 1 contains all generators and equals C (x) D.

The composite is zero. We have (g (x) 1)(f (x) 1) = (g f) (x) 1 on pure tensors. Since g f = 0, the composite is zero on pure tensors, so it is zero. Hence the image of f (x) 1 lies in the kernel of g (x) 1.
For the reverse inclusion, let I be the image of f (x) 1 in B (x) D. Let pi: B (x) D -> (B (x) D)/I be the quotient map. We build a map from C (x) D to this quotient.
Define beta: C x D -> (B (x) D)/I by beta(c, d) = pi(b (x) d), where b is any element of B with g(b) = c. Such b exists because g is surjective.

The map beta is well defined. Let g(b) = g(b'). Then b - b' lies in the kernel of g, which equals the image of f. So b - b' = f(a), and b (x) d - b' (x) d = f(a) (x) d = (f (x) 1)(a (x) d). This element lies in I, so pi(b (x) d) = pi(b' (x) d).

The map beta is bilinear. Take b, b' with g(b) = c and g(b') = c'. Then g(b + b') = c + c' and g(r b) = r c. So beta(c + c', d) = pi((b + b') (x) d) = beta(c, d) + beta(c', d), and beta(r c, d) = r beta(c, d). Linearity in d is clear.

By the universal property there is an R-linear map psi: C (x) D -> (B (x) D)/I with psi(c (x) d) = beta(c, d). For every pure tensor b (x) d we get psi((g (x) 1)(b (x) d)) = psi(g(b) (x) d) = pi(b (x) d). Both sides are additive in the tensor, so psi (g (x) 1) = pi on all of B (x) D.

Let x be in the kernel of g (x) 1. Then pi(x) = psi((g (x) 1)(x)) = psi(0) = 0. So x lies in I, the image of f (x) 1. Together with the earlier inclusion, the kernel of g (x) 1 equals the image of f (x) 1. The sequence is exact.

applications.title: Compute the tensor product Z/4 (x) Z/6
applications.inputs: Take R = Z. Take the exact sequence Z --(4)--> Z --> Z/4 --> 0, where the first map is multiplication by 4. Tensor with D = Z/6.
applications.hypotheses: The map Z -> Z/4 is surjective. Its kernel is 4Z, which is the image of multiplication by 4. So the sequence is exact at the middle and at the end.

steps.text: Tensoring with Z/6 gives an exact sequence Z/6 --(4)--> Z/6 --> Z/4 (x) Z/6 --> 0. Here Z (x) Z/6 is identified with Z/6, and the first map is multiplication by 4.
So Z/4 (x) Z/6 is the cokernel of multiplication by 4 on Z/6. The image of this map is the set of multiples of 4 in Z/6. The multiples 4*1, 4*2 and 4*3 reduce modulo 6 to 4, 2 and 0.
The image is {0, 2, 4}. It has 3 elements. The cokernel has 6 divided by 3 elements.

applications.conclusion: Z/4 (x) Z/6 has exactly 2 elements. It is isomorphic to Z/2, which is Z/gcd(4, 6).

results.statement: Let R be a commutative ring and let M, N, P be R-modules. The map Phi: Hom_R(M (x) N, P) -> Hom_R(M, Hom_R(N, P)) defined by Phi(h)(m)(n) = h(m (x) n) is an isomorphism of R-modules. Its inverse sends k to the unique linear map Psi(k) with Psi(k)(m (x) n) = k(m)(n).
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with 1. All tensor products and Hom modules are over R.
M, N and P are R-modules.
Hom_R(N, P) is an R-module with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This uses the commutativity of R.

definitions.name: universal property of the tensor product
definitions.text: For every R-bilinear map beta: M x N -> P there is exactly one R-linear map M (x) N -> P that sends m (x) n to beta(m, n).

definitions.name: Hom_R(N, P)
definitions.text: The set of R-linear maps from N to P. Addition is pointwise: (u + v)(n) = u(n) + v(n). Scalar multiplication is (r u)(n) = r u(n).

source.alignment: Mathlib states the equivalence between bilinear maps M -> N -> P and linear maps M (x) N -> P. A bilinear map M x N -> P is the same as a linear map M -> Hom(N, P), so the authored statement is the same equivalence.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Phi is well defined. For h in Hom(M (x) N, P) and m in M, the map n -> h(m (x) n) is linear in n because (x) is linear in the second slot. So Phi(h)(m) is in Hom(N, P).

Phi(h) is linear in m because (x) is linear in the first slot: Phi(h)(m + m')(n) = h((m + m') (x) n) = h(m (x) n) + h(m' (x) n), and the same holds for scalars. Phi is linear in h because the operations on Hom are pointwise.

Construct the inverse. Let k be in Hom(M, Hom(N, P)). The map (m, n) -> k(m)(n) is R-bilinear. Linearity in m holds because k is linear and the operations on Hom(N, P) are pointwise. Linearity in n holds because k(m) is linear.

By the universal property there is exactly one R-linear map Psi(k): M (x) N -> P with Psi(k)(m (x) n) = k(m)(n). The assignment k -> Psi(k) is linear, because the defining formula on pure tensors is linear in k, and uniqueness identifies sums and multiples.
Phi Psi = id. For m in M and n in N we have Phi(Psi(k))(m)(n) = Psi(k)(m (x) n) = k(m)(n). So Phi(Psi(k)) = k.
Psi Phi = id. For h in Hom(M (x) N, P), the maps Psi(Phi(h)) and h are both linear and both send m (x) n to h(m (x) n). Pure tensors generate M (x) N, so the two maps are equal.
Phi is a linear map with a two-sided inverse Psi. So Phi is an isomorphism of R-modules.

applications.title: Count the homomorphisms from Z/4 (x) Z/6 to Z/2
applications.inputs: Take R = Z, M = Z/4, N = Z/6, P = Z/2. A Z-linear map is a group homomorphism.
applications.hypotheses: Z is commutative. Hom_Z(Z/6, Z/2) is an abelian group, so the adjunction applies.

steps.text: Compute Hom(Z/6, Z/2). A homomorphism is fixed by the image x of 1, and x must satisfy 6x = 0 in Z/2. Both x = 0 and x = 1 satisfy this, since 6 is a multiple of 2.
So Hom(Z/6, Z/2) has 2 elements and is isomorphic to Z/2. By the adjunction, Hom(Z/4 (x) Z/6, Z/2) is isomorphic to Hom(Z/4, Z/2).
Compute Hom(Z/4, Z/2). The image y of 1 satisfies 4y = 0 in Z/2. Both y = 0 and y = 1 satisfy it, since 4 is a multiple of 2. So there are 2 homomorphisms.

Cross-check with the direct computation. Z/4 (x) Z/6 has 2 elements, so it is Z/2. Hom(Z/2, Z/2) has 2 elements, the zero map and the identity. The size of Z/4 (x) Z/6 is the product 4*6 divided by lcm(4, 6) = 12.

applications.conclusion: There are 2 homomorphisms Z/4 (x) Z/6 -> Z/2. The adjunction turns a count of bilinear maps into two counts of maps out of cyclic groups.

results.name: Simple modules are quotients of the ring by maximal left ideals
aliases: classification of simple modules by maximal ideals
results.statement: Let R be a ring and let M be a left R-module. Then M is simple if and only if there is a maximal left ideal I of R with M isomorphic to R/I. For a commutative ring R, the simple R-modules are exactly the modules R/m with m a maximal ideal.
hypotheses: R is a ring with identity. It need not be commutative.
M is a left R-module. A simple module is a nonzero module whose only submodules are 0 and M.
A maximal left ideal is a proper left ideal that no other proper left ideal strictly contains.

definitions.name: correspondence theorem
definitions.text: If I is a left ideal of R, then the submodules of R/I are exactly the sets J/I with J a left ideal of R and I contained in J. The correspondence J -> J/I preserves inclusion and is a bijection.
