proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Suppose M is simple. Then M is nonzero. Choose m in M with m differing from 0. The map phi: R -> M with phi(r) = r m is R-linear. Its image R m is a nonzero submodule of M, because it contains m = 1 m.
Since M is simple, R m = M. So phi is surjective. Let I be the kernel of phi, a left ideal. By the first isomorphism theorem, M is isomorphic to R/I.
The ideal I is proper, because M is not zero. Let J be a left ideal with I contained in J. The image phi(J) is a submodule of M. So phi(J) = 0 or phi(J) = M.

If phi(J) = 0 then J is contained in I, so J = I. If phi(J) = M then for any r in R there is j in J with phi(j) = phi(r). Then r - j is in I, which is contained in J. So r is in J and J = R. Thus I is a maximal left ideal.
Conversely, suppose I is a maximal left ideal and M is isomorphic to R/I. The module R/I is nonzero, because I is proper.

Let U be a submodule of R/I. By the correspondence theorem, U = J/I for a left ideal J containing I. By maximality, J = I or J = R. So U = 0 or U = R/I. Therefore R/I is simple, and so is M, since an isomorphism preserves the lattice of submodules.
For commutative R, every left ideal is an ideal, and a maximal left ideal is a maximal ideal. So the simple R-modules are the modules R/m with m a maximal ideal.

applications.title: Simple modules over Z/12
applications.inputs: Take R = Z/12. This is a commutative ring with 12 elements. Its maximal ideals are (2) and (3).
applications.hypotheses: The ideals of Z/12 are the ideals (d) for d dividing 12. The quotient (Z/12)/(d) is isomorphic to Z/d. It is a field exactly when d is prime. So the maximal ideals are (2) and (3).

steps.text: By the theorem, every simple Z/12-module is isomorphic to (Z/12)/(2) = Z/2 or (Z/12)/(3) = Z/3. There are no others.
The ideal (2) in Z/12 has the 6 elements 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The quotient Z/2 has 12/6 elements.
The ideal (3) has the 4 elements 0, 3, 6, 9. The quotient Z/3 has 12/4 elements.
The Z/12-module Z/4 is not simple. It contains the proper nonzero submodule {0, 2}. It also has 4 elements, but a simple module has 2 or 3 elements.

applications.conclusion: The simple modules over Z/12 are Z/2 and Z/3, with 2 and 3 elements.

results.name: Finitely generated projective modules over a local ring are free
aliases: projective implies free over local rings
results.statement: Let R be a commutative local ring with maximal ideal m and residue field k = R/m. Let P be a finitely generated projective R-module. Then P is free of finite rank r, and r equals the dimension of the k-vector space P/mP.
hypotheses: R is a commutative local ring. It has exactly one maximal ideal m.
P is a finitely generated R-module.
P is projective. Every surjection of R-modules onto P has an R-linear right inverse.
The Lean declaration proves the more general statement for finitely generated flat modules. Every projective module is flat.

prerequisites.reason: The proof uses Nakayama's lemma twice: to lift a basis of P/mP to generators of P, and to show that the kernel of the resulting surjection is zero.

definitions.name: Nakayama's lemma, form used
definitions.text: Let R be local with maximal ideal m and let N be a finitely generated R-module. If N = mN then N = 0. If N' is a submodule of N and N = N' + mN, then N = N'.

definitions.name: projective module
definitions.text: An R-module P is projective if for every surjective R-linear map p: X -> Y and every R-linear map u: P -> Y there is an R-linear map v: P -> X with p v = u.

source.alignment: Mathlib proves that every finitely generated flat module over a local ring is free. A projective module is flat, so the projective case is a special case. The authored proof is a separate argument that uses the splitting of a surjection.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: The quotient P/mP is a k-vector space, because m kills it. It is finite dimensional, because the images of a finite generating set of P span it. Let r be its dimension. Choose elements p_1, ..., p_r of P whose images form a basis of P/mP.
Let P' be the submodule generated by p_1, ..., p_r. Since the images of the p_i span P/mP, we have P = P' + mP. By Nakayama's lemma, P = P'. So the p_i generate P.

Define pi: R^r -> P by pi(e_i) = p_i. It is surjective. Let K be its kernel. Because P is projective, applying the lifting property to the identity of P gives an R-linear map s: P -> R^r with pi s = id.

Then R^r = K + s(P) and K intersects s(P) in 0. Indeed, for x in R^r write x = (x - s pi(x)) + s pi(x) with x - s pi(x) in K. If s(y) is in K then y = pi s(y) = 0. So R^r is the direct sum K + s(P), and s(P) is isomorphic to P.
Reduce modulo m. Since m R^r = mK + m s(P), we get R^r/mR^r = K/mK + s(P)/m s(P) as a direct sum. Here s(P)/m s(P) is isomorphic to P/mP. Taking dimensions over k gives r = dim(K/mK) + r.
So K/mK = 0, that is K = mK. The module K is finitely generated, because K is isomorphic to the quotient R^r/s(P), via the map x -> x - s pi(x) from R^r onto K. By Nakayama's lemma K = 0.
Since K = 0, the map pi is an isomorphism from R^r onto P. So P is free of rank r = dim_k(P/mP).

applications.title: A projective module over Z/4 has 4^r elements
applications.inputs: Take R = Z/4. It is a local ring with maximal ideal m = (2) and residue field Z/2. Consider the Z/4-module P = m = {0, 2}, which is isomorphic to Z/2, and a hypothetical projective module Q with 16 elements.
applications.hypotheses: R is commutative and local. All modules here are finite, hence finitely generated.

steps.text: By the theorem, a finitely generated projective R-module is free, so it is isomorphic to R^r and has 4^r elements for some r >= 0. The sizes 1, 4, 16, 64 occur, and no other sizes occur.
The module P = m has 2 elements. The number 2 lies strictly between 4^0 = 1 and 4^1 = 4, so 2 is not a power of 4. Hence m is not projective over Z/4.
For the module Q with 16 elements, if Q is projective then Q is free of rank r, with 4^r = 16. So r = 2.
The rank can also be read from Q/mQ. It is a vector space over Z/2 with 2^r elements, so it has 4 elements, and its dimension is r = 2. This agrees with the theorem.

applications.conclusion: The ideal (2) is not a projective Z/4-module. Any projective Z/4-module with 16 elements is free of rank 2.

results.statement: Let R be a principal ideal domain and let F be a free R-module with a basis of n elements. Let N be a submodule of F. Then N is free, and N has a basis of m elements for some m <= n.
hypotheses: R is a principal ideal domain. It is an integral domain in which every ideal is generated by one element.
F is a free R-module of finite rank n.
N is any submodule of F. It need not be finitely generated a priori.

definitions.name: coordinate map
definitions.text: If e_1, ..., e_n is a basis of F, the map pi: F -> R with pi(a_1 e_1 + ... + a_n e_n) = a_n is R-linear. Its kernel is the span of e_1, ..., e_(n-1).

theorem Submodule.nonempty_basis_of_pid {ι : Type*} [Finite ι] (b : Basis ι R M)
    (N : Submodule R M) : ∃ n : ℕ, Nonempty (Basis (Fin n) R N) := by
  have := Classical.decEq M
  cases nonempty_fintype ι
  induction N using inductionOnRank b with | ih N ih =>
  let b' := (b.reindex (Fintype.equivFin ι)).map (LinearEquiv.ofTop _ rfl).symm
  by_cases N_bot : N = ⊥
  · subst N_bot
    exact ⟨0, ⟨Basis.empty _⟩⟩
  obtain ⟨y, -, a, hay, M', -, N', N'_le_N, -, -, ay_ortho, h'⟩ :=
    Submodule.basis_of_pid_aux ⊤ N b' N_bot le_top
  obtain ⟨n', ⟨bN'⟩⟩ := ih N' N'_le_N _ hay ay_ortho
  obtain ⟨bN, _hbN⟩ := h' n' bN'
  exact ⟨n' + 1, ⟨bN⟩⟩

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Induct on n. If n = 0 then F = 0 and N = 0, which has the empty basis.

Let n >= 1 and let e_1, ..., e_n be a basis of F. Let pi be the n-th coordinate map and F' = ker(pi). Then F' is free with basis e_1, ..., e_(n-1). Put N' = N intersect F'. This is a submodule of F', so by induction N' is free with a basis of m' <= n - 1 elements.
The image pi(N) is an ideal of R, because pi is linear. Since R is a principal ideal domain, pi(N) = (c) for some c in R.
If c = 0, then pi(N) = 0, so N is contained in ker(pi) = F'. Then N = N', which is free with at most n - 1 elements in its basis.

If c differs from 0, choose x in N with pi(x) = c. Let y be in N. Then pi(y) = a c for some a in R, because pi(y) is in (c). The element y - a x lies in N and pi(y - a x) = a c - a c = 0. So y - a x is in N'. This shows N = N' + R x.
The sum is direct and R x is free. Suppose a x is in N'. Then 0 = pi(a x) = a c. Since R is a domain and c differs from 0, a = 0. So N' intersect R x = 0 and a x = 0 only for a = 0.

Let b_1, ..., b_m' be a basis of N'. Then b_1, ..., b_m', x generate N. They are linearly independent: if a_1 b_1 + ... + a_m' b_m' + a x = 0, then a x lies in N', so a = 0, and then all a_i = 0. So N is free with m' + 1 <= n basis elements.

applications.title: A basis of the submodule of Z^2 spanned by (2, 4) and (6, 3)
applications.inputs: Take R = Z, F = Z^2 with the standard basis e_1, e_2, and N the submodule generated by u = (2, 4) and w = (6, 3). The map pi takes the second coordinate.
applications.hypotheses: Z is a principal ideal domain. N is a submodule of Z^2, so the theorem applies and N is free.

steps.text: The image pi(N) is the ideal generated by 4 and 3. Since gcd(4, 3) = 1, this ideal is (1), so c = 1. Find x in N with pi(x) = 1. Use 4*1 + 3*(-1) = 1.
So x = u - w. Its first coordinate is 2 - 6 = -4. Its second coordinate is 4 - 3 = 1. Hence x = (-4, 1).
Next find N' = N intersect ker(pi). An element a u + b w lies in ker(pi) when 4a + 3b = 0. The solutions are (a, b) = t (3, -4) for t in Z. Then t(3u - 4w) = t(3*2 - 4*6, 3*4 - 4*3) = t(-18, 0).

So N' is generated by (-18, 0). By the proof, N has the basis (-18, 0) and (-4, 1). Check the index of N in Z^2. It is the absolute value of the determinant of u and w, and it equals that of the basis.
The determinant of u and w is the same number up to sign, which confirms the basis.

applications.conclusion: The submodule N is free with basis (-18, 0), (-4, 1). It has index 18 in Z^2.

steps.text: Among the generators s_1, ..., s_k, choose a subset t_1, ..., t_r that is linearly independent and maximal for inclusion. This exists because the set of generators is finite. The case r = 0 is allowed. Let F be the submodule generated by t_1, ..., t_r. It is free with basis t_1, ..., t_r.
Fix j. If s_j is one of the t_i, put d_j = 1. Otherwise the family t_1, ..., t_r, s_j is dependent by maximality. So a_0 s_j + a_1 t_1 + ... + a_r t_r = 0 with the coefficients not all zero.

In this relation a_0 differs from 0. If a_0 = 0 then a_1 t_1 + ... + a_r t_r = 0 with some a_i nonzero, which contradicts independence of the t_i. Put d_j = a_0. Then d_j s_j = -(a_1 t_1 + ... + a_r t_r) lies in F.

Let d = d_1 d_2 ... d_k. Since R is a domain, d differs from 0. For every j, d s_j = (d / d_j)(d_j s_j) lies in F, because F is a submodule. Every element of M is an R-combination of the s_j, so d M is contained in F.
The map mu: M -> M with mu(m) = d m is R-linear. It is injective, because M is torsion-free and d differs from 0. So M is isomorphic to its image d M.
The image d M is a submodule of the free module F of rank r. By the result on submodules of free modules over a principal ideal domain, d M is free of rank at most r. Therefore M is free.

applications.title: The Z-module generated by 1/2 and 1/3 in Q is free of rank 1
applications.inputs: Take R = Z and let M be the subgroup of Q generated by s_1 = 1/2 and s_2 = 1/3.
applications.hypotheses: M is a subgroup of the field Q, so a nonzero integer multiple of a nonzero element is never zero. Thus M is torsion-free. M is finitely generated by s_1 and s_2.

steps.text: The elements s_1 and s_2 are linearly dependent over Z. The relation is 2 s_1 - 3 s_2 = 0. So the maximal independent subset is {s_1}, and F = Z (1/2).
Find the multipliers d_j. We have d_1 = 1. For s_2 the relation gives 3 s_2 = 1 = 2 s_1, so d_2 = 3 and 3 s_2 lies in F. Then d = 3.
The image d M = 3M is generated by 3/2 and 1, both in F = Z (1/2). In terms of the basis 1/2 of F, they are 3 and 2 times the basis. Since gcd(3, 2) = 1, 3M = F.
So M is isomorphic to the free module F of rank 1. A generator of M is 1/2 - 1/3, which equals 1/6.
Check that 1/6 generates M. We have 1/2 = 3 (1/6) and 1/3 = 2 (1/6). Both generators are integer multiples of 1/6.

applications.conclusion: M = Z (1/6) is free of rank 1, as the theorem predicts for a finitely generated torsion-free Z-module.

results.statement: For every integer n >= 1, the product n# of all primes p <= n satisfies n# < 4^n. In particular, theta(x) = sum of ln p over primes p <= x satisfies theta(x) <= x ln 4 for every real x >= 0.
hypotheses: n is an integer with n >= 1.
n# is the product of all primes p with p <= n. The empty product is 1, so 1# = 1.

theorem primorial_lt_four_pow (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≠ 0) : n# < 4 ^ n := by
  induction n using Nat.strong_induction_on with | h n ihn =>
  rcases n with - | n; · grind
  rcases n.even_or_odd with ⟨m, rfl⟩ | ho
  · rcases m.eq_zero_or_pos with rfl | hm
    · decide
    calc
      (m + m + 1)# = (m + 1 + m)# := by rw [add_right_comm]
      _ ≤ (m + 1)# * choose (m + 1 + m) (m + 1) := primorial_add_le m.le_succ
      _ = (m + 1)# * choose (2 * m + 1) m := by rw [choose_symm_add, two_mul, add_right_comm]
      _ < 4 ^ (m + 1) * 4 ^ m :=
        Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_lt_of_le (ihn _ (by lia) (by lia)) (choose_middle_le_pow _) (by simp)
      _ ≤ 4 ^ (m + m + 1) := by rw [← pow_add, add_right_comm]
  · rcases Decidable.eq_or_ne n 1 with rfl | hn
    · decide
    · calc
        (n + 1)# = n# := primorial_succ hn ho
        _ < 4 ^ n := ihn n n.lt_succ_self (by grind)
        _ ≤ 4 ^ (n + 1) := Nat.pow_le_pow_right four_pos n.le_succ

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Use strong induction on n. For n = 1 we have 1# = 1 < 4. For n = 2 we have 2# = 2 < 16. Assume n# < 4^k for all 1 <= k < n, where n >= 3.
Case n even. Then n > 2 is even, so n is not prime. Hence n# = (n-1)#. By the induction hypothesis (n-1)# < 4^(n-1) < 4^n.
Case n = 2m+1 odd, with m >= 1. Split the primes p <= n into primes p <= m+1 and primes p with m+1 < p <= 2m+1. So n# = (m+1)# * P, where P is the product of the primes in the interval (m+1, 2m+1].

Each prime p in (m+1, 2m+1] divides (2m+1)! because p <= 2m+1. We have (2m+1)! = C(2m+1, m) * m! * (m+1)!. Every factor of m! (m+1)! is at most m+1 < p, so the prime p does not divide m! (m+1)!. Hence p divides C(2m+1, m).
The primes in the interval are distinct, so they are pairwise coprime. Their product P divides C(2m+1, m). Hence P <= C(2m+1, m), because C(2m+1, m) is a positive integer.

The binomial coefficients C(2m+1, m) and C(2m+1, m+1) are equal by symmetry, and both are terms of the sum of all C(2m+1, k), which is 2^(2m+1) by the binomial theorem for (1+1)^(2m+1). So 2 C(2m+1, m) <= 2^(2m+1), which gives C(2m+1, m) <= 4^m.
Since m >= 1, we have m+1 <= 2m < n. The induction hypothesis gives (m+1)# < 4^(m+1). Hence n# = (m+1)# * P < 4^(m+1) * 4^m = 4^(2m+1) = 4^n. This closes the induction.
For the corollary, theta(x) = ln(floor(x)#) <= floor(x) ln 4 <= x ln 4, because ln is increasing and floor(x) <= x.

The primes up to m+1 = 6 are 2, 3, 5. Their product 6# is 30. The primes in (6, 11] are 7 and 11. Their product P is 77.
The binomial coefficient C(11, 5) = 11!/(5! 6!) equals 462. It is divisible by 7 and by 11, so P = 77 divides 462 and 462/77 = 6.
The bound C(11, 5) <= 4^5 holds: 462 is at most 1024.
Therefore 11# = 6# * P <= 30 * 462, and 11# is far below the bound 4^11.

applications.conclusion: 11# = 2310 < 4^11 = 4194304. So theta(11) = ln 2310 is below 11 ln 4. The proof steps are all visible in this case.

steps.text: Fix a prime p and write e = floor(log_p n), so p^e <= n < p^(e+1). For m in 1..n, v_p(m) <= e, because p^(v_p(m)) divides m and m <= n < p^(e+1). Also v_p(p^e) = e with p^e <= n. So v_p(L(n)) = e. If p > n, then v_p(L(n)) = 0.

Legendre's formula: v_p(m!) = sum over i >= 1 of floor(m/p^i). Proof: v_p(m!) is the sum of v_p(j) for j = 1..m. The integer j is counted once for each i with p^i dividing j. The number of such j with p^i | j and j <= m is floor(m/p^i).
Let 0 <= k <= n. Since C(n, k) = n!/(k! (n-k)!), Legendre's formula gives v_p(C(n, k)) = sum over i >= 1 of [floor(n/p^i) - floor(k/p^i) - floor((n-k)/p^i)].

For real numbers a, b we have floor(a+b) - floor(a) - floor(b) in {0, 1}. Reason: a = floor(a) + {a} and b = floor(b) + {b} with fractional parts in [0,1). The sum {a} + {b} is in [0,2), so floor({a}+{b}) is 0 or 1. Apply this with a = k/p^i and b = (n-k)/p^i. Every term of the sum is 0 or 1.
If p^i > n, then k/p^i < 1 and (n-k)/p^i < 1 and n/p^i < 1, so all three floors are 0 and the term is 0. Hence only the indices i = 1..e can give a nonzero term. So v_p(C(n, k)) <= e = v_p(L(n)).
For a prime p > n, p does not divide n!, so p does not divide C(n, k). Thus v_p(C(n, k)) <= v_p(L(n)) for every prime p. By unique factorization, C(n, k) divides L(n). In particular C(n, k) <= L(n).
By the binomial theorem, 2^n = (1+1)^n = sum for k = 0..n of C(n, k). There are n+1 terms and each is at most L(n). Hence 2^n <= (n+1) L(n). Take logarithms for the second form.

The sum of the binomial coefficients is 2^10.
The right side of Nair's bound is (n+1) L(n) = 11 * 2520.

applications.conclusion: 2^10 = 1024 <= 27720 = 11 * L(10). The bound holds. Each of the 11 binomial coefficients divides 2520, so none exceeds 2520.

theorem harmonic_le_one_add_log (n : ℕ) :
    harmonic n ≤ 1 + Real.log n := by
  by_cases hn0 : n = 0
  · simp [hn0]
  have hn : 1 ≤ n := Nat.one_le_iff_ne_zero.mpr hn0
  simp_rw [harmonic_eq_sum_Icc, Rat.cast_sum, Rat.cast_inv, Rat.cast_natCast]
  rw [← Finset.sum_erase_add (Finset.Icc 1 n) _ (Finset.left_mem_Icc.mpr hn), add_comm,
    Nat.cast_one, inv_one]
  gcongr
  simp only [Finset.Icc_erase_left]
  calc ∑ d ∈ .Ico 2 (n + 1), (d : ℝ)⁻¹

    _ ≤ ∫ x in 2..↑(n + 1), (x - 1)⁻¹ := ?_

steps.text: Let k = floor(log_2 n), so 2^k <= n < 2^(k+1) and k >= 1 because n >= 2. For each m with 1 <= m <= n we have 2^(v_2(m)) <= m <= n < 2^(k+1). So v_2(m) <= k, and v_2(1/m) = -v_2(m) >= -k.
Claim: v_2(m) = k for m <= n only when m = 2^k. Indeed, if v_2(m) = k then m = 2^k * q with q odd. If q >= 3, then m >= 3 * 2^k > 2 * 2^k = 2^(k+1) > n, which is impossible. So q = 1.
Split H_n = 1/2^k + R, where R is the sum of 1/m over all m in 1..n with m != 2^k. For each term of R we have v_2(1/m) = -v_2(m) >= -(k-1), because v_2(m) <= k - 1 by the claim.
The sum R is positive. It contains the term 1/1, because 1 differs from 2^k when k >= 1. All terms are positive, so R > 0. The ultrametric inequality then gives v_2(R) >= -(k-1).
We have v_2(1/2^k) = -k, which is smaller than -(k-1) <= v_2(R). The two valuations differ, so v_2(H_n) = min(-k, v_2(R)) = -k.
Since k >= 1, v_2(H_n) = -k < 0. A nonzero integer has v_2 >= 0. So H_n is not an integer.

applications.title: H_6 is not an integer, with its 2-adic valuation
applications.inputs: Take n = 6. Then k = floor(log_2 6) = 2 and 2^k = 4. The terms with m != 4 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6.
applications.hypotheses: n = 6 >= 2. The unique m <= 6 with v_2(m) = 2 is m = 4. The next candidate 3*4 = 12 exceeds 6.

steps.text: Compute the exact value of the full sum H_6.
The remainder R = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/6 equals 11/5. Its denominator 5 is odd, so v_2(R) = 0, and this is at least -(k-1) = -1.
Add the term 1/4 with v_2 = -2. The sum is 49/20.

applications.conclusion: H_6 = 49/20 has denominator 20 = 4 * 5, so v_2(H_6) = -2 = -k. It is not an integer.

theorem sum_range_pow (n p : ℕ) :
    (∑ k ∈ range n, (k : ℚ) ^ p) =
      ∑ i ∈ range (p + 1), bernoulli i * ((p + 1).choose i) * (n : ℚ) ^ (p + 1 - i) / (p + 1) := by
  have hne : ∀ m : ℕ, (m ! : ℚ) ≠ 0 := fun m => mod_cast factorial_ne_zero m
  -- compute the Cauchy product of two power series
  have h_cauchy :
    ((mk fun p => bernoulli p / p !) * mk fun q => coeff (q + 1) (exp ℚ ^ n)) =
      mk fun p => ∑ i ∈ range (p + 1),
          bernoulli i * (p + 1).choose i * (n : ℚ) ^ (p + 1 - i) / (p + 1)! := by
    ext q : 1
    let f a b := bernoulli a / a ! * coeff (b + 1) (exp ℚ ^ n)
    -- key step: use `PowerSeries.coeff_mul` and then rewrite sums
    simp only [f, coeff_mul, coeff_mk, sum_antidiagonal_eq_sum_range_succ f]
    apply sum_congr rfl
    intro m h
    simp only [exp_pow_eq_rescale_exp, rescale, RingHom.coe_mk]
    -- manipulate factorials and binomial coefficients
    have h : m < q + 1 := by simpa using h
    rw [choose_eq_factorial_div_factorial h.le, eq_comm, div_eq_iff (hne q.succ), succ_eq_add_one,
      mul_assoc _ _ (q.succ ! : ℚ), mul_comm _ (q.succ ! : ℚ), ← mul_assoc, div_mul_eq_mul_div]
    simp only [MonoidHom.coe_mk, OneHom.coe_mk, coeff_exp, Algebra.algebraMap_self, one_div,
      map_inv₀, map_natCast, coeff_mk]
    rw [mul_comm ((n : ℚ) ^ (q - m + 1)), ← mul_assoc _ _ ((n : ℚ) ^ (q - m + 1)), ← one_div,
      mul_one_div, div_div, tsub_add_eq_add_tsub (le_of_lt_succ h), cast_div, cast_mul]
    · ring
    · exact factorial_mul_factorial_dvd_factorial h.le
    · simp [factorial_ne_zero]
  -- same as our goal except we pull out `p!` for convenience
  have hps :
    (∑ k ∈ range n, (k : ℚ) ^ p) =
      (∑ i ∈ range (p + 1),
          bernoulli i * (p + 1).choose i * (n : ℚ) ^ (p + 1 - i) / (p + 1)!) * p ! := by
    suffices
      (mk fun p => ∑ k ∈ range n, (k : ℚ) ^ p * algebraMap ℚ ℚ p !⁻¹) =
        mk fun p =>
          ∑ i ∈ range (p + 1), bernoulli i * (p + 1).choose i * (n : ℚ) ^ (p + 1 - i) / (p + 1)! by
      rw [← div_eq_iff (hne p), div_eq_mul_inv, sum_mul]
      rw [PowerSeries.ext_iff] at this
      simpa using this p
    -- the power series `exp ℚ - 1` is non-zero, a fact we need in order to use `mul_right_inj'`
    have hexp : exp ℚ - 1 ≠ 0 := by
      simp only [exp, PowerSeries.ext_iff, Ne, not_forall]
      use 1
      simp
    have h_r : exp ℚ ^ n - 1 = X * mk fun p => coeff (p + 1) (exp ℚ ^ n) := by
      have h_const : C (constantCoeff (exp ℚ ^ n)) = 1 := by simp
      rw [← h_const, sub_const_eq_X_mul_shift]
    -- key step: a chain of equalities of power series
    rw [← mul_right_inj' hexp, mul_comm]
    rw [← exp_pow_sum, geom_sum_mul, h_r, ← bernoulliPowerSeries_mul_exp_sub_one,
      bernoulliPowerSeries, mul_right_comm]
    simp only [mul_comm, mul_eq_mul_left_iff, hexp, or_false]
    refine Eq.trans (mul_eq_mul_right_iff.mpr ?_) (Eq.trans h_cauchy ?_)
    · left
      congr
    · simp only [mul_comm, factorial]
  -- massage `hps` into our goal
  rw [hps, sum_mul]
  refine sum_congr rfl fun x _ => ?_
  simp [field, factorial]

steps.text: Let S(t) = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} e^(kt) in Q[[t]]. The coefficient of t^p/p! in S is sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^p, with 0^0 = 1. So S(t) = sum_p (sum_k k^p) t^p/p!.
Telescoping: S(t) * (e^t - 1) = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (e^((k+1)t) - e^(kt)) = e^(nt) - 1. Here we use e^(kt) e^t = e^((k+1)t).
Divide by t. Write e^t - 1 = t E(t). Then t S(t) E(t) = e^(nt) - 1, so S(t) E(t) = (e^(nt) - 1)/t = F(t), where F(t) = sum_{j>=0} n^(j+1) t^j/(j+1)!.
Since E is invertible with inverse sum B_i t^i/i!, we get S(t) = (sum_i B_i t^i/i!) * F(t).
Compare the coefficients of t^p. The left side gives (sum_k k^p)/p!. The right side gives, by the Cauchy product, sum_{i=0}^{p} (B_i/i!) * n^(p-i+1)/(p-i+1)!.
Multiply by p!. For each i, p!/(i! (p+1-i)!) = C(p+1, i)/(p+1), because C(p+1, i) = (p+1)!/(i! (p+1-i)!). This gives sum_k k^p = sum_{i=0}^{p} B_i C(p+1, i) n^(p+1-i)/(p+1).

Compute the integrals. f^p = t^(x-1) e^(-t), whose integral is Gamma(x). g^q = t^(y-1) e^(-t), whose integral is Gamma(y). So the right side is Gamma(x)^a Gamma(y)^(1-a).
The left side is Gamma(z). Hence Gamma(a x + (1-a) y) <= Gamma(x)^a Gamma(y)^(1-a).
Take logarithms: ln Gamma(a x + (1-a) y) <= a ln Gamma(x) + (1-a) ln Gamma(y). This is the definition of convexity of ln Gamma on (0, infinity).

source.alignment: The Lean theorem states that x ln n + ln n! - sum_{m=0}^{n} ln(x+m) tends to ln Gamma(x). Taking exp gives the product form here.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

steps.text: Approximation of the integrand. For fixed t > 0 and n > t, (1 - t/n)^n tends to e^(-t), because n ln(1 - t/n) tends to -t. For 0 <= t < n, 0 <= (1 - t/n)^n <= e^(-t), because 1 - u <= e^(-u) for all real u.

Apply dominated convergence to the functions h_n(t) = 1_{(0,n)}(t) (1 - t/n)^n t^(x-1). They converge pointwise to e^(-t) t^(x-1) and are dominated by t^(x-1) e^(-t), which is integrable on (0, infinity) because x > 0. So Gamma_n(x) tends to Gamma(x).
Substitute t = n s on (0, n). Then Gamma_n(x) = n^x * I(x, n), because dt = n ds and t^(x-1) = n^(x-1) s^(x-1).

Recurrence for I. For n >= 1, integrate by parts with u = (1-s)^n and dv = s^(x-1) ds, so v = s^x/x. The boundary term [s^x (1-s)^n / x] vanishes at s = 1 because n >= 1, and at s = 0 because x > 0. The derivative of u is -n (1-s)^(n-1), so I(x, n) = (n/x) I(x+1, n-1).
Iterate n times: I(x, n) = n!/(x (x+1) ... (x+n-1)) * I(x+n, 0). Here I(x+n, 0) is the integral of s^(x+n-1) over (0, 1), which equals 1/(x+n).
So Gamma_n(x) = n^x n!/(x (x+1) ... (x+n)). By step 2 this tends to Gamma(x). This is the stated limit.

applications.title: Recover Gamma(2) = 1 from the limit formula
applications.inputs: Take x = 2. The finite product is n! n^2/(2 * 3 * ... * (n+2)). We test n = 3 and n = 1000.
applications.hypotheses: x = 2 > 0, so the formula applies. The product 2 * 3 * ... * (n+2) equals (n+2)!.

steps.text: For n = 3 the expression is 3! * 3^2/(2*3*4*5).
Simplify in general: n! n^2/(n+2)! = n^2/((n+1)(n+2)). For n = 3 this equals 9/20, the same as above.
For n = 1000 the value n^2/((n+1)(n+2)) is 1000000/1003002, close to 1.
The distance from 1 at n = 1000 is 3002/1003002, about 0.003. It tends to 0 as n grows, because n^2/((n+1)(n+2)) = 1/((1+1/n)(1+2/n)).

applications.conclusion: The limit of n^2/((n+1)(n+2)) is 1, so the formula gives Gamma(2) = 1. This agrees with Gamma(2) = 1! = 1.

source.alignment: The Lean theorem Nat.card_multiples counts the multiples of p among 1..n and equals n/p. This is the counting step 2. The authored bounds follow from it.

steps.text: Count the set P of pairs (k, m) of positive integers with m <= N and k dividing m. Counting by m, each m contributes its d(m) divisors. So |P| = D(N).

Counting by k: for fixed k, the possible m are the multiples k, 2k, ..., jk with jk <= N. There are floor(N/k) such multiples. Also k <= m <= N. So |P| = sum_{k=1}^{N} floor(N/k). Hence D(N) = sum_{k=1}^{N} floor(N/k).
Upper bound. floor(N/k) <= N/k. So D(N) <= N sum_{k=1}^{N} 1/k = N H_N. By the harmonic bound H_N <= 1 + ln N, we get D(N) <= N (1 + ln N).
Lower bound. floor(N/k) > N/k - 1 for each k. Sum over k = 1..N: D(N) > N H_N - N. By the harmonic bound H_N >= ln(N+1), we get D(N) > N ln(N+1) - N.
Since ln(N+1) >= ln N, the two bounds give N ln N - N < D(N) <= N ln N + N. So |D(N)/N - ln N| <= 1, which is the statement D(N)/N = ln N + O(1).

source.alignment: Lean states riemannZeta 4 = pi^4/90 for the analytically continued zeta function. For real s > 1 this equals the series, which is the authored statement.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let f(x) = x^2 on [-pi, pi]. Then f is real, even and square integrable. The integral of f^2 = x^4 over [-pi, pi] is 2 pi^5/5, so (1/2pi) integral of |f|^2 = pi^4/5.
Coefficient c_0 = (1/2pi) integral of x^2 dx = (1/2pi)(2 pi^3/3) = pi^2/3.

For n != 0, f is even, so the sine part of e^(-inx) integrates to 0 and c_n = (1/pi) integral from 0 to pi of x^2 cos(nx) dx. Integrate by parts twice. The first integration gives [x^2 sin(nx)/n] from 0 to pi, which is 0, minus (2/n) integral of x sin(nx). The second gives integral of x sin(nx) = [-x cos(nx)/n] + (1/n) integral of cos(nx) = -pi (-1)^n/n + 0. So integral from 0 to pi of x^2 cos(nx) = 2 pi (-1)^n/n^2 and c_n = 2 (-1)^n/n^2. Parseval's identity then applies with these coefficients.
Parseval: pi^4/5 = c_0^2 + sum over n != 0 of |c_n|^2 = pi^4/9 + 2 sum_{n>=1} 4/n^4, because |c_n| = |c_(-n)| = 2/n^2.
Rearrange: 8 zeta(4) = pi^4/5 - pi^4/9 = 4 pi^4/45. Divide by 8: zeta(4) = pi^4/90.
The series converges since 1/n^4 <= 1/n^2 and the series of 1/n^2 converges. The rearrangement in step 5 is valid because all terms are positive.

applications.hypotheses: The terms 1/n^4 are positive and decreasing, so the integral comparison for the tail holds. We use the rational number 355/113 as an upper estimate for pi.

steps.text: Compute the exact partial sum S_5 of the series.
Compute the integral tail bound for the terms with n >= 6.
The predicted value (355/113)^4/90 is the claimed zeta(4), with pi replaced by 355/113.
The difference between the predicted value and S_5 is positive and smaller than the tail bound 1/375 = 0.00267. The difference is 0.00197.

applications.conclusion: The value pi^4/90 = 1.08232... lies between S_5 = 1.08035 and S_5 + 1/375 = 1.08302. So the formula passes an independent numerical test.

results.name: Affinely independent families have at most dim + 1 points
aliases: affine independence iff difference vectors are linearly independent
results.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space of dimension n over a field k, and let P be an affine space over V. Let p_0, ..., p_m be points of P. The family (p_i) is affinely independent if and only if the m vectors p_1 - p_0, ..., p_m - p_0 are linearly independent in V. Hence an affinely independent family in P has at most n + 1 members.
hypotheses: k is a field and V is a k-vector space with finite dimension n.
P is an affine space over V, so that the difference p - q is a vector of V for all points p and q of P.
The family (p_i), i = 0..m, is finite.

Affine independence means: if weights w_0, ..., w_m in k satisfy w_0 + ... + w_m = 0 and w_0 p_0 + ... + w_m p_m = 0 (the weighted sum of points with weight sum 0 is a vector of V), then every w_i is 0.

definitions.name: weighted sum with weight sum 0
definitions.text: For weights w_i with sum 0, the expression w_0 p_0 + ... + w_m p_m means w_0 (p_0 - q) + ... + w_m (p_m - q) for any point q. The value does not depend on q because the weights sum to 0.

source.alignment: The declaration states only the bound on the number of points. The authored statement adds the equivalence with linear independence of the difference vectors, which the proof of the bound uses.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Assume that the family (p_i) is affinely independent. Let c_1, ..., c_m be scalars with c_1 (p_1 - p_0) + ... + c_m (p_m - p_0) = 0. Define the weights w_i = c_i for i >= 1 and w_0 = -(c_1 + ... + c_m).
The weights sum to 0 by the choice of w_0. Take q = p_0 as the base point. Then the weighted sum is w_0 * 0 + c_1 (p_1 - p_0) + ... + c_m (p_m - p_0), and this vector is 0 by assumption.
Affine independence now gives w_i = 0 for all i. In particular c_i = 0 for i >= 1. Hence the vectors p_i - p_0 with i >= 1 are linearly independent.

Conversely, assume that the vectors p_i - p_0 (i >= 1) are linearly independent. Let weights w_i have sum 0 and weighted sum 0. With base point p_0 the weighted sum equals w_1 (p_1 - p_0) + ... + w_m (p_m - p_0), because the term for i = 0 is w_0 * 0.
Linear independence gives w_1 = ... = w_m = 0. The sum condition then gives w_0 = -(w_1 + ... + w_m) = 0. So the family is affinely independent. This proves the equivalence.

A linearly independent family in a vector space of dimension n has at most n members, because it extends to a basis and every basis has n elements. Hence m <= n, and the family p_0, ..., p_m has m + 1 <= n + 1 points.

applications.title: Four points in the plane are never affinely independent

steps.text: The bound gives at most n + 1 affinely independent points in the plane.
The family has 4 points, which is more than 3. So the family is not affinely independent. Find a witness: take the weights (1, -1, -1, 1). They sum to 0.
The first coordinate of the weighted sum is 1*0 - 1*1 - 1*0 + 1*1.
The second coordinate of the weighted sum is 1*0 - 1*0 - 1*1 + 1*1. Both coordinates are 0 while the weights are not all 0, so the family is affinely dependent.

applications.conclusion: The family of 4 points of the plane is affinely dependent, as the bound requires. The explicit relation is p_0 + p_3 = p_1 + p_2 (the diagonals of a parallelogram have the same midpoint).

results.name: Existence and uniqueness of the circumsphere of a simplex
aliases: circumcenter of a triangle exists and is unique
results.statement: Let P be a Euclidean affine space and let p_0, ..., p_n be affinely independent points of P. Then exactly one point c in the affine span of p_0, ..., p_n satisfies |c - p_0| = |c - p_1| = ... = |c - p_n|. Thus exactly one sphere has its center in the affine span and contains all the points p_i. Its center is the circumcenter and its radius is the circumradius.
hypotheses: P is an affine space over a real inner product space V, and |u| denotes the norm of u in V.
The points p_0, ..., p_n are affinely independent. For n = 2 this means that the three points are not on one line.
The center must lie in the affine span of the points. Without this condition, a sphere through the points is not unique when the span is smaller than P.

prerequisites.reason: It shows that the vectors p_j - p_0 are linearly independent, which makes the Gram matrix invertible.

definitions.name: Gram matrix
definitions.text: For vectors u_1, ..., u_n the Gram matrix G is the n x n matrix with entries G_ij = <u_i, u_j>. It is symmetric.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Put u_j = p_j - p_0 for j = 1..n. By the prerequisite these vectors are linearly independent. Every point c of the affine span has the form c = p_0 + v with v = t_1 u_1 + ... + t_n u_n, and the t_j are unique.
For j >= 1 we have p_j - c = u_j - v. So |c - p_j|^2 = |u_j - v|^2 = |u_j|^2 - 2<u_j, v> + |v|^2. Also |c - p_0|^2 = |v|^2. Hence |c - p_j| = |c - p_0| if and only if 2<u_j, v> = |u_j|^2.
Insert v = sum_k t_k u_k. The n conditions become the linear system 2 sum_k G_jk t_k = |u_j|^2 for j = 1..n, that is 2 G t = b with b_j = |u_j|^2.
The matrix G is injective. Suppose G s = 0. Then s^T G s = sum_jk s_j s_k <u_j, u_k> = |sum_j s_j u_j|^2 = 0. So sum_j s_j u_j = 0, and linear independence gives s = 0.
A square matrix with trivial kernel is invertible. So the system has exactly one solution t = G^(-1) b / 2. This gives exactly one point c in the span with |c - p_j| = |c - p_0| for all j.

Let R = |c - p_0|. Then the sphere with center c and radius R contains all p_i. Conversely, a sphere with center c' in the span that contains all p_i has |c' - p_i| equal for all i, so c' = c by uniqueness and its radius is R. This proves the uniqueness of the sphere.

steps.text: The diagonal entry G_11 = <u_1, u_1> equals 16.
The diagonal entry G_22 = <u_2, u_2> equals 9.

The second equation 2*9*t_2 = 9 gives t_2.

results.statement: Let A, B, C be the vertices of a non-degenerate triangle in a Euclidean space. Let O be its circumcenter and G its centroid. G = (A + B + C)/3 is the centroid.
The altitude from A is the line in the plane ABC through A that is perpendicular to the line BC. The other altitudes are defined in the same way.

source.alignment: In the Lean source the orthocenter is defined as the Monge point, and the declaration expresses it with the circumcenter and centroid. The authored statement also shows directly that this point is on the altitudes.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Take O as the origin and write a, b, c for the position vectors of A, B, C. By the prerequisite O is in the plane of the triangle, so a, b, c lie in the 2-dimensional direction space D of this plane, and |a| = |b| = |c| = R.
The centroid has position vector g = (a + b + c)/3. Define h = 3g = a + b + c. Then h is in D, so H is a point of the plane, and H - O = 3 (G - O) by construction.
Compute the inner product of h - a with b - c. We get <h - a, b - c> = <b + c, b - c> = |b|^2 - |c|^2 = R^2 - R^2 = 0. So the vector H - A is perpendicular to the side BC.

The line through A in the plane ABC perpendicular to BC consists of the points X of the plane with <X - A, b - c> = 0, because in the 2-dimensional plane the vectors perpendicular to b - c form a line. The point H has this property, so H is on the altitude from A.
The same computation with the roles of a, b, c exchanged gives <h - b, c - a> = |c|^2 - |a|^2 = 0 and <h - c, a - b> = |a|^2 - |b|^2 = 0. So H is on the altitude from B and on the altitude from C.
Thus the three altitudes meet in H. Since H - O = 3 (G - O), the points O, G, H are collinear and G divides the segment OH in the ratio OG : GH = 1 : 2.

steps.text: Take O as the origin and write a, b, c for the vertices. Then |a| = |b| = |c| = R, and by the Euler line theorem h = a + b + c. Put n = h/2, the midpoint of OH.
The side midpoint M_A = (b + c)/2 satisfies n - M_A = a/2. So |n - M_A| = R/2. In the same way |n - M_B| = |b|/2 = R/2 and |n - M_C| = |c|/2 = R/2.

The Euler point E_A = (a + h)/2 satisfies n - E_A = -a/2. So |n - E_A| = R/2. The same holds for E_B and E_C. Also M_A + E_A = h, so n is the midpoint of M_A E_A, and the segment M_A E_A is a diameter of the circle with center n and radius R/2.

Now let D be the foot of the altitude from A. Both M_A and D are on the line BC, so D - M_A is parallel to b - c. Both E_A and D are on the altitude through A, because A and H are on it, so E_A is on it too. Hence D - E_A is perpendicular to b - c.
Therefore <D - M_A, D - E_A> = 0. Write r = M_A - n, so E_A - n = -r. Then <D - M_A, D - E_A> = <(D - n) - r, (D - n) + r> = |D - n|^2 - |r|^2.
Hence |D - n|^2 = |r|^2 = R^2/4, that is |D - n| = R/2. So the foot D_A is on the circle. The feet D_B and D_C follow in the same way. All nine points are at distance R/2 from N.

results.name: Uniform convexity of inner product spaces
results.statement: Let E be a real inner product space and let 0 < eps <= 2. Put delta = 2 - sqrt(4 - eps^2). Then delta > 0, and for all unit vectors x, y in E with |x - y| >= eps we have |x + y| <= 2 - delta. Moreover delta >= eps^2/4. In particular, if |x| = |y| = 1 and |x + y| = 2, then x = y.

x and y are vectors of E with |x| = |y| = 1.

steps.text: The parallelogram identity states |x + y|^2 + |x - y|^2 = 2|x|^2 + 2|y|^2. For unit vectors the right side is 4. So |x + y|^2 = 4 - |x - y|^2.
Since |x - y| >= eps, we have |x - y|^2 >= eps^2. So |x + y|^2 <= 4 - eps^2. Because 0 < eps <= 2, the number 4 - eps^2 is in [0, 4). Taking square roots gives |x + y| <= sqrt(4 - eps^2) = 2 - delta.
We have delta > 0 because eps > 0 implies 4 - eps^2 < 4, hence sqrt(4 - eps^2) < 2.
For the bound on delta, note that (2 - eps^2/4)^2 = 4 - eps^2 + eps^4/16 >= 4 - eps^2, and 2 - eps^2/4 >= 1 > 0 for eps <= 2. So sqrt(4 - eps^2) <= 2 - eps^2/4, that is delta >= eps^2/4.
Equality case. Let |x| = |y| = 1 and |x + y| = 2. Suppose x != y and put eps = |x - y|, which is in (0, 2]. The first part gives |x + y| <= 2 - delta < 2, a contradiction. So x = y.

The theorem bounds |x + y|^2 by 4 - eps^2.
The actual value is |x + y|^2 = 1^2 + 1^2, which is at most 3.
The lower bound delta >= eps^2/4 = 1/4 gives |x + y| <= 7/4. Check that (7/4)^2 is at least 4 - eps^2 = 3.

applications.conclusion: Here |x + y| = sqrt(2), which is less than 7/4 and less than sqrt(3). The unit vectors x and y are strictly inside the bound 2 - delta.

results.name: The Minkowski functional of a convex absorbent set is sublinear
results.statement: Let E be a real vector space and let s be a convex absorbent subset of E. Define gauge(x) = inf { r > 0 : x is in r*s }. Then gauge(x) is a finite number >= 0 for every x, gauge(a x) = a gauge(x) for every a >= 0, gauge(x + y) <= gauge(x) + gauge(y) for all x, y, and gauge(x) <= 1 for every x in s.
hypotheses: E is a real vector space.
s is convex: for u, v in s and t in [0,1], the point t u + (1 - t) v is in s.
s is absorbent: for every x in E there is R > 0 such that x is in a*s for every real a with a >= R.
r*s denotes the set { r u : u in s }.

steps.text: For x let S(x) = { r > 0 : x is in r*s }. Absorbency gives a number R with x in a*s for all a >= R, so S(x) is not empty. The set is bounded below by 0, so gauge(x) = inf S(x) is a real number >= 0.
Absorbency applied to x = 0 gives 0 in a*s for some a > 0, so 0 is in s. Then 0 is in r*s for every r > 0, so S(0) = (0, infinity) and gauge(0) = 0. If x is in s, then 1 is in S(x), so gauge(x) <= 1.

Homogeneity. Let a > 0. For r > 0 we have x in r*s if and only if a x is in (a r)*s. So S(a x) = a S(x), and the infimum scales: gauge(a x) = a gauge(x). The case a = 0 is gauge(0) = 0 from the previous step.
Subadditivity. Fix eps > 0. By the definition of the infimum there are a in S(x) and b in S(y) with a < gauge(x) + eps/2 and b < gauge(y) + eps/2. Write x = a u and y = b v with u, v in s.
Then x + y = a u + b v = (a + b) ( (a/(a+b)) u + (b/(a+b)) v ). The weights a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) are positive and sum to 1. Convexity of s puts the bracket in s. So a + b is in S(x + y).
Hence gauge(x + y) <= a + b < gauge(x) + gauge(y) + eps. Since eps > 0 is arbitrary, gauge(x + y) <= gauge(x) + gauge(y).

steps.text: Fix z = a x + b y with a, b > 0 and a + b = 1. Define h(w) = (z - b w)/a. The map h is continuous because E is a topological vector space, and h(y) = (a x + b y - b y)/a = x.

Let U = interior of s. It is open and contains x = h(y). So h^(-1)(U) is an open set that contains y. Since y is in the closure of s, every open set around y meets s. So there is w in s with h(w) in U.
Put u = h(w). Then u is in U and z = a u + b w by the definition of h. Here u is in the interior of s and w is in s.
Define the map phi(v) = a v + b w. Because a != 0, phi is a homeomorphism of E (its inverse is v -> (v - b w)/a). Hence phi(U) is open, and it contains phi(u) = z.
Every point of phi(U) has the form a v + b w with v in U, so v is in s. Also w is in s, and a + b = 1 with a, b >= 0. By convexity a v + b w is in s. So phi(U) is an open subset of s that contains z.

Therefore z is in the interior of s. For the last claim, let x and y be in the interior of s. Then y is in the closure of s, so the open segment is in the interior of s. The end points x and y are in the interior by assumption. So the interior of s is convex.

  · linarith [angle_le_pi x z]
  suffices Real.cos (angle x y + angle y z) ≤ Real.cos (angle x z) by
    have H0 : 0 ≤ angle x y + angle y z :=
      add_nonneg (angle_nonneg x y) (angle_nonneg y z)
    rwa [Real.strictAntiOn_cos.le_iff_ge ⟨H0, H⟩ ⟨angle_nonneg x z, angle_le_pi x z⟩] at this

steps.text: The angle does not change if a vector is multiplied by a positive scalar. So assume |x| = |y| = |z| = 1. Put alpha = angle(x,y) and beta = angle(y,z), both in [0, pi]. Then <x,y> = cos(alpha) and <y,z> = cos(beta).
Decompose x = cos(alpha) y + x', where x' = x - <x,y> y. Then <x',y> = <x,y> - <x,y> = 0. Also |x'|^2 = 1 - cos^2(alpha) = sin^2(alpha), so |x'| = sin(alpha) because sin(alpha) >= 0 on [0, pi].
In the same way z = cos(beta) y + z' with <z',y> = 0 and |z'| = sin(beta).
Expand <x,z> = cos(alpha) cos(beta) <y,y> + cos(alpha) <y,z'> + cos(beta) <x',y> + <x',z'>. The two middle terms are 0 by orthogonality, so <x,z> = cos(alpha) cos(beta) + <x',z'>.
By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality <x',z'> >= -|x'||z'| = -sin(alpha) sin(beta). Hence cos(angle(x,z)) = <x,z> >= cos(alpha) cos(beta) - sin(alpha) sin(beta) = cos(alpha + beta).

If alpha + beta >= pi, the claim holds because angle(x,z) <= pi. If alpha + beta < pi, then angle(x,z) and alpha + beta are both in [0, pi], where cos is strictly decreasing. So cos(angle(x,z)) >= cos(alpha + beta) gives angle(x,z) <= alpha + beta.

source.alignment: The declaration states: if p1 != p2 and p all lie on both circles, then p = p1 or p = p2. This is the same as at most two common points.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Let p be a common point. Then |p - c1|^2 = r1^2 and |p - c2|^2 = r2^2. Subtract: |p - c1|^2 - |p - c2|^2 = r1^2 - r2^2.

Expand each square. The terms |p|^2 cancel, and we get 2<p, c2 - c1> = r1^2 - r2^2 + |c2|^2 - |c1|^2. Put d = c2 - c1, which is nonzero. Then <p, d> = kappa for a constant kappa that depends only on the data.

So every common point is in the set L = { p : <p, d> = kappa }. This set is not empty if there is a common point. Fix p0 in L. Then L = p0 + W, where W = { w : <w, d> = 0 } is the orthogonal complement of d.
Since dim V = 2 and d != 0, the space W has dimension 1. Choose e != 0 in W. Then L = { p0 + s e : s in R }.
A point p = p0 + s e is on the first circle if and only if |p0 + s e - c1|^2 = r1^2, that is |e|^2 s^2 + 2 s <e, p0 - c1> + |p0 - c1|^2 - r1^2 = 0.
This is a quadratic equation in s with leading coefficient |e|^2 > 0. It has at most 2 real roots. Different roots give different points because e != 0. So there are at most 2 common points.

steps.text: Put t_k = (2k+1) pi / (2n) for k = 0, ..., n-1. Then 0 < t_k < pi, and n t_k = (2k+1) pi / 2. So T_n(cos t_k) = cos((2k+1) pi / 2) = 0. Each x_k is a root.
The cosine is strictly decreasing on [0, pi]. The angles t_0 < t_1 < ... < t_(n-1) lie in (0, pi). So the numbers x_k are pairwise different, and there are n of them.

T_n has degree n and leading coefficient 2^(n-1). A nonzero polynomial of degree n over a field has at most n roots when counted with multiplicity. We have found n different roots. So these are all roots, and each is simple.
A polynomial that has n simple roots x_k and degree n equals its leading coefficient times the product of (x - x_k). This gives T_n(x) = 2^(n-1) * product (x - x_k).

For y_j = cos(j pi / n) with j = 0, ..., n, the angles j pi / n are different points of [0, pi]. Cosine is strictly decreasing there, so y_0 = 1 > y_1 > ... > y_n = -1. Also T_n(y_j) = cos(n * j pi / n) = cos(j pi) = (-1)^j.

applications.title: Product of the Chebyshev nodes for n = 4
applications.inputs: Take n = 4. Then T_4(x) = 8x^4 - 8x^2 + 1, and the nodes are cos(pi/8), cos(3pi/8), cos(5pi/8), cos(7pi/8).
applications.hypotheses: T_4 has degree 4 and leading coefficient 2^3 = 8, so the theorem applies with n = 4.

steps.text: The product formula gives T_4(x) = 8 * (x - x_0)(x - x_1)(x - x_2)(x - x_3). At x = 0 this gives T_4(0) = 8 * x_0 x_1 x_2 x_3, because there are 4 factors and (-1)^4 = 1. Also T_4(0) = 1. So the product of the nodes is 1/8.

Check by trigonometry. Since cos(5pi/8) = -cos(3pi/8) and cos(7pi/8) = -cos(pi/8), the product is (cos(pi/8) cos(3pi/8))^2. Now cos(3pi/8) = sin(pi/8), so cos(pi/8) sin(pi/8) = sin(pi/4)/2 = sqrt(2)/4. Its square is 2/16.
The identity gives T_4(1/2) = cos(4 pi/3) = -1/2 because 1/2 = cos(pi/3). The explicit polynomial agrees.
The equioscillation points are y_j = cos(j pi/4). For j = 2 we have y_2 = 0 and T_4(0) = (-1)^2 = 1, which matches the constant term of T_4.

applications.conclusion: The product of the four Chebyshev nodes is 1/8. The product formula, a direct trigonometric check and the value T_4(0) = 1 give the same result.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration bounds the leading coefficient of a polynomial of degree at most n with |P| <= 1 on [-1, 1]. The authored statement applies it to P = p / M with M the uniform norm of the monic polynomial p. The authored proof uses the alternation argument.

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: The function |p| is continuous on [-1, 1], so it has a maximum M. Suppose, for contradiction, that M < 2^(1-n).
Put R = 2^(1-n) T_n. By the leading coefficient result, R is monic of degree n. Let q = R - p. The terms of degree n cancel, so q has degree at most n - 1.

Let y_j = cos(j pi / n) for j = 0, ..., n. They satisfy y_0 > y_1 > ... > y_n and R(y_j) = 2^(1-n) (-1)^j. We have |p(y_j)| <= M < 2^(1-n), so q(y_j) = 2^(1-n)(-1)^j - p(y_j) has the sign of (-1)^j: positive for even j and negative for odd j.

For j = 0, ..., n-1, the continuous function q has opposite signs at y_(j+1) and y_j. By the intermediate value theorem, q has a root z_j with y_(j+1) < z_j < y_j. These n open intervals are pairwise disjoint, so z_0, ..., z_(n-1) are n different roots.
A nonzero polynomial of degree at most n - 1 has at most n - 1 roots. So q = 0. But q(y_0) > 0. This contradiction shows M >= 2^(1-n).
Sharpness. The polynomial 2^(1-n) T_n is monic of degree n. Since |T_n| <= 1 on [-1, 1] and T_n(1) = 1, its maximum equals 2^(1-n).

steps.text: Differentiate T_n(cos t) = cos(n t) with respect to t. The chain rule gives -sin t * T_n'(cos t) = -n sin(n t). For t in (0, pi) we have sin t > 0, so T_n'(cos t) = n sin(n t) / sin t.

Claim: |sin(n t)| <= n sin t for t in (0, pi) and n >= 1. For n = 1 this is an equality. If it holds for n, then sin((n+1)t) = sin(n t) cos t + cos(n t) sin t gives |sin((n+1)t)| <= n sin t * 1 + 1 * sin t = (n+1) sin t.
Take x in (-1, 1) and put t = arccos x in (0, pi). By the first step and the claim, |T_n'(x)| = n |sin(n t)| / sin t <= n * n = n^2.
The function |T_n'| is continuous on [-1, 1]. It is at most n^2 on the dense subset (-1, 1). So it is at most n^2 at x = 1 and x = -1 as well.

Value at 1. Take the limit of T_n'(cos t) = n sin(n t)/sin t as t tends to 0 from above. Since sin(n t)/t tends to n and sin t / t tends to 1, the quotient tends to n * n. By continuity of T_n' at 1, T_n'(1) = n^2.

results.statement: For n >= 1 and k = 0, ..., n, let b_k(x) = C(n,k) x^k (1-x)^(n-k). Then for every real x: sum_k b_k(x) = 1; sum_k k b_k(x) = n x; sum_k k(k-1) b_k(x) = n(n-1) x^2; and sum_k (n x - k)^2 b_k(x) = n x (1-x).
hypotheses: n is an integer with n >= 1, and k runs over the integers 0, ..., n.
x is any real number. For x in [0, 1] each b_k(x) is nonnegative.
C(n,k) is the binomial coefficient n! / (k! (n-k)!).

prerequisites.reason: The proof expands (x + y)^n with the binomial theorem and differentiates the expansion.

definitions.name: Bernstein basis polynomial
definitions.text: b_k(x) = C(n,k) x^k (1-x)^(n-k), for fixed n and k = 0, ..., n. For x in [0,1] it is the probability of k heads in n independent tosses of a coin with head probability x.

theorem variance (n : ℕ) :
    (∑ ν ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (n • Polynomial.X - (ν : R[X])) ^ 2 * bernsteinPolynomial R n ν) =
      n • Polynomial.X * ((1 : R[X]) - Polynomial.X) := by
  have p : ((((Finset.range (n + 1)).sum fun ν => (ν * (ν - 1)) • bernsteinPolynomial R n ν) +
      (1 - (2 * n) • Polynomial.X) * (Finset.range (n + 1)).sum fun ν =>
        ν • bernsteinPolynomial R n ν) + n ^ 2 • X ^ 2 *
          (Finset.range (n + 1)).sum fun ν => bernsteinPolynomial R n ν) = _ :=
    rfl
  conv at p =>
    lhs
    rw [Finset.mul_sum, Finset.mul_sum, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib, ← Finset.sum_add_distrib]
    simp only [← natCast_mul]
    simp only [← mul_assoc]
    simp only [← add_mul]
  conv at p =>
    rhs
    rw [sum, sum_smul, sum_mul_smul, ← natCast_mul]
  calc
    _ = _ := Finset.sum_congr rfl fun k m => ?_
    _ = _ := p
    _ = _ := ?_
  · congr 1; simp only [← natCast_mul, push_cast]
    cases k <;> · simp; ring
  · simp only [← natCast_mul, push_cast]
    cases n
    · simp
    · simp; ring

steps.text: Treat x and y as independent variables. The binomial theorem gives the polynomial identity (x + y)^n = sum_k C(n,k) x^k y^(n-k).
Substitute y = 1 - x. Then x + y = 1, so 1 = sum_k b_k(x). This is the first identity.

Differentiate the identity with respect to x, keeping y fixed. The result is n (x+y)^(n-1) = sum_k k C(n,k) x^(k-1) y^(n-k). Multiply by x and put y = 1 - x. Since x + y = 1, we get n x = sum_k k b_k(x).

Differentiate twice with respect to x. For n >= 2 the result is n(n-1)(x+y)^(n-2) = sum_k k(k-1) C(n,k) x^(k-2) y^(n-k). Multiply by x^2 and put y = 1 - x. We get sum_k k(k-1) b_k(x) = n(n-1) x^2. For n = 1 both sides are 0.
Expand (n x - k)^2 = n^2 x^2 - 2 n x k + k(k-1) + k. Multiply by b_k(x) and sum. The sum equals n^2 x^2 * 1 - 2 n x * n x + n(n-1) x^2 + n x.
Simplify: n^2 x^2 - 2 n^2 x^2 + n^2 x^2 - n x^2 + n x = n x - n x^2 = n x (1 - x). This is the fourth identity.

applications.title: Check the identities for n = 3 and x = 1/3
applications.hypotheses: n = 3 >= 1 and x = 1/3 is real, so all four identities apply. The values b_k are computed from the definition.

steps.text: First identity. The four values sum to 1.
Second identity. The sum of k b_k is (0*8 + 1*12 + 2*6 + 3*1)/27, and n x = 1.
Fourth identity. Here n x = 1, so (n x - k)^2 equals 1, 0, 1, 4 for k = 0, 1, 2, 3. The weighted sum is (8*1 + 12*0 + 6*1 + 1*4)/27.
The right side is n x (1 - x) = 3 * (1/3) * (2/3).

applications.conclusion: For n = 3 and x = 1/3 both sides of the variance identity equal 2/3, and the first two identities hold with the values 1 and 1.

results.name: Bernstein's uniform approximation by Bernstein polynomials
aliases: Bernstein's proof of the Weierstrass theorem
results.statement: Let f: [0,1] -> R be continuous. For n >= 1 define the Bernstein polynomial B_n f(x) = sum over k = 0..n of f(k/n) C(n,k) x^k (1-x)^(n-k). Then B_n f converges to f uniformly on [0,1]: for every e > 0 there is N such that |B_n f(x) - f(x)| < e for all n >= N and all x in [0,1].
hypotheses: f is a continuous real-valued function on the closed interval [0,1].
n >= 1 is an integer. B_n f is a polynomial of degree at most n.
The number N depends on f and e but not on x.

prerequisites.reason: The proof uses sum b_k = 1 and the variance identity sum (n x - k)^2 b_k = n x (1-x).
The proof uses uniform continuity of f on [0,1] (Heine-Cantor theorem).
The proof uses a bound M for |f| on [0,1] (extreme value theorem).

definitions.name: Bernstein polynomial of f
definitions.text: B_n f(x) = sum_k f(k/n) b_k(x) with b_k(x) = C(n,k) x^k (1-x)^(n-k). It is a weighted average of the values f(k/n).

definitions.name: uniform convergence
definitions.text: g_n converges uniformly to g on a set S if sup over S of |g_n - g| tends to 0.

theorem bernsteinApproximation_uniform [LocallyConvexSpace ℝ E] (f : C(I, E)) :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => bernsteinApproximation n f) atTop (𝓝 f) := by
  let : UniformSpace E := IsTopologicalAddGroup.rightUniformSpace E
  have : IsUniformAddGroup E := isUniformAddGroup_of_addCommGroup
  /- Topology on a locally convex TVS is given by a family of seminorms `‖x‖_U = gauge U x`,
  where the open symmetric convex sets `U` form a basis of neighborhoods in this topology,
  and are the open unit balls for the corresponding seminorms.
  For technical reasons, we neither assume `U`s to be open, nor symmetric. -/
  suffices ∀ U ∈ 𝓝 (0 : E), Convex ℝ U →
      ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∀ x : I, gauge U (bernsteinApproximation n f x - f x) < 1 by
    rw [(LocallyConvexSpace.convex_basis_zero ℝ E).uniformity_of_nhds_zero_swapped
      |>.compactConvergenceUniformity_of_compact |> nhds_basis_uniformity |>.tendsto_right_iff]
    rintro U ⟨hU₀, hcU⟩
    filter_upwards [this U hU₀ hcU] with n hn x
    exact setOfPred_gauge_lt_one_subset_self hcU (mem_of_mem_nhds hU₀) (absorbent_nhds_zero hU₀)
      (hn x)
  intro U hU₀ hUc
  /- Choose a constant `C` such that `‖f x - f y‖_U ≤ C` for all `x`, `y`.
  For a normed space, this would be twice the norm of `f`. -/
  obtain ⟨C, hC⟩ : ∃ C, ∀ x y, gauge U (f x - f y) ≤ C := by
    have : Continuous fun (x, y) ↦ gauge U (f x - f y) := by fun_prop
    simpa only [BddAbove, Set.Nonempty, mem_upperBounds, Set.forall_mem_range, Prod.forall]
      using isCompact_range this |>.bddAbove
  have hC₀ : 0 ≤ C := le_trans (gauge_nonneg _) (hC 0 0)
  /- Use uniform continuity of `f` to choose `δ > 0` such that `‖f x - f y‖_U < 1 / 2`
  whenever `dist x y < δ`. -/
  obtain ⟨δ, hδ₀, hδ⟩ : ∃ δ > 0, ∀ x y : I, dist x y < δ → gauge U (f x - f y) < 1 / 2 := by
    have := CompactSpace.uniformContinuous_of_continuous (map_continuous f)
    rw [Metric.uniformity_basis_dist.uniformContinuous_iff
      (basis_sets _).uniformity_of_nhds_zero_swapped] at this
    exact this {z | gauge U z < 1 / 2} <| tendsto_gauge_nhds_zero hU₀
      |>.eventually_lt_const <| by positivity
  -- Take `n ≠ 0` such that `C / δ ^ 2 / n < 1 / 2`.
  have nhds_zero := tendsto_const_div_atTop_nhds_zero_nat (C / δ ^ 2)
  filter_upwards [nhds_zero.eventually_lt_const (half_pos one_pos), eventually_ne_atTop 0]
    with n nh hn₀ x
  -- The idea is to split up the sum over `k` into two sets,
  -- `S`, where `x - k/n < δ`, and its complement.
  set S : Finset (Fin (n + 1)) := {k : Fin (n + 1) | dist k/ₙ x < δ}
  calc
    gauge U (bernsteinApproximation n f x - f x)
      = gauge U (∑ k : Fin (n + 1), bernstein n k x • (f k/ₙ - f x)) := by
      simp [bernsteinApproximation.apply, smul_sub, ← Finset.sum_smul]
    _ ≤ ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), gauge U (bernstein n k x • (f k/ₙ - f x)) :=
      gauge_sum_le hUc (absorbent_nhds_zero hU₀) _ _
    _ = ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) := by
      simp only [gauge_smul_of_nonneg, bernstein_nonneg, smul_eq_mul]
    _ = (∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x)) +
          ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) :=
      (S.sum_add_sum_compl _).symm
    -- We'll now deal with the terms in `S` and the terms in `Sᶜ` in separate calc blocks.
    _ < 1 / 2 + 1 / 2 := add_lt_add_of_le_of_lt ?_ ?_
    _ = 1 := add_halves 1
  · -- We now work on the terms in `S`: uniform continuity and `bernstein.probability`
    -- quickly give us a bound.
    calc
      ∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) ≤ ∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x * (1 / 2) := by
        gcongr with k hk
        refine (hδ _ _ ?_).le
        simpa [S] using hk
      _ = 1 / 2 * ∑ k ∈ S, bernstein n k x := by rw [mul_comm, Finset.sum_mul]
      -- In this step we increase the sum over `S` back to a sum over all of `Fin (n+1)`,
      -- so that we can use `bernstein.probability`.
      _ ≤ 1 / 2 * ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), bernstein n k x := by gcongr; exact S.subset_univ
      _ = 1 / 2 := by rw [bernstein.probability, mul_one]
  · -- We now turn to working on `Sᶜ`: we control the difference term just using `C`,
    -- and then insert a `(x - k/n)^2 / δ^2` factor
    -- (which is at least one because we are not in `S`).
    calc
      ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, bernstein n k x * gauge U (f k/ₙ - f x) ≤ ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, C * bernstein n k x := by
        simp only [mul_comm (bernstein n _ x)]
        gcongr
        apply hC
      _ = C * ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, bernstein n k x := by rw [Finset.mul_sum]
      _ ≤ C * ∑ k ∈ Sᶜ, ((x : ℝ) - k/ₙ) ^ 2 / δ ^ 2 * bernstein n k x := by
        gcongr with k hk
        conv_lhs => rw [← one_mul (bernstein _ _ _)]
        gcongr
        simpa [one_le_div₀, hδ₀, sq_le_sq, S, abs_of_pos, ← Real.dist_eq, dist_comm (x : ℝ)]
          using! hk
      -- Again enlarging the sum from `Sᶜ` to all of `Fin (n+1)`
      _ ≤ C * ∑ k : Fin (n + 1), ((x : ℝ) - k/ₙ) ^ 2 / δ ^ 2 * bernstein n k x := by
        gcongr; exact Sᶜ.subset_univ
      _ = C * (∑ k : Fin (n + 1), ((x : ℝ) - k/ₙ) ^ 2 * bernstein n k x) / δ ^ 2 := by
        simp only [← mul_div_right_comm, ← mul_div_assoc, ← Finset.sum_div]
      -- `bernstein.variance` and `x ∈ [0,1]` gives the uniform bound
      _ = C / δ ^ 2 * x * (1 - x) / n := by rw [variance hn₀]; ring
      _ ≤ C / δ ^ 2 * 1 * 1 / n := by gcongr <;> unit_interval
      _ < 1 / 2 := by simpa only [mul_one]

steps.text: Fix e > 0. The function f is continuous on a compact interval, so f is bounded, |f| <= M, and uniformly continuous. Choose d > 0 with |f(s) - f(x)| < e/2 whenever |s - x| < d.
For x in [0,1] we have b_k(x) >= 0, and sum_k b_k(x) = 1. So B_n f(x) - f(x) = sum_k (f(k/n) - f(x)) b_k(x). Hence |B_n f(x) - f(x)| <= sum_k |f(k/n) - f(x)| b_k(x).
Near terms. Let A be the set of k with |k/n - x| < d. For k in A the factor |f(k/n) - f(x)| is less than e/2. The sum over A is at most (e/2) sum_(k in A) b_k(x) <= e/2.
Far terms. For k not in A, |f(k/n) - f(x)| <= 2M and (k/n - x)^2 / d^2 >= 1. So the sum over k not in A is at most 2M sum_k ((k/n - x)^2 / d^2) b_k(x) = (2M / (n^2 d^2)) sum_k (n x - k)^2 b_k(x).
By the variance identity, the last quantity equals 2M x (1-x) / (n d^2). Since x (1-x) <= 1/4 on [0,1], it is at most M / (2 n d^2). This bound does not depend on x.
Choose N > M / (e d^2). For n >= N, M / (2 n d^2) < e/2. Then |B_n f(x) - f(x)| < e/2 + e/2 = e for all x in [0,1]. This proves uniform convergence.

applications.title: Bernstein polynomials of f(x) = x^2
applications.inputs: Take f(x) = x^2 on [0,1]. The moment identities give B_n f(x) = x^2 + x(1-x)/n exactly.
applications.hypotheses: f is continuous on [0,1], so the theorem applies. B_n f has degree 2, and the identities for sum k b_k and sum k(k-1) b_k are exact for all n.

steps.text: Compute B_n f exactly. B_n f(x) = sum_k (k/n)^2 b_k = (1/n^2) (sum k(k-1) b_k + sum k b_k) = (n(n-1) x^2 + n x) / n^2 = x^2 + x(1-x)/n.
Check with n = 2 and x = 1/2. The definition gives B_2 f(1/2) = f(0)/4 + f(1/2)/2 + f(1)/4.
The formula gives x^2 + x(1-x)/n at n = 2, x = 1/2.
The error is x(1-x)/n <= 1/(4n) for all x in [0,1]. For n = 26 it is below 1/100, because 4 * 25 = 100 gives 1/100 exactly at n = 25.
For n = 26 the error bound is 1/104, which is below 1/100.

applications.conclusion: B_n(x^2) = x^2 + x(1-x)/n converges to x^2 uniformly, with sup error exactly 1/(4n). The error is below 1/100 for every n >= 26.

results.name: Orthogonality of the trigonometric system
aliases: orthonormality of exp(i n x) on the circle
results.statement: For integers m, n, the integral of exp(i m x) exp(-i n x) over [-pi, pi], divided by 2 pi, equals 1 if m = n and 0 if m != n. Equivalently, for integers m, n >= 0: the integral over [-pi, pi] of cos(m x) cos(n x) dx is 0 if m != n, pi if m = n >= 1, and 2 pi if m = n = 0; the integral of sin(m x) sin(n x) dx is 0 if m != n and pi if m = n >= 1; and the integral of sin(m x) cos(n x) dx is 0 for all m, n.
hypotheses: m and n are integers. In the real forms m, n >= 0, and sin(0 x) = 0 gives the zero case.
The interval has length 2 pi, the common period of the functions. Any interval of length 2 pi gives the same values.
The inner product is <u, v> = (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of u(x) conj(v(x)) dx.

prerequisites.reason: The proof evaluates the integral of exp(i k x) by an antiderivative.
The proof uses exp(i y) = cos y + i sin y to pass between exponentials and cos and sin.

definitions.name: trigonometric system
definitions.text: The functions e_n(x) = exp(i n x), n an integer, on [-pi, pi]. With the normalized inner product they are orthonormal.

source.alignment: The Lean declaration states that the functions fourier n on AddCircle T are orthonormal in L2 for normalized Haar measure, for any period T > 0. The authored statement takes T = 2 pi and adds the real forms, which the proof derives.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; no local Lean check

proof.verification: authored proof; agent inference review pending; no local Lean check
proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Put k = m - n, an integer. Then exp(i m x) exp(-i n x) = exp(i k x). We must compute (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of exp(i k x) over [-pi, pi].
If k = 0, the integrand is 1, and the average is (1/(2 pi)) * 2 pi = 1.
If k != 0, the function exp(i k x)/(i k) is an antiderivative of exp(i k x). The integral equals (exp(i k pi) - exp(-i k pi))/(i k) = 2 sin(k pi)/k = 0, because sin(k pi) = 0 for integer k.

Real forms. Since cos a cos b = (cos(a+b) + cos(a-b))/2, the integral of cos(m x) cos(n x) is half the sum of the integrals of cos((m+n)x) and cos((m-n)x). By the real part of the previous step, the integral of cos(k x) over [-pi, pi] is 2 pi for k = 0 and 0 for k != 0.

Evaluate the cases. If m != n, both k values m+n and m-n are nonzero when m, n >= 0, so the result is 0. If m = n >= 1, the result is (0 + 2 pi)/2 = pi. If m = n = 0, it is (2 pi + 2 pi)/2 = 2 pi. For sin(m x) sin(n x) = (cos((m-n)x) - cos((m+n)x))/2 we get 0, pi, and 0 in the same way.
The function sin(m x) cos(n x) is odd, and [-pi, pi] is symmetric about 0. So its integral is 0 for all m, n.

applications.title: Extract coefficients and the mean square of a trigonometric polynomial
applications.inputs: Take f(x) = 3 + 2 cos(2x) - sin(5x) on [-pi, pi].
applications.hypotheses: f is a finite linear combination of the functions 1, cos(2x), sin(5x), which belong to the trigonometric system, so the orthogonality relations apply term by term.

steps.text: Integrate f(x) cos(2x). The term 3 cos(2x) integrates to 0. The term 2 cos(2x)^2 integrates to 2 pi. The term sin(5x) cos(2x) integrates to 0. The coefficient of pi in the total is 0 + 2 * 1 - 0.
So the coefficient of cos(2x) equals (1/pi) times the integral of f cos(2x), which is 2. This agrees with the definition of f.
Square f and integrate. All cross terms vanish by orthogonality. The remaining terms give: 3^2 * 2 pi + 2^2 * pi + 1^2 * pi. Dividing by 2 pi gives the mean square 3^2 + 2^2/2 + 1/2.
So the integral of f(x)^2 over [-pi, pi] is 2 pi times 23/2, which has the coefficient 23 in front of pi.

applications.conclusion: Orthogonality extracts the coefficient 2 of cos(2x), and it gives the integral of f^2 over [-pi, pi] as 23 pi with no integration of products.

results.name: Fourier coefficients of a derivative on an interval
results.statement: Let a < b and T = b - a. For an integrable g, define c_n(g) = (1/T) times the integral over [a, b] of g(x) exp(-2 pi i n x / T) dx. Let f: [a,b] -> C be differentiable at every point of [a,b] with integrable derivative f'. Then for every integer n != 0, c_n(f) = (1/(-2 pi i n)) * ( exp(-2 pi i n a / T) (f(b) - f(a)) - T c_n(f') ). In particular, if f(a) = f(b), then c_n(f') = (2 pi i n / T) c_n(f).
hypotheses: a < b are real numbers, and T = b - a.
f is complex valued and differentiable on the closed interval [a, b] (one-sided at the ends). The derivative f' is integrable on [a, b].
n is a nonzero integer. For n = 0 the formula fails because of the factor 1/n.

prerequisites.reason: The proof is one integration by parts on the integral that defines c_n(f).

theorem fourierCoeffOn_of_hasDerivAt {a b : ℝ} (hab : a < b) {f f' : ℝ → ℂ} {n : ℤ} (hn : n ≠ 0)
    (hf : ∀ x, x ∈ [[a, b]] → HasDerivAt f (f' x) x) (hf' : IntervalIntegrable f' volume a b) :
    fourierCoeffOn hab f n = 1 / (-2 * π * I * n) *
      (fourier (-n) (a : AddCircle (b - a)) * (f b - f a) - (b - a) * fourierCoeffOn hab f' n) :=
  fourierCoeffOn_of_hasDerivAt_Ioo hab hn
    (fun x hx ↦ hf x hx |>.continuousAt.continuousWithinAt)
    (fun x hx ↦ hf x <| mem_Icc_of_Ioo hx)
    hf'

source.alignment: The Lean declaration uses fourierCoeffOn, the Fourier coefficient of the function lifted to the circle AddCircle (b - a), with the character fourier(-n) at the point a. The authored formula writes this character out as exp(-2 pi i n x / T).

proof.scope: The complete stated result under every listed hypothesis.

steps.text: Put w = 2 pi n / T, so that the kernel is exp(-i w x). Because n != 0, w != 0. The function exp(-i w x) / (-i w) has derivative exp(-i w x).

Integrate by parts with u = f and dv = exp(-i w x) dx. We get the integral of f exp(-i w x) over [a,b] equal to [f(x) exp(-i w x) / (-i w)] evaluated from a to b, minus the integral of f'(x) exp(-i w x) / (-i w) dx.
Since w T = 2 pi n, exp(-i w b) = exp(-i w a) exp(-2 pi i n) = exp(-i w a). So the boundary term is exp(-i w a) (f(b) - f(a)) / (-i w).

Divide the identity by T. The boundary part becomes exp(-i w a) (f(b) - f(a)) / (-i w T) = exp(-i w a) (f(b) - f(a)) / (-2 pi i n). The integral part becomes - c_n(f') / (-i w) = T c_n(f') / (2 pi i n).

Combine: c_n(f) = (1/(-2 pi i n)) ( exp(-i w a)(f(b) - f(a)) - T c_n(f') ), because T c_n(f') / (2 pi i n) = - T c_n(f') / (-2 pi i n). If f(a) = f(b), solve for c_n(f') to get c_n(f') = (2 pi i n / T) c_n(f).

applications.title: Fourier coefficients of x and x^2 on [-pi, pi]
applications.inputs: Take a = -pi, b = pi, T = 2 pi. First apply the formula to f(x) = x with f'(x) = 1. Then apply it to f(x) = x^2 with f'(x) = 2x.
applications.hypotheses: Both functions are differentiable on [-pi, pi] with continuous derivatives. Take n = 3 and n = 1, which are nonzero. For f = x^2 we have f(pi) = f(-pi), so the boundary term vanishes.

steps.text: For g = 1 we have c_n(1) = 0 for n != 0, because the integral of exp(-i n x) over a full period is 0. For f(x) = x with n = 3, exp(-2 pi i n a / T) = exp(3 i pi) = (-1)^3. The formula gives c_3(x) = (1/(-6 pi i)) * ((-1)^3 * 2 pi - 0) = (-1)^3 / (-3i) = i (-1)^3 / 3. The imaginary part is (-1)^3/3.

For f(x) = x^2 we have f(pi) - f(-pi) = 0. So the formula gives c_n(x^2) = (T / (2 pi i n)) c_n(2x) = (2/(i n)) c_n(x), using T = 2 pi. With c_3(x) = -i/3 we get c_3(x^2) = (2/(3i)) * (-i/3) = (2/3) * (-1/3).
General n. Since c_n(x) = i (-1)^n / n, we get c_n(x^2) = 2 (-1)^n / n^2. For n = 1 this is -2.
Check n = 3 with the general formula. It gives 2 (-1)^3 / 3^2.
The coefficient -2 for n = 1 and n = -1 gives the cosine term -4 cos x in the Fourier series of x^2, as in the classical expansion x^2 = pi^2/3 - 4 cos x + cos(2x) - ...

applications.conclusion: The formula gives c_n(x) = i (-1)^n / n and c_n(x^2) = 2 (-1)^n / n^2 for n != 0 on [-pi, pi]. The coefficient decay of x^2 is one order faster than that of x, as the smoothness of the periodic extension predicts.
